en: The Vāyavīya Saṃhitā: Now begins the seventh Saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, within the Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaurī and Śaṅkara.
Now begins the seventh [section], the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā.
Chapter 1. Vyāsa said:
Salutations to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, by his attendants, and by his son. *Śiva Purāṇa* 7.1.1ab.
To the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
whose power is indeed incomparable and whose sovereignty is all-pervading—
[the wise] declare his nature to be lordship and omnipresence.
I go for refuge to that unborn Viśvakarman, the eternal, auspicious,
and imperishable Mahādeva,
the Great-Souled One, at the field of Dharma, the great sacred ford at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī.
At Prayāga, in the Naimiṣa forest, on the path to the world of Brahmā,
sages of purified souls, devoted to the vow of truth,
possessed of great luster and great fortune, performed a great sacrificial session (mahāsatra).
There, having heard of that sacrificial session of those whose actions are untainted,
[the king approached] the wise Veda-Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
who was himself a high-souled and intelligent disciple renowned throughout the three worlds.
He was a knower of the merits and defects of speech consisting of five members;
he was a superior debater even against Bṛhaspati himself as he spoke,
and his voice was sweet to the ears with its charming words and rhythmic cadences.
Skilled in narration, a speaker of eloquence, knowing the proper time and discerning the rules of conduct,
that Sūta, the best of Paurāṇikas, arrived at that place. Seeing the Sūta approaching, the sages were delighted in their hearts.
They offered him both hospitality and worship according to the prescribed rites. Having accepted the worship of the virtuous presented by the sages, he—
being duly appointed and with his mind directed toward that which was appropriate for himself— engaged in the task assigned to him.
Then, by that very meeting, the minds of the sages of purified souls became filled with longing to hear the ancient narrative. At that time,
the great seers honored him with favorable words.
Turning toward him with great devotion, they spoke these words:
The sages said:
"O omniscient Romaharṣaṇa, by the weight of our good fortune, you [have appeared before us]."
O highly fortunate one, O great-minded King of the Śaivas,
today you have attained the entire science of the Purāṇas, having received it directly from Vyāsa;
therefore, you are indeed a worthy vessel for these most wonderful stories.
Like the ocean, the mine of jewels, for those gems that are vast and essential;
whatever has been, whatever is yet to be, and whatever other thing exists—
there is nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you.
"You have come here for the sake of seeing us by the power of destiny;
having performed no meritorious deed whatsoever, you ought not to depart in vain.
Therefore, [listen to] this most worthy of being heard, the merit consisting of the knowledge of sacred narratives."
"Quickly recite for us the Purāṇa, which is the very essence of the entire Vedānta.
Thus requested by the sages who were exponents of the Vedas,
Sūta replied with auspicious words that were gentle and consistent with reason.
Sūta said:
"Having been honored, favored, and urged by you in this way,
how could I not fully expound the Purāṇa revered by the Ṛṣis?"
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the Goddess, Skanda, and Vināyaka,
as well as to Nandin and Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī himself,
I shall proclaim this most meritorious Purāṇa, which is equal to the Vedas.
The *Śivajñānārṇava* (The Ocean of the Knowledge of Śiva), which directly bestows the fruits of devotion and liberation,
is adorned with the meanings of the Āgamas joined with the logic of words and their referents;
it was formerly narrated by Vāyu in connection with the Śveta Kalpa.
Listen as I speak of all the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), the traditional sequence of the Purāṇas, and likewise the origin of this Purāṇa:
the four Vedas, the auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive system of Nyāya.
The Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and these fourteen sciences—
namely, in order, Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—
and above those, the Arthaśāstra; indeed, eighteen sciences are thus remembered.
Regarding these eighteen branches of knowledge that follow divergent paths,
the sacred tradition declares that the trident-bearing Lord himself is their direct author.
For he, the Lord of the entire universe, desiring to create the whole world, [is the source].
He directly appointed Brahmā as his eternal son at the beginning. To that Brahmā, the first-born son and source of the universe,
the Lord formerly imparted these sciences for the purpose of creating the world.
Then he gave the god Hari the power of protection for the sake of preservation; indeed,
he gave his middle son Viṣṇu as the protector even of Brahmā, while Brahmā,
having acquired the sciences, was expanding the creation of progeny.
First, the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā as the source of all scriptures;
immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths.
From that, the manifestation of all scriptures arose from his mouth.
When the people on earth were unable to comprehend its full extent, then,
at the command of the Lord of the Universe,
Viṣṇu— the soul of the universe, the sustainer of all, and the sovereign lord— condensed the meaning of that knowledge at the end of the Dvāpara ages.
Having descended to the surface of the earth under the name of Vyāsa, he moves about in this world.
O twice-born ones, in this manner the Vedas are divided in every Dvāpara age;
thereafter, the Purāṇas and other [texts] are likewise composed.

Furthermore, in this Dvāpara age, he was born of Satyavatī by the one known as Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana, like the sacrificial fire from the kindling wood. That sage, having condensed the Vedas, divided them again into four.
Because he divided the Vedas in the world, he is known as Vedavyāsa.
Furthermore, that which was a condensed version of the Purāṇas measuring four hundred thousand [verses] has,
even today, expanded to a magnitude of one billion verses in the realm of the gods.
If a twice-born man should know the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and the Upaniṣads,
yet does not know the Purāṇa, he would not truly be wise.
One should augment the Veda by means of the Itihāsas and the Purāṇas.
"The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He will deceive me.

The Purāṇa, characterized by five features, consists of the primary creation (sarga), the secondary creation (pratisarga), genealogy (vaṃśa), the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of dynasties (vaṃśānucarita)."

This Purāṇa is taught in ten ways and in eight ways by the sages who are the best among the knowers of reality, through the distinction between the extensive and the subtle. These are the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata.
The Bhaviṣya, the Nāradīya, and after that the Mārkaṇḍeya;
the Āgneya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Laiṅga, and the Vārāha;
the Skānda, the Vāmana, the Kaurma, the Mātsya, and the Gāruḍa.
And the *Brahmāṇḍa*—this is the meritorious sequence of the Purāṇas.
Among them, the fourth is the *Śaiva*, which belongs to Śarva and accomplishes all goals;
that text, measuring one hundred thousand verses, is divided into twelve *saṃhitās*.
That [system] was indeed created by Śiva himself; therein Dharma is established.
By the very Dharma taught therein, men of the three twice-born classes become Śaivas.
Therefore, one who seeks liberation should take refuge in Śiva alone.
Relying on this alone, even the gods attain liberation, and not otherwise.
Listen as I briefly describe the divisions of this Purāṇa which has been proclaimed as Śaiva and is equal to the Vedas.
Likewise, the Vidyeśvara, the Raudra, and the unsurpassed Vaināyaka;
the Auma, the Mātṛpurāṇa, and the Rudraikādaśaka;
as well as the Kailāsa, the Śatarudra, and that which is called the Śatarudrīya.

Beyond that is the Vāyavīya, known as the *Sahasrakoṭirudra*, and the Purāṇa called Dharma; thus there are twelve Saṃhitās. The Vidyeśa is declared to consist of ten thousand verses by way of its textual count.
Then follow the Raudra, the Vaināyaka, the Cauma, and thereafter the one called Mātṛka;
each of these consists of eight thousand verses, while the Trayodaśasahasraka consists of thirteen thousand,
and that which is called the eleven Raudras consists of six thousand verses, as does the Kailāsa.
The Śatarudra, the Trisāhasra, and beyond that the Koṭirudra;
then the one joined with nine thousand [verses], endowed with the knowledge of all things;
and the one called Sahasrakoṭirudra, consisting of eleven thousand [verses].

The Vāyavīya Purāṇa consists of four thousand verses and is unsurpassed; that which is known as the Dharmapurāṇa consists of twelve thousand verses. Thus, the Śaiva Purāṇa is declared to comprise one hundred thousand verses according to the division of its branches.
That Purāṇa, the essence of the Vedas, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
was condensed by Vyāsa into twenty-four thousand verses.
Among them, the Śaiva Purāṇa is indeed the fourth, consisting of seven Saṃhitās.
Among them, the first is called Vidyeśvara; the second is the Rudrasaṃhitā;
the third is named Śatarudra; the fourth is Koṭirudra;
the fifth is said to be Umā; and the sixth is the Kailāsasaṃhitā.

The seventh is called the Vāyavīya; thus, there are seven compendia (saṃhitās) here. The Vidyeśvara consists of two thousand [verses], the Raudra of ten thousand five hundred, and the [Śatarudrīya] is said to consist of thirty-two hundred and one hundred and fifty.
Likewise, there is Śatarudra and Koṭirudra, which exceed the sky by two yugas;
then Dvisāhasra and Dviśata, as well as Uma, which is one thousand earths;
and Kailāsa, which is one thousand earths plus four hundred and forty.
Beyond that, there are two hundred and forty [verses] concerning Vāyu; thus,
by this division of numbers,
the Purāṇa named after Śiva, which is supremely meritorious, is heard to consist of four thousand verses in total.
That which has been proclaimed as the Vāyavīya section consisting of four thousand [verses],
this very same work, comprising two parts, I shall now set forth.
This unsurpassed scripture must not be spoken to one who does not know the Vedas.
It should not be given to one who lacks faith, nor likewise to one who is ignorant of the Purāṇas; rather,
it should be imparted to a tested disciple who is righteous, free from malice,
devoted to Śiva, and follows the path of Śiva’s dharma.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, by whose grace this Purāṇa-saṃhitā exists within me.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Descent of Knowledge," in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 2. Sūta said:
In former times, after a vast period had elapsed, this occurred again and again at the end of a kalpa.
When this eon had arrived and the work of creation had commenced,
when the means of livelihood were established and living beings had awakened,
the sages belonging to the six lineages were conversing with one another.
"This is supreme, this is not"—thus a very great dispute arose. Because the Supreme is difficult to define, no certainty was reached there. They went to see the Creator, the imperishable Brahmā.

There, on the auspicious and beautiful peak of Mount Meru, crowded with gods and dānavas, frequented by siddhas, cāraṇas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, the Blessed Brahmā dwells while being praised by the gods and asuras.
Resounding with flocks of birds, adorned with jewels and coral,
and beautified by groves, caves, mountain clefts, dwellings, and waterfalls—
there lies the forest named Brahmavana, teeming with various kinds of wild animals.
It was ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long,
containing delightful lakes filled with the sweet water of the Surasā river,
where beautiful flowering trees were covered by intoxicated bees.
There was a great and beautiful city, resembling the rising sun,
belonging to the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas who were arrogant because of their invincible strength;
it was made of refined gold and possessed lofty walls and gateways.
It was adorned with hundreds of turrets, balconies, pinnacles, and gateways;
it seemed to lick the sky with its many costly and variegated jewels;
and it was embellished by many millions of great palaces.

In that place dwells Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, together with his assembly. Having gone there, the sages and gods beheld the high-souled Grandfather of the worlds in person, attended by hosts of celestial rishis.
Resembling pure gold, adorned with all ornaments,
with a serene countenance, gentle, and with eyes as broad as lotus petals;
endowed with divine luster and anointed with divine perfumes.

He was wearing divine white garments and adorned with celestial garlands; his lotus feet were being venerated by the lords of the gods and asuras and by the masters of yogis. He was attended by a woman whose limbs were endowed with every auspicious mark, who held a chowrie in her hand.
Shining like the sun with the splendor of the Sarasvatī,
all the sages, upon seeing him, their faces and eyes bright with joy,
placed their joined palms upon their heads and praised that bull among the gods.
The sages said:
"Salutations to you, the threefold-formed one, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
to the ancient Puruṣa, to Brahman, the Supreme Self."
Salutations to the one whose body is primordial matter (pradhāna), who causes the agitation of primordial matter;
to the one who, though unchanging, is manifested through twenty-three divisions.
Salutations to the one whose body is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), who dwells within the interior of the cosmic egg.
Salutations to Him who has accomplished all that was to be done and who has perfected all instruments of action; salutations to the one who is all worlds and the ordainer of all worlds;
salutations to the cause of the laws governing the union with and separation from the body of the universal self.
"By you alone has this entire world been created, withdrawn, and protected.
Nevertheless, O Lord, O Grandfather, we do not know you because of your Māyā.
Sūta said:
Thus praised by the highly fortunate great seers, Brahmā spoke with a deep voice, as if gladdening the sages. Brahmā said:
"O highly fortunate sages, you who possess great being and great splendor,
for what purpose have you all assembled here together? To the god Brahmā, who was speaking thus, those most excellent knowers of Brahman replied:
With words pregnant with discipline, they all spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, we are enveloped by a great darkness."
Exhausted and disputing among ourselves, we see nothing here that is superior;
for you are indeed the sustainer of the entire world and the cause of all causes.
O Lord, there is nothing here that remains unknown to you.
Who is that person who is more ancient than all beings,
the Supreme Person, pure, perfect, eternal, and the Supreme Lord?
By what creative act is the world first created?
"O one of great wisdom, speak the truth for the sake of dispelling my own doubt.
Thus questioned, Brahmā, his gaze smiling with wonder,
[spoke] in the presence of the gods, the dānavas, and the sages.
Rising up and meditating for a very long time while uttering the word "Rudra," his entire body drenched with tears of bliss,
he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Sages' Introduction," in the first section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said: From which [Reality] words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it. (Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.3.1ab)
The wise man indeed does not fear anything from any quarter regarding that bliss,
from which this entire universe— headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—
is first brought forth together with all the elements and the senses.
He who is the sustainer of all causes, the meditator, the supreme cause— He is never produced from anything else at any time. Endowed with all sovereignty, He is Himself the Lord of All by name.
Śambhu, who dwells in the midst of space, is to be meditated upon by all those seeking liberation.
He who appointed me as his son in the beginning and bestowed knowledge upon me—
it was through his grace that I attained this station of Prajāpati.
The Lord stands firm like a tree, the one who dwells alone in heaven;
by that Great-Souled Puruṣa, this entire world is filled.
He is the one among many creatures, and he is active while they are inactive.

He who alone makes the one seed manifold is Maheśvara; he who, as the Lord, rules over all these worlds by means of these individual souls (jīvas). Rudra is the one blessed lord; there is no second whatsoever.

Though He is eternally seated within the hearts of all people, He remains unperceived by others; yet, perceiving the universe Himself, He presides over it at all times. Furthermore, He is that which [presides over] all causes whatsoever, even those released from Time.
The Lord alone, possessing infinite power, presides over all;
for him there is neither day nor night, neither equal nor superior [time].
His supreme power is innate, as are his eternal knowledge and action.
That which is the perishable unmanifest, and that which is the immortal imperishable—both these are of the nature of the Imperishable;
they are the one God, Hara himself.
Through meditation upon Him, he who possesses the power of yoga and the cultivation of pure being exercises lordship over them.
For at the end of this sacrificial animal, the entire illusion (*viśvamāyā*) ceases;
that in which lightning does not shine, nor the sun, nor the moon—
that by whose light all this is illumined— such is the eternal Vedic revelation.
The one God, Mahādeva, is to be known as Maheśvara.
No state superior to his is ever found.
He is the beginning, without beginning or end, and is pure by his very nature.

He is independent and complete, sovereign over all that moves and is stationary; he possesses a non-material body, is glorious, and is devoid of both the object of definition and its defining characteristics. He is the liberated one and the liberator, beyond time, yet the impeller of time.
He whose dwelling is above all, who is the abode of all, and the knower of all;
he is the Lord of this entire universe consisting of the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan),
the highest among all beings that exist in ascending order, and the one beyond whom there is nothing higher.
He is a bee for the honey of the nectar of infinite and endless multitudes;
he is skilled in the compounding of all the unbroken cosmic eggs;
he is an ocean of magnanimity, heroism, profundity, and sweetness.
There is no object whatsoever equal to him, nor indeed anything superior;
he stands as the peerless King of Kings among all beings.
By means of this wondrous creative act, the universe is first brought forth.

Furthermore, at the time of the end, when this [universe] is about to undergo dissolution, all beings become subject to him; he is the director of all. Yet, he is perceived only through supreme devotion and never otherwise.

Vows, all forms of giving, ascetic penances, and likewise restraints—these were declared of old by the virtuous for the sake of attaining true being; of this there is no doubt. Hari, I, Rudra, and likewise other gods and asuras [are established therein].
Even today,
he remains invisible to those who, though desiring a vision of him, are fallen, deluded, wicked, or contemptible;
yet he is to be worshipped and spoken with by devotees, both internally and externally.
This form is threefold: gross, subtle, and beyond that.
The gross is visible to us and the immortals, while the subtle is seen by yogins. (Note:
The absence of the *śap* suffix is an archaic Vedic usage.)
Beyond that, however, is that which is eternal, consciousness, bliss, and imperishable;
it is perceived by devotees who are established in it, intent upon it, and who have taken recourse to its vow.
What is the use of saying more here? It is the supreme secret, more secret than the secret.
There is no doubt that devotion to Śiva exists; one endowed with it is liberated.
That devotion arises solely from grace, and grace is born of devotion.
Just as a seed comes from a sprout, or as a sprout comes from a seed.
For a devotee, all accomplishments everywhere are preceded by grace alone;
that very grace is attained at the end through every means of practice.
Dharma is the means for attaining grace, and it has been revealed by the Veda.
By the power of that practice, there arises an equilibrium between the previously accumulated merit and demerit.
From that equilibrium comes contact with grace, and from that, an excellence of dharma.
Having attained this excellence of dharma, the animal’s (paśu) demerit is completely destroyed.
Thus, for one whose sins have been gradually destroyed over many births,
devotion preceded by knowledge arises toward the Lord of All, who is accompanied by Ambā.
In accordance with that disposition, the grace of the Lord is further increased.
Through grace, there is the renunciation of action in terms of its fruit, but not in terms of its essential nature.
Therefore, from the renunciation of the fruits of action, there arises the auspicious lineage of the Śiva-dharma.
And that [lineage] is twofold: independent of a guru and dependent upon one.
In this regard, that which is dependent is a hundred times superior to that which is independent.
For one who follows the lineage of the Śiva-dharma, there is the attainment of the knowledge of Śiva.
Through the power of the attainment of knowledge, a person perceives the defects within saṃsāra.

From that comes detachment from sense objects; from detachment, the means of attaining the true state (bhāva). For one who has achieved the true state, there is steadfastness in meditation, not in ritual action.
Yoga proceeds for the person who is devoted to knowledge and meditation.
Through yoga, however, supreme devotion arises, and immediately thereafter grace (prasāda). By grace, a living being is liberated; once liberated, he becomes equal to Śiva.
This sequence of the manner of bestowing favor is not intended [as a rigid rule].
The grace accorded to a person corresponds exactly to his capacity.
One is liberated while still in the womb; another likewise at the moment of birth;
yet another is liberated as a child, a youth, or even an old man.
One who has entered the womb of an animal is liberated; another, a denizen of hell, is likewise freed.
Yet another, having attained a [higher] station, is liberated when that station perishes.
Still another, having reached the end of his station, returns once more and is then liberated.
Someone traveling on that path, by stopping and resting there again and again, is liberated.
Therefore, liberation for human beings is not held to occur through a single means alone;
rather, nirvāṇa comes only through grace (prasāda) in accordance with the state of one's knowledge.
Therefore, for the sake of his grace, let us all— wives, sons, and the sacred fires— be free from defects of speech and mind; meditating on Śiva alone, being devoted to him,
intent upon him, united with him, and taking refuge in him.
Performing all their ritual acts, they remained with their minds fixed upon him alone.
A thousand divine years passed while the sacrifice was undertaken with great deliberation;
at the conclusion of the sacrificial session, Vāyu shall go there through the application of mantras.
He himself will explain to you the means for your ultimate welfare.
Therefore, one must go to the holy city of Vārāṇasī, which is supremely beautiful,
where Viśveśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow, dwells together with the Goddess.
The glorious one always dwells there for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
Having seen a great marvel there, you shall come into my presence;
then, O best of the twice-born, I will tell you the means to liberation.
By means of this, liberation in a single birth rests in the palm of your hand—
liberation that effects release from the bondage of the cycle of existence through many births. This mind-made wheel, created by me, is now being released.
"Wherever its rim is worn away, that place is auspicious for penance.
Having spoken thus, and having beheld the mind-made discus which was radiant as the sun,
the Grandfather prostrated before Mahādeva and dismissed him.

Those brahmins, even more delighted, bowed to the Lord of the worlds and proceeded to the place where the rim of that wheel had shattered. That wheel, too, was reduced to a fine, smooth, and beautiful stone surface.
In a certain part of his own forest, where the water was pure and sweet,
that forest became renowned as Naimiṣa, honored by sages and crowded with many yakṣas, gandharvas, and vidyādharas.
Purūravas, having conquered the eighteen islands of the ocean,
fell under the sway of Urvaśī’s charms, impelled by fate;
and out of delusion, he seized the golden sacrificial enclosure in an improper manner.

Where, in ancient times, the sages, desiring to create the universe, being seekers of Brahman and householders, commenced a divine sacrificial session (*sattra*) while the Creator himself was struck down by the sage-sages who were enraged and [wielding] *kuśa*-grass as thunderbolts.
There, by the learned sages who were experts in grammar, semantics,
and logic, the ritual was performed through the application of power, wisdom, and action.
There, those who knew the Vedas constantly [refuted] those excluded from the Vedic teachings.

Excessive disputants strike down others with their words through the force of debate and sophistry. That Naimiṣa forest was suitable for the asceticism of those sages; it was delightful with clear water flowing from rocks at the foot of the crystal mountain that resembled nectar, abounded with trees bearing exceedingly sweet fruit, and was free from predatory beasts.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Naimiṣa," in the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 4 Sūta said:
In that region, highly fortunate sages of celebrated vows,
worshipping Mahādeva, then commenced a sacrificial session (*satra*).
And that sacrificial session of the great seers proceeded, filled with every wonder.

It was like the ancient sacrifice of the creators of the universe when they desired to bring forth the world. Then, as time passed and that sacrificial session, in which abundant gifts were distributed,
had come to an end, Vāyu himself arrived there by the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The divine disciple of the Self-Existent One is the self-controlled master who perceives everything directly;
under his command reside the Maruts, seven groups of seven. (Note:
The absence of the long vowel [in "marutaḥ"] is an archaic Vedic usage.)
Constantly impelling the limbs by means of its own functions, such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and others,
it maintains the bodies of all living beings;
and it is endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
He who supports the worlds through the intermediate directions, time, and other pure principles;
who has space as his source and possesses double the qualities due to the presence of touch and sound;
and whom the seekers of truth call the primordial nature of the luminous elements—[to him I bow].
Seeing him arrived at the hermitage, the sages performing long sacrificial sessions recalled the words of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and experienced incomparable joy; then,
all of them rose and bowed to the one born from the sky.
They prepared for him a seat made of gold.
Seated there, duly honored by the sages,
he greeted them all and then inquired after their welfare.
Vāyu said:
"O Brahmins, is all well with you here now that this great sacrifice has commenced?
I hope that the Daityas, those enemies of the gods who destroy sacrifices, do not cause you any trouble."
Did no expiation or ill-performed rite ever arise?
Having worshipped the gods with hymns and weapons and the ancestors with ancestral rites in their respective temples,
was the ritual duly performed by you?
"And now that the great sacrifice has concluded, what do you intend to do next?
Thus addressed by Vāyu, who was devoted to Śiva, all the sages—
purified and with joyful minds— replied with humility.
The sages said:
"Today all is well with us;
today our ascetic merit shall become truly auspicious, since you have come here for the sake of increasing our spiritual welfare."
Listen to this ancient account concerning those whose minds were overcome by darkness:
"In former times, we worshipped Prajāpati for the sake of higher knowledge;
he, the protector, having shown favor to us who had come to him for refuge, spoke thus."
O Brahmins, Rudra is superior to all and is the supreme cause;
only one possessed of devotion perceives his true nature, which is beyond ratiocination.
Devotion toward him arises through his grace, and from that very grace comes liberation.

Therefore, for the sake of his grace, perform a long sacrificial session (*sattra*) at Naimiṣa through the practice of a sacrificial union; worship Rudra, the supreme cause. By his grace, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, Vāyu will come there.

"From his mouth, the attainment of knowledge will come; therein lies your highest good. Having thus instructed us, O highly fortunate one, we were all sent by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), desiring your arrival in this place.
"Seated in a long sacrificial session for a thousand divine years,
we have nothing else whatsoever to pray for beyond your arrival.
Having heard this account of the sages who were engaged in a long sacrifice, [he spoke].
Vāyu, having become pleased in mind, remained there surrounded by the sages.
Then, questioned by those sages for the sake of increasing their devotion,
the omnipresent Lord spoke briefly of the sovereignty of Śiva beginning with the creation.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Meeting with Vāyu," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 5 Sūta said:
There, first of all, the illustrious residents of the Naimiṣa forest,
having prostrated according to the prescribed rule, questioned the lord Pavana. The inhabitants of Naimiṣa said:
"How have you attained this knowledge that is the domain of the Lord?
And how did you come to possess the nature of Śiva, [which belongs even] to Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest?
Vāyu replied:
The nineteenth kalpa should be known as Śvetalohita.
In that kalpa, the four-faced one, desiring to create, performed austerities.
By those intense austerities, his father himself was pleased.
Assuming a divine youthful form, the best among the beautiful, Maheśvara,
the God of gods, became a sage named Śveta and, uttering divine speech,
granted him his vision.
Having seen his father, the Lord and Master of Brahmā, Brahmā bowed down and received supreme knowledge along with the Gāyatrī. Then, having attained that realization, the four-faced Viśvakarman—
He created all beings, both stationary and moving;
for it was from him that Brahmā obtained the nectar upon hearing it from the Supreme Lord,
and from his very mouth I too obtained it through the power of my ascetic penance.
The sages said:
What is that auspicious knowledge obtained by you, which is more truthful than truth itself,
and by attaining supreme steadfastness in which a person reaches happiness?
Vāyu said:
"The knowledge of the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), the fettered soul (Paśu), and the fetter (Pāśa), which was obtained by me in the past—
therein a man seeking happiness should establish himself with supreme steadfastness."
Suffering arises from ignorance and is ceased by knowledge alone.
Knowledge is the discernment of reality, and reality is traditionally held to be twofold:
the non-inert and the inert; and there is also the Controller of both.
The bound soul (paśu), the bond (pāśa), and the Lord (pati)— these three are described in sequence as the perishable (kṣara),
the imperishable (akṣara), and that which is beyond both the perishable and the imperishable (kṣarākṣarapara).
This triad is extensively expounded by those who know the true principles (tattva).
The imperishable (akṣara) is called the animal (paśu), while the perishable (kṣara) is declared to be the bond (pāśa).
That which is beyond both the perishable and the imperishable is designated as the Lord (pati).
The sages said:
"What is that which is called the Imperishable (akṣara), and what is cited as the Perishable (kṣara)?
And what is the supreme among those two? Tell me this, O Māruta.
Vāyu said:
"Prakṛti is said to be the perishable (kṣara), while Puruṣa is called the imperishable (akṣara).
Another, the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), impels these two.
The sages said:
"What is this called 'prakṛti' (primordial nature), and who is considered this 'puruṣa' (spirit)?
What is the relationship between these two, and who is this impelling Lord (Īśvara)?
Vāyu said:
Māyā is declared to be Prakṛti, and Puruṣa is enveloped by Māyā.
Their connection arises from primordial karma; Śiva is the impeller, the Lord.
The sages said:
"What is this that is called Māyā? What is the nature of one who is enveloped by Māyā?
What is its root, and from where does it arise? What is the state of Śiva-hood, and from where does Śiva come? Vāyu said:
Māyā is the power of Maheśvara; he is of the nature of consciousness, yet enveloped by Māyā. Impurity (mala) is innate and obscures consciousness, while purity and the state of Śiva are inherent.
The sages said:
"How does Māyā veil [the soul], and for what reason?
For what purpose is there this veiling of the person (puṃs), and by what means is it removed?
Vāyu said:
The obscuration (āvṛti) may belong even to that which is all-pervasive, because even the constituent powers (kalā) and so forth are pervasive.
Karma alone is the cause for the sake of experience; it ceases upon the destruction of impurity (mala).
The sages said:
What is that which is called *kalā* and so forth? Or what is it designated as *karma*?
What is its beginning, what is its end, what is its fruit, and what is its substratum?
By whose enjoyment is what enjoyed, and what is the means for that enjoyment?
"What is the cause of the destruction of impurities? What is a person like whose impurities have been destroyed?
Vāyu replied:
"Kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, and niyati..."

The Kalās and so forth have been fully described; he who is the enjoyer is the Puruṣa. Action, consisting of merit and demerit, which has pleasure and pain as its fruit, is beginningless, ends with experience, and rests upon the self through ignorance.
Experience leads to the destruction of karma; experience is said to be unmanifest.
The body, which serves as the means for experience, functions through the gateway of the external and internal organs.
Through the grace obtained by the excellence of one's disposition, there occurs the destruction of impurity.
And when that impurity of the self is exhausted, the person becomes equal to Śiva.
The sages said:
"What are the individual functions of the five principles beginning with Kalā? Please tell us."
By what is the Self designated as "the enjoyer" and "the person"?
Of what nature is that unmanifest, and in what form is it experienced?
What is its refuge during enjoyment, and what is called the body?
Vāyu said:
Space, action, and knowledge are the manifestors; time and attachment are the motivators.
Therein, time is the delimiting factor and necessity (niyati) is the regulator.
That which is the unmanifest cause, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), and characterized by manifestation and dissolution—
what the seekers of truth call Pradhāna and Prakṛti—
is manifested from the Kalā, though its essential nature remains unmanifest.
The self, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is experienced in three ways through the qualities (*guṇas*). Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities born of *prakṛti*;
they exist within *prakṛti* in a subtle form, like oil in a sesame seed.
Happiness and the cause of happiness are briefly remembered as being of the nature of *sattva*.
That which is the opposite of this is *rājasa*; while arrogance and delusion are of the nature of *tamas*.
An upward movement is declared to be *sāttvika*, whereas a downward movement would be *tāmasa*.
That which is the intermediate state is declared to be the *rājasa* (passionate) path.
It consists of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five gross elements (*bhūta*),
the fivefold unity of the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), and the five organs of action (*karmendriya*).
The fourfold group consisting of primordial matter (pradhāna), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas)—
this is briefly described as the unmanifest (avyakta) along with its modifications. When that [unmanifest] has entered the state of being a cause, it is called the "unmanifest" (avyakta).

The manifest, having reached the state of an effect— such as the body and so forth— is like a jar and the like. Just as an effect such as a jar does not differ significantly from its material cause, such as clay, so too the manifest, such as the body, does not differ significantly from the unmanifest.
Therefore, the unmanifest alone is the cause of unity, as are the instruments;
the body is its substratum, and it is also that which is to be experienced, and nothing else.
The sages said:
Vāyu said: "How could there be, even in reality, the existence of anything denoted by the word 'self' that is distinct from the intellect, the senses, and the body?"
The distinction of the omnipresent [Self] from the intellect, the senses, and the body is certain;
yet the reason that "there truly exists some Self" is very difficult to establish therein.
For the wise do not accept that the intellect, the senses, or the body possess the nature of the Self.

Because memory consists of indeterminate cognitions that persist as long as the body exists, the one who remembers all objects of experience is therefore celebrated in the Vedas and the Vedāntas as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī), whose sphere encompasses the entirety of all that is knowable.
He, the eternal one, remains pervading everything there and everywhere;
nevertheless, he is not clearly perceived anywhere by anyone.
He cannot be grasped by the eye, nor even by the other sense organs.
The Great Self is realized through the mind alone when it is fully illumined.
It is neither female, nor male, nor even neuter;
it is not above, nor across, nor below, nor from any direction whatsoever.
The wise man always perceives that which is bodiless within bodies, immovable within the moving, and imperishable—through constant self-reflection.
What is the use of saying more on this point? The Person is distinct from the body.
But those who perceive no difference— that is, they do not see the vision [of truth] within those things that are unreal—
for them, this body which is said to belong to the Puruṣa does not exist as something beyond [the self],
nor is it impure, nor powerless, nor suffering, nor transient.
Joined with that which has become the seed of calamities,
a person becomes happy, miserable, or deluded through his own karma,
just as a field saturated with water produces a sprout.

Karma, flooded by ignorance, likewise produces a body; [bodies] that are known to be utterly unpleasant dwellings and whose death is certain. His bodies, both those yet to come and those already past, are in their thousands.
As embodied beings arrive again and again, their bodies decay;
nowhere is an eternal dwelling found by anyone.
In these [bodies], one is seen both covered and separated from them.
Like the lunar orb in the sky amidst shimmering masses of clouds,
the activity of the Self here appears divided through the differentiation of various bodies; indeed,
it is perceived like a single die within the roll of a game of eight-sided dice.
No one shall belong to him, nor does he belong to anyone;
this union with wives, sons, and kinsmen is merely a meeting on the road.
It is just as when two pieces of wood come together upon the great ocean.
Having come together, they depart from one another; such is the meeting of the elements.
He sees that body, yet he does not see that body [as his own]. A certain other sees both of them, but neither of them sees him.
It is determined that all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary [plants], are proclaimed to be *paśus* (bound souls). This illustration has been declared for all *paśus* indeed.
This very creature, who consumes pleasure and pain, is bound by fetters;
the wise declare that he has become the instrument for the sport of the Lord.
This ignorant being is not the master of its own pleasure and pain.
"Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Anila, the sages were delighted in their minds.
Having bowed to that Vāyu, who was an expert in the Śaiva Āgamas, they spoke [as follows].

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge of the Reality of Śiva," in the first section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 6]
The sages said:
"Regarding this one who is called the 'bound soul' (paśu) and that which is described as the 'bond' (pāśa)—
what is this Lord who exists as distinct from these two?"
Vāyu said:
There is a certain Lord, the creator of the universe, the refuge of boundless and beautiful qualities, who liberates bound souls from their fetters.

In the absence of that [Lord], how could this creation of the universe come to be? Because both of these—the individual soul (*paśu*) and the bond (*pāśa*)—are insentient and devoid of knowledge. Whatever is insentient, such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, [is likewise incapable of it].
That [world] was seen by him himself to have been created by an intelligent cause;
for the universe, being an effect composed of parts, depends upon an agent.
Therefore, the agency over the effect belongs to the Lord (pati), and not to the bound souls (paśu) or their fetters (pāśa).
Even the agency of the individual soul (paśu) is preceded by the impulsion of the Lord (pati),
just as the movement of a blind man [requires a guide] and his knowledge of acting improperly.
Having considered oneself as distinct, and the Impeller as distinct from that [self], [one attains liberation].
When he is thus favored by Him, he indeed becomes fit for immortality.

In reality, there exists a supreme state belonging to the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (pati). Having known that very source through the knowledge of Brahman, one shall become liberated.
This pair, consisting of the perishable and the imperishable, is joined together;
the Lord, the liberator of the universe, sustains the manifest and the unmanifest.
The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—this is remembered as the threefold nature of that which is to be contemplated.
Indeed, for those who know, there is nothing further to be known beyond this.
Just as oil is contained within sesame seeds, or clarified butter within curd;
just as water pervades a stream, or as fire exists within the fire-drill wood.
In this very way, one who is constantly disciplined through truth and austerity perceives the Great Soul within oneself, distinct from the individual self—
that one Lord who possesses the net, together with his sovereign powers as his own energies.
Having made all these worlds his own, he alone rules as the sole Lord.
At that time, Rudra was indeed one; there was no second whatsoever.
Having created the entire universe, he who is its protector withdrew it back into himself.
The absence of the *ślu* suffix is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
He indeed has eyes on every side, and likewise he has faces on every side;
similarly, he is endowed with arms on every side and feet on every side.
The one God, Maheśvara, generating heaven and earth,
is himself the source and the origin of all the gods;
he brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha as the first among the deities.
For the Veda declares: "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe.
"I know this Great Puruṣa, the immortal and eternal, the Lord who stands beyond darkness, resplendent like the sun."
There is nothing higher than this, nor anything lower than the Supreme Self;
there is nothing smaller and nothing greater, for by Him this entire world is filled.
He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere dwells in the secret cave of all beings.

The Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent. With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, he stands encompassing everything.
He is the manifestation of the qualities of all the senses, yet he is devoid of all senses;
he is the Lord and Master of all, the refuge and friend of all.
He is one who sees though he has no eyes, and he hears though he has no ears.

He knows everything, yet no one knows Him; they call Him the Supreme Puruṣa. Subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, this Imperishable One, Maheśvara, is hidden within the cave of the heart of every living being.
Through the grace of the Creator,
one who is free from sorrow beholds that Lord, who possesses will, whose essence is will, and who is endowed with an excellence of majesty;
"I know him, the undecaying, the ancient, the all-pervading, the omnipresent."
The exponents of Brahman declare that he is the cessation of birth;
though he is one, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), through the application of his manifold powers, creates these three worlds at the beginning and withdraws the universe at the end.

The Supreme Śiva’s manifold form is called the "All-Sustainer" (Viśvadhātrī) and the "Unborn" (Ajā). Another [the individual soul], desiring his own nature, lies upon that single Unborn One— who is red, white, and black— the progenitor who bestows offspring.
But another goat, being unattached, abandons that very same she-goat after having enjoyed her.
Two birds, inseparable companions, dwell upon the same tree;
one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
A person submerged in this tree, hidden from view, grieves.
But when he beholds another, the Lord who is the supreme cause,
then, freed from sorrow, he shall become happy and perceive His majesty.
The Vedas, sacrifices, seasons, and all that has been and all that is to be—
into this universe the Supreme Lord, the wielder of *māyā*, creates through *māyā*.
One should know *māyā* to be *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) to be the wielder of *māyā*.
By her very limbs, this entire world is pervaded;
she perceives the Lord, who is subtler than the subtlest, even within the midst of an embryo.
(The use of the verb *vicetoti* is due to its being an archaic Vedic form.)

By virtue of the grammatical rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (irregularities occur frequently), this form is correct. Having known Śiva alone as the Lord—the creator of the universe and its enveloper—one attains ultimate peace. (ŚivP 7.1.6.35)
He alone is Time, the protector, the sovereign lord, and the master of the universe.
By knowing Him, the sovereign lord of the universe, one is liberated from the noose of death.
Having known the Lord who abides as subtle as the cream upon clarified butter, one is released.
Hidden within all beings, one is liberated from all sins.
He alone is the supreme deity, the architect of the universe, Maheśvara;
by knowing Him as dwelling within the heart, one attains immortality.
When everything was neither day nor night, neither existent nor non-existent—
since the ancient wisdom [perceived] that Śiva alone was the one and only—
no one could grasp him above, nor across, nor in the middle.
There is no likeness for him whose name is Great Renown.
Some who are fearful at birth perceive this very one as unborn;
they seek refuge in the right-hand bliss of this Rudra for the sake of protection.
Two syllables, infinite and supreme to Brahman, have been proclaimed;
they are known as Vidyā and Avidyā, wherein they are hidden as if in secret.
Indeed, the perishable is called Avidyā, while the immortal is celebrated as Vidyā.
He who rules over both of them is indeed the other, Maheśvara.
Manifesting his single net in many ways and yet remaining as one,
that majestic one exercises supreme sovereignty after having created all beings.
He shines by himself, illuminating the quarters— above, below, and across.
He alone, the most excellent, presides even over that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva),
transforming all words that denote intrinsic nature as well as their referents.
Through the qualities (guṇas), it presides over that entire universe in its capacity as both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment. Indeed,
the gods and great seers know that supreme Brahman, which is higher than the highest, hidden in the secret Upaniṣads,
as the primordial womb of the world and the source of Brahmā.
Those who know the Lord— who is to be grasped through contemplation, who is called "effortless," who brings about both existence and non-existence, who is auspicious,
and who effects the creation of the *kalās*— they have abandoned the body.
Some, being deluded, consider inherent nature (*svabhāva*) [to be the cause], while others consider time (*kāla*).
For such is the majesty of the Lord by which this world is set in motion;
since it is eternally enveloped by Him, whose nature is the Time of time,
this action impelled by Him revolves together with the elements.
Having repeatedly performed that action and having withdrawn again,
and indeed having attained union with the principle (tattva) together with the principle,
[he proceeds] by means of eight, three, two, or even one [element].
In due time, by means of his own qualities, he himself [causes] the entire world to arise through those qualities;
he should then join it to actions such as those arising from its own nature (*svabhāva*).
In the absence of these [qualities], there would be the destruction even of action already performed.
Upon the exhaustion of karma, he then truly proceeds to another state;
he himself is the beginning, the cause of yoga for both the enjoyer and the enjoyment.
Beyond the three times, he is the partless one, the Supreme Lord himself.
The all-knowing one, the lord of the three qualities, Brahman himself, higher than the high; him,
the universal-formed, the unborn, Bhava, the adorable Lord of Creatures,
the God of gods, worshipped by the world— we worship him who dwells within our own hearts.
Because from Him the phenomenal world revolves through time and other factors—
He who brings about righteousness, dispels evil, is the Lord of enjoyments, and the abode of the universe; Him,
the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme deity among deities.
May we know the Lord, the supreme among lords, beyond all else, the God who is the Lord of the lords of the worlds. For him no effect exists, nor does any cause exist;
neither his equal nor his superior is seen anywhere in the universe.
His manifold power is heard in the Veda to be innate;
it consists of knowledge, strength, and action, by which this entire universe was created.
He has no lord over him, nor any mark [of office], nor any ruler.
He is the cause of causes and the sovereign lord over them all.
There is no progenitor for him, nor is there any birth for him from anywhere.
Likewise, the factors known as *mala*, *māyā*, and so forth, do not serve as causes for his birth.
He alone is hidden within all beings and pervades them on every side;
he is called the inner self of all beings and the presiding lord of dharma.
He is the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, and devoid of qualities.

He alone is the sovereign of the many who are powerless and devoid of self-control; he is the eternal among the eternal and the conscious among the conscious. Though he is one and free from desire, the Lord bestows the objects of desire upon the many.

Having known that Lord— the cause of the worlds, attainable through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the Master of all beings— the bound soul (paśu) is liberated from all fetters (pāśas). He is the creator of the universe, the knower of the universe, the one who knows his own self as the source, the maker of time, and the possessor of qualities.
The primordial Lord of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Master of the Guṇas, the Liberator from bonds—
he who in the beginning created Brahmā and himself taught him the Vedas;
having realized that God through the clarity of my own intellect, I [bow to him].
Desiring liberation from this saṃsāra, I take refuge in Śiva—
He who is fruitless, actionless, peaceful, blameless, and stainless;
the supreme bridge to immortality, like the wind that has consumed its fuel.
When men shall wrap up the sky like a piece of leather,
then, having failed to recognize Śiva, there will be an end to suffering.
Through the power of their austerity and by the grace of the Lord, O great seers, [this shall come to pass].
This knowledge, appropriate for those beyond the stages of life (*atyāśrama*), is pure and destructive of sin;
it is the supreme secret of the Vedānta, proclaimed in a former age.
By the weight of my good fortune, I have obtained this from the mouth of Brahmā.
This unsurpassed knowledge must not be given to one who is not tranquil;

it must never be given to a son of improper conduct, nor to one who is not a disciple. [It should be given] to one who possesses supreme devotion toward the God, and toward the Guru just as toward the God.
For these truths have been declared to that high-souled one, and they shine clearly before him.
Therefore, listen to this summary: Śiva is beyond both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
At the time of creation, he brings forth everything; at the time of dissolution, he withdraws it all once again.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Śiva-Tattva," in the first part of the Vāyavīya-Saṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva-Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 7 The Sages said:
Everything arises from time, and everything perishes by time alone;
for nothing whatsoever exists that is independent of time.
Since the entire universe, with its eternal cycle of transmigration, is contained within it.
By means of the mudrās of creation and withdrawal, it revolves like a wheel.
Brahmā, Hari, Rudra, and likewise other gods and asuras,
having encountered the destiny ordained by Him, are unable to transcend it.

Wearing away all creatures by dividing them into the past, present, future, and so forth, this most terrifying one acts according to his own will as the supreme lord. Who is this venerable Time, and under whose control does he abide?
"O wise one, tell me this: who would not be under his control?
Vāyu replied:
[He whose body is composed of] the divisions of time, such as *kāla*, *kāṣṭhā*, *nimeṣa*, and so forth..."
That which is known as Kālātman is the supreme splendor of Maheśvara;
it is inviolable for all that is stationary and moving,
the power of the Lord in the form of his command that governs the entire universe.
Liberation consists of portions of that [time], residing within the Great Self who is time itself.
Having emerged from Him, it is transferred and cast forth like iron by fire.
Therefore, the universe is subject to the power of time; He does not abide under the power of the universe.
Time is indeed under the control of Śiva, but Śiva is not under the control of Time;
for the unimpeded splendor of Śarva is established even over Time.
Therefore, the great boundary of Time is indeed difficult to transcend.
Who is able to transcend Time by means of any distinction in wisdom?
No one can transcend the action ordained by Time.
Even those who, through their prowess, rule the entire earth under a single umbrella [are subject to it].
Even those who, having restrained the collection of their senses, conquer the entire world, do not transcend Time, just as the oceans do not overstep the limits of the tide. They do not conquer Time;
rather, Time conquers even them.

Even physicians who know the science of Ayurveda and have practiced the elixirs of rejuvenation do not transcend death; for time is indeed difficult to overcome. [They may possess] prosperity, beauty, character, strength, and noble lineage.

A living being thinks one thing, but Time forcibly does another. Indeed, the Lord unites and separates all beings with things both unpleasant and pleasant, whose arrivals and departures are beyond thought.

At the very moment that someone is suffering, another is happy; oh, how wondrous is the variety of Time, whose nature is so difficult to comprehend! He who was young becomes old, and he who was strong becomes weak.
O twice-born ones, even he who is glorious becomes devoid of glory through Time, for Time moves in diverse ways. Neither noble birth, nor character, nor strength,
nor skill is sufficient for the accomplishment of a task, for Time is indeed irresistible.

Time acts with impartiality toward those who have protectors and are generous, attended by songs and musical instruments, as well as toward those who are helpless and subsist on the food of others. Even elixirs and medicines, though properly administered, do not bear fruit when the time is not right.
Those very same [actions], when gathered together by Time, quickly attain fruition and bestow happiness.

One is not born nor does one die before the appointed time; one does not attain supreme nourishment before the appointed time. One is not made happy or miserable before the appointed time; there exists no thing whatsoever that is untimely.
In due time the cool wind blows; in due time the rain-clouds bring forth rain.
In due time the heat subsides; in due time everything attains fruition.
Time is the cause of all existence; by time the crops constantly come to be.

In time the crops go to their dissolution; in time the world of living beings comes back to life. He who understands in this way the true nature of Time according to reality, having transcended the self of Time, beholds that which is beyond Time.

Salutations to that supreme Parameśvara, the auspicious Śiva of manifold forms, who is neither time nor bondage and liberation, who is neither the individual soul (puruṣa) nor primordial nature (prakṛti), nor the universe. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Time," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 8.
The Sages said:
By what measure is the calculation of the lifespan determined in this time?
"What, then, is the ultimate limit of time in its numerical form?
Vāyu replied:
"In this context, that which is called a *nimeṣa* is declared to be the first measure of life."
Regarding time in its numerical form, up to the limit of the past kalās of the Śāntva period, a single blink of an eyelash is defined as a *nimeṣa*. Fifteen such *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*.

Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are called a *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*. Thirty *muhūrtas* are declared to be one day and night (*ahorātra*). A month, consisting of two fortnights (*pakṣa*), is composed of thirty such days and nights.
A month, consisting of the dark and light fortnights, is to be known as a day and night of the ancestors (pitṛs).
Six such months are considered an *ayana*, and two *ayanās* are held to be a year. This is the human year according to the worldly measure that is traditionally recorded.
This is the divine day and night; such is the determination of the scripture.
The southern solstice is the night, and likewise, the northern solstice is the day.
A month is known to consist of thirty divine days and nights, just as in the human reckoning.
Likewise, a year of the gods consists of twelve months;
it should be known that three hundred and sixty human years constitute one divine year,
as proclaimed in the human reckoning.
The calculation of the Yugas proceeds by divine measure alone.
The wise know that there are four Yugas in Bhārata-varṣa:
first is that which is named Kṛta-yuga, and after that, Tretā is ordained.

Dvāpara and Kali—these are all the ages in their entirety. The Kṛta age consists of four thousand years; its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three [ages], along with their twilights and twilight-portions,
they proceed by a decrease of one thousand and one hundred [years].
This twelve-thousand-year period, augmented by these, constitutes a cycle of four ages (caturyuga).

That which consists of a thousand cycles of the four yugas is called a *saṃkalpa*. Seventy-one such cycles of four yugas are said to constitute the interval of a *manu*. Within a single *kalpa*, there are fourteen such successions of *manus*.
By this sequential process,
hundreds and thousands of kalpas and manvantaras have passed away along with their inhabitants;
furthermore, because all of them are unknowable and incalculable.

Indeed, it is not possible to describe their details in full even in successive order. A single day of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, is called a *kalpa*. A thousand such *kalpas* are here said to constitute one year of Brahmā.
Eight thousand years constitute one *yuga* of Brahmā, the lotus-born. A thousand such *yugas* form a single *savana* of Brahmā. And three thousand such *savanas* likewise constitute his *trivṛt*.
The entire lifespan of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin is calculated as follows:
in a single day of his, fourteen Indras pass away;
and in one month, four hundred and twenty [Indras] pass away.
In the lifespan [of Brahmā], there are five hundred and forty thousand years;
and in the lifespan [of Viṣṇu], there are five hundred and forty thousand years.
One day of Viṣṇu is equal to one day of Rudra.
In the day of Īśvara, Rudra is likewise Īśvara;
he who is Sadākhya is Śiva himself, and he too is Sadāśiva with that same number [of days].
His lifespan is five hundred thousand and forty thousand [years].
In that [state], this very soul of Time proceeds directly from Śiva himself.
O twice-born ones, that which has been described here as the interval of time for creation—
this interval of time should be known as the day of the Supreme Lord.
The night of the Supreme Lord should be known to be of the same duration as his day.
His day is traditionally held to be creation, and his night is dissolution.
One should maintain the understanding that for him there is neither day nor night.
This ritual service is performed out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The subjects, the lords of subjects, and the forms of the gods and asuras;
the sense organs, the objects of the senses, and the five great elements—[all these are manifestations of Him].

Then the subtle elements, the source of the gross elements (bhūtādi), and the intellect, together with the divine [ego], all remain during the day of the wise Supreme Lord. At the end of that day they dissolve; at the end of the night, the origin of the universe [re-emerges].

Salutations to that Great Śaṅkara, the Soul of All, whose power over objects such as action, time, and inherent nature cannot be transgressed; to Him by whose command alone this entire universe is governed. Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Lifespans of the Three Devas," in the section on the Power of Time within the first part of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 9.
The sages said: How did he create and then place this entire world? Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.9.1ab.
By his command, the Supreme Lord performs the supreme sport.
What was that which first came into being? By whom was this entire universe pervaded?
And by whom, moreover, is this swallowed by the one of vast belly?
Vāyu said:
"Śakti was first produced, following the state beyond peace (śāntyatīta).
Then from the Lord Śiva, who possesses power, came Māyā, and then the Unmanifest (avyakta)."
From that [Śakti-tattva] arises the state of Śāntātīta through the sequence of the states of Śānti;
from that, the state of Vidyā; from that, the emergence of the state of Pratiṣṭhā;
and from the state of Pratiṣṭhā, the state of Nivṛtti arises in due order.

Thus has the creation impelled by the Lord been described in brief; likewise, their dissolution occurs in reverse order. Beyond this which has been designated as the fivefold state, the Supreme Creator is intended.
Therefore, this entire world is pervaded by five constituent parts (kalās).
That which is the unmanifest cause is presided over by the Self;
it is also accepted that [the Self] creates everything from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa).
However, even in that case, agency belongs neither to the unmanifest (avyakta) nor to the self (ātman);
for prakṛti is insentient and the puruṣa is ignorant.
Whatever is insentient, such as pradhāna, atoms, and so forth, [lacks agency].
That [world] was seen by him himself to have been created without an intelligent cause;
yet the world is dependent upon a creator, because it is an effect composed of parts.
Therefore, he who is capable, independent, possessed of all powers, and all-knowing—[is that creator].
He is without beginning or end, endowed with great sovereignty;
he alone is the creator of the world, Mahādeva, the Great Lord.
He is the protector and the destroyer of all, yet he is distinct from and unrelated to them.
The transformation of Pradhāna and the activity of Puruṣa—
all this proceeds solely by the command of Satyavrata.
This eternal principle dwells within the minds of the virtuous.
And one of limited intelligence does not abide by this position [of permanence],
for from the beginning of creation until the great dissolution,
all this passes away within a hundred autumns of Brahmā.
"Parama" is the name of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest;
half of that is called "para," and half of that is designated as a "parārdha.
When the dissolution arrives at the end of the period of two parārdhas, [all things are withdrawn].

Taking up its own unmanifest effect, it abides within itself. When the unmanifest has been established in the self and transformation has been withdrawn, both Pradhāna and Puruṣa abide together in a state of shared nature.

These two qualities, *tamas* and *sattva*, exist in a state of equilibrium; they are undifferentiated, infinite, and mutually interwoven. At that time, when there is an equality of the qualities, in that undivided state where *tamas* prevails—
In that place where the wind was stilled and there was only water, nothing at all could be discerned.
When this world was thus unknowable, Maheśvara alone remained.
Then, after having spent the entire night in supreme devotion to Maheśvara, [he arose].
When the night had turned to dawn, Maheśvara, through the application of his *māyā*, entered both of those two principal beings and agitated them. Thereupon,
he [became] the source and the place of dissolution for all beings without exception.
From the Unmanifest, creation arose by the command of Parameṣṭhin,
whose single fraction of power suffices for all the various and ever-increasing desires of the universe.
Salutation to Him, whom those who know the paths call the Self and the Lord of the paths, and who is distinct from all worlds.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Agency in Creation, Preservation, and Dissolution," in the first part of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Ten. Vāyu said:
First, by the command of the Lord, from the unmanifest (avyakta) presided over by Puruṣa,
the transformations beginning with intellect (buddhi) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa) arose in succession.
Then, from those transformations, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha [were born].
As the cause of all things, the three gods were born;
they possess an unimpeded power to pervade the universe everywhere,
as well as incomparable knowledge and eternal sovereignty, such as the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) and the rest.
Maheśvara, together with his sovereignty, is pleased with these [beings] regarding their causality in the three activities known as creation, maintenance, and dissolution. However,
in another kalpa, there arises a rivalry among them whose intellects have become deluded.
And he assigned to each of them the duty of creation, protection, and dissolution.
These, born from one another, support one another;
they flourish through one another, being devoted to one another.
In some places Brahmā is praised, in some Viṣṇu, and in others Rudra;
yet by this, no superiority or preeminence of sovereignty is established for them.
Fools, driven by agitation and dogmatic attachment, revile them with their words.
They undoubtedly become *yātudhānas* and *piśācas*.
Maheśvara is the Lord who transcends the three *guṇas*, the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*),
the one with parts (*sakala*), and the support of all, the cause of the origin of power (*śakti*).

This very Self is established in the state of Lordship, effecting the creation of the world through His divine play, out of these three: primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual soul (puruṣa), and Himself;
He who is the Supreme Lord, eternal, partless, and superior to all.
He alone is its support, its very self, and its presiding lord.
Therefore, Maheśvara is both Prakṛti and Puruṣa;
Sadāśiva, Bhava, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are all essentially Śiva.
From Pradhāna was first born Vṛddhi, Khyāti, Mati, and Mahān. From the agitation of the Mahat-tattva, the threefold Ahaṃkāra arose.
And from Ahaṃkāra came the elements, the subtle essences (tanmātras), and the sense organs.
From the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is characterized by the predominance of *sattva*, the *sāttvika* creation proceeds;
that *vaikārika* creation manifests simultaneously as the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) and the five organs of action (*karmendriya*).

The eleventh [organ] therein is the mind (*manas*), which by its own nature partakes of both [qualities]. From the *ahaṃkāra* associated with *tamas*, there arises the origin of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*bhūta*). Because it is the primary source of the gross elements, it is called *bhūtādi*.
From *bhūtādi* there arises mere sound (*śabda-mātra*), and from that, the origination of space (*ākāśa*).
From space, touch (*sparśa*) is produced; from touch, the emergence of wind (*vāyu*). From wind comes form (*rūpa*), and from that, fire (*tejas*); from fire, the production of taste (*rasa*).
From taste, water was produced; from them, fragrance arose.
From fragrance, earth was born, and from the elements, all else—both moving and non-moving.
This occurred through the presiding presence of the Puruṣa and by the grace of the Unmanifest.

For those [principles], beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas, produce the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). When the effect and the instrument of Brahmā were fully perfected therein, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), designated as Brahmā, became fully developed within that egg.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa.
He is the original creator of all beings, and Brahmā appeared at the beginning.
The likeness of that Lord is characterized by knowledge and dispassion.

The intellect (*buddhi*) of that one who possesses pride in sacrifice is of the nature of Brahmā (*brāhmī*), bestowing sovereignty over all phenomena (*dharma*). From the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), whatever he desires arises through his mind;
yet, due to its transformation, its threefold qualities (*triguṇya*), its dependence, and its inherent nature, it remains subject to control.
Dividing himself threefold, he proceeds throughout the three worlds;
by means of these three, he himself creates, devours, and beholds.
In the state of Brahmā he is four-faced, and in the state of Time he is known as the Ender (Antaka).
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads; there are three states of the Self-born One:
in the state of Brahmā, there is *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; in the state of Time (*kālatva*), there is *rajas* and *tamas*;
and in the state of Viṣṇu, there is *sattva* alone—the increase of the qualities (*guṇavṛddhi*) is thus threefold in the All-pervading Lord.

In the state of Brahmā, he creates the worlds; in the state of Kāla, he also withdraws them; and in the state of Puruṣa, the All-pervading Lord is utterly indifferent. Such is the threefold activity of the Lord. Because he is thus divided into these three modes, Brahmā is said to possess the three qualities (triguṇa).
Because he is divided fourfold, he is proclaimed as the Cāturvyūha (the Fourfold Manifestation).
Because he is the beginning, he is known as Ādideva; because he is unborn, he is remembered as Aja.
Since he protects all creatures, he is remembered as Prajāpati.
The golden Mount Meru is the amnion of that Great-Souled One;
the oceans are the fetal fluids, and the mountains are the placenta. Within that egg are these worlds, and within them is this entire universe.
The moon and the sun, along with the constellations, the planets, and the wind, [are contained within];
the egg is surrounded on the outside by water ten times its size,
and that water is surrounded on the outside by fire ten times its size.
Fire is surrounded on the outside by air ten times its size;
air is surrounded by space, and space is surrounded by the source of the elements (bhūtādi).
Likewise, the source of the elements is surrounded by the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle is surrounded by the Unmanifest (avyakta).
The egg is surrounded on the outside by these seven coverings;
and enveloping this [egg], the eight primordial natures (prakṛtis) stand in mutual relation,
O best of the twice-born, performing the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Thus, arising from one another, they support one another;
for the modifications exist within the modified through the relationship of container and contained,
just as a tortoise first extends its limbs and then withdraws them.
Having likewise created the modifications and the unmanifest, he again withdraws them.
Everything originating from the unmanifest is born in the forward order;
but when the time of dissolution arrives, it is absorbed in the reverse order.
By the power of time alone, the *guṇas* become either unbalanced or balanced.
When there is equilibrium of the *guṇas*, it should be known as dissolution (*laya*); when there is imbalance, it is called creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
This very thing is the womb of Brahmā; this is the great, solid cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*).
"The field of Brahmā is designated as such, and Brahmā is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Such millions of cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) are to be known by the thousands;
because Pradhāna is all-pervading, they are situated horizontally, above, and below."
In those various places, four-faced Brahmās, Haras,
and Bhavas were created by Pradhāna; having thus obtained the presence of Śambhu,
Maheśvara— who is beyond the unmanifest— [created] the cosmic egg born from the unmanifest.
From the egg was born the pervasive Brahmā; by him these worlds were created.
This first creation of *pradhāna*, which proceeded without prior conscious intent, has been described by me.
Furthermore, at the time of the final dissolution, there occurs an absolute dissolution, which is performed solely as the sport (*līlā*) of the Lord.
That which is known as the immeasurable cause— Brahmā, the Pradhāna, the progenitor of Prakṛti—
is without beginning, middle, or end, possessed of infinite power, white yet intensely red, and joined with Puruṣa.
Because of its productivity and the predominance of the quality of rajas, it is the cause for the expansion of the continuity of the world.

Having created even the eight transformations at the time of the beginning, he likewise consumes them at the time of the end. Both the state of persistence and the subsequent activity of those causes established within primordial nature— all that belongs to the Great Lord, whose power is non-material, through his mere volition.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Structure of the Cosmic Egg," in the seventh section, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 11 The Sages said:
"Tell us of all the Manvantaras and all the various divisions of the Kalpas,
as well as the intermediate creation and the secondary creation within them.
Vāyu said:

A *parārdha* is recorded as the duration of Brahmā’s life, which is measured by the number of years in his lifespan. An equal period of time is ordained for him as well, at the end of which he is dissolved. This occurs day after day for that Brahmā of the preceding birth.
There have been fourteen cycles of the highly fortunate Manus;
because they are without beginning, without end, and entirely unknowable,
it is impossible to describe the Manvantaras and Kalpas individually.
Even though all these have been spoken, since you are listening to my words, what further fruit could there be here? Therefore, I do not venture to speak anything more than this.
Indeed, that very kalpa which is currently prevailing among the kalpas—[it is this].
Therein, the creations and re-creations proceed in brief.
This present aeon (kalpa), known by the name Vārāha, is that which is currently occurring;
even within this, O best of the twice-born, there are fourteen Manus.
There are seven Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva, and seven others beginning with Sāvarṇika.
Among them, the seventh Manu, named Vaivasvata, is currently presiding. Throughout all the Manvantaras, the processes of creation and dissolution continue.
A wise person should employ reasoning, for [all things] generally become equal again.
When the previous kalpa has turned back and the wind of time has set in,
when the trees and the forests have had their roots completely uprooted.
When the god of fire burns, even those who have mouths as small as blades of grass survive;
when the earth is drenched by rain and the oceans overflow,
and when all directions are submerged in a vast flood of water— Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.11.11ab–12ab.
Then, as the waters of the dissolution began their fierce dance with circles of wave-arms and restless tossing,
Brahmā, having become Nārāyaṇa, slept peacefully upon the water.
Reciting this mantra and verse concerning Nārāyaṇa,
listen, O best of sages, to it and to its meaning which rests upon the syllables:
"The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *Nara*."
Since they are his place of rest (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
While the Lord of the Thirty Gods was performing his sleep consisting of Śiva-yoga,
the Siddhas dwelling in Janaloka stood with their palms joined in reverence.
At the time of dawn, the gods awakened him with hymns of praise,
just as the Vedas formerly awakened the Lord at the time of creation and other such occasions.
