Then, having awakened and risen from his bed, he emerged from the midst of the waters.
With eyes languid from yogic sleep, he gazed upon all directions;
yet he saw nothing then that existed apart from his own self.
Sitting as if filled with wonder, he fell into deep reflection.
"Where is that blessed, delightful, and vast earth,
with its various great mountains, rivers, cities, and forests?
While Brahmā was reflecting thus, he could not perceive the existence of the earth at all.
Then he remembered his father, the three-eyed Lord;
by the remembrance of Bhava, the God of gods of immeasurable splendor,
the lord of the earth realized that the earth was submerged in the waters.
Then, desiring to lift the earth from the waters, Prajāpati meditated upon his divine boar-form, which was suited for sporting in the water,
possessing the stature of a great mountain and the roar of a massive rain-cloud.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with a blazing roar and terrifying, it had thick,
rounded, and dense shoulders and broad, elevated hips;
its thighs and forelegs were short and round, and its snout was very sharp and circular.
Resembling a ruby gem, with round and terrifying eyes;
with large, rounded, and long limbs, and blazing with stiff ears;
agitating the ocean of dissolution with his heaving inhalations and exhalations.
Beautiful with its cheeks and shoulders covered by shimmering, fine manes;
adorned with jewels, ornaments, and variegated great gems;
it shone like a towering mass of clouds illuminated by flashes of lightning.
Assuming a vast and immeasurable boar-form,
the Creator entered the subterranean realm (rasātala) for the purpose of uplifting the earth.
At that time, that boar, resembling a mountain, shone exceedingly.
Just as one who has reached the soles of the feet of Maheśa in his linga-form,
the upholder of the earth then lifted the submerged earth,
embraced it with his tusks, and emerged from the netherworld (rasātala).
Seeing him, the sages and Siddhas dwelling in Janaloka rejoiced,
danced, and strewed flowers upon his head;
the body of the Great Boar, covered with flowers, shone resplendently.
The mountain of collyrium appeared as if covered by falling fireflies.
Then, having brought the great earth to its proper place, the omnipresent Lord Varāha,
assuming his own form, established it.
Having leveled the earth and established the mountains upon it,
he fashioned the four worlds beginning with Bhūr as before;
thus, from the midst of the great waters of the dissolution situated beneath the earth, he [reconstructed] the vast earth together with its mountains.
And having placed [the seed] above, Viśvakarman created once again the world of both the moving and the unmoving.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of Creation and Other Matters," in the seventh section (Vāyavīya Saṃhitā) of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 12.
Vāyu said:
As he was then contemplating creation with deliberate intent,
at the moment of deep meditation, a delusion consisting of darkness (tamas) appeared.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and that which is called andhatāmisra—
this fivefold ignorance (avidyā) manifested from the Great-Souled One. Thus, as he was meditating with self-consciousness, the creation became established in five ways.

Completely enveloped by darkness like a seed within a jar, they are without light both inside and out— stunned and utterly unconscious. Therefore, their intellect, their faces, and their sensory organs are all shrouded.

Therefore, those mountains were proclaimed to be the foremost among those whose selves are restrained. Having seen that first creation to be such an ineffective one, Brahmā became displeased in mind and conceived a second [creation].
From his desire to express [it], the stream of animals (tiryaksrotas) turned forth.
These animals have internal illumination but are again obscured on the outside;
born from that, they are of the nature of bound souls (paśu) and they follow wrong paths.
Knowing that [creation] also to be unsuccessful, he reflected upon another creation.
Then the upward-streaming (ūrdhvasrotas) creation of the gods, characterized by goodness (sāttvika), took place. They abound in happiness and joy, and are unobstructed both internally and externally.

They are designated as being luminous both externally and internally by their very nature. Then, from the Unmanifest (avyakta) which was meditating, there arose the downward-flowing stream (arvāk-srotas),
the human-named creation, which is intense with suffering.
Those in whom *tamas* predominates are external to light (*prakāśa*), while those in whom *rajas* predominates are internal.
The fifth creation is that of grace (*anugraha-sarga*), which is established in four ways:
through error (*viparyaya*), power (*śakti*), contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and likewise through attainment (*siddhi*).
They were all without possessions and delighted in sharing;
furthermore, those beginning with the Bhūtas are proclaimed to be ungrateful and lacking in virtuous conduct.
This was the first creation of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, known as the Mahat-sarga.
The second creation is said to be that of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*);
the third is known as the *vaikārika* (or *aindriyaka*) creation of the senses.
Thus, this creation from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has arisen without prior conscious intent.
The fourth is the primary creation (*mukhyasarga*), for the immobile beings (*sthāvara*) are indeed known as primary.

That which is called the transverse-streamed (*tiryaksrotas*) is the fifth, the animal womb (*tiryagyoni*). The sixth is that of the upward-streamed (*ūrdhvasrotas*), which is known as the divine creation (*devasarga*).

After that, the seventh creation is that of the downward-streaming beings (*arvāk-srotas*), which is human. The eighth is the creation of grace (*anugraha-sarga*), and the ninth is recorded as the creation of the youthful (*kaumāra*).
The first three creations are primordial (*prākṛta*), and they were not preceded by conscious deliberation.
The five secondary [creations], beginning with the principal one, proceed from prior intelligence. In the beginning, Brahmā indeed created from his own mind the mental sons who were equal to himself:
Sananda, Sanaka, the learned Sanātana, and [Sanatkumāra].
Long ago, Prajāpati [appointed] Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra;
all of them were to be known as yogins, free from passion and devoid of envy.
With their minds attached to the Lord, they did not set their thoughts upon creation.
When Sanaka and the others had departed, having no desire for creation,
Brahmā, wishing to create once more, performed supreme austerity.
While he was thus performing penance, nothing at all came into being.

Then, after a long time, anger was born from his suffering. From the eyes of him who was possessed by anger, drops of tears fell. Then, from those drops of tears, the *bhūtas* and *pretas* came into being at that time.
Seeing all those born of tears, Brahmā reproached himself. A fierce fainting spell, arising from anger and indignation, came upon him.
Having fainted, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), possessed by rage, gave up his life.
Then Rudra, the Lord of Prāṇa, the blessed Nīlalohita,
appeared from the mouth of the Lord in order to grant incomparable grace;
the sovereign Lord divided himself tenfold and onefold.

Those high-souled ones were addressed by him: "O children, you have been created by me in ten ways and as one, for the sake of showing grace to the worlds. Therefore, for the establishment and the welfare of the entire world..."
"And for the sake of the continuity of progeny, exert yourselves without weariness.
Having been addressed thus, they wept and fled in all directions;
because of their weeping (*rodana*) and fleeing (*drāvaṇa*), they are known by the name Rudras.

Those who are Rudras are indeed the vital breaths (prāṇas), and those who are the vital breaths are the Great-Souled Ones. Therefore, Maheśvara, the compassionate son of Brahmā, restored the vital breaths once more to the deceased god Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin.
With a joyful countenance due to the return of the Lord’s life-breath, Rudra,
the Lord of the Universe, addressed these supreme words to Brahmā:
“Do not fear, do not fear, O highly fortunate Viriñca, O teacher of the worlds!”

"I have restored your vital breaths; rise up in comfort, O you of noble vows. Having heard those enchanting words, which were like an experience in a dream, he slowly opened his eyes, which possessed the luster of blooming lotuses, and gazed upon Hara.
Then, having regained his life-breaths, Brahmā addressed him with palms joined in reverence, speaking these words in a voice that was both affectionate and profound: "Indeed,
by the mere sight of you, you gladden my mind."
"Who are you, who stand here in the form of the universe as the elevenfold self?
Having heard those words of his, Maheśvara,
the Lord of the gods, spoke while touching Brahmā with his two very pleasant hands.
"Know me to be the Supreme Self who has come to you as your son.
And these eleven Rudras have arrived to protect you.
Therefore, by my grace, shake off this intense fainting spell."
"Awakened as before, you ought indeed to create living beings.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Brahmā became joyful in mind;
the Soul of the Universe then praised the Supreme Lord with eight various hymns.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, O Blessed Rudra, whose splendor is immeasurable like that of the sun.
Salutations to the god Bhava, the essence, whose nature consists of water.
Salutations to Śarva, who has the form of the earth, the source of joy for the gods;
salutations to you, Īśa, the Vasu, whose self consists of the element of touch.
Salutations also to Paśupati, the fire of exceeding brilliance.
Salutations to you, Bhīma, whose form is space and who consists of sound alone;
salutations to Ugra, whose nature is fierce and who is the self of the sacrificer;
salutations to Mahādeva, to Soma, to you whose form is nectar.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
entreated the Lord of the Universe with words preceded by prostration:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, my son Maheśvara!"

"You were born from my body for the purpose of creation, O destroyer of Ananga. Therefore, O Lord of the World, as I am engaged in this great task, provide assistance in every way; you ought to create all living beings."
By that [act], the god Rudra, the destroyer of Tripura, was purified for them.
"So be it," Śaṅkara accepted those words.
Then the blessed Brahmā, having greeted him who was joyful, [spoke].
Permitted by him to create, he likewise brought forth other progeny:
Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha; these he created by his mind alone.
In the beginning, Brahmā created Dharma and Saṃkalpa as well.
These twelve sons of Brahmā are proclaimed to have been born in the beginning;
together with Rudra, they were ancient householders.

They shall have twelve lineages, divine and accompanied by hosts of gods; they will be possessed of progeny, engaged in sacred rites, and adorned by great seers. Then there are the fourfold groups: gods, asuras, pitṛs, and humans.
Desirous of creating these waters together with Rudra,
Brahmā indeed concentrated his mind for the sake of creation and joined himself in yoga.
From his mouth he generated the gods, and from his flanks the ancestors.
From his hips he produced all the Asuras, and from his generative organ, the humans.
From his dung-pit were born the Rākṣasas, possessed by hunger;
these were his sons, night-stalkers who were powerful and dominated by the qualities of darkness and passion (tamas and rajas).

Serpents, yakṣas, as well as bhūtas and gandharvas were born; birds were created from his wings, and he produced winged creatures from his chest. He likewise brought forth goats from his mouth and serpents from his sides.
From his feet were born horses, elephants, śarabhas, gavayas, and deer;
as well as camels, khaṭvāṅgas, nyaṅkus, and other species.
From his body hair grew medicinal herbs, fruits, and roots.
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī meter, the Ṛg-veda hymns, the Trivṛt Sāman, the Rathantara,
and the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice among sacrifices;
likewise, the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh meter, and the Pañcadaśa Stoma.
From his right mouth, he created the Bṛhat-sāman, as well as the Uktha;
likewise, from [his other mouths], he created the Sāmans, the Jagatī meter, and the seventeen-fold Stoma.
From his western mouth, he created the Vairūpya, the Atirātra,
the twenty-first [Sāman], the Atharvans, and the Āptoryāma;
and from his northern mouth, he created the Anuṣṭubh and the Vairāja.
From his limbs were born various beings, high and low:
yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise hosts of apsarases;
as well as nāgas, kinnaras, rākṣasas, birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents.
And this imperishable world— whether stationary or moving, such as trees or animals—
whatever actions they performed in previous creations,
those very same actions they assume again and again when being created.

Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood—impregnated by these, beings resort to them; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which corresponds to its own nature.
This diversity exists within the great elements, in the objects of the senses, and in the various forms of liberation.

The Creator himself ordained the specific functions of all beings; and at the beginning, that Grandfather fashioned the names, forms, and the manifold expansion of all elemental beings from the very words of the Veda.
The Unborn One gave to those born at the end of the night the very names of the sages and the modes of expression found in the Vedas;
just as the various signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle.
Those very same things are seen in such a manner during the beginnings of the Yugas.
Thus, this creation of the world by the Self-born One arises from the instruments [of the senses];
it is a transformation of Prakṛti itself, beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa).
It was graced by the splendor of the moon and sun, adorned with planets and constellations;
it was further embellished by rivers, oceans, and mountains,
as well as by various other delightful and prosperous regions.
In that forest of Brahman, the all-knowing Brahmā,
unmanifest and born from the seed of the Unmanifest, moves about, sustained by the grace of the Lord.
He has the intellect as his trunk and great branches, and the internal senses as his hollows.

The eternal Brahma-tree is the source of livelihood for all beings; it has the great elements as its trunk, the stainless sprouts as its branches, virtue and non-virtue as its abundant flowers, and the arising of pleasure and pain as its fruit.
The wise declare heaven to be his head, the sky his navel, and the moon and sun his two eyes;
the quarters are his ears and the earth his feet—he is the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings.
From his mouth the Brahmins were produced, and from the front part of his chest the Kṣatriyas.
From his thighs the Vaiśyas were born, and from his feet all the Śūdras; thus were all the castes produced from his body.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 13]
The sages said:
"The creation of Bhava, the Supreme Self, has been described by you.
However, a doubt arises in us regarding his [creation] from the mouth of the Four-faced One."
Virūpākṣa, the best of gods, the radiant Hara who wields the trident;
the Lord Rudra, the soul of Time, with matted hair and blue-and-red in hue—
he [overcomes] this world together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and even Agni.
He who, filled with wrath when the end of the age has arrived, brings all things to destruction;
he before whom both Brahmā and Viṣṇu bow down out of fear;
he by whom those two are brought under his control as the one who contracts the worlds.
That very Lord who formerly created Brahmā and Viṣṇu from his own body is indeed the eternal Master who provides for their security and prosperity;
how then can that Blessed One, Rudra, the primordial and ancient God, [be otherwise]?
Śambhu became the son of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest;
and we have heard previously that Prajāpati and Viṣṇu likewise arose from one another’s limbs for the sake of creation, each from the other.
Furthermore, how does the manifestation of all beings from one another occur through the relationship of cause and effect, and by way of the predominance or subordination of the qualities?
There is nothing that you have not asked about, nor is there anything whatsoever that you have not heard.
"Since you have become a disciple of the Blessed One, you remember everything. Tell us the truth, just as the all-pervading Brahmā told it to the sages.
O father, we are full of faith and eager to hear the glorious account of the Lord."
Vāyu said:
"O Brahmins, you who are skilled in inquiry have asked this most appropriately.
In former times, when I was questioned about this very matter, my grandfather (the Grandfather) spoke thus to me."
I shall now fully explain how Rudra came into being,
and how, furthermore, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were born from one another;
for these three, whose nature is causal, were born directly from Maheśvara.
They are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and end of the entire universe, including all that is mobile and immobile;
they are endowed with supreme sovereignty, permeated by the Supreme Lord,
eternally presided over by His power, and capable of performing His work.
Formerly, all three were appointed by their father to three tasks:
Brahmā for creation, Hari for protection, and likewise Rudra for destruction.
Nevertheless, due to mutual jealousy, they sought to surpass one another.
Having gratified his own father, the Supreme Lord, through ascetic penance,
and having obtained [the power] from the grace of that Parameṣṭhin with his whole being,
Rudra formerly created Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa in another kalpa.
In another kalpa, moreover, Brahmā—the one who consists of the universe—created Rudra and Viṣṇu;
and the Lord Viṣṇu again created Rudra and Brahmā;
and Brahmā again created Nārāyaṇa, and [Nārāyaṇa] again created Brahmā.
Thus, in age after age, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are born from one another,
each seeking the welfare of the others;
this is recounted by the great sages with reference to the specific events occurring at the end of each respective kalpa.
Their power is described as arising from their mutual interaction.
Listen to their wondrous, meritorious, and sin-releasing narrative,
which took place during the *Tatpuruṣa* Kalpa of the supreme Brahmā.

Formerly, in the eon named Meghavāhana, Nārāyaṇa indeed became a cloud and carried the Earth for a thousand divine years. Having observed his disposition, Viṣṇu, the teacher of the entire world, [acted].
With his entire being, he bestowed the imperishable power (*śakti*).
Having then received that power from Śiva, the Lord of All,
Viṣṇu, whose self is everything, created the universe together with the Creator of the Universe.
Having witnessed that majesty of Viṣṇu, the Grandfather (Brahmā), created by him, was seized by supreme envy; laughing, he spoke these words:
"Go, O Viṣṇu! I have understood the cause of your creation."
Rudra is superior to us both; of this there is no doubt.
By the grace of that Supreme Lord, the God of gods, you are the primordial Blessed One, the creator and, in the ultimate sense, the protector.
"And having propitiated Rudra, the leader of the thirty gods, through ascetic penance, I shall create the entire world together with you; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus reproached Viṣṇu, the Lord born from the lotus [spoke].
Having attained Śaṅkara through his ascetic penance, he made this request:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the universe, Great Lord!
Viṣṇu is born from your left limb, and I am indeed born from your right limb."
Nevertheless, Acyuta created the entire world together with me;
yet, out of envy, he was reproached by me through the power of your support,
with the thought that "he is not superior to my own state"— such is my feeling toward you, Maheśvara.
Since our origin is from you alone and is thus similar for both of us,
just as you previously bestowed grace upon him through his devotion,
so too, O Śaṅkara, it behoves you to grant all of that to me as well.
Thus petitioned by him, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes—
who is a treasury of compassion— righteously granted everything to him as well.
Having thus obtained from the Lord himself the state of being the self of all in an instant, Brahmā—
Hurrying, he then approached and beheld Puruṣottama in a brilliant celestial chariot,
resembling the sun, which was situated in the abode of the Ocean of Milk;
it was divine, adorned with gold and jewels, and fashioned by his own mind.
He saw the lotus-eyed one reclining upon a bed of infinite splendor,
four-armed, with noble limbs, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a conch and a discus, gentle, and with a face like the orb of the moon.
The god, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, has a serene and sweet smile;
his lotus-feet are reddened by the touch of the earth’s soft lotus-like hands,
and he lies like the nectar of the Ocean of Milk, absorbed in yogic sleep.
Through *tamas* he is known as Kālarudra; through *rajas*, he is the one born from the golden egg;
through *sattva*, he is the all-pervading Viṣṇu; and in his state beyond qualities (*nirguṇatva*), he is Maheśvara.
Having beheld that Puruṣa, Brahmā spoke these bold words: ŚivaP 7.1.13.40–41ab.

"I shall swallow you, O Viṣṇu, just as you [swallowed] yourself in the past. Having heard those words of his, the mighty-armed one, awakening to the Grandfather (Brahmā), looked up at him and smiled slightly.
At that moment, Viṣṇu was swallowed by that Great-Souled One;
and at that very instant, he was effortlessly created from the middle of Brahmā’s eyebrows.
At that time, the Lord himself, adorned with the moon, appeared.

In order to bestow incomparable grace upon them, he who is formless assumed a form so that their power might be seen; for he had previously granted them a boon. He arrived at that place where Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were staying.
Then, both pleased and yet fearful out of curiosity, they praised the God;
and with great reverence, they bowed down many times from a distance.
The Lord Bhava, the wielder of the Pināka bow, having thus shown them favor, [spoke].
Even as they were gazing with reverence, he vanished from their sight.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Creation of Brahmā and Viṣṇu," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 14.
Vāyu said:
I shall describe for each kalpa the cause of Rudra’s manifestation,
by which the creation of Brahmā proceeds once its continuity has been severed.

In age after age, Brahmā, who is born from the cosmic egg, having created living beings, became deeply distressed and fell into delusion due to the lack of increase among those creatures. For the sake of pacifying his sorrow and for the proliferation of his progeny—
In each respective Kalpa, Rudra— the soul of time and lord of the hosts of Rudras—
is designated by the Supreme Lord as Maheśa Nīlalohita;
having become the son and younger brother of Brahmā, he bestows grace upon him.
He alone is the Blessed Lord Īśa, a mass of splendor,
free from ailment; he is the beginningless and endless Sustainer, the all-pervading one who causes the contraction of beings,
endowed with supreme sovereignty, and permeated by the state of the Supreme Lord.
Constantly presided over by His power and marked by His very signs,
he bears His name, possesses His form, and is capable of performing His work; his conduct is equal to His own,
and he is the observer of His command.
Resplendent like a thousand suns, adorned with the moon as his ornament;
wearing serpents as necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, and a girdle of *muñja* grass;
shining with the skull-fragments of Jalandhara, Viriñca, and Indra.
His hair and face were tawny like the half-rippled waves of the Gaṅgā;
his beautiful lips were pressed against the tips of his broken fangs;
and his earrings were drawn into circles along the side of his left ear.
He who has the departure of a great bull, whose voice is like the roar of a great cloud,
who resembles a great fire, and who possesses great strength and prowess—
thus, Maheśvara, assuming a terrible and great form, [approached] the daughter of Brahmā.

Having bestowed consciousness upon Brahmā, it also assists him in the act of creation. Therefore, by the grace of Rudra, the creation of progeny proceeds eternally for the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) in the form of a continuous stream in every kalpa.
Once, when requested by Brahmā to create, the omnipresent Nīlalohita,
by means of his own mind, created all beings similar to himself—
those with matted hair, free from fear, blue-necked, and three-eyed.
[He saw] those who were liberated from old age and death, bearing blazing tridents as their excellent weapons.
By them, the entire fourteen-fold world was completely covered.
Having seen those various Rudras, the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke to Rudra.
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods! Do not create such offspring as these. Create other beings, may prosperity be yours—beings who are endowed with death.
Thus addressed, the Supreme Lord, smiling, spoke to Brahmā.

"I have no such creation; you create inauspicious progeny. However, these great-souled and mighty ones who have been created by my mind—all of them shall indeed move about with me as performers of sacrifice."
Having spoken thus to Viśvakarman, Hara, the Lord of all beings,
together with the Rudras, withdrew from the creation of progeny and remained detached.
From that time forward, that God did not produce auspicious offspring.
"Remaining with his vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), he stands as firm as a pillar until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Rudra," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 15]
Vāyu said:
When the creatures created by the Creator did not multiply,
Brahmā then resolved to bring about creation through sexual union.
Because the race of women had not previously emerged from the Lord,
the Grandfather was unable to effect creation through sexual union; thereupon,
he formed a resolution directed toward a definitive purpose.
"O Supreme Lord, you must be questioned for the sake of the very increase of these subjects;
without your grace, these subjects will not flourish.
Having reflected thus, the Soul of the Universe proceeded to perform penance.
Then there is the primordial, supreme power, infinite and the creator of the worlds;
she is the first, most subtle, pure, accessible through contemplation, and captivating. She is devoid of qualities, free from phenomenal expansion, partless, and undisturbed.
Inseparable, eternal, and always by the side of the Lord—
with that supreme power (śakti), Brahmā meditated upon the Blessed Three-eyed One in his heart and performed supreme austerity.
As that supreme being was engaged in intense austerity,
his father became well-pleased with him in a very short time. Then, having entered some form by means of a certain portion of himself, [he appeared].
Having become Ardhanārīśvara, Lord Hara himself departed.
Beholding that supreme deity, who is beyond darkness, immutable, non-dual, indefinable, and invisible to those of unrefined souls— Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.15.9cd–10ab; 7.1.15.10cd–11ab.
The creator of all worlds, the Lord of the lords of all worlds,
joined with the supreme power that ordains all worlds—
beyond reasoning, without appearance, immeasurable, undecaying, and eternal.
It is immovable, devoid of qualities, peaceful, and the abode of infinite majesty;
all-pervading, the giver of all, free from the manifestation of both the existent and non-existent;
liberated from all points of comparison, the refuge, eternal, and auspicious.
Having prostrated like a staff and then rising with palms joined in reverence, Brahmā [spoke] with words endowed with faith and humility, worthy of being heard, refined by sacred preparation,
consistent with the true meaning of all things, and augmented by the purport of the Vedas.
He praised the God and the Goddess with hymns whose scope was the subtle meaning.
Brahmā said:
"Victory to you, O God, Mahādeva! Victory, O Īśvara, Maheśvara!"
Victory to you, O most excellent of all virtues; victory to you, O sovereign of all the gods!
Victory to you, O auspicious Prakṛti; victory to you, O mistress of Prakṛti!
Victory to you, who are beyond Prakṛti; victory to you, O beautiful one of Prakṛti!
Victory to you, O you of unfailing great illusion; victory to you, O you whose desires are unfailing!
Victory to you, O you of unfailing great play; victory to you, O you of unfailing great power!
Victory, O Mother of the entire world; victory, O you who consist of the entire world!
Victory to you, O sustainer of the entire world! Victory to you, O friend of the entire world!
Victory to you, O possessor of eternal sovereignty! Victory to you, O eternal abode!
Victory to you, O eternal form! Victory to you, O eternal follower!
Victory to you, the creator of the threefold self; victory to you, the protector of the threefold self!
Victory to you, the destroyer of the threefold self; victory to you, the leader of the threefold self!
Victory to you, whose expansion as the cause of the world depends upon your glance!
Victory to You, whose physical elements have been consumed by the fire arising from Your side-long glances of indifference toward worldly victory!
Victory, O Lord, who are unknowable even to the gods and others, and who shine with the subtle vision of Your own Self!
Victory, O Lord of the Power of the Gross Self! Victory to You who pervade all that is moving and unmoving!
Victory to you, who have unified the entire collection of cosmic principles within your single name!

Victory to you, who possess a multitude of excellent attendants stationed upon the heads of the asuras! Victory to you, who are most skillful in the arrangement of protection for those who have sought refuge in you!
Victory to you, who have uprooted the sprouting shoots of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra! Victory to you, who manifest the power, heroism, and valor of supreme sovereignty!
Victory to you, who transcend the universe and have cast aside the majesty of all others!

Victory to you, the supreme nectar of the application of the five-fold meaning! Victory to you, whose very nature is the hymn of the nectar of the knowledge of the five-fold meaning! Victorious one, the best of physicians for the great disease of terrible saṃsāra!
Victory to you, the moonlight that dispels the thick veil of darkness consisting of the impurities of primordial ignorance!
Victory to you, the fire of destruction for Tripura! Victory to you, O Bhairavī of Tripura!
Victory to you, who are liberated from the three qualities (guṇas)! Victory to you, the crusher of the three qualities!
Victory to you, the first omniscient one; victory to you, the awakener of all!
Victory to you whose limbs are abundant with divinity; victory to you, the bestower of what is prayed for!
O Lord, where is your supreme abode, and where is our trivial speech?
Nevertheless, O Blessed One, forgive me as I lament out of devotion. Having addressed him with such well-spoken words, the four-faced Viśvakarman bowed down again and again to Rudra and to Rudrāṇī.

This excellent hymn of praise, meritorious and proclaimed by Brahmā, is named Ardhanārīśvara; it increases the joy of both Śiva and Śivā. Whoever recites this with devotion, whether under the instruction of anyone at all—
He obtains that fruit by reason of pleasing Śiva and Śivā—
those two who bring about the existence of all beings in every world, whose forms are devoid of birth and destruction,
and who eternally assume the bodies of the most excellent man and woman; to those two Śaṅkaras, I am perpetually prostrate.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn to Śiva and Śivā," in the first part of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 16. Vāyu said:
Then the god Mahādeva, with a voice like the roar of a great rain-cloud,
spoke in words that were sweet, profound, auspicious, and composed of gentle syllables;
words endowed with meaning and characterized by the marks of royalty.
With a pure and tireless skill in protecting against the onset of all objects without exception,
and preceded by a most captivating, noble, and sweet smile,
the Lord, being well-satisfied, addressed Viśvakarman.
Īśvara said:
"O child, O child, O highly fortunate one, my son, O Grandfather!
I already know all the gravity of your words."
"Now you have performed penance for the very sake of the prosperity of all creatures.
I am pleased by this penance and I grant you your desire," having spoken these most noble words, which were sweet by their very nature.
From a portion of his own form, Hara, the best of gods, created the Goddess,
whom those who know Brahman call the Goddess endowed with divine qualities—
the supreme power of Bhava, the Supreme Self.
In her, indeed, birth, death, old age, and the like do not exist;
she is Bhavānī, who truly manifested from the body of Bhava.
Of her, words turn back along with the mind and the senses.
She appeared as if born from a portion of her husband’s own body; that goddess,
who stands pervading this entire universe with her majesty,
was perceived as if she were the personified form of his wondrous power.
She deludes this entire world with her illusory power (māyā).
She was born from the Lord, yet in the ultimate sense she is unborn.
Her supreme nature is not within the range of perception even for the gods.
And she, the sovereign of all the immortals, was manifested from the body of her husband.
Having seen that Supreme Goddess, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds—
she who is omniscient, omnipresent, subtle, and devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence— [he was struck with wonder].
Having prostrated before the Great Goddess, who illuminates this entire world with her supreme light, the Virāṭ indeed made this request. Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, I was created by the God in the beginning, O you who pervade the entire world;
appointed to the creation of progeny, I create the whole universe.
All the gods and others were fashioned by me through my mind, O Goddess."
They do not increase even though they are created again and again. Therefore,
having established creation as originating solely from sexual union,
I wish to cause all my progeny to flourish.
"In former times, the imperishable lineage of women did not emerge from you;
therefore, I possess no power to create the race of women.
Indeed, the origin of all powers is truly from you."
Therefore, I pray to you alone— the sovereign goddess of the gods, the Māyā who bestows all powers upon everyone everywhere— and who grants boons; O omnipresent one,
for the sake of the growth of the moving and the unmoving, through one of your portions.
"O destroyer of worldly existence, become the daughter of my son Dakṣa.
Thus entreated by Brahmā, whose source is Brahman,
the Goddess emitted from the middle of her eyebrows a single Śakti whose splendor was equal to her own.
Looking at her, Hara, the best among the gods of gods, spoke with a smile:
"Having propitiated Brahmā through austerity, fulfill his desire.
Having received that command of the Supreme Lord upon her head, she—
At the word of Brahmā, the Goddess became the daughter of Dakṣa.
Having thus bestowed that incomparable power, which is the very form of Brahman, upon Brahmā,
she entered the body of the God, and the God vanished.
From that time forward in this world, enjoyment became established in women;
and, O best of Brahmins, the creation of progeny proceeded through sexual union.
O preeminent sages, even Brahmā attained joy and satisfaction.
All this has been narrated to you regarding the origin of the Goddess’s power;
it increases merit and is worthy of being heard as it follows upon the creation of beings. Whoever constantly recites this account of the origin of the Goddess’s power—
One obtains all merit and gains auspicious sons.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Emergence of the Goddess's Power," in the first section of the seventh book, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 17.
Vāyu said:
Having thus obtained from the Lord himself that supreme and eternal power,
the Prajāpati, desiring to perform creation originating from sexual union, [proceeded].
He himself was wonderful; he became a woman with one half and a man with the other.
She who was the woman by that half gave birth to Śatarūpā.
Brahmā created Virāj, and he became a man with one half.
He was indeed the first Manu, the Self-born (Svāyaṃbhuva) Puruṣa.
That goddess Śatarūpā, having performed extremely difficult austerities,
obtained as her husband none other than Manu of radiant fame.
From him, Śatarūpā gave birth to two sons,
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, the best among those who possess sons;
and she also bore two highly fortunate daughters, from whom these progenies were born.
Ākūti is to be known as one [daughter], while Prasūti is remembered as the other.
The Lord Svāyambhuva gave that Prasūti to Dakṣa;
and Prajāpati Ruci likewise took Ākūti as his wife.
From the mental Ruci, through Ākūti, a beautiful pair was born:
Yajña and Dakṣiṇā, by whom the world was brought into existence.
Furthermore, from Prasūti, the daughter of Svāyambhuva, were born the mothers of the worlds.
The lord Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Medhā, Kriyā,
as well as Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapu, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti as the thirteenth.
The Lord Dharma accepted the daughters of Dakṣa as his wives.
Of those, eleven younger sisters with beautiful eyes remained:
Khyāti, Satī, Saṃbhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and Kṣamā.
Sannati, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā;
Bhṛgu, Śarva, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
Pulastya, Atri, Viśiṣṭha, Pāvaka, and the Pitṛs.

The most excellent sages, Khyāti and the others, took those maidens as wives. As for the thirteen sons of Dharma, beginning with Kāma and ending with Yaśas, from them were born Śraddhā and the others, who culminated in supreme happiness.
Indeed, from the continuity of unrighteousness and violence arose those characterized by suffering,
as well as sons such as Nikṛti and others who were marked by dharma;
yet they are recorded as having neither wives nor sons, for all of them were without fixed constraints.
This very creation, characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*), was born as the regulator of dharma.
She who was the daughter of Dakṣa and the beloved wife of Rudra, Satī,
having abandoned her body born of Dakṣa on account of the censure of her husband—
Having censured Dakṣa and the wife of Dakṣa along with their kinsmen, she appeared as the daughter of Himavat, the mountain, born of Menā. (Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.17cd–19ab) 1 Prathamārṣī 519a.

Rudra, having seen that Satī, created Rudras equal in splendor to himself; the manner in which he created those innumerable beings has already been described. Lakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, was born to Bhṛgu from Khyāti.

The two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are the sustainers of the Manvantaras. Their sons, grandsons, and descendants by the hundreds and thousands were all brought [to this state] during the Svāyambhuva interval; they are all considered to be Bhārgavas.
From Marīci also was born Paurṇamāsī;
she gave birth to four daughters, and their descendants were most illustrious.
In their lineage was born Kaśyapa, the father of many sons.
Smṛti, the wife of Aṅgiras, gave birth to two sons,
Āgnīdhra and Śarabha, as well as four daughters;
their sons and grandsons passed away by the thousands.

From Prīti, the wife of Pulastya, Dantogni was born as a son. In a previous birth, during the Svāyaṃbhuva interval, he was known as Yogi. Many descendants of his lineage became renowned as the Paulastyas.
Kṣamā, however, gave birth to three sons of the patriarch Pulaha:
Kardama, Suri, and Sahiṣṇu. All three possessed the splendor of the three sacred fires, and their lineage remains well-established.
Sannati bore to Kratu sons equal to Kratu himself.
They had no wives nor sons, for they were all perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
These sixty thousand are remembered as the Vālakhilyas.
They proceeded in front of Anūru, surrounding the sun.
And Atri’s wife, Anasūyā, gave birth to five Ātreyas and a daughter named Śruti,
who was the mother of Śaṅkhapada.
Satyanetra, Havya, Āpomūrti, Śanaiścara,
and Soma as the fifth— these are proclaimed as the five Ātreyas.
The sons and grandsons of those high-souled Ātreyas [are likewise known].
In the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, hundreds and thousands have passed away.
Now, in the city of Ūrjā, seven sons were born to Vasiṣṭha;
their eldest sister was Puṇḍarīkā, who possessed a slender waist.
Raja, Gātra, Ūrdhvabāhu, Savana,
Anaya, Sutapas, and Śukra— these are remembered as the seven great sages (Saptarṣis).
These are the lineages and names of those high-souled members of the Vasiṣṭha clan.

In the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, hundreds of billions have passed. Thus, O twice-born ones, this creation of the sages has been proclaimed along with its descendants; it cannot be described in detail, for it is impossible to speak of it exhaustively.
That fire which is of the nature of Rudra, the mind-born son of Brahmā—Svāhā obtained as her beloved three sons of immeasurable luster:
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci; these are the three for you.
The Pavamāna fire is produced by friction; the Pāvaka fire is said to be of lightning origin.
That which blazes in the sun is declared to be the Śuci fire, born of the sun.
Havyavāha, Kavyavāha, and Saharakṣas—these are the three.

The sons of these three were, respectively, the Devas, the Pitṛs, and the Suras. Their sons and grandsons numbered forty-nine, and they were established in the three types of ritual acts: those performed for specific desires (kāmya), occasional rites (naimittika), and constant duties (ajasra).
All are to be known as ascetics, and likewise all are observers of vows;
all have Rudra as their very self, and all are devoted to Rudra.
Therefore, whatever may be offered as an oblation by anyone into the mouth of the fire [is offered to them].
"All that shall be considered as given unto Rudra; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus has the determination of the fires been recounted exactly as it is, O Brahmins, without excessive detail. Hereafter, I shall speak of the Pitṛs.

Because the six seasons are the abode of those who identify with their respective stations, it is said in the Vedic revelation: "The seasons are the ancestors. For indeed, all things—both stationary and moving—are born from you, the seasons.
Therefore, it is heard in the Śruti that these Pitṛs are the Ṛtus;
thus, these great-souled Pitṛs, who preside over the seasons,
remain here by their own sovereign power until the gathering of the clouds.
The ancestors are recorded as being of two kinds: the *agniṣvātta*s and the *barhiṣad*s.
These householders are, respectively, those who have not performed sacrifices and those who have performed sacrifices. From Svadhā were born two daughters for the ancestors, world-renowned.
And Menā and Dharaṇī, by whom this entire universe is supported;
Menā was the daughter of Agniṣvātta, and Dharaṇī was the daughter of Barhiṣat. Menā was the wife of Himavat, and [gave birth] to Maināka and Krauñca.

She gave birth to Gaurī and Gaṅgā, who is purified by her embrace with the body of Bhava. Dharaṇī, the wife of Meru, gave birth to a son, Mandara, who was endowed with divine medicinal herbs and possessed shoulders as beautiful as a painting.
That very glorious Mandara, the son of Meru, by the power of his asceticism,
became the actual abode of Lord Śiva, the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha. Dharaṇī gave birth once more to thirty renowned daughters.
Velā, Niyati, and the third, Āyati—
Āyati and Niyati were the two wives of the two sons of Bhṛgu.
Thus has their lineage been described to you previously during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.

From the ocean, the shoreline gave birth to one irreproachable daughter, Sāmudrī by name, who was of the same caste as her father; she became the wife of Prācīnabarhis. Sāmudrī bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis.

All of them were named Prācetasa and were masters of the science of archery (dhanurveda). In former times, during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu, Dakṣa attained the status of their son through the curse of Tryambaka.
Thus, O Brahmins, these divine lineages of the high-souled sons of Brahmā, beginning with Dharma,
have been described by me in due order— neither too briefly nor too extensively—
and accompanied by the hosts of gods.
They were active, possessed of progeny, and adorned with great supernatural powers.
This settlement of subjects originated from Prajāpati;
indeed, it is not possible to enumerate them even in hundreds of millions of years.
The lineage of kings also proceeds in two ways:
the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa) and the Lunar dynasty (Somavaṃśa), which are most meritorious on earth.
[Among them were] Ikṣvāku, Ambarīṣa, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, and others.
The kings of virtuous fame who have been heard of here were born in that lineage;
so too were other royal sages endowed with various heroic powers.
What fruit is there in mentioning those ancient ones who have already passed away?
Moreover, since discourse concerning Īśvara has already occurred here and there,
the praising of others is not approved by the virtuous; considering this, I do not wish to speak at length,
even though it is relevant and serves to illuminate the power of Īśvara alone.

"The creation and so forth have also been told; herein lies their detailed exposition. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narration of Creation," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 18.
The sages said:
"How did the goddess, the daughter of Dakṣa, having cast off her body as Dākṣāyaṇī,
formerly become the daughter of Himavat through Menā?"
And how was Rudra censured by the high-souled Dakṣa? What was the cause there by which Bhava came to be reviled? And how was Dakṣa born as a result of the curse of Bhava?
"O Mārutas, first tell me [the history] of Cākṣuṣa Manu. Vāyu said:
"Listen, I shall relate [the account] of Dakṣa, who was of fickle mind."
This conduct, born of sin and negligence, was a reproach to all the immortals.
Long ago, all the gods, asuras, siddhas,
and supreme ṛṣis once went to the peak of the Himavat to behold Īśāna.

Then, O best of the twice-born, both the God and the Goddess, seated upon their divine throne, granted their vision to those gods and others. At that very moment, Dakṣa also arrived there together with the immortals.
Then, out of respect for himself, the God [Brahmā] went to see his son-in-law Hara and his own daughter Satī when Dakṣa had arrived;
however, he never once remembered [to invite] the gods and others with particular distinction.
Because he did not know her true nature at all,
and was utterly deluded, thinking only "she is my daughter," enmity toward her arose within him.
Then, impelled by that very enmity and by fate, [he acted].
The skillful Dakṣa did not bring his daughter-in-law, even though he was initiated for the sacrifice;
yet, having summoned all his other sons-in-law in due order,
he honored each of them individually with hundreds of abundant gifts.
Then, having heard from the mouth of Nārada that they had assembled in such a manner, Rudrāṇī informed her father and went to his abode. Then,
a divine celestial chariot, facing every direction, appeared nearby.
Rich in auspicious marks, easy to ascend, and exceedingly captivating;
resembling molten gold, adorned with various jewels;
featuring a canopy of pearls and beautifully decorated with garlands and tassels.
It had turrets of molten gold, was surrounded by hundreds of jeweled pillars, possessed stairs fashioned from diamonds, and featured coral pillars and archways. (Note:
The use of the nominative case at the beginning of the verse is an archaic Vedic usage.)
It was spread with flowered cloths and featured a great throne of variegated jewels;
its jeweled floor was flawless, with gaps filled by a lattice of diamonds,
and it was adorned with a beautiful jeweled staff bearing the emblem of the Great Bull.
Its frontage was adorned with a banner as white as a cloud;
its great gate was presided over by invincible lords of the qualities (guṇeśvaras), whose bodies were protected by jeweled armor and who held variegated cane-staffs in their hands.
Surrounded by many women skilled in the playing of the mṛdaṅga drum, rhythmic clapping, singing, and the flute and lute, and possessing clever dress and speech,
the Great Goddess ascended together with her dear female companions.
Taking two beautiful yak-tail whisks with charming vajra handles,
the two auspicious daughters of Rudra fanned her.
At that time, the Goddess’s face shone between those two whisks.
Between the two of them as they fought like two swans over a lotus, Sumālinī,
overflowing with love, held over her crest a moon-like parasol encircled by pearls.
That radiant parasol shone above the goddess’s face,
like the orb of the moon above a vessel of nectar. Then,
seated before her, was Śubhāvatī, her face graced with a gentle smile.
He indeed delighted the virtuous Satī with the diversion of dice-play; then Suyaśas, placing the auspicious sandals adorned with jewels between his breasts,
served the Goddess.
Another woman, with limbs as beautiful as gold, took up a shining mirror;
another a palm-leaf fan, and another a box of betel.
A certain beautiful woman held a lovely pet parrot in her hand.
One lotus-eyed woman carried very pleasing and fragrant flowers; another bore ornaments;
and yet another carried an ointment of excellent unguents and auspicious collyrium.
And other similar women, each performing their appropriate duties,
attended upon that Great Goddess from all sides in turn.
In the midst of them, the Supreme Goddess shone most brilliantly.
In the midst of Tārā’s retinue, she was like an autumnal crescent moon.
Then, immediately after the sound arising from the conch,
the great drum of departure was struck.
Then, sweet-sounding musical instruments, along with the sounds of raised cymbals, resounded spontaneously,
as did hundreds of trumpets;
and so too did the lords of the Gaṇas, who were armed and possessed splendor equal to that of Maheśa.

At that time, eight hundred thousand [attendants] went before him. In their midst, the illustrious leader of the Gaṇas, Somanandīśvara— who is worshipped by the Lord— proceeded mounted upon a bull, like Bṛhaspati mounted upon an elephant.
The divine drums resounded in the sky, and the clouds brought celestial bliss; all the sages danced, and the perfected yogis rejoiced. And the clouds released a rain of flowers over the canopy above.
Then, accompanied everywhere along the way by hosts of gods and others,
the Great Goddess entered her father’s house as if in a mere moment.
Seeing her, Dakṣa became enraged because she was the cause of his own destruction.
She offered respectful and honored worship even to his younger sisters. Then the moon-faced goddess Ambikā, seated in the assembly, spoke these words— appropriate, composed, and noble— to her father.
The Goddess said:
"O dear one, that Lord under whose command everything from Brahmā down to the Piśācas must abide—
surely he has not yet been worshipped according to the prescribed rites."
"Let that be; why have you performed such a despicable act, disregarding the disrespectful treatment shown to my eldest daughter? Thus addressed, Dakṣa, provoked by anger, spoke to her.
"My young daughters are superior to you, more distinguished, and worthy of worship;
and their husbands are held by me with great joy.
In all virtues, they even surpass your husband, Tryambaka."
"O Śarva, you are of a rigid nature and characterized by darkness (tamas); you have resorted to this [state]. Therefore, I hold you in contempt, for Bhava is indeed adverse to me.
Having been addressed thus, the enraged Goddess spoke to her father, Dakṣa.
While all those present in the sacrificial assembly were listening, you, O Dakṣa,
have suddenly defamed my husband with your speech— the manifest Great Lord of the World, who is free from every blemish.

The thief of knowledge, the betrayer of the guru, and the reviler of the Vedas and the Lord—these are all great sinners who must be punished; such is the Vedic revelation. Therefore, [this punishment] is most fitting for such an exceedingly grave sin.
"By fate, a terrible punishment shall suddenly befall you,
because you have not worshipped Tryambaka, the God of gods;
therefore, know for certain that your wicked lineage is destroyed."
Having spoken thus to her father, Satī, filled with wrath and casting off all fear,
abandoned her body and went to the Himavat mountain.
That glorious mountain, devoted to the supreme, had attained the arising of the fruits of his merit.
For that very purpose, he performed difficult austerities for a very long time.
Therefore, the Sovereign Lady bestows her grace upon that Lord of Mountains;
by her own will, through her power of yoga-māyā, she has made him her father.

When Satī had departed, censuring Dakṣa and overwhelmed by fear, the mantras then vanished and the sacrifice was destroyed. Having heard of the Goddess's departure, the Destroyer of Tripura [Śiva]— Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.18.53ab–54ab; 7.1.18.53cd–54ab.
He became enraged at Dakṣa and the ṛṣis, and he cursed them:
"Since Satī, though innocent on my account, was insulted by Dakṣa,
while all his other daughters were honored along with their husbands."

Therefore, in the Vaivasvata interval, these sons-in-law of yours shall all be born together, not from a womb, during the sacrifices of Brahmā. And you shall become a human king in the lineage of Cākṣuṣa.
I am the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of Pracetas;
even there, O evil-minded one, I shall create obstacles for you again and again,
even in those actions joined with virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
Thus addressed by Rudra of immeasurable splendor,
Dakṣa abandoned his body born of Svāyambhuva and fell to the earth in grief.
Thereafter, Dakṣa was indeed born as the son of Pracetas during the Cākṣuṣa interval.
The grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of the Pracetasas—
Bhṛgu and the others were indeed born during the interval of the Vaivasvata Manu,
when Brahmā was performing a sacrifice while assuming the body of Varuṇa.
Then, while that sacrifice of the evil-minded Dakṣa was proceeding for the sake of dharma,
Maheśa created an obstacle while Manu Vaivasvata was present.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Satī’s Body," in the first section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the seventh book, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 19.
The Sages said:
How did it come to pass for the evil-minded Dakṣa, who was engaged in the pursuit of dharma and wealth?
We wish to know why Maheśa created this obstacle.
Vāyu said:
"By the power of the asceticism of the Goddess, the mother of the entire universe..."
When the Himavat mountain was delighted, having attained the status of father-in-law,
and when the God, whose abode is the peak of Himavat,
had performed that marriage and was sporting with her, a great deal of time passed.
When the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, Dakṣa Prācetasa himself,
intending to perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), set about his preparations.
Then, on the ridge of the Himavat mountains, Dakṣa indeed performed the sacrifice.
At that auspicious region of Gaṅgādvāra, frequented by sages and perfected beings,
all the gods, led by Śakra,
gathered at his sacrifice and then resolved to depart.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Sādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts;
the drinkers of steam (ūṣmapās), the drinkers of soma, the drinkers of clarified butter, and likewise the drinkers of smoke;
the two Aśvins, the Pitṛs, and other great ṛṣis as well.

"Accompanied by Viṣṇu, all of you have arrived as sharers of the sacrifice. Seeing the entire assembly of gods arrived without the Lord (Śiva), Dadhīca, overcome with indignation, spoke thus to Dakṣa.
Dadhīca said:
"By performing worship of those who are unworthy of worship, and by failing to worship those who are worthy of worship, a man incurs great sin; of this there is no doubt."
Where there is the approval of the wicked and likewise the contempt of the virtuous,
there a terrible punishment ordained by the gods falls instantly.
Having spoken thus, the brahminical sage addressed Dakṣa once more.
"Why do you not worship the Lord, the Master of Creatures (Paśubhartṛ), who is worthy of adoration? Dakṣa replied:
"I have many Rudras with tridents in their hands and matted hair."
"I know no other Great Lord than these eleven who are established here.
Dadhīca said:
"What fruit is there in worshipping these other immortals in the sacrifice?"
"O King, if Rudra is not worshipped by you in this sacrifice—
He who is the imperishable Lord and Creator of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
He before whom all beings from Brahmā down to the Piśācas proclaim their service."
He who is beyond the primal natures (prakṛti) and even beyond the Puruṣa,
is meditated upon by the seers who are learned in Yoga and perceivers of reality;
he is the imperishable, supreme Brahman, who is both non-being and being-and-non-being.
Without beginning, middle, or end, inconceivable, and eternal—
he who is the creator, the destroyer, and the sustainer, the Great Lord (Maheśvara)—
I see no one other than him, whose self is Śaṅkara, in this sacrifice.
Dakṣa said:
"I shall now take this entire oblation, purified by ritual and mantras, from the golden vessel of the Lord of Sacrifice;
having divided it, I shall offer the portion of the peerless Lord Viṣṇu that is to be conveyed."
Dadhīca said:
"O Dakṣa, because Rudra, the Lord of the lords of all gods, has not been propitiated by you,
this entire sacrifice of yours shall not come to fruition."
Having spoken these words, the enraged Dadhīca, the best of sages,
departed from that place and went to his own hermitage.
Even after the sage had left, the gods did not abandon Dakṣa.
Because the inevitable future misfortune was certain to occur,
at that very time, O brahmins, having learned all this from the Lord, the Goddess urged the God to consume Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Urged by the Goddess with the intent to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the Lord suddenly created the heroic Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas—
a god with a thousand faces and a thousand lotus-eyes.
Holding a thousand mallets and having a thousand arrows in his hands,
with tridents, axes, and clubs in his grasp, he bore a blazing bow;
terrible, he held a discus and a thunderbolt, and had the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
His hand was illuminated by a thunderbolt, and his hair blazed like lightning;
he bore a great mouth with terrifying fangs and a massive belly;
his tongue was like a flash of lightning, his lips were pendulous, and his voice resounded like the clouds or the ocean.
He was wearing a great tiger skin dripping with blood,
his earrings were formed into circles pressed against his two cheeks,
and his crest was adorned with a garland of the heads of excellent gods.
Adorned with great golden ornaments, including tinkling anklets and armlets,
it was illuminated by a mass of jewels and its chest was covered by a necklace of bright pearls;
its prowess was equal to that of the great śarabha, the tiger, and the lion.
With a gait as languid as that of a noble, rutting elephant,
possessing a luster like a conch shell, a chowrie, a kunda flower, the moon, or a lotus stalk,
he was like the king of mountains covered in snow, yet had attained a state of manifest mobility.
Surrounded by a garland of flames, adorned with radiant pearls,
and blazing with splendor like the fire at the end of an eon—
he then knelt upon the earth, bowing down with palms joined in reverence.
The Lord of the Gaṇas stood at the side of the God of gods; and out of wrath, he created the Great Goddess Bhadrakālī-Bhadrā so that she might go along with him as a witness to his deeds.
Seeing Vīrabhadra standing there, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction and accompanied by Bhadrā, Śaṅkara said, "May it be well. And he,
together with the Goddess, addressed Maheśvara.
"Command me, O Great God; what task shall I perform?
Then the Destroyer of Tripura, desiring to please the daughter of Himavat, spoke with a voice of great resonance to the mighty-armed Vīrabhadra.
The God of gods said:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, together with Bhadrakālī, you must immediately destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas; this is the task for you."
"I too, staying together with her near the hermitage of Raibhya,
shall witness your unbearable prowess, O Lord of the Gaṇas—
[the prowess] of those trees which are at Kanakhala and in the vicinity of Gaṅgādvāra."
In that region, on the mountain Suvarṇaśṛṅga, which resembles Meru and Mandara, Dakṣa’s sacrifice is currently taking place.
Swiftly bring about the destruction of that sacrifice; do not delay.
When the Lord had spoken thus, the Goddess, daughter of the King of the Snowy Mountains,
gazing upon her son with auspiciousness and well-being— just as a cow gazes upon her own calf—
embraced him and, like a six-faced one, smelled his head.
Smiling, she herself spoke these very sweet words:
The Goddess said:
"O child, O auspicious one, O highly fortunate one of great strength and prowess!"
"You were born for the sake of my pleasure, O Eraser of my wrath!
Since he has become intent on sacrificial rites without having invited the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñeśvara),
therefore, O Lord of the Gaṇas, destroy Dakṣa and that sacrifice through your enmity."
"O Bhadra, by my command, having turned the auspiciousness of the sacrifice into misfortune,
and having slain that sacrificer, O child, destroy [the rite] with Bhadrā.
Carry out this command of the two Śivas, whose deeds are wondrous, as if it were their entire will."

Placing [the bull] upon his head and paying homage, Bhadra set out to depart. Then the Blessed One, Vīrabhadra— the great god who makes his abode in the dwellings of the departed and who wipes away the wrath of the Goddess— became enraged.
From the pores of his skin, he created the hosts of Gaṇeśvaras known as Romajas;
from the region of his right arm, he created hundreds of millions of Gaviśvaras;
likewise, from his feet, thighs, back, sides, face, and throat.
Then, from the secret parts, the ankles, the middle of the head, the throat, the mouth, and likewise the belly,
the entire world— including the spaces of the sky— became completely covered by the auspicious lords of the Gaṇas, whose prowess was equal to that of Bhadra himself.
All of them had a thousand arms, and in their hands they held a thousand weapons. All were attendants of Rudra, and all possessed a splendor equal to that of Rudra.
With tridents, spears, and maces in their hands, they carried clubs, stones, and boulders.
Resembling Kālāgnirudra, three-eyed and wearing matted locks,
hundreds of them with lion-vehicles fell violently from the sky;
and like clouds, those noble-born ones let out great roars.

Surrounded by those auspicious ones, the Blessed Lord Madra shone like Kālabhairava at the end of time accompanied by hundreds of fires of cosmic destruction. Having mounted his lordly bull in their midst, the one whose banner is the bull [Śiva] appeared.
The blessed Bhadra departed like the auspicious cloud of Bhava;
when he had mounted his bull,
one radiant with ashes held a pearl umbrella while grasping white chowries.
Then he, radiant with the luster of ashes, shone at the side of Bhadra like the Lord Śiva,
the teacher of the entire world, beside the king of mountains;
and Bhadra also shone by his presence, holding a white chowrie in his hand.
Like the gentle Bālasoma, who bears the excellent trident as his weapon,
he blew the auspicious white conch, *Bhadra*, in front of Bhadra.
Then Bhānukampa, of great splendor and adorned with gold and jewels, [blew his conch].
The divine drums resounded with a tumultuous celestial sound;
hundreds of clouds rained down a shower of flowers upon his head—
flowers that were in full bloom, filled with honey, and whose fragrance was like the kin of the wind.
And winds favorable to the journey blew along the path. Then all the lords of the Gaṇas, intoxicated and exultant in their martial strength, danced, rejoiced, shouted, laughed, spoke, and sang.
Then, standing amidst the host of Bhadra-gaṇas, that Bhadra shone with Bhadrā,
just as Tryambaka shines with Ambikā while standing amidst the host of Rudra-gaṇas.
At that very moment, Dakṣa’s sacrificial enclosure was made of gold.
The mighty-armed Vīrabhadra entered, accompanied by a great retinue. Then Bhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, entered the sacrificial ground of that preeminent sacrifice offered by Dakṣa,
like Rudra at the end of time desiring to consume the world.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vīrabhadra," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa. Vāyu said:
Then he beheld a great sacrificial session (*satra*) belonging to the gods of immeasurable splendor, led by Viṣṇu; it was adorned with variegated banners and equipment,
strewn with excellent *darbha* grass according to the season, and featured a well-kindled sacrificial fire.
It was adorned with radiant sacrificial vessels made of gold,
and by sages skilled in sacrifice who performed the rites according to rule; there,
many ritual procedures were properly executed in accordance with the injunctions seen in the Vedas.
Abounding with thousands of celestial women and served by hosts of apsarases,
graced by the sounds of flutes and lutes and amplified by the chanting of the Vedas—
the heroic and majestic Vīrabhadra beheld this at Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Then he let out a lion’s roar, deep as a thundercloud. Thereupon, a great sound of "kila-kila" was raised by the lords of the Gaṇas, filling the sky as it were and surpassing the roar of the ocean.

Seized by that great sound, all the inhabitants of heaven fled in every direction, terrified, their garments and ornaments falling away. "Is the great Mount Meru being shattered? Is the earth being rent asunder? they cried.
"What is this? What is this? the gods cried out loudly, like lordly elephants in a dense forest hearing the roar of lions;
having heard such a sound, some abandoned their lives out of fear.
The mountains shattered and the earth trembled;
the winds whirled about and the ocean was agitated.
The fires did not blaze, nor did the sun shine.

The planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars did not shine. At that very time, the Blessed Lord Bhadra, together with his auspicious attendants and Bhadrā, arrived at that radiant sacrificial enclosure.
Seeing him, though terrified, Dakṣa stood as firm as if he were steadfast;
he spoke these words like one enraged: "Who are you, and what do you desire here?
Having heard those words of the evil-minded Dakṣa...
Vīrabhadra, of great splendor and with a roar as formidable as a thundercloud,
looked upon Dakṣa and the gods and the officiating priests as if smiling. (Śivapurāṇa 7.1.20.14cd–15ab)
Vīrabhadra spoke these fitting words, pregnant with meaning and free from confusion: "Indeed,
we are all attendants of Śarva, who possesses immeasurable splendor."
"We have arrived with the desire for a share; let a share be granted to us.
If no share has been assigned to us in this sacrifice, then let the reason for that be told, or else let me fight with the immortals."
Thus addressed by the lord of the Gaṇas, the gods led by Dakṣa replied: "The mantras are our authority; we are not the masters. The mantras said to the gods: "Your minds are afflicted by delusion."
Because you do not worship Maheśvara, who is worthy of the first portion,
even though those gods have been addressed by the mantra, they are all deluded in mind;
desiring his exclusion, they did not grant a share to Bhadra.
When their own words, though true and beneficial, had thus become futile,
they then departed slowly for the eternal world of Brahmā.
Then the leader of the Gaṇas spoke to the gods, headed by Viṣṇu.
"The mantras were not authorized by you who are arrogant in your strength;
because we have been thus insulted by the gods in this sacrifice,
I shall therefore remove your pride along with your lives."

Having spoken thus, the Lord, filled with wrath, consumed the Yakṣavāṭa and Mahākūṭa with the fire from his eyes, just as Hara did with the three cities. Then all the lords of the Gaṇas, whose bodies were as lofty as mountains, [advanced].
Having uprooted the sacrificial posts and bound them with ropes around the necks of the Hotṛ priests,
and having broken and pulverized the various sacrificial vessels in the water,
they seized the components of the sacrifice and cast them into the current of the Gaṅgā.
There, there were mountain-like heaps of divine food and drink;
rivers of milk flowing with nectar, and very smooth curds as thick as mud;
and various kinds of meat, both savory and fragrant.
Indeed, those heroes partake of flavorful drinks, as well as foods to be licked and sucked; they snatch them with their mouths, devour them,
and scatter them about with thunderbolts, discuses, great tridents, spears, nooses, and sharp-edged axes.
With pestles, swords, ṭaṅkas, bhidhipālas, and axes,
those powerful heroes born from the body of Vīrabhadra pierced all the arrogant gods led by the world-protectors.
"Cut! Pierce! Cast down! Cast down quickly! Let him be slain! Let him be torn asunder!
"Seize him! Strike him! Rend him! Uproot him!
Such were the cruel words, born of fury, which were like spikes to the ears.
In various places, there arose hosts of Gaṇeśas who were intent on battle;
some had rolling eyes, while others bit their lips, fangs, and palates.
Having dragged away those dwelling in hermitages, they killed the ascetics whose wealth was their penance.
Carrying away the *sruva* ladles and casting the fire into the waters,
they broke the jars and shattered the jeweled altars;
singing, shouting, and laughing again and again.

And drinking the blood-liquor, the leaders of the Gaṇas danced. Having churned the gods including Indra, those lords of the Gaṇas— whose essence was like that of bulls, serpents, and lions, and whose nature was incomparable— performed many joyful gestures that caused their hair to stand on end.
Some rejoiced, some struck out, some ran, and some prattled;
some danced, some laughed, and some of the Pramathas leaped about with great force.
Some desired to seize the water-laden clouds, while others flew up to catch the sun.
Some of those terrifying Pramathas, stationed in the sky, desired to rush forth along with the wind;
others, having seized excellent weapons like Garuḍas seizing great serpents,
wandered through the circle of the sky while even the gods fled before them, for they resembled the peaks of mountains.

Uprooting house after house—along with their latticed windows, balconies, and pavilions—the Pramathas, resembling dark rain-clouds, hurled them again and again into the midst of the waters and roared. They overturned doors, panels, and walls; they destroyed halls, roofs, and windows.
Alas! The sacrificial enclosure was shattered like a helpless man, or like a word that has lost its true meaning.
"O Lord! O Father! O Son! O Brother! O Mother!
O Uncle!"—thus did the women cry out many times with cries of helplessness as their houses were being torn down.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Destruction of the Sacrifice," in the first section of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vāyu said:
Then those leaders of the thirty gods, headed by Viṣṇu and Śakra,
all fled, terrified and overwhelmed by fear. Seeing the gods thus harassed, with their own limbs unblemished [by injury], they were struck with alarm.
Thinking that those who deserved punishment had not been punished, the bull among the Gaṇas became enraged.
Then, raising his trident— which destroys even the power of Śarva—
the mighty-armed one, with his gaze fixed upward, emitted flames from his mouth.
He rushed even at the immortals as a lion does at elephants;
as he charged them, his exceedingly beautiful gait became a sight to behold,
like that of an elephant in rut in Vārāṇasī.
Then the powerful one agitated that great army of the gods,
just as a rutting leader of an elephant herd agitates a vast lake;
manifesting himself in many forms of blue, pale-white, and red.
Wearing a tiger skin as his garment, with its excellent stars of gold, he moved among the hosts of gods—
cutting, piercing, splashing, tearing, and even crushing them—
like a fierce fire consuming dry grass.
Moving with great speed here and there, bearing his trident,
all the gods perceived that single being as if he were a thousand.
And Bhadrakālī, enraged and arrogant with the pride increased by battle, [advanced].
With his spear emitting blazing flames, he pierced the gods in battle.
That auspicious weapon, born from the wrath of Rudra,
shone with it like the fire at the end of an eon, smoky-grey and flickering with radiance.

Then Bhadrakālī shone in that battle like the fire of universal destruction at the end of the aeon (kalpa), having consumed the entire world with her flames. (Note: The elision of the letter *n* in "vidrutatridaśā" is an archaic Vedic usage.)
Then Bhadra, the leader of the Rudra hosts,
playfully struck Sūrya along with his horse on the head with his left foot;
Bhadra struck Agni with swords, and Yamī struck Yama with *paṭṭiśa* spears.
With a firm trident he struck the Rudras, and with solid mallets, Varuṇa;
with iron clubs, Nirṛti; and with axes himself, the wielder of the axe—the heroic lord of the Gaṇas—pierced Vāyu in battle as if in mere play.

He instantly [struck] all the hosts of gods and the sages who were hostile to Śambhu. Then, with the tip of his fingernail, the Lord likewise cut off the beautiful tip of the nose of Sarasvatī and that of the Mother of the Gods.
And with an axe, he cut off the staff-like arm of Vibhāvasu;
and in front of his mother, the Goddess, he lopped off her tongue by two finger-breadths.
Likewise, the Lord [cut off] the right nostril of the goddess Svāhā.
With the tip of his claw, he tore at her left nipple;
then Bhadra, possessing supreme speed, forcibly plucked out the two large eyes of the vulva, which were as radiant as lotus petals.
With the tip of his bow, he struck Pūṣan’s row of teeth, which were as radiant as a string of pearls;
by that blow, Pūṣan became indistinct in speech.
Then the Lord playfully touched the moon with his big toe.
Having seized him for a moment like a worm and dragged him to the ground,
Bhadra, in supreme rage, severed Dakṣa’s head;
even as Vairiṇī was crying out, he gave it to Bhadrakālī.
Greatly delighted, that goddess took up his head, which resembled a palm fruit, and played with it like a ball upon the field of battle. Then,
Dakṣa’s sacrifice became as wretched as women are when their husbands have been slain.
He was struck with both feet and both hands by the lords of the Gaṇas.
[They struck] Ariṣṭanemi, Soma, and Prajāpati Dharma;
as well as Aṅgiras Bahuputra, Kṛśāśva, and Kaśyapa.
Seizing him by the throat, the powerful leaders of the Gaṇas, possessing the prowess of lions,
rebuked him severely with words and struck him on the head with their fists. His wives, sons, and dependents were likewise assaulted by the Bhūtas and Vetālas.
Just as in the Kali age, noble women are violated by paramours through force;
and that [city] had its water-jars shattered, its sacrificial posts broken, and its festivities ceased;
its great halls were set ablaze, and its gates and archways were shattered.
The army of the gods had been torn asunder, and the ascetics were being slaughtered;
the sound of Vedic recitation had been silenced, the crowds of people had perished,
the distressed women were wailing, and the entire retinue had been destroyed.
Then the sacrificial enclosure, being thus afflicted, became like a desolate wilderness.
Struck down by the force of the trident, with their arms, thighs, and chests shattered,
and their heads severed, the foremost of the gods fell upon the earth.
When those gods had been slain by the thousands and fallen,
Gaṇeśāna entered the sacrificial fire-altar in an instant. Then,
seeing him who was as formidable as the fire of cosmic destruction enter, Bhadra—
Terrified of death, Yajña fled, assuming the form of a deer.
Stretching his great bow, which was terrifying with the sound of its firm string,
Bhadra pursued him while discharging his arrows.

Drawing his cloud-like bow back as far as his ear, he made the bowstring resound in every direction—through the heavens, the sky, and the earth. Hearing that roar, [the enemy] became overwhelmed, crying out, "I am slain! in his distress.
With his curved mouth,
which was like a crescent moon, that hero rendered the person of the sacrifice headless as he fled in the form of a deer— trembling, deprived of luster, his feet faltering from great fear.
Seeing that son of the Sun thus treated with contempt,
Viṣṇu became exceedingly enraged and prepared for battle;
he bore him away with great speed upon his shoulder, its joints bent.
Garuḍa, the consumer of serpents and king of all birds, [assisted him];
and the gods who remained after the slaughter, led by the king of the gods,
rendered him aid as if prepared to give up their very lives.
Seeing the gods together with Viṣṇu like jackals [before] a lion,
the Lord of Beings laughed, as a lion [might] feel distressed [at the sight of them].
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Punishment of the Gods," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
At that moment, a chariot appeared in the sky,
resplendent like a thousand suns, adorned with beautiful garments, and bearing the bull-emblem on its banner.
Exalted by two jewel-like horses and possessing four wheels,
it was adorned with a collection of many divine missiles, weapons, and jewels;
indeed, he alone shall be the charioteer of that preeminent chariot.

And just as in the battle of Tripura, he who had previously been stationed on Śarva’s chariot— Brahmā, having brought that excellent chariot near Hara by the very command of the Wielder of the Trident, spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Bhagavan-bhadra, O Bhadrāṅga! The Lord Indubhūṣaṇa,
the immutable Hero, who dwells near the hermitage of Rebhya together with Ambikā, commands you, Tryambaka, to mount his chariot."
"O mighty-armed one, he beheld your unbearable prowess.
Having heard those words of his, that heroic elephant among the Gaṇas,
honoring the Grandfather, ascended the divine chariot.
Thus, while that excellent chariot was occupied by Brahmā as the charioteer,
Bhadra’s splendor increased like that of Rudra, the enemy of the cities.
