Then [he blew] an excellent, radiant conch shell, possessing a luster equal to the full moon.
The exceedingly powerful Bhānukampa placed it to his mouth and blew [the conch].
Hearing that sound of the conch, which resembled the cry of a distressed crane,
the digestive fire of the gods flared up with fear.
In an instant, the quarters of the sky, including their intermediate spaces, became densely packed with Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, lords of serpents, and Siddhas who were eager to witness the battle. Then,
from the corner of his bow, the Śārṅga, that cloud-like Nārāyaṇa [discharged his arrows].
With a great rain of arrows, he tormented the bull of the Gaṇas.
Seeing him approaching, showering arrows by the hundreds,
Bhadra took up his victorious bow and released thousands of shafts.
Having taken up that divine bow, which was terrifying in battle,
he slowly drew it back, just as the Lord drew Mount Meru [when lifting it]. As that bow was being drawn, there arose a great sound.
With that great sound, he caused the earth to tremble. Then the illustrious leader of the Gaṇas, himself of fierce prowess, seized a formidable and excellent arrow, blazing like a venomous serpent.
When the arrow was extracted, his arm, joined to the mouth of the quiver,
appeared like a serpent about to enter an anthill;
as it was raised in his hand at that moment, it shone brilliantly with the shafts.
Like a young snake bitten by a great serpent,
Bhadra— possessing the prowess of Rudra—
being enraged, deeply pierced the imperishable Viṣṇu with a thick and fierce arrow in the forehead.
Viṣṇu, who had been struck on the forehead and previously insulted, became enraged at the lord of the Gaṇas like a bull at a lion. Then,
with a great arrow that was like a thunderbolt and possessed a cruel point—
He pierced the arm of the lord of the Gaṇas, which resembled a serpent; and Vīrabhadra, possessed of great strength, again swiftly discharged an arrow, radiant as ten thousand suns, into his arm.

And that Viṣṇu again [struck] Bhadra, and Bhadra likewise again [struck] Viṣṇu; O Brahmins, they both pursued and struck one another with arrows. As they were swiftly discharging arrows at each other with great speed, [the battle continued].
A tumultuous and hair-raising battle took place between the two. Seeing that tumultuous combat between those very two, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! was uttered by the sky-dwellers in the heavens.
Then Bhadra pierced Viṣṇu’s broad chest very firmly with a fire-mouthed arrow, radiant as the sun.
Struck deeply by that arrow with its fierce impact, he was severely wounded.
Having suffered great pain, he fell down unconscious;
then, Hari, having regained consciousness as if rising again after a moment,
discharged all his divine weapons against him.
And that general of Śiva’s army, Viṣṇu,
suddenly warded off all those arrows discharged from the bow with his own terrible counter-arrows.
Then Viṣṇu [discharged] an arrow marked with his own name, which was nowhere obstructed.

He discharged that arrow, blood-red with rage, aiming it at the Lord of the Gaṇas. But the Blessed One, Bhadra, by means of his excellent arrow called Bhadra, severed that shaft into a hundred pieces on its path before it had even reached him.

Then, with a single arrow he cut the Śārṅga bow, and with two arrows the wings of Garuḍa; all this occurred in the mere twinkling of an eye, and it was like a marvel. Thereupon, by the power of yoga, Viṣṇu [emerged] from his body along with the most formidable gods.
He discharged thousands [of beings] with conchs, discs, and maces in their hands;
the mighty-armed one, in a mere moment, utterly consumed them all with the fire emitted from his eye, just as Śaṅkara burned the inhabitants of Tripura.
Then Viṣṇu, becoming even more enraged, quickly raised his discus; at that moment, the hero became intent on hurling it at him. Seeing him standing before him with the discus raised, [he spoke].
As if smiling, Gaṇeśāna effortlessly paralyzed it;
with his limbs thus paralyzed, Viṣṇu was no longer able, even though he wished, to discharge that terrible and incomparable discus anywhere.
As if gasping for breath, he raised one arm equipped with the discus and stood there,
becoming listless and motionless like a stone;
he was like a soul without a body, or like a bull without horns.
And as Viṣṇu stood there with his fangs bared like a lion,
Indra and the other gods beheld Viṣṇu fallen into such a wretched state,
overpowered by the Lord of the Gaṇas, just as bulls are by a lion.
With weapons raised, they stood ready to fight in their fury.
Seeing them in battle— like a lion [regarding] small deer— the hero Bhadra,
whose very body was Rudra himself, was surrounded by a host of excellent warriors.
By that terrible, loud laughter, the right hand of the censured Indra, though still holding his thunderbolt, was struck with fear; even as he desired to hurl it, his arm,
deprived of the bolt, became as if paralyzed with wonder.
Even the arms of all others, though full of passion,
turn back like the undertakings of the indolent;
for thus was their entire majesty thwarted by that Blessed One.

The immortals were unable to stand before him in battle; with their limbs paralyzed, they fled, overwhelmed by fear. Agitated by the terror of his heroic splendor, they could no longer maintain their position in the fight.
Vīrabhadra, the mighty-armed, pierced the fleeing heroic gods with sharp arrows,
just as Maghavat strikes mountains with showers of rain;
many were the arms of that hero, resembling iron clubs.

With their blazing weapons, they shone like serpents with flames of fire. Discharging numerous missiles and weapons, that hero shone like the Source of the Universe (Viśvasambhava) at the beginning of time, emitting all living beings.
Just as the sun covers the earth with its rays,
so too did the hero in an instant cover the quarters with his arrows;
the gold-adorned shafts of the lord of the Gaṇas filled the circle of the sky.
Leaping up like flashes of lightning, those great beings became the very model of comparison;
like large water-snakes devouring frogs, they deprived the hosts of gods of their lives and drank the wine of their blood.
Some with their arms severed, some with their noble faces cut away,
and others with their sides rent open, the immortals fell to the earth;
their many limbs were mangled by arrows and their joints were shattered.
Some, with their eyes rolling back, fell dead upon the ground;
as if wishing to enter the earth or desiring to go into the sky, they collapsed,
unable to restrain themselves, merging into one another.
Some entered the earth, others the caves of the mountains;
some went into the sky, and others entered the water.
Thus, with all his limbs severed by the gods, that hero shone forth.
The host of subjects was seized by Bhairava as if he were the Blessed Lord himself;
it became like the enemy of Tripura after he had burnt the triple city. Thus, the entire army of the gods was dejected and loathsome to behold.
Then, born from Gaṇeśvara, he assumed a wretched form. At that time, a terrible river began to flow, carrying the blood and water of the gods' heroes, foreboding fear for all living beings.
Then the sacrificial ground, drenched with blood,
shone like a dark-complexioned Kaiśikī woman whose garment is wet with blood after she has slain Śuṃbha.
While that great and exceedingly terrible battle was taking place, [the earth appeared thus].
As if terrified by fear, the earth trembled;
the great ocean, filled with massive waves and whirlpools, was agitated;
meteors fell as great portents, and trees shed their branches.

All the quarters became gloomy and an inauspicious wind blew. "Alas! What a reversal of fate is this, that this horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*)—performed by Dakṣa himself, the Prajāpati and son of Brahmā—should come to such a pass!"
Dharma and the other members of the assembly are protected by the one whose banner is Garuḍa;
and Indra and the other gods receive their respective shares in person.
Nevertheless, this pertains to the sacrificer, the sacrifice, and the officiating priests.

Only then does the severing of the head immediately result in the desired fruit. Therefore, one should never perform an action that is not prescribed by the Vedas, nor one that is excluded by the Lord, nor one that is undertaken with false intent.
Even after performing very great merit or sacrificing with hundreds of rituals,
one who lacks devotion to Maheśvara does not obtain that fruit.
Yet, even after committing very great sin, he who worships Śiva with devotion [attains it].

He is liberated from all sins; there is no need for deliberation on this point. What is the use of saying more here? For one who delights in reviling Śiva, charity is in vain, austerity is in vain, sacrifice is in vain, and the fire-oblation is in vain.

Then the hosts of gods in battle—along with Nārāyaṇa, the Rudras, and the world-protectors—pierced by arrows shot from the bow of the Lord of the Gaṇas, fled, overwhelmed by intense pain. Some, with their hair disheveled, stumbled here and there; others, with their limbs prostrate, sank down in various places.

In some places, certain gods perished with their mouths agape; in other places, some of the divine heroes fled. There, certain deities fell down, ruined and with their garments, ornaments, missiles, and weapons cast aside, displaying a most piteous appearance as they abandoned their intoxication, pride, and strength.
Having scattered the sacrifice of Dakṣa— which had set out upon an evil path— with his invincible and unassailable weapons,
that Lord of the Gaṇas shone resplendent in the midst of the lords of the Gaṇas, like a lion among bulls.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the first section (Pūrva-khaṇḍa) of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 23. Vāyu said:
Thus, with their limbs cut and shattered, the gods, led by Viṣṇu, [fell]. (Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.23.1ab)
In an instant, having fallen into a miserable state, those who remained were few and trembled. As those heroes and other gods were terrified in battle,
the Pramathas, exceedingly enraged and urged on by Vīrabhadra, [attacked them].
And having thus seized him, they bound his hands, feet, neck, and belly with firm iron shackles.
At that moment, Brahmā [spoke] auspicious words to the daughter of the mountain king.
Having gained affection through his role as charioteer, he bowed down and spoke with entreaty:
"O Blessed One, enough with this anger; these dwellers of heaven have already been destroyed.
Be gracious, O you of noble vows, and let all be forgiven along with the hair-born ones."
Thus addressed by that Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
the leader of the Gaṇas became pacified and well-pleased out of respect for him;
and the gods, who were the ministers of the God of Gods, obtained their opportunity.
Holding their joined palms to their heads, they praised him with various hymns.
The gods said:
"Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the destroyer of the sacrifice, the wielder of the trident!"
To Rudrabhadra, the lord of the Rudras, the source of the Rudras;
to him who has the form of Kālāgnirudra, who took away the limbs of Kāla and Kāma;
to the slayer of the heads of the gods and of the evil-minded Dakṣa.
O hero, through association with this sinful Dakṣa of untiring deeds,
we— who are otherwise irreproachable— have been chastised by you in battle;
O Lord, we have all been scorched and are terrified of you.
"You alone are our refuge; protect us who have come to you for shelter.
Vāyu said:
"Thus praised, the Lord was indeed pleased and, having dismissed the gods, released them from their fetters."
He brought the immortals here into the presence of the God of gods.
There, the Lord, the Blessed One, the Sovereign, stood in the intermediate space—
Śarva, the omnipresent Great Lord of all worlds, accompanied by his attendants.
Seeing that Supreme Lord, the gods, led by Viṣṇu,
were both delighted and terrified, and they bowed down to Maheśvara.
Seeing those immortals frightened, Hara, the remover of the distress of those who prostrate, [acted].
Having looked at Pārvatī, Mahādeva spoke this while smiling.
Mahādeva said:
"Do not fear, O all you gods; you are indeed my offspring."

"The rod of punishment has been wielded here by the compassionate one solely for the sake of favoring you, the immortals; indeed, your transgression has been forgiven by us. For if we were to become angry, neither your stability nor your very lives would remain."
Vāyu said:
Having been addressed thus by Śarva of immeasurable splendor, all the thirty gods,
their doubts instantly dispelled, danced with joy.
Having become serene in mind and their hearts overwhelmed with joy,
the denizens of heaven began to offer praise to Śaṅkara.
The gods said:

You alone, O God, are the creator of all the worlds, their protector, and their destroyer; you are the Supreme Lord. You whose physical forms are sustained by the qualities of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*, appearing through the distinct manifestations known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—homage be to you, O embodiment of all, O creator of the universe, O purifier!
O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, it was indeed by your grace that the Moon, who had assumed a form for the sake of his devotee though being formless, and who was the giver of happiness,
attained bliss after dying upon immersion in you, even as he joined his palms toward the Sun.

O Lord, by worshipping you, Sīmantinī, whose husband had been slain, attained incomparable good fortune; and through the vow observed on Mondays, she obtained sons. The God granted his own unsurpassed station to Śrīkara.

Out of fear of the circle of kings, you protected Sudarśana; and the treasure-house of compassion caused Medura to cross over along with his wife. By your action, you made the widow Śāradā a woman with a husband once again.
"O Bhadrāyu, you have cut off his misfortune and bestowed happiness upon him. By serving you, Sauminī has indeed been liberated from the bond of worldly existence.
Viṣṇu said:

O Śambhu, you are Kaharīśa; through the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, you are the creator, the protector, and likewise the destroyer, desiring to bestow grace upon all beings. You are the remover of all pride and the one who manifests the splendor of all radiance.
You are hidden within all branches of knowledge and you bestow grace upon all.
O Lord of the Mountains, from you comes everything, you are everything, and everything is in you.
Save me, save me, save me again; have mercy upon me!
Then, in the meantime, Brahmā, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence,
took this opportunity and addressed the wielder of the trident.
Brahmā said:
Victory to you, O God, Great God, the dispeller of the distress of those who bow before you!
Among such offenses, who else but you would be so gracious?
Those who were previously stationed in battle shall now attain their desires.
Who would not attain restoration when the Supreme Lord is pleased? This very act of finding fault with those who have committed offenses against the gods of gods—
one should consider this a decoration, due to the weight of his acceptance.
Thus being addressed by Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin,
the God of gods looked at the face of the Goddess and,
as if smiling out of affection for Brahmā, who was born from a lotus and was like a son to him, spoke.
The Lord restored the limbs of the gods and others as they were before.
And to those goddesses, the mothers of the gods, who had been punished by the first [deity] and the others,
Giriśa likewise restored their limbs as they were before.

The Lord Brahmā himself, the Grandfather, acted toward Dakṣa in accordance with his sin, transforming his face into that of an old goat. Having regained consciousness and seeing that he was restored to life, the wise one [Dakṣa] was filled with wonder.
Terrified, with palms joined in reverence, he praised Śambhu while lamenting at length.
Dakṣa said:
"Victory to you, O God, Lord of the World, who bestows grace upon the worlds!"
Have mercy, O Great Lord; forgive my transgression.
You alone, O Lord, are the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the worlds.

"Thou art the Command. We desire to hear this, exactly as it is and in due order.
Vāyu said:
"Agni" is said to be the fierce and terrible fiery body of Rudra;
Soma is the nectar-like body of Śakti, which brings about peace.
That which is immortality is your foundation; it is itself splendor (*tejas*), knowledge (*vidyā*), and power (*kalā*).

Within all subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), those very things constitute essence (*rasa*) and splendor (*tejas*). The function of splendor is twofold: consisting of the nature of the sun and consisting of the nature of fire.
In the same way, the functioning of taste consists of the nature of soma and the nature of water;
light consists of lightning and so forth, while taste consists of sweetness and so forth.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is sustained by these various distinctions of light and taste.
The production of nectar (*amṛta*) comes from fire, and by means of that nectar, fire thrives.
For this very reason, the dynamic union of Agni and Soma is for the welfare of the world. There is the abundance of grain for the sake of the oblation (*havis*), and rain for the growth of the grain.

Rain alone is the oblation; therefore, the world is sustained by Agni and Soma. This fire blazes upwards as far as the supreme nectar of Soma, and as far as the abode of Agni, the nectar of Soma flows downwards.
For this very reason, Kālāgni is below and Śakti is above;
there shall be burning upwards and flooding downwards until [the end].
This Kālāgni, moving upwards, is supported by the Foundation Power (Ādhāra-śakti) alone.
In the same way, the moon flows downward as the locus of the feet of Śiva and Śakti.
Śiva is above and Śakti is below; Śakti is above and Śiva is below.
Thus, there is nothing here that is not pervaded by Śiva and Śakti.

The world has been repeatedly burnt by fire and reduced to ashes; they say this is the very potency (*vīrya*) of fire, and therefore that which is ash is its potency. Whoever, having thus understood the true nature of ash, bathes with ash—
Bound by mantras beginning with "Agni," one is liberated from the fetter.
However, that ash which is the potency of fire, when drenched again by Soma,
becomes fit for the governance of Prakṛti through the application of yoga.

But by means of yogic method, that ash, being drenched on all sides by the shower of nectar from the Śakti, shall cause one to turn back from [worldly] authority. Therefore, for the sake of the Conqueror of Death, there should always be this bathing with nectar.
For one who has obtained the touch of the nectar of Śiva’s power, how could there be death?
He who knows the secret fire and the flooding as it has been described,
having abandoned the state of Agni and Soma, is not born again.
Having burned the body with the fire of Śiva, he who drenches it with the nectar of the gentle Śakti according to the path of yoga is fit for immortality; indeed,
having kept this meaning in his heart, it was proclaimed by the Lord.
"The entire universe consists of the nature of Agni and Soma," according to its corresponding character.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Principle of Ashes" (Bhasmatattvavarṇana), in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 29.
Vāyu said:
I shall explain how the nature of speech and meaning was established for the world;
I shall provide a correct understanding of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) in brief, but not in detail.
There is no object that is not the meaning of a word, nor is there any word that is without meaning;
therefore, in the conventional usage [of language], every word is the indicator of every object.
This manifestation of word and meaning is a twofold transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti).
They call that the natural form (prākṛtī mūrti) of Śiva and Śivā, the Supreme Self. That manifestation whose essence is sound is said by the wise to be threefold:
gross (sthūlā), subtle (sūkṣmā), and supreme (parā). Of these, the gross is that which falls within the range of hearing.
The subtle [power] is said to consist of thought, while the supreme is devoid of thought.
That which is Power is the Supreme Power, resting upon the principle of Śiva;
through its union with the power of knowledge, it likewise strengthens the power of will.
The essence of the collective totality of all powers, known by the name of the *Śakti-tattva*,
has become the primordial material cause (*mūlaprakṛti*) of the entire range of effects.
That very power is Kuṇḍalinī, Māyā, the supreme reality of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*).
She, whose very nature is differentiation, unfolds as the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Among them, three paths are said to consist of words (śabda) and three of meanings (artha).
For all men indeed, according to their own respective purity, [these paths manifest].
There are the spheres of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority according to the differentiation of all the principles (*tattva*). Those principles are pervaded by the *kalās* exactly as they are;
this occurs first through the fivefold transformation of the supreme *prakṛti*.
And it is certain that those *kalās*, beginning with *nivṛtti* and the rest, are sufficient.
From the perspective of sound (*śabda*), there are the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*), the path of words (*padādhvan*), and the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*);
from the perspective of meaning (*artha*), they are respectively the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), and the path of *kalās* (*kalādhvan*).
In this regard, the mutual relationship of pervader and pervaded among all [these categories] is stated:
mantras are pervaded by all words because of their nature as sentences;
and words, indeed, are said by the wise to be a collection of phonemes (varṇas).
The castes (varṇas), however, are pervaded by the worlds, because they are perceived within them;
and the worlds,
too, are pervaded by the multitudes of principles (tattvas), because they are repeatedly commenced by causal principles through the process of internal and external origination.
Some worlds here have arisen from within;
others are to be known as those belonging to the Purāṇas in the Śiva-āgama,
as well as certain principles (tattvas) well-known from Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Furthermore, all other principles well-known in the Śiva-śāstras are likewise pervaded by these *kalās* exactly as they are;
this occurs at the outset through the fivefold transformation of the supreme *prakṛti*.
And those five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are pervaded in successive order.
Therefore, the supreme power (parā śakti) is the pervader of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), being undivided from the state of supreme primordial nature (paraprakṛti),
because that existence [of the paths] arises from the Śiva-tattva.
From the power (śakti) up to the earth (pṛthivī), all that has arisen from the Śiva-principle is pervaded by that very [Śiva] alone,
just as a jar and other objects are pervaded by clay.
That supreme abode of Śiva is what is to be attained through the six paths.
The pervasive and non-pervasive power [is purified] through the purification of the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
By means of *nivṛtti*, the stability of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) is purified up to the level of Rudra;
by means of *pratiṣṭhā*, however, it is purified from there upwards as far as the domain of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Above that, in the middle, up to the limit of Viśveśvara, purification occurs through Vidyā;
above that, at the end of Madhu, purification occurs through Śānti;
and beyond that, through Śāntyatītā, which they call the supreme ether (paramaṃ vyoma) due to its union with the supreme primordial nature (paraprakṛti).
These are the five principles (pañcatattva) by which the entire world is pervaded;
indeed, all of this must be perceived by practitioners right there.
He who desires to effect purification without understanding the pervasion of the paths (adhvan) [is unable to do so].
That deceiver is not capable of attaining the fruit of purity;
his exertion is in vain and leads only to hell,
unless there is the conjunction with the descent of power (śaktipāta) regarding the principles (tattvas) as they truly are.
Thus, its pervasion and its expansion cannot be known.
The supreme power of Śiva is the sovereign command (ājñā), whose nature is consciousness and who is the mistress of Māra.
By her, acting as the causal agent, Śiva presides over everything.

Upon investigation, this is neither the self nor an illusion, nor is it a transformation; there is neither bondage nor liberation, for she is that which brings about both bondage and liberation. She is the supreme limit of all sovereignty, inseparable from Śiva.
She is his counterpart in nature through those various specific states;
he is always her husband by virtue of her, and she is always his wife by virtue of him.
Their offspring is the effect, which is the world born of the supreme primordial nature.
"He is the agent and she is the instrument; thus their distinction is established.
"Śiva alone is directly manifest, yet he exists in two ways.
"Some say that the distinction between these two consists in the state of female and male."
Others, however, maintain that the supreme power of Śiva is inherent (*samavāyinī*) to him,
like the radiance of the sun, consisting of consciousness (*cidrūpā*), and yet established as if distinct;
therefore, Śiva is the supreme cause, and his command is the Supreme Goddess.
Impelled by that very [power], the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) of Śiva— imperishable,
known as Mahāmāyā, Māyā, and Prakṛti consisting of the three qualities—
is threefold according to its functional differentiation; it brings forth the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
That path, consisting of both word and meaning, is sixfold and constitutes the entire universe;
they say that the whole collection of scriptures is merely an expansion of this very [path].
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Reality of Word and Meaning," in the first section (Pūrvakhaṇḍa) of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 30.
The Sages said:
"The deeds [of Śiva] are manifold, pertaining to householders, and profound."
Difficult to comprehend even for the gods, they delude our minds;
yet, in the essential relationship between the two Śivas, no fault is perceived.
Through their deeds, even a worldly nature is discerned in them both.
Even Brahmā and the others, who are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds,
remain subject to Śiva once they have received his powers of restraint and grace.
Śiva, however, is not the object of restraint or grace for anyone at all.
Therefore, it is certain that His sovereignty is independent.
If such sovereignty as this exists, it is characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*);
and since this is established by His very nature, it must have a formal embodiment as its locus.
A form for that which is independent cannot be established by means of a primary cause;
furthermore, since even a form is an effect, its establishment would be without a cause.
Everywhere, the supreme state is said to be one thing, and the non-supreme another.
How can the supreme and the non-supreme states coexist in one place?
For the nature of this Supreme Self is indeed devoid of fruit;
why then is that very same nature called "possessing parts" (sakala), since its nature is immutable?
If the nature [of things] were contrary [to what it is], and if [the Lord] were independent and acted according to his own will,
why would the Sovereign not cause a reversal of the eternal and the non-eternal?
One is the embodied, conditioned self, while the other is the fruitless Śiva.
And it is briefly stated everywhere that he is presided over by Śiva;
at that time, the very self of the form becomes the form of this Śiva.
For the dependence of both the form and the possessor of the form upon him is certain.
Otherwise, how could a form be assumed by one who is independent?
Therefore, the assumption of a form is due to the desire for a fruit to be accomplished through that form;
for the state of having a body at will does not truly correspond to absolute sovereignty.
For such a free will of men follows from their past actions;
indeed, they are capable of assuming a body by their own will and likewise of abandoning it. From Brahmā down to the Piśācas, are they not all subject to karma? Do they transcend their karma?
They know the creation of bodies by will to be like a magical illusion (indrajāla),
because it does not transcend the mastery over the powers (aiśvarya) such as atomization (aṇimā).
Viṣṇu, assuming a universal form (viśvarūpa), [was addressed] by the great seer Dadhīci.
While fighting, he himself assumed that very form;
thus, even though Śiva, the Supreme Self, is superior to all,
his possession of a body makes him appear to us as sharing the same nature as other beings.
They say that Śiva, the supreme cause, is the benefactor of all;
yet how is it that he, the benefactor of all, took away [the head] of the gods?
The Lord severed the fifth head of Brahmā many times over.
While Viṣṇu, in his form as Nṛsiṃha, was forcibly reviling Śiva, saying "You are my son," O dull-witted one,
[Śiva] suddenly assumed the form of a Śarabha;
having attacked him with his feet, he tore open his heart with his sharp claws.
Among the celestial women and the gods, on account of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
not a single one escaped punishment by the heroic Vīrabhadra; indeed,
he destroyed the three cities along with their women, Daityas, and children.

In a single moment, Kāma— the lord of Rati and the cause of delight for all creatures— was himself made into fuel for the fire of the god’s eye by that deity; and even as the gods cried out, he was offered as a sacrifice into the fire of the eye.
And some cows were streaming floods of milk upon the heads of sky-dwellers;
beholding this with wrath, the Lord instantly reduced the Asura Jalandhara to ashes,
having split him apart with his foot while he was encircling the waters.
Having bound Viṣṇu, he who had hurled him a hundred *yojanas* away,
was struck right there by the wielder of the trident with his very spear.
Having obtained that discus through ascetic penance, Hari, possessing regained prowess, remained ever steadfast.
As the enemies of the gods, whose hearts were devoid of compassion, sought to slay him,
Andhaka’s chest was scorched by the fire-crested trident;
then, having created the Black Goddess from his own throat, the child was struck down.
Having brought forth Kauśikī from the skin-sheath of Gaurī,
Śumbha, together with Niśumbha, was brought to his death in battle. Furthermore, the great narrative concerning Skanda has been heard in the Skānda Purāṇa.

Requested by Brahmā for the sake of slaying the lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, the enemy of Indra, the Lord went to the inner apartments of Mount Mandara. Having sported with the Goddess for a very long time, he became excessively absorbed in their amorous pastimes.
Then, as if having brought the earth down to the subterranean realm (rasātala) by that very name,
he deceived the Goddess and discharged his own seed— which was exceedingly difficult to bear—
into her, like pure, nectar-like oblation poured into the fire.
Having cast [the seed] even into the Gaṅgā and other waters, it was partially retrieved by Agni from here and there,
drop by drop and slowly;
while his wife Svāhā, in the form of the Kṛttikās, was sporting with her husband.
Having been cast upon Mount Meru in a certain reed-thicket that had turned to gold,
it ignited the ten directions with its radiance over time,
coloring all the mountains and making them golden along with Meru itself.
Then, after a long time, when that splendor had arisen there in Kumāra— whose limbs were delicate and who was the very model for all youths— they beheld his charming childhood form.
While the worlds, including the gods and the asuras, were struck with wonder and confusion,
the Lord himself arrived, longing to see his son;
he then placed him upon his lap along with the Goddess, his face beaming with a smile.
With his inner self overwhelmed by affection as if drinking yellow nectar,
even while the gods and dispassionate ascetics looked on,
he freely caused the boy to dance upon his own chest.
Having enjoyed that play and having honored one another,
they commanded the Goddess’s breast-milk and had her drink it, which was like nectar;
and they instructed her, saying, "Your incarnation is for the welfare of the worlds."
Neither the god himself nor the goddess attained satiety.
Then, having made an alliance with Śakra, who was terrified of the demon Tāraka,
[Śiva] caused him to be consecrated as the commander-in-chief of the celestial hosts.
Having placed his son in front, the Lord, the enemy of Tripura,
himself remaining invisible, [beheld] Skanda, who was protected by Indra and the other gods,
in battle by that spear of his which pierces the Krauñca mountain and is like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Even the head of Tāraka was severed out of fear of Śakra;
then the gods, headed by Hari and Dhātṛ, offered special hymns of praise.
Likewise did Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who was arrogant in his own strength, do so in person.
As he was lifting Mount Kailāsa with his own long arms,
the trident-bearing God of gods, unable to endure that offense,
crushed him into the earth so that he sank down by the mere movement of His big toe.
For the sake of a certain purpose concerning a young brahmin who had taken refuge with him and whose life was ebbing away,
the Lord arrived in haste and brought Death (Antaka) to his very feet. Furthermore,
the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala), failing to recognize his own vehicle, the king of bulls, [was likewise subdued].
Having brought all the worlds under his control, the universe then consists of nothing but water.
By means of those various modes of conduct, beautiful with bliss yet unknown to the world,
this universe has been repeatedly set in motion through the spontaneous movement of his limbs.

If Śiva, who is eternally peaceful, were to bestow grace upon everyone, he would surely fulfill all desires; why then would he grant liberation through his power? Nor can the diversity of beginningless karma be the determining factor in this matter.
Indeed, even karma may have been caused by Īśvara. What is the use of much speaking here? Atheism is the cause [of this state].
O Māruta, tell me how it might be quickly dispelled.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Inquiry into the Nature of Śiva," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Vāyu said:
O Brahmins, it is appropriate that you have harbored doubt when urged by reasons;
for among those of virtuous intellect, the desire to know does not establish atheism. I shall here state the authoritative proof which dispels the delusion of the righteous.
But for the wicked, there is a transformation into something else only through the grace of the Lord;
without the supreme favor of the perfect Śiva,
it is firmly resolved that nothing at all can be accomplished.
One's own essential nature alone is sufficient for the act of favoring others;
otherwise, nothing at all can be favored by that which lacks such a nature.
Furthermore, the entire world to be favored consists of bound souls (paśu) and their fetters (pāśa).
However, for the sake of favoring another, there is the compliance with the Lord’s command;
the Lord, as the commander, always bestows grace upon everyone.
If He accepts wealth for that purpose, how could Śiva be dependent on others?
There is indeed no grace whatsoever that is independent of one who is to be graced;
therefore, the meaning of the word "sovereignty" (svātantrya) is characterized by independence.
On the other hand, this object of grace is held to be dependent on another.
Because liberation and worldly enjoyment are not possible for him without [the Lord's] grace;
even though he possesses a formal body, he is to be graced by removing his ignorance of Śiva.
For there is nothing here that is not presided over by Śambhu through ignorance.
That Śiva, whose nature is form, by whom we perceive the partless [reality] even through his entire [manifestation],
is metaphorically designated as the "Śaiva-form" (śaivamūrti).
For he is not the partless Śiva, the supreme cause, in his direct essence.
Unperceived by any specific manifest experience,
the mere fact of being accessible through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes its essential nature.
It does not follow from that alone that there is a cognition of indifference toward it in the absence of a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Indeed, this [form] is a certain manifest embodiment of Śiva, preeminent by its resemblance to the Self;
it is the form of Śiva, whose nature is form, and it is the supreme indicator of Him. Just as fire is not perceived when it has not yet ascended into pieces of wood.

Thus, it is established that Śiva likewise does not exist as something unascended within the form (mūrti). Just as when one says, "Bring fire," fire itself cannot be brought without the burning wood, in the same way, Śiva is to be worshipped through the form.

For this very reason, in the performance of worship and other rites, one should conceive of the image as being the Self; for what is done toward the image as the Self is done directly to Śiva himself. This same practice applies to the *liṅga* and other forms, and especially so in the case of ritual worship (*arcā*).
Śiva is worshipped by us through the very nature of those respective forms;
just as that Supreme Lord is favored by his own form-nature,
so too are we, the bound souls (paśus), favored by Śiva who is established within the nature of those forms.
For the very purpose of favoring the worlds,
all [deities] beginning with Sadāśiva, though they are essentially forms [of the one], were presided over by Śiva, the Supreme Lord;
specifically, for the enjoyment and the liberation of those very selves.
The lineage of Śiva exists within those embodied beings whose natures consist of both reality and unreality.
Enjoyment is considered to consist of the ripening of karma and to be composed of pleasure and pain.
Since Śiva does not possess karma, what could his enjoyment possibly consist of?

Śiva bestows grace upon all; he does not exercise restraint toward anything at all, for those defects which belong to those who restrain others are impossible in Śiva. Furthermore, whatever instances of restraint have been shown regarding Brahmā and the other gods—
They too were created by the form of Śrīkaṇṭha solely for the benefit of the world.
For Śrīkaṇṭha’s sovereignty over the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is certain;
Śiva presides over the form known as Śrīkaṇṭha while sporting.
The gods and others were indeed subdued with their faults, as previously described;
consequently, they too became free from sin, and the subjects were likewise freed from their feverish distress.
Furthermore, even such a subjugation is not to be despised by the wise when it occurs in its true nature.
For this very reason, the infliction of punishment upon those deserving of it is praised by kings;
for it is through this that the accomplishment of the entire range of duties occurs by virtue of their sovereignty. If he were not to exercise such lordship, how could he be the Lord of the universe?
The will of the Lord is the state of being the ordainer; the ordinance is the supreme command.
This world must act under the power of that command: "one should do this" and "one should not do that.
To follow that command is the defining characteristic of goodness.
For one whose concentration is perverted, not everything may be perceived;
however, that which is good must be well protected, while that which is bad must be turned away.
For conciliation and other means may fail, and in the end, punishment is indeed the final resort.
This instruction, ending with the [proper] application of punishment, is characterized by its purpose of bringing about welfare;
therefore, that which is contrary to this is declared to be harmful. For those who are ever established in what is beneficial, there is the example of the Lord (Īśvara).

How can he be blamed by the virtuous, since he has merely suppressed the wicked? In this world, those who act improperly are censurable for their lack of discernment; that which causes distress to the world is declared to be improper.
Every form of restraint in the world is not preceded by hatred;
for a father does not hate his son when he restrains him in order to instruct him. Even one who restrains others from the path with impartiality is worthy of being restrained.
In him, too, some degree of cruelty necessarily persists;
otherwise, he would not harm others even when they are at fault.
Furthermore, by practicing neutrality, he harms those who are ignorant.

"Therefore, some insist that one who commits violence—which is essentially suffering—is indeed merciless; yet others say there is no such rule. For it is like a physician who knows the cause of the disease inflicting a necessary injury upon his patient."
There is no cruelty whatsoever; rather, it is compassion alone that is the motive here.
For even compassion is not for the sake of virtue when directed toward violent adversaries;
one who feels such compassion toward them is, through delusion, merely a cruel person whose cruelty is masked by compassion.

In this world, even equanimity toward those who must be protected and who are one's adversaries is a fault. When one has the power to act, a person who is to be protected perishes immediately due to neglect.
He who looks on with indifference while seeing a snake entering the mouth of one who is to be protected [perishes].
Having imagined faults that are merely fallacious, he too is devoid of compassion;
therefore, it is not accepted that compassion is always a virtue.
It is accepted that one should desire what is appropriate to the occasion, while everything else is considered unacceptable.
Even within the embodied selves, defects such as passion and the like truly exist;
nevertheless, these belong only to them and not to Śiva in any way. Indeed, even when copper is cast into fire, it remains blackened.
Thus, this fire is not defiled by reason of contact with copper;
nor does fire incur impurity through contact with the impure. Indeed, even from the impure, purity arises through contact with fire.
Thus, through contact with the object of purification, Śiva does not become impure;
rather, it is the object of purification itself that becomes pure through contact with Śiva.
Just as when fire enters iron, the burning belongs to the fire alone and not to the iron.
Thus, such sovereignty belongs only to the Lord, not to individual souls, within the embodied self.
Indeed, it is not the wood that burns upward; it is fire itself that burns. Just as the state of being charcoal belongs to the wood and not to the fire, so too should this be applied here.
Therefore, even in this world, within wood, stone, and clay as well,
the state of being Śiva is metaphorically attributed solely by virtue of the descent (āveśa) of Śiva.
Consequently, qualities such as friendliness and the like are merely secondary (gauṇa), for they function in a manner distinct from that [primary nature].
For those who are colored by those qualities, they lead both to defect and to merit; however,
for Śiva, who favors all that is both secondary and primary,
the functions of his qualities lead neither to merit nor to defect.
The wise do not say that the meaning of the word "favor" (anugraha) is secondary;
rather, liberation from saṃsāra is the beneficial grace (śiva) consisting of [Śiva’s] command. To carry out that command is beneficial; what is beneficial is favor.

We shall employ everything for the welfare [of all], acting as the benefactor of everyone. That which is the meaning of the word "assistance" (upakāra), they also call "favor" (anugraha). Because that too consists of welfare, Śiva is the benefactor of all.
Everything, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, is always engaged in what is beneficial;
yet, due to its inherent nature, it does not attain that same benefit.
Just as the sun causes the lotuses to bloom with its rays, so too [does He act].
They do not all blossom at once, but rather in accordance with their own respective natures.
For the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of things is indeed the cause of what is to come;
for nature does not bring about a thing that is destined to perish among its makers.
Fire, upon contact, melts gold alone and not charcoal;
likewise, [the Guru] liberates only those whose impurities have been ripened, and not those who are already devoted to Śiva.
Whatever is destined to become as it is, that shall not otherwise become of its own accord.
Without cultivation [of the self], the agent would be independent by nature,
just as Śiva— who is pure by nature— is the benefactor of all;
likewise, those called *jīvas* are impure by nature.
Otherwise, how could these beings transmigrate according to fixed laws, while Śiva does not?
Transmigration is said by the wise to be the bondage of karma and māyā for him [the individual soul];
this bondage belongs to him alone and not to Śiva—this is the reasoned conclusion.

This cause is the innate, not adventitious, impurity of the selves alone. If it were adventitious, it would have to belong to someone by means of some cause or other. This very cause, however, is one, because its nature is non-variegated.
Although there is equality in the state of selfhood (*ātmatā*), some among those who are bound are liberated while others remain bound; furthermore,
even among those who are bound, some— due to their dissolution, enjoyment, and authority—
possess a disparity in knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth, being either superior or inferior.
Some attain the nature of the physical forms (mūrti), while others have their sphere of activity nearby.
Among those whose nature is the physical forms, some are Śivas situated at the summits of the paths;
the Maheśvaras are Rudras situated in the middle, while the Rudras are situated in the lower station.
And even when Māyā is near, there is a triad due to another cause:
there, the Ātman is situated at the bottom, the Antarātman in the middle,
and the Paramātman at the top— namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Some Vasus abide taking refuge in the state of the Supreme Self (Paramātman);
some in the state of the Inner Self (Antarātman), and likewise some in the state of the Self (Ātman).
Then there are the Śaivas in the state beyond peace (Śāntyatīta), and in the state of Peace (Śānta) belonging to Maheśvara.
In the Vidyā-kalā, those who are fierce (raudra) reside; in the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā, they are indeed Vaiṣṇava;
and likewise in the Nivṛtti-kalā, they are the Ātman-s, whose origins are from the limbs of Brahmā.
Among these, the eight primary divine births are the foremost, while the human birth is the middle one.
The birds and so forth are the five lower births; these [births] constitute fourteen.
This state of higher and lower is to be known as the impurity (*mala*) of the transmigrating soul.
Just as there is a state of rawness for one who is liberated, followed later by a state of ripeness.
Even that which is impure, unripe, and ripe becomes the cause of saṃsāra. Among men, there is a gradual progression from inferiority when [the state] is unripe, to superiority when it is ripe.
The souls of bound beings (paśu) are divided into three types according to their sequence: those with one, two, or three impurities.
Among these, the northern [region] is considered to have one impurity (*ekamala*), the middle has two impurities (*dvimala*),
and the lower ones are known to have three impurities (*trimala*), established in ascending order.
Those with two impurities and those with one impurity preside over those with three impurities respectively.
Thus, this distinction of the universe is imagined as being due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*). Śiva alone presides over all beings, whether they possess one, two, or three impurities (*mala*).
Just as even that which is non-auspicious in nature is presided over by Śiva, so too is this [universe].
Thus, the world is presided over by the Rudras as being non-different from the self of Rudra.
Indeed, the great earth, extending to the edge of the cosmic egg, is presided over by the hundred Rudras and others;
while the intermediate space, extending up to Māyā, is presided over in succession by Amareśa and the rest.
It is completely covered on all sides by [deities] as small as a thumb;
the sky, extending down to Mahāmāyā, is presided over by the lords of the worlds,
beginning with Vāyu and ending with Anāśrita, who abide within the path.
For they are indeed the gods who dwell directly in heaven, as well as those who dwell in the intermediate space;
thus are the gods praised by those devoted to the gods as "those whose station is the earth. In this way, they are distinguished separately by the three impurities, whether raw or ripened.
The disease of saṃsāra prevails among men because it serves as its underlying cause.
The medicine for this disease is knowledge alone, and nothing else.
Śambhu, Śiva, the supreme cause, is the physician who issues the command.
Śiva is capable of liberating even animals without causing them suffering;
one should not entertain the doubt as to how he could inflict pain upon them.
For it is certain that this entire cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) is nothing but suffering.

How could suffering become non-suffering? For intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not subject to error. Indeed, a sick person does not become healthy merely through the efforts of a physician and medicine; rather, the physician extracts the patient from their illness and brings them to well-being by means of medicines.

Thus, Śiva liberates from suffering those bound souls who are inherently impure and by nature afflicted, through the application of the medicine of his own command. Śiva is not the cause of disease for the physician; rather, he is the cause of the cycle of worldly existence.
Even this disparity does not constitute a fault in his case. [Objection:
If suffering is established by its very nature, how can Śiva be its cause? [Response:
Impurity is innate to souls; for that indeed causes them to wander in saṃsāra.
That insentient impurity, beginning with *māyā*, which is the cause of *saṃsāra*,
would not function by itself without the proximity of Śiva;
just as a magnet is effective only through its proximity [to iron].
Just as that [movement] belongs to moving iron, so too, O wise ones, does it belong to Śiva;
his presence cannot be turned away, for it is eternal and without cause.
Therefore, Śiva is the eternal, imperceptible presiding deity of the universe.
Nothing whatsoever exists here that proceeds without Śiva;
all this is impelled by him, yet he is not deluded.
His power, consisting of his command, is the controller facing in every direction.
This entire world is perpetually pervaded by her, yet he is not defiled.
All that is not this [world] is his domain of rule; he is the Lord.
Because of his lordship, his command prevails, yet even so, he remains undefiled.
The evil-minded one who, out of delusion, conceives of it otherwise shall perish;
yet, even so, he is not truly defiled, for it is solely through the majesty of His power that this occurs.
In the meantime, an unembodied voice was heard from the sky:
"Truth, Om, the Immortal, the Gentle"— thus it appeared clearly.
Then all the sages, exceedingly delighted and with all their doubts destroyed,
were filled with wonder and paid homage to the Lord Pavana.
Even after having removed the doubts of the sages, Vāyu, thinking that their knowledge was not yet firmly established, spoke thus. Vāyu said:
Knowledge is held to be of two kinds: indirect (*parokṣa*) and direct (*aparokṣa*).
They say that the indirect is unstable, whereas the direct is very stable.
That which is attainable through the instruction of logical reasons is called indirect.
Furthermore, direct realization will arise from the performance of the supreme [practice].
Having reached the firm conviction that there is no liberation without direct realization,
strive without sloth for the accomplishment of the supreme practice.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Instruction on Knowledge," in the first section of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh book of the Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 32 The Sages said:
"What is that supreme practice by which liberation is perceived?
O Māruta, you ought to tell me now its means as well.
Vāyu said:
For the supreme Dharma is indeed Śaiva, designated as the most excellent practice,
wherein Śiva— the direct bestower of liberation— is perceived in immediate experience.
That [Dharma] should be known as fivefold, according to its sequence through five sections.
Through those very [means]— action, austerity, recitation, meditation, and knowledge— which are unsurpassed,
that supreme Dharma is considered perfected;
it is both indirect and direct knowledge, wherein liberation is bestowed.
For both the supreme and the non-supreme dharmas are indeed enjoined by the Śruti.
Regarding the meaning denoted by the word "dharma," the Śruti alone is our authority.
The supreme dharma, which culminates in Yoga, is contained within the crest of the Śruti.
Likewise, there is another dharma that arises from the mouth of the lower revelation (adhaḥ-śruti).
Because it pertains to those who are not yet fit for the supreme [path], that which is considered the supreme dharma is distinct;
whereas the other is common to all, by virtue of their respective eligibility.
And this supreme Dharma is the means for accomplishing the highest goal;
it is fully augmented by the treatises on Dharma (Dharmaśāstra) and other auxiliary sciences. This supreme Śaiva Dharma is designated as the most excellent practice.
It is somehow augmented by the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*,
endowed with the *Śaiva-āgamas* along with their extensive ancillary and subsidiary branches (*aṅga-upāṅga*),
and perfectly augmented by the qualifications for its purificatory rites (*saṃskāra-adhikāra*).
Indeed, the Śaiva Āgama is twofold: the Śrauta and the Aśrauta, both refined.
The Śrauta is composed of the essence of the Vedas (Śruti), while the other is considered independent (svatantra).
The independent [Āgama] was first tenfold, and then again eighteenfold.
Established under the names of the *Kāmika* and other scriptures, it is designated as the *Siddhānta*.
It consists of the essence of the Vedas and extends to a vast length of one hundred crores of verses;
therein the supreme Pāśupata vow and knowledge are expounded.

In each cycle of the ages, it shall remain [in existence] through one who possesses the very form of a master of yoga; it is set in motion by Śiva himself, who has descended in various places. Having condensed it, its four supreme ṛṣis as expounders [are established].
Ruru, Dadhīca, Agastya, and the highly illustrious Upamanyu—
these are to be known as the Pāśupatas, the originators of the Saṃhitās.
Furthermore, there are hundreds and thousands of gurus belonging to their lineages.
Therein, the supreme Dharma has been declared as fourfold, consisting of conduct (*caryā*) and so forth.
Among these, the Pāśupata Yoga shall firmly bring about the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of Śiva.
Therefore, the practice of Pāśupata Yoga is considered the most excellent.
In that regard, a method is prescribed by Brahmā;
indeed, that yoga consisting of the eight names was devised by Śiva.
Through that yoga, the wisdom of Śiva arises instantaneously.
Through wisdom, one quickly attains supreme and stable knowledge.
Śiva is pleased with him whose knowledge is firmly established.
Through His grace comes the supreme yoga, which brings about the direct perception of Śiva.
Through the direct realization of Śiva, one is separated from the cause of saṃsāra;
thereafter, being liberated from saṃsāra, one becomes free and equal to Śiva.
This very means proclaimed by Brahmā is stated here separately.
Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha,
the Physician of Saṃsāra, the Omniscient One, and the Supreme Self—
this is the primary eightfold name that establishes the nature of Śiva. (Śiva Purāṇa 7.1, 32.23–24ab)
The first pentad should be known according to the sequence beginning with Śāntyatīta;
the designations of Sadāśiva and the others arise from the assumption of five limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Upon the cessation of those adjuncts, however, they cease accordingly.
For that state alone is eternal, while those who possess states are known to be impermanent;
since those who possess states are liberated upon the dissolution of their states,
the attainment of that very state is said to occur again during another transformation.
The first pentad of names would be a designation for the inner self; however,
the other triad of names, due to its connection with the application of [the categories] beginning with "appropriation" (upādāna),
Śiva alone persists through the expression of the threefold limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Because there has been no connection with primordial impurity due to its prior non-existence by nature,
he is called Śiva because his self is absolutely pure;
or else, the Lord is the sole repository of all auspicious qualities.
He is called Śiva by the virtuous who speak of the true meaning of the Śiva-principle.
Indeed, among the twenty-three principles, Prakṛti is considered supreme;
they say that the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth, is higher than Prakṛti.
That which they call the primordial sound at the beginning of the Veda, by virtue of the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
which, because its true nature is to be known solely through the Veda, is established in the Vedānta;
and which is that Supreme Maheśvara who exists beyond him [the individual soul] when he is dissolved into Prakṛti.
Because the activity of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa is dependent upon Him,
this imperishable principle consisting of the three guṇas is that which is to be attained.
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā (Māyin).
He is the agitator of Māyā, infinite, through his association with Maheśvara;
he is celebrated as the Self of Time, the Supreme Self, and so forth, both gross and subtle. This Lord dispels for us that which is called "rudd" (suffering), or the cause of suffering.

Śiva, the supreme cause, is called Rudra by the virtuous. Pervading everything from the principles (tattvas) down to the elements (bhūtas), as well as bodies and other things, without weariness, Śiva presides over them here and there; therefore he is called Rudra.
Śiva is the father even of those who are the fathers of the world, existing in the form of the [eight] manifestations;
by virtue of his nature as a father, he is proclaimed the grandfather of all.
Just as a physician who knows the root cause is the one who brings about the cessation of a disease, so too is he.
Just as [a physician acts] through skillful means and medicines, so too, by virtue of his authority over the dissolution and enjoyment of the world,
the Lord is the eternal bringer of cessation to transmigratory existence along with its very root;
thus he is called the "Physician of Saṃsāra" by those who know the true meaning of all principles.

Although these sense organs exist for the sake of accomplishing the knowledge of the ten objects, the *aṇus* (individual souls), being entirely enveloped by the impurity of *māyā*, do not know at all the entities existing in the three periods of time, whether gross or subtle.
Even though all the causes for knowing all objects are absent,
Sadāśiva knows every object exactly as it exists,
without any effort; therefore, he is called omniscient.

Because he is eternally endowed with these supreme qualities as the self of all, and because there is no other self higher than himself, Śiva is himself the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Having obtained these eight names through the grace of the Teacher, [one attains the goal].
Having cut the knot of the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti* by means of the five names beginning with Śiva,
respectively and in due order, and having purified them according to their respective qualities—
either by means of those [mantras] multiplied along with the *uddhāras*, or else by means of the *aniruddhas*— [one should proceed].
Having severed [the body] at the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā—

which together form the shape of the eightfold lotus— and having drawn one's own self through the *suṣumṇā* channel up to the moon situated at the end of the twelve finger-breadths, [one should place it] above in the energy of Śiva.
Having withdrawn the face [of the deity] according to the ritual procedure following its dissolution,
and once the body has been sprinkled again with the shower of nectar from the *śakti*,
one should descend one's own self into the heart, assuming a form consisting of nectar.
Beyond the moon situated at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], upon a white lotus,
he beheld Mahādeva Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees;
the Lord who is half-female (Ardhanārīśvara), stainless, and of sweet appearance.
Having meditated in his mind upon the God, who resembles pure crystal, serene, and cool-rayed, the man, with a steady mind,
should then worship Him with the flowers of devotion using the eight names of Śiva.

At the conclusion of the worship, the person, having again performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and properly composed the mind, should mutter the eight names of Śiva. Having offered eight oblations at the navel, he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the word "namas."

Having performed the final worship by offering eight flowers, one should offer oneself through the medium of a handful of water. By doing so, after a long time, one attains the auspicious Pāśupata knowledge.
He obtains that very foundation as well as supreme conduct;
and having attained the highest yoga, he is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Excellent Practice," in the first section of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 33.
The Sages said:
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the supreme Pāśupata vow."
"Even Brahmā and the others, by performing which [rite], are all remembered as Pāśupatas.
Vāyu said:
"I shall declare to you a secret that cuts away all sins."
The Pāśupata vow is that which is heard in the Atharvaśiras;
its time is the full moon day of Caitra, and its place is a site consecrated by Śiva,
such as a sacred field, a grove, or a forest, which is praised and possesses auspicious characteristics.
There, on the thirteenth day, having bathed well and performed his daily rites,
he should take leave of his own preceptor, worship him, and prostrate before him; then,
having performed a special worship, he himself shall wear white garments.
Wearing a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
seated upon a seat of *darbha* grass and holding a handful of *darbha*,
he performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), facing either east or north.
Having meditated upon the God and the Goddess by way of petitioning them,
and having formed the resolve, "I shall perform this vow," one becomes initiated;
[this may last] until the fall of the body, or for twelve years.
Or half of that, or half of that again; or for twelve months, or half of that, or half of that again, or even for one month;
or for twelve days, or even for six days.
For half of that time, or for one day, beginning from the moment of the vow’s formal resolve,
he should establish the sacred fire according to the rules for the purpose of performing the *virajā-homa*,
offering oblations of clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, and *caru* in their proper sequence.
Having filled it once more to the brim while aiming for the purification of the principles (tattvas),
he should offer oblations with the root mantra using those very same fuel-sticks and other materials,
while recollecting: "May these principles within my body be purified."
The five elements, the subtle essences (*tanmātras*), and the five organs of action;
distinguished by the division of knowledge and action, and further divided according to the five organs of action;
the seven bodily constituents beginning with the skin, and the five vital airs beginning with *prāṇa*.

The mind, intellect, ego, and self-consciousness; the qualities (guṇas), primordial nature (prakṛti), and the individual soul (puruṣa); attachment, limited knowledge, and power (kalā); as well as necessity, time, and Māyā; and both Pure Knowledge (vidyā) and Maheśvara-Sadāśiva.
They know the principles (tattvas) in their proper order as Śakti and the Śiva-principle.
By offering oblations with pure mantras, that sacrificer becomes free from passion (viraja);
having obtained the grace of Śiva, he indeed becomes possessed of knowledge.
Then, having taken cow dung, formed it into balls, and consecrated them with mantras,
he should place them in the fire, sprinkle them with water, and eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) on that day.
Then, on the morning of the fourteenth day, having performed everything previously described, [he should proceed].
On that day, remaining without food, he should complete the remainder of the time.
Having likewise performed the oblations at dawn on the sacred festival day (parvan),
and having concluded with the final rites, he should carefully collect the ashes from the Rudra-fire.
Then, having become one with matted hair, or shaven-headed, or even with a single lock of hair,
and having bathed, he may— if free from shame— be naked;
or he may wear saffron-colored garments, or else clothes made of skin or bark.
He should wear a single garment or a bark dress, and carry a staff and a girdle.
Then, having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice,
he should take that ash produced from the fire of the *viraja* and rub it over his body.
With the six Atharvaṇa mantras beginning with "Agni," one should sequentially distribute [the ashes] over the limbs from the head down to the feet and touch them with them; then,
having gathered up the ashes again in that very same order—
One should perform the smearing of all limbs with the *praṇava* or with the name of Śiva;
then one should fashion the *tripuṇḍra*, which is called the "three-fold life-span. Having attained the state of Śiva, one should then practice the yoga of Śiva.
One should likewise perform this Pāśupata vow at the three junctions of the day;

it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and brings about the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva). Having abandoned that state of being a bound soul and having performed the Pāśupata vow...

The eternal Mahādeva, whose form is the *liṅga*, is worthy of worship. One should prepare a golden eight-petaled lotus as a seat, adorned with the nine gems and provided with a pericarp and filaments.
In the absence of those, however, one should use a red or white lotus;

and in the absence of even that, it should consist solely of meditative visualization (bhāvanāmaya). Having fashioned a small *liṅga* in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that lotus, [one should worship it].
One should worship the crystal [liṅga], together with its pedestal, according to the prescribed rites and sequence.
Having installed that liṅga— which has been purified— according to the injunctions,
one should provide it with a seat and a form consisting of five faces.

One should bathe [the deity] with full jars prepared according to one's means, such as those containing the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and others, as well as with full jars made of gold (aṣṭāpada),
using fragrant substances including camphor, sandalwood, saffron, and the like.
Having smeared the *śivaliṅga* with *śrīkhaṇḍa* paste and adorned it with ornaments,
[he should worship] with bilva leaves, lotuses, red and white water-lilies (*utpala*),
blue water-lilies, and various other fragrant flowers.

Having worshipped [the deity] according to one's means with auspicious and excellent leaves, variegated *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and so forth, in accordance with the procedure for the great worship (*mahāpūjā*),
one should likewise offer incense, a lamp, and an oblation of food (*naivedya*).
Having offered [the oblation], one should perform auspicious rites according to one's means. All desired and excellent things, acquired through righteous means,
should especially be given as offerings during that vow.

O twice-born ones, the number of *śrīpatra*, *utpala*, and *padma* flowers is considered to be one thousand each; however, there is another count, namely one hundred and eight for each. Even in that case, one should especially not omit the *bilva* leaf.
They say that a single golden lotus is superior to a thousand [ordinary] lotuses.
This same principle applies to blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*) and the like, as well as to *bilva* leaves.
Regarding other flowers, there is no fixed rule; one should offer whatever is available.

The eightfold offering (arghya) is excellent, as are incense and ointments, especially so. Sandalwood is used for the face named Vāmadeva, yellow orpiment for the Pauruṣa face, and some say that ashes are the ointment for the Īśāna face; such is the tradition.
They do not consider [ordinary] incense sufficient because of the prescription for specific types of incense:
white agallochum (sitāguru) is for the mouth called Aghora; furthermore, black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) is for the Pauruṣa mouth;
guggulu resin is for the left (Sadyojāta) mouth; and saugaṃdhika is for the Saumya (Vāmadeva) mouth.
For even in the northeast, one should especially offer incense such as uśīra;
combined with sugar, honey, camphor, and the ghee of a tawny cow (kapilā),
along with sandalwood, agallochum, and other woods, this is declared to be the general [incense].
Then, a row of lamps enriched with camphor wicks and ghee should be offered.
After that, water for the guest-offering (arghya) and water for sipping (ācamana) should be given to each face.
In the first enclosure, Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha are to be worshipped in due order.
Then, the limbs of Brahmā are worshipped in the first enclosure;
in the second enclosure, the Vighneśas who are universal sovereigns (cakravartins) are to be worshipped;
and in the third enclosure, the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtis) beginning with Bhava are to be worshipped.
There, Mahādeva and the others, as well as the eleven forms (Ekādaśamūrti),
are all to be worshipped in the fourth enclosure (caturthāvaraṇa) as the lords of the Gaṇas. Furthermore,
outside the lotus, in the fifth enclosure, they are to be worshipped in due order.
The lords of the ten directions, together with their weapons and their followers,
as well as all the mental sons of Brahmā, all the hosts of luminaries,
all the goddesses and gods, and all those who move through the sky, should likewise be worshipped.
And all others dwelling in the netherworld, as well as all the hosts of sages;
indeed, all the yogis, the *sakhās*, the *pataṅgas*, and likewise the mothers (*mātṛs*);
the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapālas*) together with their retinues, and this entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
Considering it worthy of worship for the sake of pleasing Śiva as the manifestation of Śambhu,
one should then, at the conclusion of the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā), having fully worshipped the Supreme Lord,
devotedly offer oblations (havis) that are accompanied by clarified butter, mixed with meat, and heart-pleasing.
Having offered mouth-fresheners and the like, along with betel-leaf and its accompaniments,
and having adorned [the deity] once more with various flowers and ornaments,
one should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and then complete the remainder of the worship.
One should offer a drinking cup along with its accessories, as well as a bed;
one should offer a couch adorned with a necklace resembling the moon,
and all that is primary, fit for a king, and pleasing, in a manner appropriate to each.
Having performed [the rites] oneself and having caused them to be performed by others, and having abandoned [worldly attachments], one should offer worship;
having recited the *Vyapohana-stotra* and the five-syllabled *vidyā*, one should mutter it.
Having performed circumambulation and prostration, one should dedicate oneself [to the Lord].
Then, one should worship the preceptor and the Brahmin in front of the deity;
having offered the *arghya* and eight flowers, one should dismiss the deity from the *liṅga*.
Having properly restrained the fire within the fire, one should likewise dismiss that as well.
And every day, a person should perform the aforementioned service;
then, that lotus-liṅga, together with all its accessories,
should be offered to one's own guru or installed in a temple of Śiva.
Having honored his gurus, the Brahmins, and especially those observing vows,
as well as devoted twice-born men, he should, if he is able, satisfy the poor and the helpless;
and he himself should be capable of fasting, or else subsisting on fruits and roots.
He should either observe the milk-vow, subsist on alms, or likewise eat only once a day;
he should always eat only at night, remain devoted to sleeping on the ground, and be pure;
or else he should sleep on ashes, sleep on grass, or wear rags and animal skins.
One who observes the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should always practice this vow;
likewise, on Sundays, under the asterism Ārdrā, on the fifteenth day of both fortnights,
and on the eighth and fourteenth days, one who is capable should even observe a fast.

One should avoid with every effort— through mind, deed, and speech— those who follow heretical paths, those who have fallen from their caste, women in their courses, those in a state of birth-impurity, and outcasts.
One should always be characterized by forgiveness, generosity, compassion, truthfulness, and non-violence.
Contented and tranquil, likewise devoted to recitation and meditation,
he should perform the ritual bath at the three periods of the day, or alternatively, the bath with sacred ash;
and he should perform the special worship with his mind, speech, and voice.
What need is there for much speaking here? One who observes the vow must not perform anything inauspicious.

However, if such an act is committed through negligence, one should determine its gravity or lightness and perform the appropriate expiation through worship, fire-oblations, recitation, and other rites.
Until the vow is completed, one should practice in this manner without negligence. One should perform the gift of a cow, the rite of releasing a bull, and worship with abundant offerings.
Devoted and free from all worldly desires, one should do so for the sake of pleasing Śiva.
This general rule for this vow has been declared in brief.
Now I shall describe the specific details for each month as they have been heard.
In Vaiśākha, there is a vajra-liṅga; in Jyeṣṭha, an auspicious emerald one.
One should know that in the month of Āṣāḍha it is made of pearl; in Śrāvaṇa, it is fashioned from sapphire.
In the month of Bhādrapada, it is supremely composed of ruby.
One should know that in the month of Āśvina, the excellent liṅga is indeed made of *gomedaka*.
On the full moon of Kārttika, a liṅga made of coral; on Mārgaśīrṣa, one of lapis lazuli (vaidūrya);
on Pauṣa, one consisting of topaz (puṣparāga); and likewise on Māgha, one made of sapphire (dyumaṇi).
On Phālguna, it should be made from moonstone (candrakānta), and in Caitra, either that or the reverse order.
If jewels are not available in any month, [the vessel] should be made of gold; or,
in the absence of gold, it may be made of silver, copper, stone,
or likewise of clay, lac, or even some other material as available.

Or else, one may fashion a liṅga made entirely of all types of fragrances according to one’s preference. At the conclusion of the vow, having performed the daily rites and having offered the special worship as before, one should likewise perform the fire oblation.
Having thus honored the preceptor and especially those observing the vow,
and being permitted by the instructor, facing either the east or the north,

the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) for the gods and others, and the state of being a Lord (patitva) for Śiva,
exactly as it had been taught to Kṛṣṇa by the sage Upamanyu.
Thus I shall speak in brief; listen to that without distraction. Formerly, as Upamanyu was seated, Viṣṇu, assuming a dark form, prostrated himself according to the rule and spoke these words.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the divine Pāśupata knowledge and his entire majesty as spoken by the God to the Goddess."
"How is the god Paśupati [defined], and what are the *paśus* proclaimed to be?
By what fetters are they bound, and how are they liberated?
Thus was the illustrious Upamanyu questioned by the high-souled one.
Having prostrated before the God and the Goddess, Upamanyu, being fully restored, spoke accordingly.
Upamanyu said:
"From Brahmā down to the immovable [plants], all belong to the trident-bearing God of gods."

Those subject to the power of saṃsāra are proclaimed as *paśus* (bound souls). Because he is their lord, the Lord of Gods, Śiva, is remembered as Paśupati. As the Lord, he binds those *paśus* with fetters such as *mala* and *māyā*.
He alone, when properly worshipped with devotion, is the liberator of those [souls].
These twenty-four principles— Māyā, Karma, and the Guṇas—
are called "objects" (viṣayas), the fetters that bind the individual soul (jīva).
Having bound all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the Lord Maheśvara,
the divine Master, causes them to perform his own work through these fetters. By the command of that Great Lord, Prakṛti [brings about] what is appropriate for the Puruṣa.

That [Prakṛti] gives birth to the intellect (buddhi), and that intellect gives birth to the ego (ahaṃkāra). From the command of Śiva, the God of gods and bestower of auspiciousness, there likewise arise the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (tanmātra).
By his own most exalted command,
even the subtle elements (tanmātras) bring forth all the gross elements (mahābhūtas) in due succession,
resulting in the formation of bodies for all embodied beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
By the command of Śiva, they produce all the great elements without exception;
the intellect indeed determines, the ego conceives of "I," the mind perceives,
and the mental faculty also forms volitions.
And the ears and other [senses] individually apprehend their own respective objects, such as sound and the rest,
and not others, by means of the divine power of the Lord’s command.
Likewise, those which were the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, [also functioned accordingly].
Just as they perform their respective duties and nothing else by the command of Śiva,
