so too are sounds and other objects perceived, and speech and other actions performed;
for the most venerable command of Śambhu is indeed inviolable for all.
Space, which is omnipresent, provides room for all beings without exception solely by the command of the Supreme Lord;
likewise, through various names such as "prāṇa" and others, it exists both within and without the world.
By the command of Śarva, the wind-god sustains everything;

by the command of the Supreme Lord, Agni carries the sacrificial oblation (*havya*) to the gods and the ancestral offering (*kavya*) to the consumers of *kavya*, and he also performs cooking and other such tasks.
By his command, the waters perform for all [beings] the act of reviving and so forth;
by the command of the Lord of the Universe, the Earth constantly supports the world.
He protects the gods, slays the asuras, and guards the three worlds.
By his command— which cannot be transgressed by any of the gods— the Lord of the Gods,
Varuṇa, eternally exercises sovereignty over the waters;
and by his very decree, he binds with nooses those who deserve punishment.
The Lord of Yakṣas, the master of wealth, constantly bestows riches upon all beings in accordance with their merit, by virtue of his command over men;
he also perpetually grants prosperity and wisdom to those of excellent intellect.
And by the command of Śiva, Īśāna effects the suppression of the wicked;
and by the injunction of Śiva, Śeṣa supports the earth upon his head—
him whom they call the dark, fierce form of Hari that brings about his end.
By the command of the Lord, the four-faced Brahmā creates everything without exception;
through his other forms, he protects it and at the end, he destroys it.
Viṣṇu protects the universe by the command of the one who is the death of Death.

He creates and also causes trembling by means of his own three bodies; at the end, he withdraws the entire universe by the command of that very one. Furthermore, the Soul of the Universe, divided into three, protects while also creating.
Time creates everything; Time withdraws all beings.
By the command of the Time of Time, Time protects the universe. Sustaining the world with its three portions, it ordains the rain through its splendors.
By the command of the God of gods, that sun rains down upon the heavens;
it nourishes the various species of medicinal herbs and also brings delight to all living beings.
And by the command of the Moon-ornamented Lord (Śiva), the moon is drunk by the gods.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
the sky-dwellers, sages, Siddhas, serpents, humans, and wild animals;
as well as domestic animals, birds, insects and the like, and all immobile beings.
The rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, and lakes;
the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, the scriptures, the collections of mantras, the sacrifices, and so forth;
and the worlds beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva, together with their presiding deities.
Innumerable cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*), along with their coverings—
those that are present, those that have passed, and those yet to come— in their entirety;
as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions, the divisions of time, and the *kalās* and so forth.
Whatever is seen or even heard in this world,
all that is presided over by the power of Śaṅkara’s command.
By the power of his command, the earth, the mountains, the clouds, and the oceans remain established here.
The hosts of luminaries and the gods headed by Śakra—whatever exists, whether sentient or insentient, stable or transient.
Upamanyu said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, this is most wonderful regarding Śambhu, whose deeds are immeasurable."
Listen to this command which I have heard from the mouth of Śruti:
"In ancient times, it is said, the gods together with Indra were disputing with one another, each saying,
'I am the victor, I am the victor,' after having conquered the Asuras in battle."

Then Maheśvara, assuming a choice disguise from among them, appeared like a yakṣa himself, his limbs devoid of his own characteristic marks. Taking a single blade of grass upon the ground, he said to those gods: Śiva Purāṇa 7.2.2.47ab–48ab.
"He who is able to transform this is indeed the conqueror of the Daityas.
Having heard the words of the Yakṣa, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of Śacī,
somewhat enraged, laughed and prepared to seize him as if he were a blade of grass.

It was not even possible to pick up that blade of grass with the mind; nevertheless, Indra fashioned a thunderbolt to cut it down. That thunderbolt was as if completely fused with his own thunderbolt on all sides.
Struck by that blade of grass, it fell sideways with its tip pointing horizontally.
Thereupon, the other world-protectors, possessed of great strength and highly incensed,
discharged their weapons by the thousands toward that blade of grass.
The great fire blazed forth and a fierce wind blew,
like the swollen ocean when the time of universal dissolution has arrived.
Thus did the gods diligently set about their task, aiming at that blade of grass.
"Alas, O Kṛṣṇa, it was in vain that [the Yakṣa] acted by his own power!
Then, provoked to anger, the Lord of the Gods said to the Yakṣa, "Who are you?
Thereupon, even as they were looking on, he vanished.
In that interval, the goddess Haimavatī, adorned with divine ornaments,
appeared in the expanse of the sky, radiant and smiling with a pure smile.
Seeing her, the gods, led by Śakra, were filled with wonder.
Having prostrated before the Yakṣa, they asked, "Who is this extraordinary Yakṣa?
The Goddess replied with a smile, "He is beyond your comprehension;
by him this wheel called saṃsāra, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is made to revolve."
"By him the universe is first created, and by him it is withdrawn again.
There can be no one who governs him; by him everything is governed.
Having spoken thus, that Great Goddess vanished right there.
And all the gods, filled with wonder, bowed to her and departed for heaven.
Om. Thus ends the second chapter in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in its Uttarakhaṇḍa.
Chapter 3.
Upamanyu said:
Listen, O Kṛṣṇa, to [the glory] of Maheśa, Śiva, the Supreme Self;
by means of his forms and his own self, this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded.
That Śiva, whose nature is immeasurable, presides over all this very universe through his own forms;
for it is remembered that all this consists of Brahmā,
Viṣṇu, Rudra, Maheśāna, and Sadāśiva.
His forms are to be known as those by which this entire universe is pervaded.
Furthermore, there are five other bodies called the Brahmās;
by those bodies, nothing whatsoever exists here that is not permeated.
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and likewise Sadyojāta—
these are the five celebrated Brahmans, the forms of the Lord.
Among them, that form of his called Īśāna is the first and most venerable.

The Lord presides over the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is the direct enjoyer of primordial nature (prakṛti). That form of the embodied Lord known as Sthāṇu-Tatpuruṣa presides over the unmanifest (avyakta), which consists of the substratum of the qualities (guṇas) and is the object of enjoyment.
The principle of Intellect (buddhitattva) of the wielder of the Pināka bow, which is endowed with the eight qualities beginning with dharma,
is presided over by the form known as Aghora, which is most highly honored.
[He likewise presides over] the form of Mahādeva, the Creator, called Vāmadeva.

Those who know the scriptures say that the form of Śambhu, named Sadyojāta, possesses immeasurable splendor and is the presiding deity of the ego (ahaṃkṛti). The wise declare that the mental [form] is the presiding deity of the intellect (mati).

The wise know this sovereign power of the Lord, called Īśā, as the mistress of the ear, of speech, of sound, and likewise of the all-pervading ether; and they know her as the sovereign form of the skin, of the hand, of touch, and of the wind.

All those who are experts in the meaning of the Purāṇas know that which is called Puruṣa. The wise say that the presiding form of the eye, as well as of the feet, of form, and likewise of fire, is named Aghora.
They know the form called Vāmadeva to be the Sovereign (Īśvarī) presiding over the tongue, the anus, taste, and likewise water;
as well as over the sense of smell, the generative organ, odor, and earth.

They declare that the form called Sadyojāta is the Sovereign (Īśvarī). These five forms of the Lord are to be diligently worshipped by men seeking the highest good, for they are the sole causes of all blessings.
The universe consists of the eight forms of that God of gods;
pervading it, the entire world remains within him like clusters of gems on a thread.
[These forms are] Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, and Paśupati.
This is an archaic (ārṣa) compound lacking the case-ending [in the first member].
And Mahādeva is Īśāna, as are the eight renowned forms:
Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Space, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Sun, and the Moon.
Presided over by Maheśa through his eight forms beginning with Śarva,
she, whose nature is the sustainer of the universe, supports the entire world consisting of the moving and the unmoving;
this is the firm conclusion of the scripture regarding the form of Śiva known as Śārvī-Śivā.

Consisting of water, she is the source of life for the entire world; she is celebrated as the future form of the Supreme Self, Bhava. Pervading the universe both internally and externally, she is auspicious and composed of light.
Raudrī is the immutable form of Rudra, established in a terrible aspect;
she causes the one whose self is the wind to vibrate, she sustains him, and she vibrates by herself.
This form of the fierce Creator is called Aumgrī by the virtuous.
Providing space for all, pervading all, and having the nature of the sky;
she is the form of Bhīma known as Bhīmā, who shatters the hosts of beings;
she is the presiding deity of all souls and dwells in all sacred fields.
The form of Paśupati should be known as that which severs the bonds of the bound souls (paśu-pāśa).
Illuminating the entire world, it is called by the name Divākara (the Sun).
The form of the Great Lord known as Īśāna moves through the heavens.
That which nourishes the universe, the nectar-rayed maker of night,
is the form of Mahādeva known by the name Mahādeva.
The Self is the eighth form of that Śiva, the Supreme Soul.
Because the other forms are pervaded by Him, the universe is therefore of the nature of Śiva.
Just as the branches of a tree flourish through the watering of its root,
so too does this world-body flourish through the worship of Śiva.
They know that the granting of fearlessness to all, as well as the favoring of all,
and the performing of service for all, is the worship of Śiva.
Just as a father here becomes delighted through affection for his sons, grandsons, and so forth, [so does Śiva become pleased].

Likewise, Śaṅkara becomes pleased through the universal satisfaction [of all beings]. If restraint is exercised against any embodied being whatsoever, that is undoubtedly performed against the Eight-formed One (Aṣṭamūrti) himself; of this there is no doubt.

Worship with your whole being Śiva, who stands presiding over the universe through his eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti), Rudra, the supreme cause. Om. Thus ends the third chapter in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 4.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Blessed One, [tell me] of Śarva, the Supreme Lord of immeasurable splendor.
I have heard that this entire universe is pervaded by their forms;
now I wish to know the true nature of these two lords,
and how this world, consisting of the states of female and male, is presided over by them.
Upamanyu said:
"I shall describe in brief the glorious majesty and the true nature of Śiva and Śivā;
to speak of it in detail would be impossible even for Bhava himself."
Śakti is the Great Goddess herself, and Mahādeva is the possessor of Śakti. Indeed, this entire world of moving and non-moving things is but a mere fragment of their sovereign power (vibhūtileśa).
Whatever object exists, some portion of it is insentient in nature, while another portion consists of consciousness.

There is a duality: the pure and the impure, the supreme and the non-supreme. That wheel of consciousness which revolves, accompanied by the wheel of the insentient, is the impure and non-supreme; the other, however, is the supreme and auspicious.
Furthermore, both this world and the beyond consist of the dual nature of consciousness and unconsciousness;
and by their very nature, this sovereignty belongs to Śiva and Śivā.
Indeed, the entire universe is under the control of Śiva and Śivā, but Śiva and Śivā are not under the control of the universe.
Since this [universe] is that which is to be ruled, therefore both Śiva and Śivā are the Lords of the Universe.
As is Śiva, so is the Goddess; as is the Goddess, so is Śiva. One should perceive no difference between these two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight.

Indeed, this moon does not shine without its moonlight; likewise, Śiva does not shine even though he exists without Śakti. For just as this sun is not perceived without its radiance, so it is with him.
And the radiance, depending upon that sun, shines all the more intensely.
Thus, the relationship of power and the possessor of power exists through mutual dependence;
there is no power without Śiva, and no Śiva without power.
That by which Śiva is eternally capable regarding the devotion and liberation of embodied beings—
she is that one primordial, supreme Power (*parā śakti*), consisting of consciousness (*cinmayī*) and resting in Śiva;
her they call [the power] of the Lord of All, according to his various corresponding qualities.
She alone is the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), whose nature is consciousness, sharing the same attributes as Śiva, the Supreme Self; she possesses the quality of procreation and,
by the will of Śiva, divides the universe manifoldly and brings it forth.
That primordial nature is Māyā, consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), and is remembered as being threefold;
it is by this Śivayā that this entire world is pervaded,
both as one, as two, and likewise as a hundred thousandfold.
Indeed, the powers (śaktis) are divided manifoldly according to worldly convention.
By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (parā-śakti) attains oneness with the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva).
Thereafter, at the beginning of creation, it vibrates forth like oil from a sesame seed.
Then, by means of the power called Kriyā (Action), which arises from the Possessor of Power (Śaktimat) within Śakti,
as that [power] was being agitated, Nāda first emerged.
From Nāda issued Bindu, and from Bindu came the Lord Sadāśiva.
From him Maheśvara was born, and from Maheśvara came Śuddhavidyā.

She is the sovereign power (*īśvarī*) of speech, known as Vāgīśā, belonging indeed to the Wielder of the Trident (*Śūlin*). She, moreover, unfolds even as the *Mātṛkā* in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*).

Then, through infinite immersion, Māyā brought forth Time (kāla), as well as Necessity (niyati), Limited Agency (kalā), and Knowledge (vidyā); from Limited Agency [arose] Attachment (rāga) and the Individual Soul (puruṣa). From Māyā, moreover, there came into being the Unmanifest (avyakta), which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
From that manifest [state] consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), the three qualities become distinct:
namely, sattva, rajas, and tamas, by which the entire world is pervaded. From these qualities being agitated, the three forms known as the Lords of the Qualities (guṇeśa) arise.
The principles beginning with Mahat arose in their proper sequence;
and by the command of Śiva, from them there emerged innumerable cosmic eggs (aṇḍas) and individual bodies (piṇḍas),
presided over by the sovereign Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) such as Ananta and others.
The divisions of power (śakti) are proclaimed according to the distinctions between different bodies;
they should be understood as having various forms through the differentiation of gross and subtle.
That power of Rudra is Raudrī, while that of Viṣṇu is indeed considered Vaiṣṇavī.

Brahmāṇī is said to belong to Brahmā, and Indrāṇī is called the consort of Indra. What is the use of saying more here? That which is celebrated as the universe is pervaded by His own nature, just as the inner self pervades the body.
Therefore, the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of power (*śakti*). That which is called the supreme *kalā* is the power of the Supreme Self.
Thus, this supreme power follows the will of the Lord.
It is certain that he creates the entire universe, both the stable and the moving.
By means of his three innate powers— knowledge, action, and the desire to act—
the omnipotent Lord eternally presides over the universe, pervading it entirely.

The power of will (icchā-śakti) of the Great Lord consists of the thought, "Let this be thus, let this not be thus"; it is eternal and the regulator of effects. The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), however, is its effect, as well as its instrument and its cause.

The intellect determines the purpose in its true nature; then the power of action (kriyā-śakti), taking the form of volition (saṃkalpa), fashions the entire world of effects in an instant, exactly as desired and exactly as determined.
Just as she who possesses the nature of giving birth to power gives rise to the three powers,
being impelled by the Supreme Power (paramā śakti), she brings forth the entire universe;
even so, through union with power, Śiva is called "the Possessor of Power" (śaktimān).

This world arises from Śakti and the Possessor of Śakti; it is Śaiva in nature. Just as a son is not born without a father and a mother, so too this world of moving and non-moving beings does not exist without Bhava and Bhavānī.
The universe originates from woman and man, and it consists essentially of woman and man.
It is the manifestation of woman and man, and it is presided over by woman and man. Śiva is declared to be the Supreme Self, and she is celebrated as Śivā.
Śiva is declared to be Sadāśiva, and Śivā is Manonmanī;
Śiva is to be known as Maheśvara, and Śivā is called Māyā.
Puruṣa is the Supreme Lord (Parameśāna), and Prakṛti is the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī).
Rudra is Maheśvara himself, and Rudrāṇī is the beloved of Rudra.
Viṣṇu is the god Viśveśvara, and Lakṣmī is the beloved of Viśveśvara. When Śiva is Brahmā the creator, Brahmāṇī is the beloved of Brahmā.

The Lord Bhāskara is Śambhu; the Goddess Prabhā is Śivā. Maheśvara is Manmathārāti (the enemy of Kāma); Śacī is the Daughter of the Mountain King. Jātavedas is Mahādeva; Svāhā is she whose body is half of Śarva.
The god Yama is Tryambaka, and his beloved is Girikanyakā;
the lord Nirṛti is Īśa, and Nairṛtī is the daughter of the mountain;
the lord Varuṇa is Rudra, and Vāruṇī is the daughter of Bhūdhara.
The moon-crested one is Vāyu; Śivā is the one who captivates the heart of Śiva.
The Yakṣa is the one who took the head of the sacrifice; Ṛddhi is the daughter of the lord of the snowy mountains.
The one with the crescent moon as his crest is Candra; Rohiṇī is the beloved of Rudra.

Īśāna is the Supreme Lord, and Āryā is the Supreme Goddess; Ananta is the one with infinite coils, and Anantā is the beloved of Ananta. Kālāgnirudra is the enemy of Time, and Kālī is the beloved of the Ender of Time.
Manu, known as Puruṣa, is Śambhu; Śatarūpā is the beloved of Śiva.
Dakṣa is Mahādeva himself, and Prasūti is the Supreme Goddess. Ruci is Bhava, and Bhavānī is called Ākūti by the wise.
The divine Bhṛgu is the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes; Khyāti is the beloved of the Three-eyed One.
The venerable Marīci is Rudra; Saṃbhūti is the beloved of Śarva.
Aṅgiras is to be known as Gaṅgādhara; Smṛti is said to be Umā herself.

Pulastya, whose crest is the moon, and Prīti, the beloved of the wielder of the Pināka bow; Pulaha, the destroyer of Tripura, and Śivapriyā, his beloved; Kratu, the destroyer of the sacrifice (Kratudhvaṃsī), is proclaimed as Kratu, and Saṃnati is the wife of that Lord.
The three-eyed one is Atri himself, and Umā is known by the wise as Anasūyā;
Kaśyapa is the god Kālahā, and Maheśvarī is the mother of the gods;
Vasiṣṭha is the enemy of Manmatha, and the goddess is Arundhatī herself.
All males are Śaṃkara, and all females are Maheśvarī.
Therefore, all men and women are the manifestations (vibhūtis) of those two alone.
The Blessed Lord Īśa is the subject (viṣayin), and the Supreme Goddess is the object (viṣaya).
The entire form of Umā is that which is to be heard, while the listener is he whose weapon is the excellent trident.
The aggregate of all things to be asked about is held by the beloved of Śaṅkara;
the questioner himself is that Soul of the Universe who is adorned with the crescent moon.
The beloved of the Speaker bears the form of the object to be seen;
the Lord Viśveśvara, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, is the seer.
The Great Goddess is the collection of tastes; the God Śiva is the taster.
The daughter of the mountain is the object of love, and the consumer of poison is the beloved;
thus the Great Goddess, Maheśvarī, eternally constitutes the state of the object of thought.
He alone, the Great God Maheśvara, the soul of the universe, is the thinker.
The beloved of worldly existence bears the form of the object to be known;
the Blessed Lord whose crest is the crescent moon is the knower of that very deity.
The Blessed Lord, the Master, is the vital breath (prāṇa) of all living beings.
The life-force of all beings is Ambikā, who exists in the form of water;
the Goddess, beloved of the Destroyer of Tripura, maintains the state of being the field (kṣetra).
Then, the Blessed Lord, the Slayer of Death, assumes the state of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
The god who has the trident as his weapon is Day, and Night is dear to the one who holds the trident in his hand.
The god Śaṅkara is Space, and Pṛthivī is dear to Śaṅkara.
The Blessed Lord Īśa is the Ocean, and the Daughter of the Mountain King is the Shoreline.
The tree belongs to the bull-bannered god, and the creeper to the beloved of the Lord of the Universe.
The Blessed Lord, the Subduer of Cities, assumes every masculine gender,
while the goddess, the delight of the gods, assumes every feminine gender.
She who is beloved by all bears the entire web of words without exception;
the one whose crest is the charming moon bears the entire nature of their meanings.
Whatever power is proclaimed for whichever object, [it is she who sustains it].
She is that very Goddess, the Sovereign of All; he is that very One, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
Whatever is supreme, whatever is purifying, whatever is meritorious, and whatever is auspicious—all that, O highly fortunate ones, is said to be the manifestation of the splendor of those two.
Just as the flame of a burning lamp illuminates a house,
so does this splendor of those two pervade and illuminate the world,
from blades of grass up to the form of Śiva, in a progressive sequence of increasing universal manifestation.
"Because of the sequence of their proximity, such is the supreme revelation.
These two, who consist of every form and bestow all that is auspicious,
are to be worshipped, saluted, and meditated upon at all times."

O Kṛṣṇa, this true nature of the two Supreme Lords has indeed been told by me to you today according to my wisdom; yet it cannot be fully encompassed by such a measure. For how is it possible to express the true nature of the two Supreme Lords in its entirety?
Even for all those great ones, [the Lord] has gone beyond the mind;
yet for those whose minds are focused on no other and are offered unto the Lord, He has entered within.
For others, He is not ascended upon the intellect, while for these, He is indeed ascended just as He is.
This manifestation that has been described is indeed considered the supreme *prakṛta* (natural) form;
however, those who know the secret understand another supreme form which is *aprākṛta* (non-natural) and hidden,
from which speech, along with the mind and the senses, turns back.
This supreme, non-material majesty belongs to the Supreme Lord;
it alone is the highest abode here, it alone is the supreme goal here,
and it alone is the ultimate limit of the majesty of the Supreme Being.

Those who have conquered their breath and subdued their senses strive here to attain that [state], just as those confined in a prison strive to close the door of their cell without any opening— to obtain the life-restoring medicine for one bitten by the venomous serpent of saṃsāra.

The wise man who knows the majesty of the two Śivas does not fear anything from any quarter. He who truly understands both the supreme and the non-supreme majesty transcends the non-supreme majesty and attains the supreme majesty.

"O Kṛṣṇa, this true nature of the two Supreme Souls has been told to you. Although it is a secret, I have revealed it because you are a worthy devotee of Bharga. It must never be disclosed to those who are not disciples, nor to those who are not Śaivas, nor to those who lack devotion."
"One should speak of the Bhūti of the two Lords; such is the instruction of the Vedas.
Therefore, you must not tell this to those who are not devoted to supreme auspiciousness. Tell this only to those like you who are worthy, and not otherwise."
Whoever causes this manifestation of the two Śivas to be bestowed upon those who are worthy shall be liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra and attain union with Śiva;
by the recitation of this, millions of great sins are destroyed.
By practicing [the mantra] three or four times, those who are greater than that are destroyed;
thus, undesirable enemies perish and friends likewise prosper.
Furthermore, the Śaiva knowledge increases and the intellect is directed toward truth.

If one has supreme devotion to Śiva—along with Ambā, his attendants, and his retinue—he undoubtedly obtains whatever else is most dear to him. If a devotee, pure within and full of confidence, should praise Śiva; ŚivP_7.2,4.88ab/

If the fruit [of one's practice] is obstructed by powerful past karmas, one should practice it again and again; for such a person, nothing in this world is difficult to attain. Om. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Manifestation of Gaurī and Śaṅkara," in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 5.
Upamanyu said:
This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is the body of the God of gods. *Śiva Purāṇa* 7.2, 5.1ab.
Thus, due to the weight of their bonds, these bound souls do not recognize Him;
O descendant of Yadu, they speak of that One alone as being manifold.
Not knowing the supreme state, which is free from conceptual construction, even the great seers [speak thus].
Some say that Mahādeva is the supreme being, without beginning or end, who is both the form of the lower Brahman and the essence of the higher Brahman;
he who consists of the elements, the senses, the internal organs, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and the objects of the senses.
The lower Brahman has been pointed out, while the higher Brahman consists of consciousness.
It is called "Brahman" because of its vastness (*bṛhatva*) or because of its expanding nature (*bṛhaṇatva*).
Both of these are forms of Brahman, the sovereign Lord.
Some declare that the Lord has both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) as his essential nature.
They say that knowledge is consciousness (*cetana*), while ignorance is unconsciousness (*acetana*).
Thus, the entire universe consists of both knowledge and ignorance belonging to the all-pervading Teacher of the World.
Form alone is not subject to doubt, since the universe is under its control.
They know that delusion (*bhrānti*) and supreme knowledge (*vidyā*) are the supreme form of Śiva.
Delusion is said to be the manifold misapprehension of objects.
The cognition of an object according to its true form is proclaimed as *vidyā* (knowledge).
That reality which is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is designated as the Supreme (*param*).
By contrast, that which is the opposite is called "non-existent" (*asat*) by the exponents of the Vedas.
Because he has fallen upon those two, Śiva is called the Lord of both the existent and the non-existent (sadasatpati).
They say he consists of the perishable and the imperishable, yet he is superior to both the perishable and the imperishable;
the perishable is all beings, while the one who remains fixed (kūṭastha) is called the imperishable.
Both of these are forms of the Supreme Lord, since they are under His control.
Beyond those two is Śiva, the peaceful one, who is remembered as being distinct from both the perishable and the imperishable.
He is the form of both the collective whole and the individual parts, and the cause of both the collective whole and the individual parts.
Some sages declare Śiva to be the supreme cause;
they say that the unmanifest is the totality (samaṣṭi) and likewise the manifest is the individuality (vyaṣṭi). These two are the forms of the Supreme Lord, brought forth by His will.

Those who understand the meaning of "cause" declare that Śiva is the supreme cause by virtue of being the cause of those two [the generic and the individual], acting as both the collective and the individual cause. Some describe the Lord as having the nature of both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).

That which follows along with the individual body (piṇḍa) is called "jāti" (the universal). Individuality (vyakti), which consists of differentiation, is that which rests upon the body and the universal.
Both universals and individuals are governed by His command.
Therefore, Mahādeva is remembered as having the body of both genus and individual manifestation;
Śiva is declared to be the self consisting of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla.
They call Pradhāna "Prakṛti" (Nature), and likewise, they call Puruṣa "Kṣetrajña" (the Knower of the Field).
The wise declare that the twenty-three principles constitute the manifest.
Time is the sole cause of the transformation of the entire expansion of effects.
Of these, He is the Lord, the Sovereign, the Sustainer, the initiator and the withdrawer.
The one, self-ruling, unborn cause of manifestation and disappearance possesses the nature of Pradhāna,
Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla. Therefore,
Maheśvara is declared to be their cause, leader, lord, and creator.
Some declare the Lord to be Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Ātman;
Hiraṇyagarbha is the cause of the worlds, while Virāṭ is the soul of the universe. Śiva is described by the wise as both the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) and the Supreme.
Others declare that the wise one is the self of the Taijasa and Viśva;
others call him the Fourth (Turiya), while others know him as the Auspicious One alone.
Still others say he is the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the intellect.
Others declare that the agent, the action, the effect, the instrument, and the cause are [the five states];
others describe them as consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
others speak of the fourth (turiya); and still others of that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
Some call him devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), while others know him as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*).
Some declare him to be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārī*), while others say he is beyond such existence (*asaṃsārī*).
Others declare him to be independent (*svatantra*), while others know him as dependent (*asvatantra*).
Some say he is terrible, while others know him as truly gentle;
some say he possesses passion, while others likewise say he is free from passion;
some say he is inactive, and other people say he is active.
Some say he is without senses, while others say he possesses senses;
some call him eternal, while others consider him non-eternal.
Some indeed say he is formless, while others know him as possessing form.
Some declare him to be invisible, while others know him as visible;
some declare him to be expressible, and others that he is inexpressible.
Some declare him to consist of sound, while others say he transcends sound.
Some say it consists of thought, while others say it is devoid of thought;
some say its nature is knowledge, and others call it higher consciousness (vijñāna).
Some say it is the knowable, and some say it is the unknowable.
Some call him the Supreme, while others likewise call him the Non-Supreme. Thus,
when the true nature of the Parameṣṭhin is conceptualized in this way,
the sages do not reach a definitive conclusion because of their diverse points of view.
But those who have surrendered to the Supreme Lord with their whole being,
they indeed know Śiva, the supreme cause, without effort.
As long as a bound soul does not behold the ancient Lord of the universe, the Sovereign, [he remains in bondage].
Bound by the fetters, he remains in this cycle of transmigratory existence, enduring suffering according to the rotation of a wheel's rim.
But when the seer beholds the golden-hued one— the Creator, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman—
then the wise man, having shaken off both merit and sin, becomes stainless and attains the supreme state of equanimity.
Oṃ. Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Knowledge regarding the State of Paśupati," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh part of the Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa. 1.

Regarding the term *anīśa*: although it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom there is no Lord (*īśa*)," that interpretation requires a strained construction; however, the meaning is more easily understood in the reading *yāvat paśuś ceśvaraṃ na prapaśyet* ("as long as the bound soul (*paśu*) does not perceive the Lord").

2. As for the reading *yadā paśyo vīkṣate rukmam*, it involves a break in the sequence of the grammatical construction (*bhagnaprakrama*); therefore, the correct resolution is simply that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). (550b)
Chapter 6.
Upamanyu said: For Śiva, there is no bondage consisting of *aṇava* or even that which is *māyīya*. ŚivaP 7.2, 6.1ab.
Whether he be an ordinary person or a knower, he is likewise composed of the nature of ego (ahaṃkāra).
For him, there is no mental bondage, nor any belonging to the mind (citta), nor that consisting of the senses;
nor is there any bondage of the subtle elements (tanmātra), nor any bondage of the gross elements (bhūta) whatsoever.
Neither time nor its divisions exist, nor do knowledge and destiny;
there is neither passion nor aversion in Śambhu of immeasurable splendor. Furthermore, he has no attachment, nor does he possess either virtuous or non-virtuous qualities.
Karmas and their maturation, as well as pleasure and pain which are their fruits,
have no connection with latent dispositions (*āśaya*), nor with the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of actions,
nor with enjoyments and the impressions of enjoyment pertaining to the three periods of time.
For him there is no cause, no agent, nor beginning, end, or interval;
neither action nor instrument, nor that which is not to be done, nor that which is to be done;
he has neither kinsman nor stranger, nor ruler, nor instigator.
He has neither husband nor teacher, neither protector nor superior, nor likewise any equal.
For him there is neither birth nor death, neither the desired nor the undesired. There is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither liberation nor bondage.
Whatever is inauspicious does not exist for him at any time,
and all that is auspicious exists [for him], because Śiva is the Supreme Self. That Śiva, presiding over all this very universe through his own powers, [is the source].

Because its own nature does not fall away, it is remembered as the "Stable One" (Sthāṇu). Since the world, both moving and unmoving, is presided over by Śiva, Śarva is remembered as being of all forms; knowing this, one is not deluded.
Śarva, Rudra—salutations to him! He is the Puruṣa, the supreme, the Great One;
the golden-armed Blessed One, the Lord of gold, the Sovereign;
the husband of Ambikā, the Ruler, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose vehicle is the bull.
Rudra is the one Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny;
he, the size of the tip of a hair, is to be meditated upon within the heart, inside the small cavity (dahara).
He has golden hair, lotus-like eyes, and is indeed ruddy and copper-colored.
He who advances is that god, blue-necked and golden-hued;
he is gentle, terrible, and mixed, imperishable, immortal, and undecaying.
He is the supreme, distinguished Person, the Blessed Lord, the destroyer of Death himself.
Free from both volition and the unconscious, and beyond the manifold world, he is higher than the highest.
When knowledge and sovereignty are perceived as being surpassed by Śiva,
the wise declare that [the Lord] exists as one who surpasses even the lords of the worlds.
He alone was, in the beginning, the instructor of the expansion of the scriptures for the Brahmas produced during each successive dissolution who exist within the constraints of time;
he is also the teacher of those very gurus who are likewise subject to the limitations of time.
The Lord of all is indeed the master of all, devoid of limitation by time;
His power is pure, innate, and surpasses all others.
His knowledge is incomparable and eternal, and His form is utterly uncreated.
Sovereignty without rival, absolute bliss, strength,
splendor, majesty, valor, as well as forbearance and compassion—
since he is complete through the acts of creation and the rest, there is no purpose for the Self.
The fruit of every action of his is indeed the favoring of others.
The syllable *praṇava* (Om) is the designator of that Śiva, the Supreme Self;
for the *praṇava* is traditionally held to be superior even to words such as "Śiva" and "Rudra."
O Śambhu, that perfection which is attained by dwelling upon and by the recitation of the Praṇava—which is denoted by You—is indeed the supreme attainment;
of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, those who have reached the further shore of the Āgamas declare You, O Lord, to be the Single Syllable (Ekākṣara).
Considering the identity of the signified and the signifier,
the wise have declared its four measures at the summit of the Veda:
the letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and also the resonance (*nāda*).
They say that the syllable *a* is the Rigveda, the syllable *u* is called the Yajurveda, and the syllable *ma* is the Sāmaveda;
the Atharvaveda is remembered as the sound of this [syllable *om*].
Furthermore, the syllable *a* is the great seed, the quality of passion (*rajas*), and the four-faced Creator.

The syllable *ukāra* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the womb; it is the essence (*sattva*), the protector Hari. The syllable *makāra* is the person (*puruṣa*), the seed; it is darkness (*tamas*), the destroyer Hara.
The *nāda* is the supreme Person, the Lord, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), free from action (*niṣkriya*), the Auspicious One (*śiva*).
Having designated this entire universe in its threefold form through these very three measures (*mātrās*),
it awakens the Self that is Śiva by means of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*).
For there is nothing whatsoever beyond it, nor anything smaller or greater than it.
Like a tree, He stands alone, motionless in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is filled.
Om. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Śiva-Tattva," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 7.
Upamanyu said:
His power is innate, and his knowledge is distinct from all else;
it shines in both singular and manifold forms, like the radiance of the sun.

She possesses infinite powers, such as will, knowledge, and action; and from her, Māyā and the others have arisen, just as sparks arise from fire. Indeed, [from her come] Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and the rest, as well as Vidyā, the lords of Avidyā (Avidyeśvaras), and so forth.
The Puruṣas and her Prakṛti, which is higher than the highest,
as well as the forms beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas, along with Aja and the others—
all that exists else is her effect; of this there is no doubt.
That power is all-pervading, subtle, and consists of the nature of awakening and bliss.
The Lord Śiva, adorned with the moon, is said to be the possessor of that power (Śaktimat).
Śiva is the object of knowledge; Śivā is wisdom, as well as intelligence, the Vedas, and the Smṛtis.
This is steadfastness, stability, and finality; it is the powers of knowledge, will, and action;
it is the command and the supreme Brahman; it is both the higher and lower knowledge (*vidyā*);
it is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and pure limited agency (*śuddhakalā*), since everything is produced by power (*śakti*).

She is Māyā, Prakṛti, the individual soul (jīva), transformation (vikāra), and likewise the transformed (vikṛti). Whatever is non-existent and whatever is existent—all this is pervaded by her. That Goddess, through her Māyā, [pervades] the entire cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) with all its moving and unmoving beings.
She deludes effortlessly and liberates with ease;
together with her, who has twenty-seven forms, the Lord of All pervades the universe and remains therein. Therefore, liberation proceeds from this [union].
In ancient times, certain sages who were seekers of liberation and exponents of Brahman, their minds possessed by doubt, reflected upon the matter as it truly is:
"What is the cause? From where have we been born? And by what do we live?"
Where is our firm foundation, and by whom are we presided over?
By whom do we perpetually abide in pleasures and other states at all times?
And by whom was this inviolable order of the universe established?
In this matter, it is not logical to claim that time, inherent nature, necessity, or chance [is the cause].
Rather, the elements, the womb, the person, or the yogi is the supreme among these;
for while time and the rest are insentient, the self possesses sentience.
Because pleasure and pain are derived from the elements and lack autonomy, they are investigated;
for one who follows the yoga of meditation perceives that divine power (*aiśvarī śakti*),
which directly severs the bonds, though it is intensely concealed by its own qualities.
With their bonds severed by her, they beheld with divine vision Mahādeva, the possessor of power, the cause of all causes;
he who [is the source] of all causes without exception, together with Time and the Self.
He who presides over everything by means of this immeasurable power—
through the yoga of grace, through supreme yoga,
and through the visible yoga of devotion— attains the divine goal.

Therefore, those who behold Śiva in their hearts together with His power (śakti) attain eternal peace; for others, it is not so—this is the Vedic revelation. Indeed, there is never any separation between the possessor of power and His power.
Therefore, because of the identity between power and the possessor of power, the accomplishment of both occurs simultaneously;
yet, a sequence of knowledge and action is certainly intended regarding liberation.
For when grace is present, that form [of the Lord] rests as if in the palm of one's hand.
Whether a god, a dānava, a beast, or even a bird;
whether a parrot or even a worm—one is liberated by his grace.
Whether situated in the womb, being born, a child, or even a youth.
Whether old or dying, whether dwelling in heaven or in hell,
whether fallen or righteous, whether learned or even a fool—
a virtuous soul is liberated at that very moment by His grace; of this there is no doubt.

Out of compassion for even those who are unworthy, the Supreme Lord becomes gracious toward his devotees; of this there is no doubt. Having seized hold of their various impurities, he is pleased. Indeed, that devotion arises from his grace, and grace itself is born of devotion.

Having discerned the distinctions between these states, the wise man is not deluded therein. This [grace] which precedes favor and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation cannot be attained by men in a single lifetime.

Maheśvara is pleased with those who have attained perfection over many births, who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti, who are dispassionate, and who are awakened. When that Lord of Gods is pleased, he acts toward that bound soul (paśu).
The thought "I have a protector" is a small degree of devotion preceded by intellectual understanding.
Through various forms of asceticism and Śaiva duties, a person becomes united with [the Lord].
In that yoga, through its practice, supreme devotion arises.
And through that supreme devotion, the highest grace is obtained.

From grace comes liberation from all fetters; for one who is liberated, there is bliss. Even that mortal who possesses only a small measure of devotion, after three births at most, [attains the goal].
It will not lead to the suffering of the womb-contraption; of this there is no doubt.
Service that is both with limbs and without limbs is called devotion (*bhakti*).
That, moreover, is divided threefold according to the means of mind, speech, and body.
That which consists of meditating upon the form and other attributes of Śiva is known as mental service (*mānasī sevā*).

Verbal service (*vācikī sevā*) includes recitation (*japa*) and so forth, while physical service (*kāyikī sevā*) consists of ritual action (*karma*), worship (*pūjā*), and the like. This service, accomplished through these three means, is called the *Śivadharma*.
That [discipline] is declared by Śiva, the Supreme Self, to be fivefold in brief:

austerity, ritual action, recitation, meditation, and knowledge. Ritual action consists of the worship of the *liṅga* and so forth, while austerity includes the *cāndrāyaṇa* fast and other such practices.

Recitation (*japa*) is the threefold practice of Śiva, while meditation (*dhyāna*) is contemplation of Śiva. That knowledge which is declared in the Śiva-āgamas is what is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) here. The Śiva-āgama was spoken by Śiva, the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha, to Śivā.

Out of compassion for those who have taken refuge in Śiva, [he is] the sole means for attaining all that is auspicious. Therefore, a wise man seeking his own welfare should increase his devotion toward Śiva, the supreme cause, and abandon attachment to sense objects.
Om. Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Śiva-Tattva," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 8.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear that knowledge of Śiva,
spoken by Śiva himself, which is the essence of the Vedas and leads to the liberation of those who take refuge in it;
[a knowledge] that is beyond the reach of the non-devotees, the unintelligent, and the undisciplined."
Endowed with ten and five topics, it is profound and censured by the unwise;

in some respects it is contrary to the duties (dharma) established for the castes and stages of life, yet in others it is identical to them. Having extracted [the essence] entirely from the Veda with its six limbs, as well as from Sāṃkhya and Yoga—
It was spoken by the Supreme Lord as being extensive, numbering one hundred crore verses. In that [work], O Lord, how is the worship of the Master described?
Who has the authority for the worship and other rites, and how do knowledge, yoga, and so forth proceed?
"O you of noble vows, you ought to explain all of that in detail.
Upamanyu said:
"The Śaiva [teaching], as declared in the Vedas and expounded by Śiva in brief—"
Free from praise, blame, and the like, it is the cause of immediate conviction;
born of the grace of the Guru, divine, and bestowing liberation without effort—
I shall relate it in brief, for its full expansion cannot be grasped.
In the past, out of a desire to create, the Lord Śiva— the immovable Maheśvara— manifested himself from the unmanifest,
endowed with both cause and effect as his true nature. Then that Lord, the seer who transcends the universe, brought [the world] forth.
Brahmā beheld the first god of the gods, Brahmā,
the Lord of the Veda (Brahmaṇaspati), as he was being born;
and that divine father beheld him, his son, as he was being born, by his own command.
Beheld by Rudra, that Lord, the Sovereign, emitted the universe;
he established the distinct regulations for the social classes and stages of life.
He created Soma for the sake of sacrifice, and from Soma, heaven was born.
The Earth, Fire, the Sun, Sacrifice, Viṣṇu, and the Lord of Śacī—
these and other gods praised Rudra with the Rudrādhyāya.
With a gracious countenance, the Lord stood before the gods.

Having withdrawn their knowledge for the sake of his own sport, Maheśvara, the gods, being thus deluded, then asked him: "Who are you? He, the Blessed Lord Rudra, replied: "I alone am the ancient one."
"O best of gods, I alone existed in the beginning;
I shall exist in the future as well, and there is no one else distinct from me.
I alone satisfy the entire universe with my own splendor."

"There is none superior to me, nor is there one equal to me; he who knows me is liberated. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished right there. Not seeing that Īśāna, they continued to praise him with Sāman hymns.
Having performed the Pāśupata vow established in the Atharvaśiras,
the immortals then became covered entirely in ashes.
Then, for the sake of bestowing grace upon them, the Lord, the Master of Creatures (Paśupati), [appeared].
The Lord, together with his attendants and accompanied by Umā, made his presence known there.
That God, whom sleepless yogis— having conquered their breath and burnt away their sins—
behold within their hearts, was seen by those foremost of gods.
Those who have shaken off saṃsāra and attained the supreme state of Śiva do not behold that Vāmalocanā of Maheśa, whom they call the supreme power that follows the will of the Lord.

And those other lords of the Gaṇas who are eternally perfected were also seen there. Then the gods, together with the Goddess, praised Maheśvara with divine hymns to Maheśvara and with ancient (paurāṇika) chants.
The god whose banner is the bull, having looked upon the gods with compassion, spoke these words, naturally sweet, being well-pleased: "I am satisfied.
Then, having prostrated before the bull-bannered god whose mind was well-pleased—
The gods respectfully asked him about this most significant matter.
The gods said:
"O Blessed One, by what path are you to be worshipped on the surface of the earth?"
"Whose authority regarding worship is it? You should tell me this according to the truth.
Then, having looked at the Goddess with a smile, Hara, the best of gods, revealed his own supreme form, which was terrible and of the nature of the sun.
Endowed with all sovereign qualities, consisting entirely of splendor, and supreme;
surrounded by powers (śaktis), forms (mūrtis), limbs (aṅgas), planets (grahas), and deities;
having eight arms, four faces, and the wondrous form of half-woman (ardhanārīka).
Having seen this wondrous form, the gods, led by Viṣṇu,
recognized the god Divākara (the Sun), as well as the goddess Niśākara (the Moon),
the remaining five elements, and all that is moving and unmoving as being composed of them.
Having spoken thus, they indeed paid homage to him and offered him the *arghya*—
to you who are the color of vermilion, who possess a beautiful mandala, and who wear ornaments of golden hue;
to you whose eyes resemble lotuses, who hold a lotus, and who are the cause of Brahmā, Indra, and Nārāyaṇa.

"O Blessed One, please be gracious; accept this excellent *arghya* offered with a golden vessel, filled with precious gems, containing water with gold, saffron and other fragrances, along with *kuśa* grass and flowers. Homage to Śiva, the peaceful one, who is accompanied by his attendants and is the primordial cause."
The use of the *parasmaipada* ending is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).
To Rudra, to Viṣṇu, to You, to Brahman in the form of the Sun—[he who, being composed, has worshipped Śiva in the solar mandala]...
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, one should offer the excellent *arghya* oblation;
or one should prostrate and recite these verses which have the Vedas as their source.
For such a person, nothing is difficult to attain; if he is a devoted follower, he is surely liberated.
Therefore, one should constantly worship Śiva, who has the form of the Sun,
with mind, action, and speech, for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation.
Then, having looked upon the gods, Maheśvara, stationed within the mandala, [spoke].

Having bestowed this scripture, which is the supreme among all scriptures, Hara vanished. Having understood that "this entitlement to worship therein belongs to the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas," the gods bowed to the Lord of Gods and departed as they had come.
Then, after a long time, when that scripture had disappeared,
Maheśvarī, seated upon his lap, questioned her husband.
Thus urged by the Goddess, the Moon-ornamented Lord [responded].
Raising his hand, he spoke this scripture, the supreme among all traditions:
"And it was set forth in the world by my command, O Parameṣṭhin,
by me, by Agastya, by the teacher, and by the great seer Dadhīca."
Descending himself to the earth during the cycles of the Yugas,
the wielder of the trident (Śiva) establishes a lineage of knowledge for the sake of the liberation of those who take refuge in him.
O twice-born ones, these are Ṛbhu, Satya, Bhārgava, Aṅgiras, and Savitṛ.
Mṛtyu, Śatakratu, the wise Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages;
Sārasvata, Tridhāman, and Trivṛta, the bull among sages;
Śatatejas, Dharma himself, and he who is known as Nārāyaṇa.
Svarakṣa, the wise Āruṇi, and likewise Kṛtañjaya; Kṛtañjaya, Bharadvāja, Gautama, and the supreme sage Kavi;
the sage Vācaḥsravas himself, as well as the pure Sūkṣmāyaṇi.

The sage Tṛṇabindu was Kṛṣṇa; the supreme Śākteya was Śakti; Jātūkarṇya was Hari himself; and the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was Vyāsa. Listen now to the incarnations of Vyāsa, the lords of yoga, in their proper sequence.
Indeed, during the Dvāpara ages, there are incarnations of Vyāsa among those of excellent vows;
likewise, there are incarnations of the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva) as teachers of Yoga among his disciples.
In each of those instances, the Lord shall have four disciples of great splendor.
Their disciples and grand-disciples are by the hundreds and thousands;
through their honor in the world, such as by carrying out the commands of Śiva,
the fortunate ones, being thoroughly permeated by devotion, are liberated.

Om. Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of Vyāsa," within the section on the Knowledge of the Reality of Śiva (Śivatattvajñāna) in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the seventh part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Nine.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"In all the cycles of the ages (yugāvarta), through the guise of teachers of yoga,
tell me, O Blessed One, of the incarnations of Śarva and his disciples.
Upamanyu said:
Śveta, Sutāra, Madana, Suhotra, and Kaṅka; Laugākṣi, Mahāmāya, and likewise Jaigīṣavya;
Dadhivāha, Ṛṣabha, the sage Ugra, and Atri as well. (ŚivP 7.2.9.2–3ab)
Supālaka and Gautama, as well as the sage Vedaśiras; Gokarṇa, Guhāvāsī, and another known as Śikhaṇḍin; Jaṭāmālī, Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka, and likewise Lāṅguli.
Mahākāla, Śūlin, Daṇḍin, Muṇḍīśa,
Saviṣṇu, Somaśarman, and Lakulīśvara—
these [are the Rudras] during the interval of the seventh Manu in this Vārāha Kalpa.
There were twenty-eight Yoga-teachers in successive ages;
each of these had four disciples with tranquil minds, beginning with Śveta and ending with Ruṣya. I shall name them in their proper order.
Śveta, Śvetaśikha, Śvetāśva, and Śvetalohita; Dundubhi, Śatarūpa, Ṛcīka, and likewise Ketumān;
Vikośa, Vikeśa, Vipāśa, and Pāśanāśana.
Sumukha and Durmukha, Durgama and Duratikrama;
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana; Sudhāman, Viraja, Śaṅkha, and Aṇḍaja.
Sārasvata, Megha, Meghavāha, Suvāhaka,
Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and Bāṣkala;
as well as Parāśara, Garga, Bhārgava, and likewise Aṅgiras.
Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, Ketuśṛṅga, Tapodhana;
Laṃbodara, Lamba, Lambātmā, and Lambakeśaka;
Sarvajña, Samabuddhi, as well as Sādhyasiddhi.
Sudhāmā, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Viraja;
Atri, Ugra—the best of teachers—Śravaṇa, and Śraviṣṭaka;
Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, Kuśarīra, and Kunetraka.
Kāśyapa, Uśanas, Cyavana, Bṛhaspati,
Utathya, Vāmadeva, Mahākāla, Mahānila,
Vācaḥśravas, Suvīra, Śyāvaka, and Yatīśvara.
Hiraṇyanābha of Kosala, Lokākṣi, Kuthumi, Sumantu,
Jaimini, Kubandha, Kuśakandhara,
Plakṣa, Dārbhāyaṇi, and Ketumān Gautama.
Bhallavī and Madhupiṅga, as well as Śvetaketu;
Uśija and Bṛhadaśva, Devala and Kavi;
Śālihotra, Suveṣa, Yuvanāśva, and Śaradvasu.
Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, Ulūka, and Vatsa,
as well as Kulika, Garga, Mitraka, and Ruṣya—
these were the disciples of Maheśa, who appeared in the form of a master of yoga.
The number of these is one hundred and twelve;
all are perfected Pāśupatas whose bodies are smeared with ashes,
who know the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, and who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs.
All were devoted to the stage of life dedicated to Śiva and intent upon the knowledge of Śiva;
all were free from attachment, with their minds fixed solely on Śiva;
they were wise, enduring all dualities, and delighted in the welfare of all beings.
They were upright, gentle, self-composed, having conquered anger and subdued their senses;
they wore ornaments of rudrākṣa beads and had their foreheads marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra);
some had tufts of hair, some had matted locks, some had no matted locks at all, and others had shaven heads.
Subsisting primarily on fruits and roots, devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
endowed with the realization that Śiva is their own self, and solely intent on meditation upon Śiva,
they have utterly uprooted the sprouting shoots of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra.

They are indeed prepared to depart toward the supreme city of Śiva. He who, regarding these [deities] as his constant teachers, worships Śiva eternally—he attains union with Śiva; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Om! Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Descent of Yoga of Śiva," in the seventh part, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Śivamahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Ten.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Blessed One, Lord of all masters of yoga, Sovereign of the hosts, Lord of sages;
O Preceptor, equal in splendor to the six-faced one, treasury of all knowledge!
You have likely descended upon the earth for the purpose of severing the bonds of men.
O Supreme Lord, you remain here having assumed the body of a great seer;
for otherwise, in this world, whether it be a god or even a demon,
who other than you could know the supreme state whose essence is Śiva?
Therefore, having drunk the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva poured forth from your mouth as if from the Pināka-wielder himself, my mind has not yet reached satiety.
I have taken refuge on the lap of the Lord himself, the creator of the entire universe.
"O Blessed One, what indeed did the Supreme Goddess ask her husband?
Upamanyu said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you have asked a fitting question; I shall tell it to you exactly as it is."
For you, who are devoted to existence, disciplined, and of auspicious mind,
Mahādeva, together with the Goddess, became absorbed in divine meditation upon the excellent and divine Mandara mountain, which possesses beautiful caves.
Then the goddess’s dear friend, the auspicious Susmitāsyā,
brought forth most beautiful blossoming flowers.
Thereupon, the best of gods placed the goddess upon his own lap.
Having adorned her with those flowers, he himself remained exceedingly joyful.
Then the ladies of the inner apartments, adorned with divine ornaments,
and the intimate lords of the *gaṇas*, [approached] the Great Sovereign of all the worlds.

With chowries held in their hands, they attended upon the Goddess and the God— the Lord who is complete and the Great Sovereign of all the worlds. Then, pleasant conversations took place for the amusement of the two Great Lords.

And for the protection of men in the world, those who have gone to Śiva for refuge— then, perceiving that opportunity, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds questioned her husband, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds.
The Goddess said:
By what means is Mahādeva brought under control by mortals of dull intellect,
who are incapable of realizing the truth of the Self and whose minds are undisciplined?
The Lord said:
"Neither by ritual action, nor by austerity, nor by recitations, nor by yogic postures and the like,
nor by knowledge, nor by anything else am I brought under control without faith."

If men possess faith in me by whatever means, they shall be brought under my control, touched by me, seen by me, worshipped by me, and even conversed with by me. Therefore, faith in me must be cultivated by one who desires to bring me under their influence.

Faith is the cause for the protection of one's own dharma by those belonging to the [four] stages of life (varṇins) here. That man who conducts himself according to the dharma of his own caste and stage of life—
for him alone does faith in me arise, and not for anyone else.

"All the dharma of those in the various stages of life (āśramas) established by tradition was previously declared here by Brahmā, preceded by my own command. That dharma of the Grandfather, however, is accompanied by rituals requiring great wealth."
It is not excessively abundant in fruit, yet it is accompanied by the exhaustion of afflictions.

Having attained that great dharma which is so difficult to obtain, those belonging to the [four] castes who take refuge in me with no other resort, having gained my rare faith— // ŚivP_7.2,10.20cd–21ab //
Through that path of happiness, dharma, kāma, artha, and liberation [are attained].
Furthermore, I have ordained the conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama);
indeed, for my devotees among those belonging to the castes who possess devotion toward that [path], [these fruits are secured].

"No others have this authority; such is my final decree. By the path thus commanded, those belonging to the castes who take refuge in me shall be liberated from the bonds of *mala*, *māyā*, and the rest, through my grace.
Having reached my supreme state, from which return is difficult to obtain,
they attained my highest similarity of nature and reached ultimate bliss. Therefore, whether one has obtained or not obtained the duties of the castes as proclaimed by me, [one attains this].
If my devotee, relying [on me], should uplift himself by means of his own self,
this is indeed the attainment of what was previously unattained, exceeding [all other gains] by millions upon millions of times.
Therefore, one should practice the duty of one's caste as received from my mouth.
For my incarnations, O auspicious one, exist within all the inner [scriptures] under the guise of Yoga teachers, O noble lady, and their lineage is indeed thousandsfold;
yet they are for those who are undisciplined, lacking in wisdom, and devoid of devotion, O Goddess of the Gods.
The knowledge of the lineage is difficult to attain; therefore, one should rely upon it with effort.
That [failure] is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is delusion, and that is blindness and dumbness—to labor elsewhere while being excluded from the path to liberation.
"O Goddess of the Suras, knowledge, action, conduct, and yoga—
this is declared to be my eternal dharma consisting of four quarters.
The knowledge of the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (pati) is designated as 'knowledge'."

The purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaśuddhi*) performed according to the prescribed rule under the guidance of the Guru is called *kriyā* (ritual action). The practice of my own dharma, consisting of worship and so forth, which is enjoined by me alone and applied according to the [rules of] castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), is called *caryā* (conduct).
For one whose mind is established in me by the very path I have described,
that which is the cessation of other mental fluctuations is designated as *yoga*.
O Goddess, this purification of the mind is superior to a multitude of horse-sacrifices.
For this [yoga] bestows liberation and is indeed difficult to attain for those who crave sense-objects;
it belongs to one whose group of senses has been conquered through restraint and discipline. Yoga, which destroys prior sins, is said to belong only to the dispassionate.

From dispassion arises knowledge; from knowledge, yoga proceeds. Even one who has fallen, if he is a knower of yoga, is liberated—of this there is no doubt. One should always practice compassion, non-violence, and the accumulation of knowledge.
Truthfulness, non-stealing, faith, and restraint of the senses;
likewise, teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, and officiating at sacrifices;
meditation, the state of being the Lord, and constant devotion to knowledge and virtuous conduct.
The Brahmin who conducts himself in this manner for the sake of attaining the yoga of knowledge,
having acquired higher realization (vijñāna) very soon, finds that yoga.
O Dear One, having burned away this body in an instant by the fire of knowledge, the man of wisdom [attains liberation].
Through my grace, the knower of yoga shall cast off the bondage of karma—
both the meritorious and the demeritorious karma that obstructs liberation.
Therefore, by necessity, the yogi should abandon both merit and demerit.
One is obstructed by performing action with a desire for its fruit;
therefore, one should not perform mere action, but should renounce the fruit of action.
O beloved, having first worshipped me externally through the sacrifice of action (karmayajña), [one should proceed].

Having become devoted to the yoga of knowledge, one should thereafter practice yoga thoroughly. Once my true nature is known, embodied beings who are disciplined and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal do not worship me through the sacrifice of ritual action.
The sage who is ever-disciplined, my devotee, and composed in mind—

such a yogi devoted to the yoga of knowledge shall attain union with me. Furthermore, those belonging to the social orders (*varṇa*) who have not yet attained dispassion of heart but have taken refuge in me, [shall likewise attain their goal].
Those who are worthy of it should apply themselves specifically to knowledge, conduct, and ritual action.
My worship is to be known as twofold: external and internal.
Furthermore, they know my devotion to be threefold, according to the distinctions of speech, mind, and body.
Austerity, ritual action, recitation, meditation, and knowledge— these are said by the wise to be the fivefold worship of Him in successive order. Furthermore,
that which is known by others as external consists of our own acts of adoration and the like.
That very [consciousness], when experienced within oneself, is declared to be internal;
the mind that is inclined toward Me is called *citta*, and not merely the faculty of thought (*manas*). Speech that is devoted to My name is indeed considered true speech, and no other.

Marked with the signs prescribed in my teachings, such as the triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra) and others, and devoted to my service—that body is my body, and no other. My worshipful rite is to be understood as that performed externally through sacrifice and so forth; it is not otherwise.
The emaciation of the body for my sake, as well as penances such as the *kṛcchra*, are not considered by us [to be true austerity].
Recitation (*japa*) is the practice of the five-syllabled mantra and the practice of the *praṇava* (om);
it is the practice of the *Rudrādhyāya* and so forth, and not the study of the Vedas and the like.
Dhyāna is the contemplation of my form and so forth, not concentrations on objects such as the self;
jñāna is the thorough knowledge of the meaning of my scriptures, not the cognition of other matters.
Whether externally or internally, wherever the mind finds delight— ||| Śiva Purāṇa 7.2.10.54ab–55ab |||
O Goddess, by the power of prior latent impressions (vāsanā), one should practice steadfastness in the ultimate reality (tattva).
That which is internal is superior to that which is external,
being a hundred times more excellent because of the absence of the intermixture of defects and because even those defects already observed are impossible there.
One should know that purity is internal; external purity is not what is called purity. For one whose soul is devoid of internal purity is impure even if he is externally clean.
Both external and internal worship should be performed preceded by devotion to Bhava.
"O Goddess, that which is devoid of true being is the sole cause of deception.
For me, who have accomplished my purpose and am purified, what can men do?
Indeed, whether external or internal, it is only true being that is perceived by me."
O Goddess, my eternal dharma consists solely in the state of being [devoted] to action;
for in thought, deed, and speech, I never look toward any fruit whatsoever. O Mistress of the Gods, my refuge is considered inferior if it is undertaken with a view toward a reward.

For one who desires fruit is capable of abandoning me in its absence. O blameless lady, even for one who seeks fruit but whose mind is fixed upon me alone, I shall grant a result corresponding to his inner disposition.
Those whose minds, regardless of results, are inclined toward me— even if they should later pray for a fruit— such devotees are dear to me. Likewise, those who,
by the force of prior impressions alone, have reflected upon what is fruitful and what is fruitless [and remain so], [are dear to me].
Helpless, they seek refuge in me; they are considered my most beloved.
Truly, there is no gain for them greater than the gain of me;
O Supreme Goddess, for me too, there is no gain greater than the gain of them.
Through my grace, their devotion has been offered to me;
it bestows the supreme fruit of liberation as if by its own power.
This is the case for those great-souled ones who are single-minded and have surrendered their hearts to me.
They say that the characteristic of those who hold authority over my dharma is eightfold:
affection for my devotees, rejoicing in worship,
performing worship oneself, and bodily exertion for my sake.
Devotion to hearing my stories, transformations of the voice, eyes, and limbs,
constant remembrance of me, and whoever subsists upon me—
these eightfold signs, even if they exist in a barbarian (mleccha), [qualify him as a devotee].
He is the lord of sages, the illustrious ascetic, and the wise one;
he is not dear to me even if he knows the four Vedas, but rather even a dog-eater who is my devotee.
To him gifts should be given, from him they should be accepted, and he is to be honored just as I am.

"Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—to him I am never lost, and he is never lost to me. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Devotion to Śiva," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa. Om.
Chapter 11.
The Lord said:
Now, O Goddess of gods, I shall speak concerning those devotees who possess the requisite qualification.
For the learned and foremost of the twice-born, [the duties] are summarized as follows:
bathing three times a day, the fire-ritual, the sequential worship of the Liṅga,
giving gifts, devotion to the Lord, and compassion toward all at all times.
Truthfulness, contentment, faith, and non-violence toward all living beings;
modesty, faith, study, yoga, and constant teaching;
exposition, celibacy, listening [to scripture], austerity, and forbearance.
Purity, the topknot, the sacred thread, the turban, and the upper garment;
the avoidance of prohibited things, and the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads;
and, O Goddess, worship on festival days, especially on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī).
And month after month, according to the prescribed rule, one should drink the *brahmakūrca* [mixture];
O beloved, having bathed me with that very substance, one should perform worship in a special manner.
There should be a renunciation of all ritual actions and the avoidance of food offered with faith.
Likewise, there is the avoidance of stale food, especially barley-gruel (yāvaka),
as well as liquor, the smell of liquor, and food offerings (naivedya);
this is common to all castes, but particularly for Brahmins.
Forgiveness, peace, contentment, truthfulness, and non-stealing;
celibacy, my knowledge, detachment, and the application of ashes;
and the cessation of all attachments—these ten are especially [to be observed].

Furthermore, the marks of yogins and likewise eating alms during the day are prescribed as common for those established in the forest-dwelling stage of life (*vānaprastha-āśrama*). No eating at night should be performed by any of those who are celibate students (*brahmacārin*).

Teaching and officiating at sacrifices, as well as the non-acceptance of gifts, are not specifically prescribed by me for the Kṣatriya; nor are they prescribed for the Vaiśya. Rather, [their duties are] the protection of all social classes and the slaying of enemies in battle.
The destruction of wicked birds and beasts, and of wicked men;
distrust toward everyone everywhere, yet trust in my yogis;
association with women at the proper times, and likewise the protection of the army.
Constantly employing spies to learn the news of the world,
always bearing weapons, and wearing the mantle of ashes—
this is the summary of the dharma for kings who abide in my hermitage.

The protection of cattle, trade, and agriculture are declared to be the duties of the Vaiśya. Service to the other castes is declared to be the duty of the Śūdra. Furthermore, the cultivation of gardens and taking refuge in my sacred fields [are his duties].
For a householder, sexual union with his lawful wife is ordained;
for forest-dwellers, ascetics, and celibate students, the practice of celibacy is prescribed.
For women, however, service to their husband is the eternal dharma, and no other.
"O auspicious lady, my worship may be performed if there is the husband's command.
That woman who, abandoning service to her husband, is intent upon religious vows, goes to hell; there is no need for deliberation on this point."
Now I shall declare the eternal dharma for a woman who is bereft of her husband:
vows, charity, austerity, purity, sleeping on the ground, eating only at night,
celibacy, and constant bathing with either ashes or water.
Peace, silence, and constant forbearance; the distribution [of food] according to rule on the eighth and fourteenth days, especially on the full moon day,
as well as fasting and the worship of Śiva according to the injunctions on the eleventh day.
Thus, O Goddess, I have briefly declared for those who dwell in the stages of life— the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, as well as for ascetics, students,
forest-dwellers, and householders, O beautiful one.
This is the eternal dharma for Śūdras and women as well:
"O Queen of the Gods, I am to be meditated upon by you at all times, and the six-syllabled mantra is to be recited.
This is the summary of the dharma and its purpose, encompassing the entirety of dharma as declared in the Vedas.
Now, those men in the world who have assumed a physical body by their own will,
who are endowed with an excellence of disposition and possessed of prior latent impressions (saṃskāra),
whether they are detached or even attached to objects such as women and the like—

Sins do not smear them, just as water does not stain a lotus leaf. For those pure and discerning ones who possess self-knowledge through me, there is no suffering due to the maintenance of their stage of life, because they have been purified by my grace.
For them, there is neither duty nor non-duty, nor meditative absorption as a final resort;
for them there is neither injunction nor prohibition, just as it is for me.
Likewise, here there is nothing further to be accomplished for me who am already perfected;
and likewise, there is no doubt that even for them, who have fulfilled their purpose, there is nothing more to be done.
It is only for the sake of benefiting my devotees that they have assumed a human state.

Having fallen from the world of Rudra, they are indeed Rudras; of this there is no doubt. Just as my instruction is the impeller for Brahmā and the others, so too is his command the impeller for other men.
By virtue of being the support for my command and through the excellence of its true existence,
the destruction of all sins occurs merely by the sight of it;
and signs arise that indicate auspicious fruits.
In men who possess devotion toward me,
there shall repeatedly and spontaneously arise trembling, perspiration, the shedding of tears, a change of voice in the throat,
and the experience of bliss and other such states, even regarding objects never before perceived.
By those unerring signs, whether taken individually or collectively,
and by their states of mind— whether dull, middling, or superior— those best of men are to be recognized.
Just as iron, through its immersion in fire, does not become fire itself, [so too are they distinguished].
Because of my very presence,
those who possess human bodies— though they are Rudras due to their commonality with humans in hands, feet, and other such features—
a wise person, considering them as if they were ordinary beings, should not treat them with contempt.
Disrespect has been shown toward them by men of deluded intellect;
having abandoned longevity, prosperity, lineage, and virtue, it leads to hell.
Even the station of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Lord of the Gods seems as light as a tuft of cotton compared to it.
For those great-souled ones who have risen above and no longer depend on *māyā*,

as well as for the lords of the *guṇas* who seek the state beyond the *guṇas*, the impure sovereignty— whether derived from the intellect (*bauddha*), from the Lord (*aiśvara*), or likewise from primordial nature (*prākṛta*) or the individual soul (*pauruṣa*)— must therefore be renounced.
"Now, what is the use of saying more? The sole means for attaining the highest good is the fixing of the mind upon me by whatever cause possible.
Upamanyu said:

Thus, for the welfare of the worlds, this compendium of the essential meaning of knowledge was spoken by Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, Śiva, the Supreme Self. Within this compendium of realized wisdom, all the Vedas and Śāstras are contained in their entirety.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the sciences, and the detailed expositions;
knowledge, the object of knowledge, that which is to be practiced, the qualification, the means,
and the goal— this is the compendium of the six topics.
The knowledge pertaining to the Guru, that which is to be known, the fetter (pāśa), the bound soul (paśu), and the Lord (pati);
the performance of the worship of the Liṅga and other rites; the devotee who is authorized;
the means consisting of the Śiva-mantras and so forth; and the goal, which is equality with Śiva.
Through the knowledge of this compendium of the six topics, omniscience is said to be attained.
