First, one should perform the ritual of sacrifice and so forth with devotion according to one's wealth;
having worshipped Śiva externally, one should thereafter become devoted to the internal sacrifice.
For one whose delight is within and not in the external due to the weight of merit,
there is indeed no further duty to be performed externally by that great-souled one,
who is satiated by the nectar of knowledge and whose self is auspicious through devotion to Śiva.
O Kṛṣṇa, there is never any activity either within or without;
therefore, having gradually abandoned both the external and the internal,
one should perceive the object of knowledge through knowledge and likewise relinquish ignorance.
If the mind is not one-pointed upon Śiva, what is the use of performing ritual action?
And if the mind is indeed one-pointed, what is the use of performing ritual action?
Therefore, whether one has performed rituals or not, [one should focus] internally and externally in due order.

By whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Śiva. For those virtuous ones whose minds are fixed on Śiva and whose intellects are firmly established, there shall be supreme bliss everywhere— both in this world and in the hereafter.

Through this mantra, "I bow to Him who is Śiva," the supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained; therefore, it should be mastered for the sake of attaining both the higher and lower manifestations. Om. Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge of Śiva," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 12.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O best of great sages, omniscient one, great ocean of all knowledge! Śiva Purāṇa 7.2, 12.1ab.
"I wish to hear the greatness of the five-syllabled mantra according to its true essence.
Upamanyu said:
"The greatness of the five-syllabled mantra cannot be fully told even in hundreds of millions of years."

It is impossible to describe this in detail; therefore, listen to it in brief. In both the Veda and the Śiva-āgama, this six-syllabled mantra accomplishes all the goals of every devotee of Śiva without exception.

This statement consists of few syllables yet is rich in meaning; it is the essence of the Vedas, bestowing liberation. It is established by the command [of the Lord], free from doubt, and identical with Śiva.
Endowed with various supernatural powers, it is divine and delights the hearts of the world.

The omniscient one, the Lord of all embodied beings, spoke that profound and well-determined word of the Supreme Lord— the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya"— which is easily uttered and leads to the attainment of all goals.

That seed-syllable of all sciences, the primordial six-syllabled mantra, should be known as exceedingly subtle yet of great significance, like the seed of a banyan tree. The Lord transcends the three qualities; He is omniscient, the doer of all, and the Sovereign.
The all-pervading Śiva resides within the single-syllable mantra "Om. Furthermore,
the subtle Brahmas beginning with Īśāna are established in their respective order within the single-syllable mantras of the six-faced [mantra] "Namaḥ śivāya."
In the subtle six-syllabled mantra, Śiva, whose body is the five Brahmans,
exists by his very nature as the direct signifier through the relationship of the signified and the signifier.
Because Śiva is the object to be expressed (*vācya*), the mantra is traditionally held to be its signifier (*vācaka*).
This relationship of signifier and signified between these two has existed since beginningless time.
Just as this terrible ocean of saṃsāra has been set in motion from the beginningless past,
so too Śiva stands as the liberator from that beginningless saṃsāra.
Just as a medicine is by its very nature the antidote to diseases,
so too is Śiva remembered as the antidote to the defects of saṃsāra.
If this Lord of the World did not exist, this universe would become nothing but darkness.
Because primordial matter (prakṛti) is insentient and the person (puruṣa) is ignorant,
whatever is insentient— beginning with primordial matter and atoms—
is not seen to be an agent by itself without an intelligent cause.
Instruction in dharma and adharma, as well as bondage and liberation, result from investigation;
without an omniscient being, the initial creation of men cannot be established,
just as patients suffer in misery without a physician.

Therefore, there exists the Lord Sadāśiva, who is beginningless, omniscient, and eternally perfect; he is the protector who rescues men from the ocean of saṃsāra. He is the Sovereign, free from beginning, middle, and end, and pure by his very nature.
In the Śiva-āgama, Śiva is to be known as omniscient and perfect.
This mantra is His designation, and He is remembered as the designated object.
Because of this relationship between designation and the designated, the perfected mantra is Supreme Śiva.
This much indeed is the knowledge of Śiva; this much is the supreme state:
that which is the six-syllabled speech of Śiva, "Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya.
This injunction of Śiva is not a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), for it is identical with Śiva himself.
How could He—the omniscient one, perfectly complete, pure by nature, and auspicious;
the benefactor of the worlds—speak what is false?
For whatever object exists exactly as it is, with its inherent qualities and defects, [He knows it as such].
And that fruit shall be fulfilled exactly as the Omniscient One declares.
Because one is seized by defects such as passion and ignorance, one might speak untruth;
yet since those do not exist in the Lord, how could He speak otherwise?

That stainless word which has been composed by Śiva—the omniscient one who is free from all defects—is authoritative; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, the words of the Lord should be trusted by the wise.

He who lacks faith in merit and sin as they truly are goes downward. That most beautiful speech uttered by the peaceful and eminent sages for the sake of attaining heaven and liberation should be understood as "subhāṣita" (well-spoken).
That speech which follows after passion, hatred, falsehood, anger, desire,
and craving is called "ill-spoken" because it is a cause for hell. Of what use is that speech, even if it be refined, soft, or elegant?
By means of a statement concerning ignorance and passion, which are the causes of the afflictions of saṃsāra,
that which is heard gives rise to spiritual welfare and the cessation of doubts regarding passion and the like;
even if such a statement appears contrary, it should be understood as beautiful.
For even though there are many mantras, there is nowhere a pure mantra equal to that which was composed by the omniscient Śiva;
the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences are all established within the six-syllabled mantra.

Therefore, there is no other mantra anywhere that is equal to it. Just as a single aphorism (*sūtra*) is differentiated by its commentary (*vṛtti*), the six-syllable mantra is likewise distinguished by the seven crores of great mantras and various subsidiary mantras.
Whatever knowledge of Śiva there may be, and whatever branches of learning exist as well— all those are,
in brief, the commentary on the six-syllable Sūtra.
What need has he for many mantras or for scriptures of great extent?
By whomsoever this mantra, "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," is established in the heart,
by him everything has been studied, heard, performed, and accomplished;
by whomsoever the practice of the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya" has been made firm.
He on whose tongue-tip the three syllables "Śivāya," joined with the salutation and so forth, reside— the life of that person is fruitful,
whether he be an outcaste, a low-born man, a fool, or even a scholar.
"One who is steadfast in the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra is liberated from the cage of sins.
Thus was it spoken by the Supreme Lord, the wielder of the trident, when questioned by the Goddess,
for the benefit of all mortals and especially for the twice-born.

Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh section, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," ends here.
Chapter 13. The Goddess said:

In the Kali age, a turbid time difficult to conquer and hard to transcend, when the world is shrouded by the deepest lack of merit and turned away from dharma; when the conduct of the castes and stages of life has declined and a great crisis has arisen— ŚivaP 7.2.13.1ab–13.2ab.
When all authority is in doubt or when the succession has been determined,
and when instruction is obstructed and the lineage of teacher and disciple has passed away,
O Maheśvara, by what means are your devotees liberated?
The Lord said: Having taken refuge in my supreme, heart-pleasing five-syllabled lore (pañcākṣarī),
men born in the Kali age whose souls are purified by devotion are liberated.
For those defiled by faults born of mind, speech, and body that are beyond the reach of expression or recollection;
for the ungrateful, the slanderers, the deceitful,
the greedy, and even those of crooked minds who have turned their hearts toward me.

"My five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī vidyā*) is the deliverer from the fear of saṃsāra. O Goddess, I have thus repeatedly declared on this earth that even one who has fallen may be liberated through this mantra if he is my devotee."
The Goddess said:
"If a mortal were to become fallen in every respect, he would be unfit for ritual action;
indeed, any action performed through a lack of fitness for action leads to hell."
"Then how could one who has fallen [into sin] be liberated by this knowledge?
Īśvara said:
"What you have spoken is true; therefore, listen, O beautiful one."
Thinking this to be a secret, I previously concealed it;
if one who has fallen [into sin], being deluded, should worship me along with the mantra,
he would become a denizen of hell— of this there is no doubt— without my five-syllable [mantra].
Those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and others who are emaciated by vows— even for them,
there is no attainment of my world through these observances.
However, he who worships me even once with devotion using the five-syllabled mantra [attains it].
He too shall go to my abode solely through the majesty of this very mantra.
Therefore, austerities, sacrifices, vows, and likewise observances—
even all these combined— are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of the five-syllabled [mantra].
Whether bound or liberated from the noose, whoever worships me with the five-syllabled mantra shall be released; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whether one is without Rudra or with Rudra, whoever [worships] even once with the five-syllabled mantra...
Whether he be fallen or even deluded,
a man who worships me with devotion— either with the six-syllable mantra or likewise with the five-syllable mantra, accompanied by the Brahma-aṅga— is liberated.
Whether fallen or not fallen, one should worship with this mantra:
"My devotee, who has conquered anger— whether he has attained [the goal] or not attained it—
even if he has not attained it, he alone here is superior by many millions of millions of times."
Therefore, O Goddess, having indeed obtained me, one should worship with this mantra.
He who, endowed with virtues such as friendliness and devoted to celibacy, worships with devotion,
shall attain similarity to me.
What is the use of saying more in this matter? All devotees are qualified [for this]. Therefore, he indeed excels all others through my five-syllabled mantra;
by the power of the five-syllabled mantra, the great sages of the world and the Vedas [attain their goals].

The eternal dharmas remain, as do the gods and this entire world. When the dissolution has arrived and all that is stationary and moving has perished, everything returns to primordial nature (prakṛti) and will merge therein.
"I stand alone, O Goddess; there is no second anywhere.
At that time, the Vedas and all the scriptures were established in the five-syllabled mantra.
Protected by my power, they did not meet with destruction."
Then, from me, creation arose through the differentiation of *prakṛti* and the self;
and from that came the internal dissolution of those whose nature consists of the qualities (*guṇas*) and the forms (*mūrtis*). At that time, the god Nārāyaṇa lies within his body composed of *māyā*.
Reclining upon his serpent-couch in the midst of the waters,
the Grandfather (Brahmā), born from the lotus at his navel, possessed five faces; yet,
desiring to create the three worlds, he was unable to do so as he lacked assistance.
In the beginning, the Lord of Sages created seven mind-born sons of immeasurable splendor.
For the sake of increasing their spiritual perfection, the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke to me:
"O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, grant power to my sons."
Thus requested by him, I, who indeed bear five faces,
proclaimed the five syllables in their proper order to the Lotus-born One.
Grasping them with his five faces, the Grandfather of the World [received them].
Having recognized me, Maheśvara, through the relationship of the signified and the signifier,
and having understood the various applications [of mantra], Prajāpati—
having mastered the mantras— bestowed the mantra and the true meaning of the mantra upon his sons exactly as they are.
And having obtained that jewel of a mantra directly from the Grandfather of the World, they,
desiring to worship me according to the path commanded by him,
[went to] the mountain named Muñjavat on the beautiful peak of Meru.

He is my constant beloved, glorious, and always protected by my devotees. In his presence, eager to create the world, they performed intense penance for a thousand divine years, subsisting only on air.
Beholding their devotion, I immediately became manifest before them.
[I taught them] the sage (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), the peg (*kīla*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the power (*śakti*), and the deity (*daivata*);
as well as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the binding of the directions (*digbandha*), and the application (*viniyoga*) in their entirety.

I spoke this for the sake of the expansion of the world-creation of the noble ones. Then, by the power of that mantra, those sages who had been emaciated by austerity properly extended the creation consisting of gods, asuras, and humans.
Now the essential nature of this supreme vidyā is being described:
first the word "namaḥ" should be employed, and after that, "Śivāya.
This very five-syllabled vidyā resides at the head of all the Vedas.
She is the eternal seed of all that is born;
first uttered from my own mouth, she is my very speech.
She resembles molten gold and possesses full, elevated breasts.
She has four arms and three eyes, with the young moon as her crest-jewel;
holding a lotus and a water-lily in her hands, she is serene, with hands granting boons and fearlessness;
endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
Seated upon a white lotus throne, her hair was dark and curly.
Her five-colored rays, forming a shimmering mandala,
were yellow, black, smoky, golden-hued, and red.
If these are employed separately, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, [the result is as follows]:
the *bindu* resembles a half-moon, and the *nāda* has the form of a lamp-flame.
O fair-faced one, this is the second seed-syllable among the seeds of this mantra.

One should assign the fifth [syllable] of the fourth [quarter], which has a long vowel at the beginning, as the *śakti*. Vāmadeva is the name of the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *paṅkti* meter is declared for it.
O fair-faced one, I, Śiva myself, am the deity of this mantra.
O beautiful woman, Gautama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, and likewise Aṅgiras,
as well as Bharadvāja, are remembered as the sages of the social classes in their respective order.
Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Virāj are the meters.
Indra, Rudra, Hari, Brahmā, and Skanda are their presiding deities.

O fair-faced one, they say that my five faces correspond to these [deities] in their respective places. Starting from the east and ending with the upward direction, they correspond to the letters beginning with *na* in due order.
The first syllable is unaccented (adātta), the fourth is the second [high-pitched] tone,
the fifth is circumflex (svarita), and the third is known as depressed (nihata).
Thus is the root-vidyā, the Śiva-mantra, the Śaiva-sūtra, the five-syllabled [mantra].
One should know its names; this great heart-mantra of mine belongs to Śiva. The syllable *na* is said to be the head (*śiras*), while the syllable *ma* is called the crest (*śikhā*).
Likewise, the syllable *śi* is the armor (*kavaca*), and the syllable *va* is called the eye (*netra*).
When the syllables *ya*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*,
and also *phaṭ* are appended at the end of the phonemes,
then this root mantra [becomes the weapon-mantra] due to its slight modification and connection. (ŚivP 7.2.13.53–54ab)

In that [mantra] as well, the fifth syllable is adorned with the twelfth vowel. Therefore, by means of this mantra, one should perform the worship of us two through the divisions of mind, speech, and body, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth.
According to one's wisdom, according to the time, according to the scriptures, and according to one's own intelligence;
according to one's power, according to what is available, according to what is appropriate, and according to one's inclination;
whenever it may be, or wherever it may be, performed with devotion—ŚivP 7.2.13.56–57ab.
O Goddess, by whatever means worship may lead one to liberation.
O beautiful one, whatever is performed with a mind attached to me—
whether it be my own beloved [rites] or those of Śiva, whether in due order or out of order— it shall bring the same result.
Nevertheless, for those among my devotees who are not entirely helpless,
I have established a rule regarding all the scriptures.
In that regard, I shall first explain the auspicious collection of mantras.
Without which the recitation is fruitless, or by means of which it becomes fruitful.

Om. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the seventh book of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 14.
The Lord said: O fair-faced one, that which is devoid of the command, devoid of ritual action, devoid of faith,
and devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of the command— though constantly muttered, it is always fruitless.
That which is accomplished through command, that which is accomplished through ritual action, that which is accomplished through faith, and that which is my own self—
if it is thus endowed with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the accomplishment of the mantra yields great fruit.
Having approached a Brahmin preceptor (*ācārya*) who is a teacher and a knower of reality...
One who is endowed with virtuous qualities, devoted to meditation and yoga,
and possessed of purity of intention, should strive to please him with speech, mind, body, and wealth.
A Brahmin should always worship his teacher with the utmost diligence.
[He should offer] elephants, horses, chariots, and jewels; fields and houses;
ornaments and garments; grains and wealth.
One should give these to the guru with devotion, provided one has the means;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires one's own spiritual success.
Afterwards, one should offer oneself to the guru along with all one's belongings.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules and to the best of one's ability without deception,
one should receive the mantra and the knowledge from the Guru in due order. Thus satisfied, the Guru [bestows them upon] the disciple who has been worshipping him for a year.
Having bathed one who is eager to learn, free from ego, purified by ritual bathing, clean, and fasting,
for the sake of complete purification, he should indeed bathe him with full jars of ghee,
water sanctified by mantras, and auspicious substances.
Having adorned him with fine attire and ornaments of perfumes, garlands, and garments,
and having caused the Brahmins to pronounce an auspicious day and having honored them,
[one should perform the rite] on the shore of the ocean, by a river, in a cow-pen, or even in a temple.
In a pure place or even in a house, at a time that brings success, on an auspicious lunar day,
under a favorable constellation and yoga, and free from all defects—
having thus shown favor, one should then bestow my knowledge according to the prescribed rule.
With a very serene mind, one should properly recite it aloud in a secluded place.
Having recited and recited again that supreme mantra of us two, [one should say]:
"May there be Śiva; may there be auspiciousness; may there be well-being; may there be what is dear."

In this manner the Guru should give the mantra and likewise the command thereafter. Having thus received the mantra and the command from the Guru, being composed in mind, one should form a formal resolve and recite it daily, preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite.
One should recite [the mantra] eight hundred and more times daily for as long as one lives;
becoming single-minded and devoted to that alone, he attains the supreme goal.
Indeed, with devotion, one should recite one hundred thousand syllables four times over.
Eating only at night and self-restrained, he is remembered as one who has performed the *puraścaraṇa* rite.
He who, having completed the *puraścaraṇa*, becomes a constant reciter of mantras, has no equal in the world; he is a perfected one (*siddha*) and shall become a bestower of perfection (*siddhada*).
Having bathed in a pure place and fixed your mind on what is pleasing, you should meditate upon me in your heart and then repeatedly meditate upon your own guru. Then,
facing either north or east, remaining silent and with a one-pointed mind—
Having purified the five principles (pañcatattva) through burning, flooding, and other rites;
having performed the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and so forth, and thus made his body fruitful;
meditating upon the forms of us two and restraining the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Having recollected the field of knowledge, one's own form, the seer, the meter, the presiding deity,
the seed-syllable, the power, and likewise the mantra, one should mutter the five-syllabled [mantra].
Mental recitation is the best, while that which is whispered is middling.
Those expert in the meaning of the scriptures declare that vocal [recitation] is the lowest;
the highest has Rudra as its deity, the middle has Viṣṇu as its deity,
and the lowest has Brahmā as its deity— thus they say in due order.
When one recites the mantra with speech using high, low, and circumflex tones, and with words and syllables that are either clear or indistinct,
this is known as *vācika* (vocal) *japa*.
Or, when it is uttered even slightly through the mere movement of the tongue, [it is also considered vocal].

That which is not heard by others, or only slightly heard, is called whispered (*upāṃśu*). When one repeatedly contemplates the meaning of the words through the mind, following the sequence of syllables from letter to letter and word to word, that is declared to be mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*).
The vocal [recitation] is said to be one-fold, while the whispered is said to be a hundredfold;

the mental is declared to be a thousandfold, but when accompanied by *garbha* (the internal focus), it is more than a hundredfold. Recitation joined with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is called "with *garbha*" (*sagarbha*).
Prāṇāyāma is praised even when it lacks the initial and final [limbs].
Having performed forty repetitions of breath control, one who is wise and knows the meaning of the mantra should meditate upon it; if incapable, he should recite it according to his strength.

One should perform five, three, or even one breath control (prāṇāyāma), whether it be "without seed" (agarbha) or "with seed" (sagarbha); among these, the "with seed" is praised. Recitation (japa) accompanied by meditation (dhyāna) is said to be superior to even a thousand "with seed" breath controls.
Among these five types, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity. Counting the recitations with a finger is declared to be a single unit;
one should know that with a line it is eightfold, and with *putrajīva* seeds it is ten times more.
With conch shells there would be a hundred; with corals, a thousand;
with crystals, ten thousand; with pearls, it is said, a hundred thousand (a lakṣa);
with lotus seeds, ten lakṣas; and with gold pieces, ten million (a koṭi) is said [to be the result].
With knots made of *kuśa* grass and *rudrākṣa* beads, the merit becomes multiplied infinitely. A rosary fashioned with thirty beads bestows wealth during the act of recitation (*japa*),
while one consisting of twenty-seven beads grants nourishment.
That which is made with twenty-five [beads] bestows liberation;
however, one made with fifteen beads yields the fruit of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).
One should know that the thumb grants liberation, while the index finger destroys enemies.
Indeed, this ring finger brings about peace, bestows wealth, and is the giver of prosperity.
A rosary of one hundred and eight beads therein is the most excellent of the excellent;
a rosary of one hundred beads is excellent, while one of fifty is middling.
"With fifty-four beads, the *hṛcchreṣṭhā* is indeed proclaimed [to be the best]. Thus one should perform the recitation (*japa*) with a rosary; to whom should it not be shown?
The little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) is said to be the 'flowing' (*kṣariṇī*), auspicious for the rite of recitation."
One should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers;
for a recitation performed without the thumb is fruitless.
One should know that recitation in the house is equal [to the ordinary], while they know it to be a hundredfold when performed in a cow-pen.
In a sacred forest or a grove, it is said to be a thousandfold;
ten thousandfold on a holy mountain, and a hundred thousandfold by a river.
They say it is ten millionfold in a temple, and infinite in my presence.
Japa is recommended in the presence of the sun, fire, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, brahmins, and cows.
Facing east for that [purpose], it is for subjugation; facing south is for malevolent rites.
One should know that the western direction bestows wealth, while the northern direction brings peace.
In the presence of the Sun, fire, Brahmins, deities, and one's gurus,
as well as in the presence of others who are present, one should not recite the mantra with averted face.
One who wears a turban, one in a bodice, one who is bent over, one with disheveled hair, or one whose neck is wrapped;
one whose hands lack the purificatory thread (*apavitrahasta*), one who is impure, or one who is lamenting—none of these should ever recite [the mantra].
Anger, intoxication, and sneezing—these three, along with spitting and yawning, [are likewise forbidden].
One should avoid the sight of dogs and low-caste people during the practice of recitation.
If they are present, one should sip water for purification, or else meditate upon me together with you;
or one may gaze at the luminaries, or perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should not recite [the mantra] while lying down without a seat, nor while walking or standing;
nor in an impure place such as a street, nor in the midst of darkness. One should not recite with the feet outstretched, nor while in the "cock-posture" (kukkuṭāsana).
Whether mounted on a vehicle or lying down, or perhaps distracted by anxious thoughts—if one is capable, one should perform all of this; if incapable, one should recite according to one's ability.
What is the use of much speaking here? Listen to my words in brief.
One who always practices right conduct, recites pure prayers, and meditates on what is auspicious attains well-being.
Right conduct is the supreme dharma; right conduct is the supreme wealth.
Right conduct is the supreme knowledge; right conduct is the supreme goal.
A person devoid of proper conduct is censured in this world;
moreover, he shall not be happy in the next world. Therefore, one should be possessed of good conduct.
Whatever action has been prescribed for anyone in the Veda and in the Vedic scriptures—
His conduct by that [standard] is considered right conduct (*sadācāra*), and not otherwise. Because it is practiced by the virtuous (*sadbhiḥ*), it is called right conduct.
They say that the root cause of such right conduct is faith in the existence of the hereafter (*āstikyam*).

If one is a believer (*āstika*) and does not fall away from right conduct due to negligence or other such causes, that person is never defiled; therefore, one should embrace the state of being a believer.
Just as there is happiness and suffering here in this world through good and evil deeds, so it is elsewhere.
Likewise, the conviction that [the Lord] exists in the other world is called *āstikya* (faith).
O beloved, I shall tell you another secret; this must be kept hidden.
It should not be spoken to just anyone, nor to an atheist (*nāstika*), nor to a bound soul (*paśu*).
For one devoid of good conduct, for the fallen, and for the outcaste,
there is no protection greater than the five-syllabled mantra in the Kali age—
whether one is walking, standing still, or performing actions according to one's own will.
Whether one is impure or pure, this mantra is never fruitless.
Even for men who lack proper conduct and whose six pathways (ṣaḍadhvan) remain unpurified,
this mantra is not fruitless even if it has not been formally enjoined by a guru.
Even for one who is an outcaste, a fool, a deluded person, or fallen;
even for one who is lawless and base— this mantra is not fruitless,
provided that he possesses supreme devotion toward me, regardless of his condition.
It succeeds indeed, there is no doubt, and not for anyone else.
O beloved, for this [mantra], the conjunctions of the lunar day, the asterism, the weekday, and so forth, are not to be considered at all;
it is ever-arisen and does not depend on the seven [planets].
This Great Mantra (mahāmanu) is never the enemy of anyone;
it will become either a Susiddha, a Siddha, or even a Sādhya. When instructed by a perfected Guru, it is called a Susiddha.
Or even by one who is unaccomplished, that which is given—
even if it is merely an unproven means of proof—
is undoubtedly established as a proven truth for one who possesses an excess of faith in me, in the mantra, and likewise in the guru.
Therefore, having abandoned other mantras that involve obstacles due to a lack of qualification,
the wise person should directly take refuge in the supreme knowledge, the five-syllabled mantra, within this stage of life.
Even when other mantras have been mastered, this mantra will not be mastered [without it].

When this great mantra is mastered, they too become mastered. O Maheśvarī, just as I am not obtained when the gods are obtained, yet I am obtained [when they are], so too when I am obtained, they are obtained; the rule regarding these mantras is the same.
Whatever defects exist in all other mantras do not occur in this one either,
because this mantra operates without regard for caste and other such factors;
nevertheless, it is certainly not directed toward inferior fruits.
Therefore, he employs it with sudden force; hence he is possessed of great power.
Upamanyu said:
Thus was it [spoken] directly by Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident, to Mahādevī.
The five-syllable ritual has been declared as beneficial for all worlds. Whoever recites this with devotion or listens to it with a concentrated mind,
being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme goal.
1. The meaning is "that which is impermanent because it is subject to destruction.
Om. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh book of the Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 15.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Lord, O Master, you have described the greatness of the mantra,
as well as its method of application, which is equal to the direct revelation of the Vedas.
"Now I wish to hear about the supreme rite of purification for Śiva;
something was merely hinted at during the collection of mantras, but it was not forgotten.
Upamanyu said:
"Come, I shall tell you of that supreme and meritorious consecration (*saṃskāra*), which purifies all sins and was spoken by Śiva himself,
by means of which a man becomes fully qualified for worship and other rites."
By that [rite], the purification of the six paths is said to be the *saṃskāra*;
by which higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) is bestowed and the bondage of the fetters (*pāśabandhana*) is destroyed.
Therefore, this very *saṃskāra* is also called *dīkṣā*.

In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is taught by the Supreme Self, Śiva, as threefold: the Śāmbhavī, the Śāktī, and the Māntrī. [It is attained] merely by the glance of the Guru, or by touch, or even by conversation.
The consciousness that arises in the living being at once brings about the destruction of the bonds;
that is declared to be the *śāmbhavī* initiation. It is further divided into two types:
the intense (*tīvra*) and the more intense (*tīvratarā*), according to the degree of the destruction of the bonds.
That [initiation] by which immediate liberation is attained is considered the most intense (*tīvratarā*).

However, the intense (*tīvrā*) initiation purifies the sins of a man as long as he lives. Then, the initiation possessing power (*śaktī*) and knowledge (*jñānavatī*), having entered the body of the disciple...
By means of the path of yoga and with the eye of knowledge,
the Guru performs the initiation consisting of mantra and ritual action, preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit and the mandala.
This should be performed by the Guru externally for those who are dull or even more dull in their faculties.
A disciple deserves grace according to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*),
because, in brief, conformity with the Śaiva dharma is rooted in that.
Where power has not descended, there no purification arises.
There is no knowledge, no conduct of Śiva, no liberation, and no supernatural powers [for one who lacks devotion].
Therefore, having observed the signs of an abundant descent of power (śaktipāta),
the Guru should purify the disciple through either knowledge or ritual action.
The foolish-minded person who acts otherwise out of delusion perishes;
therefore, the teacher should examine the disciple in every way.
The characteristic sign of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is the arising of awakening and bliss.
Since she is the supreme power whose nature is awakening and bliss,
the modifications of the internal organ (antahkarana) serve as the signs of that bliss and awakening—
just as trembling, horripilation, changes in voice, and movements of the eyes and limbs [are signs of intense emotion].

The disciple, too, should perform an examination of the guru by means of these characteristics. This may be done through association with him, or by observing his worship of Śiva and so forth, or by associating with those who are devoted to him. For the disciple is to be instructed, and because of the necessity for reverence toward the guru.
Therefore, with every effort, one should show reverence to the Guru.
He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru.
Whether it be the Guru or indeed Śiva himself, he exists in the form of knowledge.

As is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is Vidyā, so is the Guru. The fruit obtained through the worship of Śiva, Vidyā, and the Gurus is identical. Indeed, the Guru is the embodiment of all deities and consists of all mantras.

Therefore, one who seeks the highest good should carry the command of the Guru upon his head with every effort; he should not transgress the Guru's command even in his mind. For by observing the Guru's command, one attains the perfection of knowledge.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, he should not perform any other action;
if he should act in the presence [of his teacher], he must do so entirely with the teacher's permission.
In the teacher’s house or in his presence, he should not sit as he pleases.
Since the Guru is the Lord himself in person, his house is a temple of the Divine.
Just as one falls [into sin] through association with sinners and by their evil deeds, so too [is purity gained];
just as gold here sheds its dross through contact with fire.
In the same way, through contact with a guru, a human being abandons sin;
just as a pot of ghee melts when placed near a fire,
so too does sin melt away in the presence of the teacher.
Just as a blazing fire consumes both the dry and the moist,
so too does this satisfied Guru burn away sin in an instant.
One should not provoke the anger of the Guru through thought, deed, or word.
By his anger, indeed, one's lifespan, prosperity, knowledge, and virtuous deeds are consumed.
For those who provoke his wrath, even their sacrifices become fruitless;
there is no need for further deliberation regarding this, nor regarding their restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*).

A person should never speak words that are contrary to the guru. If, out of great delusion, he should speak them, he shall go to the Raurava hell. Therefore, one should strive with effort toward the guru through mind, deed, and speech.
If a wise man desires his own welfare, he should not practice false conduct.
Whether commanded by his guru or not, he should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to him. He should perform his duty for him, whether in his presence or out of sight.

Thus, a disciple who possesses proper conduct, is devoted, always has a mind intent on exertion, and acts for the pleasure of the Guru, is therefore worthy of the Śaiva dharmas. This is so provided that the Guru is virtuous, wise, and the illuminator of supreme bliss.
One who is devoted to Śiva and knows the reality (tattva) bestows liberation, and no other;
that reality is the generation of consciousness arising from supreme bliss.
He by whom that very reality is known is indeed the one who reveals bliss.
But he who is devoid of true realization merely by means of the name alone cannot save another; can a boat save a stone, or can one stone save another stone?
By the mere name of this [practice], liberation is indeed merely nominal.
But those by whom reality has been known are liberated and liberate others as well.
How can there be awakening for one devoid of reality? For how can there be the grasping of a self?
One who is completely free from such grasping is designated a "bound soul" (paśu).
Even if impelled by other beings, one does not transcend the state of being a beast.
Therefore, in this world, he who knows the reality is considered both liberated and a liberator;
though he may be endowed with all auspicious marks and learned in all the scriptures, [he alone is so].

Even one who knows all methods and rituals is fruitless if devoid of the ultimate reality (tattva). However, for one whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it reaches the stage of direct experience,
supreme bliss arises through such means as his very glance.
Therefore, a wise man should choose only that teacher through whose contact the arising of awakening and bliss occurs, and no other;
such a teacher is worthy of being served by disciples who are skillful in humble conduct.
As long as he is known [as the Lord], he should be served by those seeking liberation;
once he is known, devotion should remain steadfast until one takes refuge in the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
One must never abandon that reality, nor should one ever neglect it in any way.
If neither bliss nor awakening is perceived there even in the slightest,
after a year the disciple should seek another guru.
Even when he has approached another guru, he should not despise his former one.
Likewise, [he should approach] the guru’s brothers, sons, instructors, and even those who urge him on;
first, having approached there, he should propitiate a wise guru— a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas, who is auspicious and pleasant to behold.
One should diligently please with mind, deed, and speech that giver of fearlessness to all, whose mind is pervaded by compassion;
the disciple should worship him until he becomes well-pleased.
When he is pleased, the disciple’s sins are instantly destroyed.
Therefore, [one should offer] wealth, jewels, fields, and houses;
ornaments, garments, vehicles, beds, and seats.
One should give these to the Guru with devotion according to one's means;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires the supreme goal.
He alone is the father, the mother, the husband, the kinsman, the wealth, and the happiness.
Since he is both a friend and a companion, one should offer everything to him.
Having first offered oneself, along with one's lineage and dependents,
and having surrendered even one's water-vessel to him, one should remain perpetually under his authority.

When one has offered oneself to Śiva, who is the soul of the Guru, then that embodied being becomes a devotee of Śiva (śaiva); there is no further rebirth after that. And the Guru should examine the disciple who has sought refuge with him for one year.
Having treated Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas— who were two or three years of age—
with commands involving the surrender of life or property,
both equal and unequal; and having relegated those of high status to low tasks and those of low status to noble deeds.
Those who do not fall into despondency even when reviled or beaten,
who are self-controlled, pure, non-violent, compassionate, and always possessed of a diligent mind— they are fit for the rite of Śiva-consecration.
Free from pride, wise, having abandoned rivalry, and speaking kindly;
upright, gentle, pure, humble, and steady-minded;
endowed with purity and right conduct—such are the twice-born devotees of Śiva.
Thus, those endowed with proper conduct through the actions of speech, mind, and body are to be purified and awakened according to the rule; this is the certainty established in the scriptures.
A woman has no inherent right to the rite of Śiva-initiation.
If she is endowed with devotion to the Lord by the command of her husband,
then likewise for a woman deprived of her husband, there is indeed the right [to perform it] with the permission of her son or others;
and for a maiden, there is the right by the command of her father.
For Śūdras, for those of mortal birth, and especially for the fallen,
as well as for those born of mixed castes, purification by the path (adhva-śuddhi) is not prescribed; however,
if they possess a genuine, unartificial devotion toward Śiva, the Supreme Cause, [then it is permitted].
They should perform the purification of sins through the offering of water for the feet and other rites.
Those born in the natural order (anuloma) who are properly integrated among the twice-born— on their behalf,
one should perform the purification of the path and other ceremonies appropriate to the mother's lineage.

But that maiden who has been dedicated by her father or others to the Śiva-dharma should be given to a devotee, and not to another who is antagonistic. If she is given to one who is adverse, she should, out of negligence, awaken her husband [to the truth].
Being unable [to endure it], she should abandon him and practice dharma with her mind,
just as the devoted wife Atri, having abandoned her husband, the best of sages,
became one who had fulfilled her purpose in the past by propitiating Śaṅkara through asceticism.
Just as she obtained the Pāṇḍavas as husbands by propitiating the god Nārāyaṇa through austerity,
though she was not directed by her elders in accordance with dharma,
in reality there is no fault here arising from a lack of independence.

For one who is devoted to the *Śivadharmas* out of reverence for the teaching of Śiva— what need is there to say more here? Whoever takes refuge in Śiva, even if they are dependent on a guru for their consecration (*saṃskāra*), that consecration does not differ [from the standard rite].

For one whose wisdom arises simply from the sight of the Guru, or even from his touch or conversation, there is no defeat. That purification which is performed by means of the mind through the path of yoga— [is the true cause of liberation].

That secret [initiation] has not been described here, as it is accessible only through the mouth of the Guru. However, that ritualistic consecration which is preceded by the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) will be explained in brief;
its detailed exposition is impossible.

Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh part, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Dīkṣā-vidhāna, the fifteenth chapter titled "The Greatness of the Guru" concludes.
Chapter 16.
Upamanyu said:
On an auspicious day, in a pure place free from many defects,
the preceptor should first perform the consecration known as the *samaya*.
Having examined the ground according to the rules by means of its smell, color, taste, and other qualities.

One should construct a pavilion there according to the methods prescribed in the treatises on architecture. Having prepared an altar in its center, one should arrange sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the eight directions and likewise in the intermediate directions, proceeding in order starting from the northeast.
One should construct the primary sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or else [construct it] from the western side; or,
having made only one primary pit,
one should arrange for its beauty with various and numerous canopies, banners, and garlands.
Then, in the middle of the altar, one should prepare a maṇḍala possessing auspicious characteristics,
suitable for the invocation of the Lord, using powders of red gold and other such materials;
or, if one is poor, with powders of vermilion and *nīvāra* grain.
It may be one cubit or two cubits in size, and either white or red.
For a lotus of one cubit, the pericarp (karṇikā) is considered to be eight finger-breadths;
the filaments (kesara) are half of that, and the remainder is for the eight petals and so forth.
Having made the pericarp and other parts of a two-cubit lotus double that size, one should arrange it, rich with primary and secondary ornaments, in the northeast of that [lotus]. Furthermore,
the altar-maṇḍala should be one cubit or half of that.
On a surface strewn with rice, husked grain, white mustard seeds, sesame, flowers, and *kuśa* grass,
one should there prepare the auspicious *śiva-kuṃbha*, endowed with the proper characteristics,
whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.

It was strewn with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice, and covered with sprouts of *kuśa* and *dūrvā* grass; it was encircled at the neck with a white thread and draped with a pair of new garments;
it was filled with pure water, provided with a *kūrca* of grass, accompanied by ritual substances, and fitted with a lid.
One should arrange a water-pot (*bhṛṅgāra*), a sprinkling-vessel (*vardhanī*), a conch, or even a discus—
omitting the ritual thread and other such items— or alternatively, a lotus leaf,
upon the northern petal of that lotus-seat.
In front [of the mandala], he should prepare the vardhanī vessel for the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) with sandalwood water;
then, to the east of the mandala, having performed the great worship of the Lord according to the rules as before, he should perform it using the mantra-pitcher.
Then, either on the shore of the ocean, at a river, in a cow-pen, or on a mountain;
or in a temple, in a house, or in any other pleasing place—
having performed everything previously described, or even without the pavilion and such.
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before and the sacrificial mound for the Fire-god,
the Guru, with a joyful countenance, entered the hall of worship,
accompanied by all auspicious rites and having performed his daily obligations.
Having performed the great worship of Maheśa in the center of the maṇḍala,
one should then invoke Śiva into the Śiva-vessel and worship him;
having meditated upon the Lord, the protector of the sacrifice, as facing toward the west.
One should worship the weapon of the Lord in the *astravardhanī* vessel to the right;
and having placed the mantra in the mantra-pitcher (*mantrakumbha*), the one proficient in mantras,
having performed all the mudrās and so forth, should carry out the mantra-sacrifice (*mantrayāga*).
Then the best of preceptors should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the Śiva-fire;
other twice-born ones should offer oblations all around the principal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
For them, the oblation is prescribed to be one-quarter or one-half of that of the preceptor.
Then, at the principal sacrificial pit (pradhānakuṇḍa), the most excellent preceptor should perform the oblation;
others should engage in sacred study, hymns of praise, and the recitation of auspicious verses;
and still others, devoted to the worship of Śiva, should perform the ritual recitation (japa) according to the rules.
Having performed dance, song, instrumental music, and other auspicious rites,
and having properly conducted the worship of the members of the assembly according to the prescribed rules,
he then caused the declaration of a "holy day" (puṇyāha) and once again worshipped Śaṅkara.
The preceptor, desiring to bestow grace upon his disciple, should pray to the God:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; entering my body, O Lord of the universe, O treasure-house of compassion, release him out of your mercy."
Then, having received permission with the thought, "I shall do thus," the preceptor brings the disciple— who has fasted, or who has eaten only sacrificial food (haviṣya),
or who has taken a single meal, is self-restrained, bathed, and performed his morning rites.

Standing himself facing east, with his upper body erect and his hands joined in *añjali*,
the Guru should sprinkle him on the head with water consecrated by the *prokṣaṇa* mantra while employing the *astra* mudrā; then,
having struck him with a scattering of flowers, the Guru should bind his vision.
Then, with half of a new *dukūla* garment that has been consecrated with mantras,
the Guru should cause the disciple to enter the mandala through the door. Impelled by him, the disciple should likewise perform three circumambulations of Śambhu.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers mixed with gold to the Lord,

facing either the east or the north, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff. Then, as before, he should sprinkle his head with water while reciting the Mūla-mantra and the Astra-mantra.
Having struck him, the preceptor should release his eye-bandage.
Having seen the maṇḍala again, he should bow to the Lord with palms joined in reverence.
Then, the Śivācārya [sees him] seated to the south of the maṇḍala.
Having seated the disciple upon a seat of *darbha* grass to his left, the Guru,
having worshipped Mahādeva, should bestow the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*).
He should utter the Śiva-mantra over that hand, which is composed of the splendor of Śiva.
Endowed with the conceit of being Śiva, the preceptor should place [the hand] upon the head of the disciple;
he, the teacher, should also perform the support of all the limbs by means of that very [hand].
The disciple, too, should prostrate on the ground before the Lord who has been manifested through the form of the preceptor.
Then, having worshipped the Lord in the fire of Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
and having offered three oblations, he should seat the disciple as before;
touching him with the tips of *darbha* grass, he should cause the Self to enter him through the Vidyā.

Having paid homage to Mahādeva, one should perform the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*). Having caused the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) according to the path taught in the *Śiva-śāstra*, and having brought about its entry into the body of the disciple, one should satisfy the mantras with offerings.
For the sake of satiating the Root-mantra, ten oblations should be offered with that very mantra;
likewise, three oblations for the Limbs should be given with the Limb-mantras in their proper order.
Then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the sake of expiation, the Preceptor—
The knower of mantras should again offer ten oblations with the root mantra;
having once more worshipped the Lord of Gods and properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the preceptor,
having offered according to the rule, shall indeed uplift the Vaiśya by means of his own caste-mantra.
In this manner, the preceptor should generate for him the status of a Kṣatriya and then again effect his elevation;
likewise, having established him in the state of a Brahmin, he should elevate the Kṣatriya and then establish both of them as Brahmins once more.
One should generate the state of Rudra in the Brahmin and accomplish the very name of Rudra;
having performed the sprinkling and the striking,
one should contemplate one's own self within the Self as being of the nature of Śiva, flashing like sparks of fire.

The Guru should expel the breath through the aforementioned channel with the mantra; having exited, he should likewise enter the heart of the disciple through that channel. Having entered, he should visualize the disciple's consciousness as resembling a dark blue drop.
One should meditate upon Him as blazing, with all impurities cast away by His own splendor.
Taking Him up through that channel with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, the practitioner of mantras,
without using inhalation (*pūraka*), should establish Him for the sake of unification with his own self.
Just as before, by means of *kumbhaka*, *nāḍī*, and *recaka*,
he should take that [power] from the disciple's heart and establish it there.
Having touched him and given him the sacred thread (*upavīta*) obtained from Śiva, he should bestow it upon him.
Having offered three oblations, he should thereafter offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Then,

having seated the disciple on an excellent seat to the right of the deity— which is strewn with *kuśa* grass and flowers— the preceptor, with palms joined in reverence, [should address] him who faces north.
Having caused [the deity] to assume the svastika posture, he himself, facing the east and seated upon an excellent seat,
should take up the full jar— which has been rendered perfectly propitious— while reciting mantras accompanied by the sounds of great auspiciousness.
While meditating upon Śiva, the preceptor should consecrate the disciple.
Then, having removed the water used for bathing and put on white garments, the disciple— having sipped water and being adorned— should go to the pavilion with palms joined in reverence.
Having seated him as before upon a seat of darbha grass, the Guru,
having worshipped the deity within the mandala, should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
Then, the preceptor, meditating upon the deity in his mind, [should apply] the sacred ash.

He should touch the child with both hands and utter the auspicious name "Śiva. Then, the preceptor of Śiva, having performed the rites of cremation and immersion and the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa according to the method of the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās, [should proceed].

Then, having meditated upon the seat of Śiva above the head of the disciple, the preceptor, having invoked Śiva there according to the rule, should worship Him mentally. With palms joined in reverence, he should pray to the God: "Be ever present here."
Having thus informed him, he should meditate upon that [disciple] as radiant with the splendor of Śambhu.
Then, having worshipped Śiva and received the Śaiva command which is identical with Śiva,
he should slowly utter the Śiva-mantra into the ear of the disciple.
Having heard the mantra with his mind fixed upon it, the disciple, with palms joined in reverence, should slowly recite it at the command of the Śiva-ācārya. Then,
the expert in mantras, having imparted the Śākta mantra, [should proceed].
Having uttered [the mantra], one should bestow happiness and auspiciousness upon him. Then,
having briefly explained the meaning of the mantra through the connection between the signified and the signifier,
one should indicate the form of the Lord, as well as yoga and the posture (āsana).
Then, by the command of the Guru, the disciple, in the presence of Śiva, the fire, and the Guru,
shall utter the words of initiation with devotion, having resolved thus:
"Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of my head."
But I would not eat without having worshipped the three-eyed Lord;
for he alone, being self-restrained, bestows [the fruit] until the reversal of delusion occurs.
Therefore, one should propitiate the God, remaining fixed in him and devoted solely to him.
Then, in the hermitage of Śiva, there shall be one named Samaya;
having obtained authority, he shall obey the command of his Guru and remain under his control.
After this, with hands folded in reverence, he shall take ashes from his own hand.
He should give to the disciple a rudrākṣa consecrated with the root mantra;
or else an image of the Lord, or even his secret body (the liṅga),
as well as the means for worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and meditation, whenever they are available.
That disciple, having received [the teachings] from the Śivācārya with great honor,
should accept them by the command of that preceptor and not otherwise;
having placed everything obtained from the teacher upon his head with devotion.
One should protect and worship Śambhu either in a monastery or in one's own home.
Beyond this, the preceptor should instruct him in the conduct of Śiva,
according to his devotion, faith, and the level of his intelligence.
Whatever has been spoken, whatever has been authorized, and whatever else has been proclaimed by the Śiva-ācārya during the sacred observance— all that one should bear upon one's head. Likewise,
the receiving, the reciting, and the hearing of the Śiva-āgama [should be done].
"One should perform it according to the instruction of the teacher, neither by one's own whim nor otherwise.
Thus has been briefly declared the sacrament known as the *samaya*,
which is the supreme means for men to attain the city of Śiva directly.
Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh section, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttarakhanda, the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Purification of the Disciple," ends.
Chapter 17.
Upamanyu said:
Thereafter, having duly examined the disciple’s fitness, the Guru should perform the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-śuddhi*) for the sake of liberation from all bonds. These are:
*kalā*, *tattva*, *bhuvana*, *varṇa*, and *pada*. Furthermore—
Together with mantra, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) are thus enumerated in brief.
The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are called the path of kalā by the wise.
The other five paths are pervaded by these five kalās, each by five.
The path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) is proclaimed to extend from the principle of Śiva down to the earth (*bhūmi*),
consisting of twenty-six elements and being of a dual nature— pure, impure, or both.
Furthermore, the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is celebrated as extending from the foundational support (*ādhāra*) up to *unmanā*.
Excluding its primary divisions and subdivisions, it is endowed with a number of sixty.
The fifty forms of Rudra are the phonemes known as the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan).
The path of words (padādhvan) is declared to be composed of manifold subdivisions.
The path of mantras is pervaded by all the mantras through supreme vidyā.
Just as Śiva, the leader of the principles (tattvas), is not counted among the principles themselves, so too he,
the leader of the mantras, is not counted within the path of mantras.

He who does not know, in accordance with reality, the pervasiveness of the path of *kalā* and the state of being pervaded by it on the part of the other paths, is not at all fit for the purification of the paths (*adhva-śodhana*). This applies to one by whom the nature of the sixfold path has not been understood.
Therefore, it is impossible for him to know the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader.
Consequently,
having correctly understood the nature of the paths (*adhvan*) as well as their state of being pervaded and pervading, one should perform the purification of the paths (*adhva-viśodhana*).
Having constructed there, as before, the area extending to the edge of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the mandala,
he should fashion a pitcher-mandala (kalaśamaṇḍala) measuring two cubits in the eastern direction.
Then, having bathed and performed his daily obligatory rites, the Śivācārya, together with his disciples, [should proceed].

Having entered the mandala of Śambhu, one should perform the worship as before. There, having offered half of the milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared for the Lord from rice measuring at least an āḍhaka, one should set aside the remainder for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa).
Or else, in a mandala prepared before him and adorned with colors,

the preceptor should place five water-pots in the cardinal directions and in the center. Within those, he should [place] the Brahma-mantras together with the root syllables, accompanied by the bindu and nāda.
The best of those skilled in ritual procedures should arrange [the mantras] beginning with "Namaḥ" and ending with "Ya".
He should place Īśāna in the central jar, Puruṣa in the one situated in front,
Aghora in the southern [jar], Vāma in the northern, and Sadyojāta in the western.
Having performed the protection rite and bound the mudrās, and having performed the consecration of the water-jar (kumbha),
he should commence the fire-oblation (homa) with the fires of Śiva as before.
As for that half of the milk-rice (pāyasa) which was previously set aside for the purpose of the oblation—
Having performed the oblation, he should prepare the remainder for the disciple to eat.
Having completed the rites for the mantras up to the libation (tarpaṇa) as before,
and having offered the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for them, he should then perform the illumination (pradīpana).

After the syllable *oṃ*, one should utter *huṃ*, then the root mantra ending with *phaṭ* and *svāhā*; these they call the limbs (*aṅga*) for the rite of illumination (*dīpana*), in their proper order. Three oblations of these should be offered in the ritual of illumination.
Having meditated upon each of those [deities] individually with mantras as having blazing forms,
and having tripled the white thread made by a brahmin girl,
one should consecrate that thread with mantras and tie it at the tip of the child's crest-lock (śikhā).
While the body stands upright with the feet together, having suspended that thread down as far as the big toe, the knower of mantras should join it there to the *suṣumṇā* channel,
taking hold of it with the *śāntā* mudrā while reciting the root mantra.
Having offered three oblations into her, one should effect her presence;
having struck the heart of the disciple with a flower as before,
and having extracted the consciousness and offered it at the *dvādaśānta*.

Having joined the thread with the *sūtra* mantra and protected it with the *astra* and *varma* mantras, one should then veil that thread and contemplate the body of the disciple as being composed of the three roots— the bond characterized by the state of being an enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment.
One should meditate upon that which generates the objects of the senses, the sense organs, the body, and so forth.
The *kalās*— Śāntyatītā and the others— which have the nature of the elements beginning with space,
should be joined with their own names in the thread and worshipped with the word "namas" appended.
Alternatively, having performed that previously mentioned sequence by means of the seed-syllables (*bīja*),
he should then observe the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of impurity (*mala*) and the other factors within the principles (*tattva*) and so forth.
Having offered oblations for the pervasion of the limited power (*kalā*) within impurity and the rest, he should inflame the *kalās*.
Having struck the disciple on the head, one should mark the thread upon the body in due order;
reciting the mantra, one should mark the thread at the level of the *śāntyatīta* (the state beyond peace).
Having done this, one proceeds in sequence through the levels ending with *nivṛtti*, up to the *śāntyatīta*.
After having offered three oblations, one should then worship Śiva in the mandala.
Having seated the disciple to the south of the deity, facing north,
the Guru should give the sacrificial caru-remnant upon a mandala strewn with darbha grass.
The disciple, having respectfully received what was given by the Guru with "Śiva" uttered first, should eat;
then, having sipped water twice, he should recite the Śiva-mantra.
Likewise, the Guru should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) upon another mandala.
Having drunk that [water] by its power and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) twice, he should meditate upon Śiva.
Having seated the disciple in the third mandala as before,
he should provide him with a tooth-stick possessing the characteristics prescribed in the scriptures.
Facing either the east or the north,
the disciple, having restrained his speech and sitting down, should clean his teeth with the soft tip of that [twig].
Having rinsed the tooth-stick and discarded it, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and meditate upon Śiva.

Instructed by the preceptor, he should enter the Śiva-maṇḍala with palms joined in reverence. If that tooth-cleansing twig is seen by the Guru to have been cast toward the east, north, west, or in front, it is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious.
In that face of the inauspicious quarter, the Guru, for the sake of pacifying those defects,
should perform oblations one hundred times, or fifty, or twenty-five, using the root mantra.
Then, having touched the disciple and having whispered the name of Śiva into his ears, [he should proceed].
On the right side of the deity, he should cause that disciple to dwell.
Pure, upon a bed of *darbha* grass spread over an unwashed cloth,
he should lie down at night with his head toward the east, meditating on Śiva within the consecrated space.
The Guru, having tied his own topknot with the thread bound to [the disciple's] topknot,
and having covered him with an unwashed cloth and the armor-mantra,
should draw three lines all around with ashes, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.

Having performed this, he should offer an oblation to the lords of the directions outside that [area] with mantras consecrated by the Astra-mantra. The disciple, likewise having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) while fasting thereafter,
should rise at dawn and report the dream he has seen to the Guru.
Om. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Procedure for Śiva-initiation," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Upamanyu said:
Then, having completed all the rites such as bathing and being urged by the preceptor,
he should go to the side of the *śivamaṇḍala* with palms joined in reverence, meditating upon Śiva.
Alternatively, having performed everything on the previous day exactly as before, but without the worship [on that day], [he should proceed].

The Guru should show the maṇḍala up until the binding of the eyes. When the disciple has cast flowers while his eyes are bound, the Guru should assign him the name corresponding to where the flowers fall.
Having initiated him, one should worship the Lord Īśāna within this mandala of floral remains as before,
and offer oblations into the fire of Śiva.
If a bad dream has been seen by the disciple, this should be done for the pacification of that defect.
One should offer oblations with the root-vidyā one hundred times, or fifty, or half of that. Then, having suspended the thread tied at the crest as before,
[one should perform] from the worship of the support (ādhāra-pūjā) onwards that which rests upon the nivṛtti-kalā.
One should perform the worship of Vāgīśvarī, preceded by the fire-oblation (homa). Then,
having prostrated before Vāgīśa and Satī, who pervades the Nivṛtti-kalā,
and having worshipped the Deity in the mandala and offered three oblations, [one should proceed].
And he should cause the disciple to attain [the state] simultaneously in all wombs. Then,
having performed the striking, sprinkling, and other rites upon the thread-body of the disciple,
and having taken up the Self and offered it at the end of the twelve [fingers], [he should proceed].
Then, having taken [the soul] by means of the root-mantra and the mudrā as seen in the scriptures,
the preceptor should simultaneously unite it with all wombs through the mind.
There are eight classes of gods and five classes of animals.
And with a single birth as a human, there are fourteen wombs; for the sake of the disciple’s simultaneous entry into all of them, he should,
according to the rule, cause the disciple’s self to enter Vāgīśānī through his own intellect.
Having fully worshipped and prostrated before the Deity for the sake of the completion of the embryo,
and having offered oblations according to the rule, one should meditate upon that which has been completed.
Thus, one should contemplate the birth of that which is completed and its continued existence through action.

Straightforwardness brings about the fulfillment of enjoyments and likewise produces supreme joy. Having offered three oblations for the sake of atonement and for the perfection of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of caste, lifespan, and experience, the best of teachers should pray to the God.
The purification of that body consists in cleansing it of the stain of attachment to the objects of the enjoyer.
Having performed this very [purification] for the disciple, one should then sever the three bonds (pāśatraya),
through the absolute destruction of the bond by means of the ritual excision (nikṛti) of that which is bound around it.
Having rendered the consciousness of the disciple completely pure, one should consider it as absolute.
Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire, one should worship Brahmā.
Having offered three oblations to him, one should impart the command of Śiva.

"O Grandfather, you must not place any obstacle in the way of this traveler toward the supreme state of Śiva; this is the most weighty command of Śiva. Having thus instructed him, having honored him, and having dismissed him according to the prescribed rites—
"Having caused [him] to abandon [the bonds]"—this is the ellipsis.
Having worshipped Mahādeva thoroughly, one should offer three oblations.
Having extracted the disciple’s self, purified by the *nivṛtti*-kalā, as before...
Having established Vāgīśa within himself and upon the thread, he should then worship him;
having offered three oblations to him and bowed down, he should dismiss her.
Having withdrawn, he should perform the reconnection along with the *kalā* for the sake of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having performed worship simultaneously during the conjunction and having offered three oblations,
one should then contemplate the entry [of the deity] into the installation of the disciple’s self.
Then, having invoked the Installation (Pratiṣṭhā) and performed everything previously described, [the rite is complete].
One should meditate upon Vāgīśānī, who pervades that [Viṣṇu] as its all-encompassing power,
resembling the orb of the full moon; having performed the remaining rites as before,
one should communicate the command of Śiva, the Supreme Self, to Viṣṇu.
Having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) of Viṣṇu and so forth, and having completed the remainder through the *vidyā*,
one should attend to the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) therein, just as before;
and having performed it, one should reflect upon its pervasion (*vyāpti*) and [the installation of] Vāgīśā in due order.
Having performed the rites up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in the blazing fire, and having completed the remainder as before,
he should invoke Nīlarudra and likewise perform worship and other services for him; then,
according to the previously mentioned method, he should grant the command of Śiva.
Having caused even that [state] of supreme austerity to depart and having performed [the rite] for its pacification,
one should then establish the Vidya-kalā and contemplate its pervasion—
just as before— one's own self-pervading Vāgīśī.
Resembling the rising sun, she illuminates the ten directions.
Then, having restored the remainder as before, one should invoke and worship the god Maheśvara;
having offered oblations to him, one should mentally convey the command of Śiva.
Having likewise emitted Maheśvara and formed this other digit (kalā),
one should lead it to the digit beyond tranquility (śāntyatītā) and contemplate its pervasiveness;
in the same way, one should meditate upon Vāgīśā as that which pervades one's own self.
Having made [the linga] resemble the circle of the sky and complete it as before,
and having worshipped Sadāśiva according to the remaining rites,
he should issue to him the command of Śambhu, whose deeds are immeasurable.
There too, as before, having worshipped Śiva on the head as previously described, and having bowed to Vāgīśa, one should dismiss him. Then,
having sprinkled the disciple on the head with water consecrated by Śiva as before, [one should proceed].
Then one should contemplate the dissolution of the Śāntyatītā [kalā] into the Śaktitattva;
that supreme [power], which pervades all paths, resides on the further shore beyond the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan).
One should meditate upon the power of Śiva (śaivī śakti), which resembles ten million suns in brilliance.
Having brought the disciple before him, who is as pure as clear crystal,
and having washed the scissors according to the path prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra,
the preceptor should perform the cutting of his topknot along with the thread.
Then, having placed that lock of hair upon cow dung, one should offer it as an oblation into the Śiva-fire with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. Having washed the scissors again,
one should withdraw the consciousness from the disciple's body into one's own hand.
Then, having had the child bathe, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and have the rites for auspiciousness performed,
he led him into the vicinity of the mandala; and having prostrated himself like a staff,
he performed worship according to the rules for the sake of purifying any deficiency in the ritual acts.
One should offer three oblations with the very mantra used for recitation;
one should offer three oblations by means of whispering (upāṃśu) pronunciation.
Then, for the purification of any deficiency in the mantra, one should worship the Lord of Gods once again.
One should offer three oblations by means of mental recitation; there,
having propitiated Śambhu who resides within the mandala together with the Mother,
the Guru, after offering the three oblations, should then pray with palms joined in reverence.
"O Blessed One, by your grace, the purification of these six paths has been accomplished;
therefore, lead him to your supreme, imperishable abode.
Having thus informed the God, [he performed] the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*).
Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* as before, one should then purify the elements (*bhūtas*).
For the sake of purifying the stable and unstable, and then for the two states of cold and heat,
one should meditate upon them in the form of a single pervasion during the rite of purifying the elements.
Having severed the knots of the elements and abandoned them along with their presiding deities,
he who recites [the mantra] within the supreme Śiva while remaining in a state of yoga—
having purified his body, burnt it, and drenched it with drops of nectar— [attains liberation].
Then, having established himself [in that state], he should fashion a body composed of the pure path (*viśuddhādhvamaya*).

Therein, first, he should place the pure *kalā* of his own path, which is beyond tranquility (*śāntyatītā*) and all-pervading, upon the head of the child; likewise, he should place the *kalā* of Tranquility (*śānti*) on the face.
One should assign Vidyā from the throat up to the navel, and Pratiṣṭhā sequentially below that;
one should assign Nivṛtti below that, reaching down to the knees, and contemplate it accordingly.
Having assigned the Sūtra-mantra with its own seed-syllables, one should assign that which is of the nature of Śiva by means of the fingers.
Having realized that [Self] within the lotus of the heart, the Guru should invoke and worship the Lord.
Having prayed for His eternal presence and the child's identity with Śiva,
the Guru should instill in this child qualities consisting of the splendor of Śiva.
Saying, "Be gracious to [the powers] beginning with *aṇimā*," he should offer three oblations;
in the same way, he should again bestow upon him the very qualities:
omniscience, contentment, and consciousness devoid of beginning and end.
[He should worship] that very power which is infinite, whose sovereignty is unimpaired;
then, having obtained permission from the Lord, he should consecrate the Lord of Gods with the jars beginning with Sadyojāta,
while meditating upon Him in his heart according to the prescribed order.
Then, having seated that disciple and worshipped Śiva as before,
and having received permission from Śiva, he should impart to him the Śaiva Vidyā—
preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, enclosed [by mantras], and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should likewise instruct [the disciple] regarding Śiva conjoined with Śakti, and the corresponding Śakti-vidyā;
as well as the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity, and likewise the state of Śiva-hood of both Śiva and Śivā;
furthermore, one should instruct on the worship of Śambhu along with its enclosures (āvaraṇas) and the seats (āsanās).

Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, he should inform Śiva: "Please make all that which has been performed by me a well-done deed. Then, together with his disciples, the Guru should prostrate himself like a staff upon the surface of the earth before the God.
Having prostrated, one should dismiss [the deity] from that maṇḍala as well as from the fire.
Then, all those worthy of worship who are members of the assembly (sadasyas) should be honored in due order;
the members of the assembly, along with the officiating priests (ṛtvijas), should be served according to one's means.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth if one desires one's own welfare.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purification of the Six Paths (Ṣaḍadhva-śuddhi) and Other Matters," in the latter section of the seventh book, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 19.
Upamanyu said:
"Henceforth I shall proclaim the name of the practitioner (sādhaka) by its very name;
the greatness of the consecratory mantra has been indicated by me in this narration."
