Having worshipped the deity in the mandala and installed him in the water-pot as before,
and having offered oblations, he should cause the disciple— who is without a turban— to enter the mandala on the ground.
Having performed the preliminary rites as before, he should likewise offer one hundred oblations.
Having satiated [the deity] with the root mantra using the water-pots, the supreme preceptor,
having kindled [the fire] as before and performed the sequence previously described,
should sprinkle [the disciple] as before and bestow the supreme mantra.
There, having performed the instruction in the Vidyā in detail and in due order,
one should entrust the Śaiva Vidyā into the hand of the disciple with water and flowers:
"This [Vidyā] bestows the fruit of all accomplishments for you in both this world and the next."
"The great mantra indeed becomes effective through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Having spoken thus and having worshipped the God, the Guru, having received permission from Śiva,
should instruct the practitioner in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and in Śiva-yoga.
Having heard that command of the Guru, the practitioner of the mantra should, in due order,
perform the mantra-sādhana prior to the viniyoga.
The practice of the root-mantra is called puraścaraṇa.
Because it must be performed beforehand for the rite known as viniyoga,
the practice of mantras is not something that must be done excessively by one seeking liberation; yet,
if it has been performed here or elsewhere, it will bring auspiciousness even to him.

On an auspicious day, in a sacred place, or at a time free from defects; having bathed with white teeth and nails, having performed his morning rites, and having adorned himself with whatever perfumes, garlands, and ornaments were available; ŚivP_7.2,19.11cd–12ab.
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, composed and entirely clad in white,
he should take his seat with ease upon a previously practiced posture, whether in a temple, another house, or some other very pleasant place.
Having assumed his own form as Śiva according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures,
he worshipped the Lord of the gods, the Lord Nakulīśvara;
having offered him milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and completed the sequence of worship in due order.
Having prostrated before that God and having received permission from his mouth,
one should recite the name of Śiva ten million times, or half of that, or half of that again;
or twenty lakhs, or even ten lakhs.
Thereafter, he should always eat only a single measure of milk-rice (pāyasa) that is free from pungent and salty flavors;
he should be non-violent, patient, tranquil, and self-controlled.
In the absence of milk-rice, he may eat fruits, roots, and the like.
These were ordained by Śiva himself, each succeeding one being superior to the last:
sacrificial porridge (caru), food, barley meal (saktu), and parched grain (yāvaka);
as well as vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, and water.
Having consecrated the foods to be chewed, eaten, and so forth with the mantra, the observer of the vow,
restrained in speech, should always eat these specifically during this practice.
The practitioner, being pure, should do so with clean water purified by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should bathe in water drawn from rivers or streams, or otherwise sprinkle oneself according to one's ability;
likewise, one should daily perform libations and offer oblations into the fire of Śiva with seven,
five, or three substances, or even with clarified butter alone.
In this way, for that practitioner of the Śiva-path who accomplishes Śiva through devotion,
there is nothing whatsoever difficult to attain, either in this world or the next.
Alternatively, he should recite the mantra day after day with a one-pointed mind.
Even without eating, by means of this thousand-fold [recitation] even without the formal ritual of mantra-sādhana,
nothing is difficult for him to obtain, and nowhere does anything inauspicious exist for him.
Having attained knowledge, prosperity, and happiness in this world, he finds liberation.
In the performance of rites, in ritual application, and likewise in daily or occasional ceremonies,
one should recite [the mantra] after bathing with water, ash, and mantras in the proper sequence;
being pure, with the topknot tied, wearing the sacred thread, and likewise holding the *pavitra* in the hand.
Wearing the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) and Rudrākṣa beads, one should mutter the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī).

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Mantras for the Initiatory Rites of the Seeker," in the latter section of the seventh book, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
[Chapter 20]
Upamanyu said:

Then, one should consecrate the disciple who has been thus purified and has performed the Pāśupata vow to the office of an Ācārya, provided he possesses the requisite yoga; otherwise, it should be done differently.
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before and worshipped the Supreme Lord,
he should place five water-pots in the cardinal directions and in the center, as previously described.
He should then install the kalā Nivṛtti in front [of the central pot] and the kalā Pratiṣṭhā in the western pot.
Having placed the Vidyā-mantra to the south, the Śānti-mantra to the north, and the supreme mantra in the center,
and having performed the protection rites (*rakṣā*) there and bound the *dhainavī* mudrā;
having consecrated the jars and offered oblations up to the final full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*) as before.
Having led the disciple into the maṇḍala, the preceptor— provided he is not wearing a turban—

should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites for the mantras, beginning as before and concluding as before. Then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods and obtained his permission as previously done, [he should proceed].
One should cause that disciple to ascend the seat for the consecration.
Having subsequently performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon him— who now embodies the five kalās—
and having bound his body with the deposited mantras, one should present the disciple to Śiva.
Then, having sequentially lifted the jars for withdrawal and the others from the middle one onwards, the preceptor should consecrate that disciple with Śiva himself. Then,
placing the Hand of Śiva upon the head of the child, the preceptor—
Having attained the state of Śiva, one should designate him as a Śivācārya.
Then, having adorned that deity and worshipped him within the Śiva-maṇḍala,
and having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more and prostrated on the ground like a staff,
the Guru, placing his joined palms upon his head, should address Śiva:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, this man has been made my preceptor."
"O Lord, having shown favor, let the divine command be bestowed upon him.
Having thus informed [the Lord] and bowing again together with his disciple,
the Guru should worship Śiva and the divine Śivāgama as he would Śiva himself.
Then, having again obtained permission from Śiva, the preceptor should give the book of Śiva-knowledge to the disciple with both hands. He [the disciple],
having placed that [book] upon his head, [should place] the Vidyā upon the seat of knowledge.
Having installed him according to the rule and having saluted him, one should worship him;
then the Guru should also give him the royal insignia,
since he who has attained the station of an Ācārya is worthy even of a kingdom.
Then he should provide instruction as practiced by the ancients,
in accordance with what is declared in the Śiva-śāstra, and in such a way that it is honored in the worlds;
having carefully examined the disciples for the characteristics described in the Śiva-śāstra.

And having consecrated the knowledge of Śiva, the teacher should bestow it upon them. In this way, one should diligently cultivate all these qualities without effort: purity, forbearance, compassion, as well as freedom from desire and absence of envy.
Having thus instructed that disciple and dismissed Śiva from the mandala,
he should worship the Śiva-pitcher, the fire, and so forth, as well as the members of the assembly;
or else, the Guru, together with his retinue, should perform the purificatory rites all at once.
In that regard, wherever even a pair [of rites] is taught as part of the ritual application (*prayoga*),
one should first prepare the water-pots (*kalaśa*) according to the procedure for the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*).
Having performed the consecration of the initiatory rules (*samayasaṃskāra*), everything else is accomplished without the formal ablution (*abhiṣeka*).
Having worshipped Śiva once more and performed the purification of the paths (*adhva-viśodhana*),
when that is completed, one should again worship the Lord.
Having offered oblations, having satisfied [the deity] with mantras, having kindled [the fire], and having offered prayers to Īśvara...
Having placed the mantra into the hand of the disciple, the preceptor should complete the remainder;
or else, having reflected upon the entire sequence of the mantra-consecration in its proper order,
the preceptor should perform the purification of the paths (adhva-śuddhi), concluding with the consecration (abhiṣeka).
In that regard, whatever ritual procedure has been prescribed for the kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā,
all of that must be performed during the purification of the three principles (tattvas).
These three principles are declared to be the principle of Śiva, the principle of Vidyā, and the principle of Ātman.
From that, Śiva [arose] within Śakti; from her, the Self (Ātman) emerged.

By Śiva, the path beyond peace (śāntyatītādhvan) is pervaded; the next, the supreme [path], is pervaded by Vidyā. Indeed, the remaining path is pervaded by Vidyā, and the entire [path] is pervaded by Ātman in due order.
"Considering the Śāmbhava [initiation] to be difficult to attain,
the wise, having mastered the meaning of the Śiva scriptures, should praise the Śākta purification as the root of mantra.
Thus has everything regarding the rite known as *saṃskāra* been explained to you.
"O Kṛṣṇa, this fourfold [classification] has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
Om. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Purificatory Rites such as Viśeṣa," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 21.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the obligatory and occasional rites prescribed in the scriptures of Śiva for those who dwell in the hermitages of Śiva."
Upamanyu said:
Having risen from bed in the morning and meditated upon the God together with his Mother,
and having reflected upon his duties, he should depart from the house when the dawn has appeared.
Then, in an uninhabited place free from obstacles, one should attend to the calls of nature.

Having performed purification according to the prescribed rule, one should practice the cleansing of the teeth. Even when tooth-sticks are unavailable, or on days such as the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī), one should do so.
One should cleanse the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water;
having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the rules, one should thereafter perform the Vāruṇa bath in a river,
a natural pool dug by the gods, a lake, or even at home.
Having placed the bathing materials on its bank and having removed external impurities,
he should smear himself with clay, bathe, and then smear himself with cow-dung;
having bathed again and again, he should discard his garment and then purify himself.

Having bathed well, one should again wear clean garments like a king. A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), an ascetic (*tapasvin*), and likewise a widow should not perform a bath for removing dirt, nor a bath with perfumes and the like, nor the cleansing of the teeth.

Having put on the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and tied his topknot (*śikhā*), he should enter the water. Having immersed himself and performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), he should draw three circles (*trimandala*) in the water.
Submerged in the northern direction, he should again mutter the mantra according to his ability and meditate upon Śiva.
Having risen and sipped water, he should sprinkle himself with that very [water] using either a cow’s horn with *darbha* grass, a leaf of the *pālāśa* tree,
a lotus leaf, or with his two hands, five or three times.

In a garden, at home, or indeed anywhere, one should perform an ablution with water consecrated by mantras using either a *vardhanī* vessel or a *kalaśa* pitcher during the time of immersion. Alternatively,
if one is unable to perform the *vāruṇa* rite, one may do so with a clean cloth.
One should purify the body, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, with water.
One may perform a bath that is fiery, or mantra-based, or performed by means of Śiva.
For one who is disciplined, the bath consisting of supreme contemplation upon Śiva is said to be one's own true bath.
Having first performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth with mantras according to the procedure prescribed in his own sūtra,
he should perform the rites up to the *brahmayajña*, having offered libations to the gods and others;
then, having meditated upon Mahādeva seated within the mandala and worshipped him according to the rules.
Then one should offer the *arghya* to that Śiva, who exists in the form of the Sun;
or else, having performed this as prescribed in one's own *sūtra*, one should purify both hands.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*) upon the hands, one whose body has been made complete (*sakalīkṛtavigraha*).

Having sprinkled [the area] with water held in the left hand, mixed with fragrant white mustard seeds and a bundle of *kuśa* grass, while reciting the root mantra and the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should indeed smell the remainder of the water.
One should contemplate the white deity through the left nostril alone;
having taken the *argha* water residing within the body,
one should contemplate the dark-colored [deity] situated outside, as present upon the stone, through the right nostril.
Then he should satisfy the gods and especially the sages;
he should offer the *arghya* according to the rules to the spirits and the ancestors.
With water mixed with red sandalwood, he should draw a mandala one cubit in size.
One should prepare a well-rounded circle on the ground, adorned with red powder and other ornaments.
Therein, one should worship the Sun together with his own attendants,
using the mantra "svakholkāya" along with its ancillaries for the sake of easy accomplishment.
Furthermore, having fashioned a mandala and worshipped it with its constituent parts,
one should place there a golden vessel measuring one *prastha* of Magadha;
it should be filled with scented water mixed with red sandalwood.
With red flowers, sesame seeds, along with *kuśa* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
as well as *dūrvā* grass, *apāmārga*, products of the cow (*gavya*), or even with water alone;
having knelt upon the ground and bowed to the Lord within the mandala.
Having placed that vessel upon his head, he should offer that *arghya* to Śiva;
or else, with water and *darbha* grass held in his joined palms (*añjali*),
he should cast it toward the sky for Śiva in the form of the Sun, reciting the root-mantra (*mūla-vidyā*).
Having again performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) preceded by the purification of the hands,
and having realized Śiva as consisting of the five Brahmans beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta,
one should take up the sacred ash with the mantras, rub it [on the hands], and touch the limbs of the body.
With the [mantras] ending in *din*, one should touch the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet in sequence;
then, having rubbed all the limbs with the root mantra (*mūla*), put on another garment,
perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice, and sprinkle oneself with water consecrated eleven times.
Having covered his body with water and sipped water twice, he should meditate upon Śiva; then,

having again placed his hands [in the *nyāsa* positions], the practitioner of mantras should draw the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes on his forehead using fragrant water, clearly applied in the proper sequence.
Whether it be circular, square, a dot, or even a half-moon—
whatever mark (*puṇḍra*) has been drawn on the forehead with ashes,
one should likewise draw that same mark on the base of the arms, on the head, and between the breasts.
Moreover, smearing the entire body with ashes is not equal to the triple marks (tripuṇḍra);
therefore, one should apply only the triple mark, even without the smearing.
One should wear Rudrākṣa beads on the head, the neck, the ears, and likewise on the hands.

It should be of golden color, unbroken, auspicious, and not worn by others; it is most excellent when yellow, red, or black, respectively for the Brahmins and the other castes. In the absence of such, it should be worn as it is available, provided it is unblemished.

In that regard, one who is superior should not wear [the rosary] below [his heart], nor should one who is inferior wear it above; one who is impure should not wear the *akṣa* bead. One should always wear it at the proper times—either at the three junctions of the day, or at two junctions, or even just once.
Having performed his ablutions and other rites according to his ability, he should worship the Supreme Lord.
Having reached the place of progeny and assumed a beautiful posture,
he should meditate upon the God and the Goddess, facing either the east or the north.
One should bow to the Guru and his disciples, beginning with Śveta and ending with Nakulīśa;
then, having bowed again to the Lord Śiva, one should mutter the eight names:
Śiva, Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.

"The Omniscient One, the Physician of Saṃsāra, the Supreme Self"— this is the group of eight verses. Alternatively, for the pacification of diseases and other afflictions, one should recite the name of Śiva alone eleven times more, while meditating on a mass of splendor at the tip of the tongue.

Having washed his feet and having smeared his hands with sandalwood paste, he should perform the ritual placement of the syllables (*karanyāsa*) preceded by the purification of the hands. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of Daily and Occasional Rites," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa. *Oṃ*.
Chapter 22.
Upamanyu said:
"Renunciation (nyāsa) is said to be threefold, according to the sequence of maintenance, creation, and dissolution."
For householders, it is the placement of stability; for celibate students, the placement of origination;
for ascetics and likewise for forest-dwellers, the placement of withdrawal.
That very same [placement] shall be the stability for a housewife who is bereft of her husband.
I shall now describe the re-creation of the maiden and the characteristics of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
The *sthitinyāsa* is declared to proceed from the thumb to the little finger.
Furthermore, it begins from the right thumb and ends at the left thumb.
The placement [of mantras] for creation has been explained; the reverse, however, is that for withdrawal.
One should place the phonemes beginning with *na* together with the *bindu* (*ṃ*) in their proper sequence upon the fingers.
One should place Śiva on the palms and on the two ring fingers.
Then, having performed the ritual placement of the weapons (*astranyāsa*) in the ten directions with the weapon-mantras,
one should [worship] the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, which have the nature of the five elements,
together with the lords of the five elements and endowed with their respective emblems.
Residing in the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
one should meditate upon those respective knots with their corresponding seed-syllables (bīja).
For the sake of purifying them, one should recite the five-syllabled Vidyā.
Having restrained the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) according to the number of the qualities (*guṇa*), one should then sever the knot of the elements with the *astra-mantra* and the *astramudrā*. Then,
by means of the *suṣumṇā* channel, one should impel the self by means of the vital breath.
One should unite that which has emerged through the aperture of Brahmā with the splendor of Śiva;
having subsequently dried the body with the wind, one should burn it with the fire of time (kālāgni).
Then, by means of the wind, one should withdraw the constituent powers (kalās) from above.
Having withdrawn the body that was indeed burnt, and having touched the *kalās* along with the ocean,
one should drench the body with nectars and establish it in its proper place. Alternatively, having withdrawn [the body] that was indeed burnt, one may do so even without the creation of the *kalās*.

Then, one should perform the immersion in nectar for that which has indeed been reduced to ashes. Then, one should join the Self, which has emerged from Śiva in the form of a lamp-flame, with that body consisting of knowledge through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
Having meditated upon Him who has entered within the body in the lotus of the heart,
one should again sprinkle that body composed of knowledge with a shower of nectar.
Then, preceded by the purification of the hands, one should perform the ritual placement (*karanyāsa*) on the hands.
Thereafter, one should perform the deposition of the body (dehanyāsa) with the Great Mudrā;
then, having performed the deposition of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) according to the path taught by Śiva,
one should then perform the deposition of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) in the joints of the hands, feet, and so forth.
Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs together with the six seed-syllables (jāti),
one should subsequently perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) starting from the southeast (āgneya) in due order;
or alternatively, one may simply perform the placement of the five limbs starting from the head.

Likewise, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and so forth, even without the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Having thus performed the purification of the body and the self in this concise form, and having attained the state of Śiva, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
Now, he who has the opportunity— or even if he lacks it— and whose mind is free from delusion,
should perform the rite of Nyāsa according to the extensive ritual manual (kalpa).
Among these, first is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, and after that follows the Brahma-nyāsa.
The third is the placement of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), and following that is the placement of the *haṃsa*.
The fifth, known as the placement consisting of the five syllables (*pañcākṣara*), is taught by the virtuous.
Among these, one may perform either one or all of them during rites such as worship.
Having placed the syllable *a* on the crown of the head and the syllable *ā* on the forehead;
likewise, *iṃ* and *īṃ* on the two eyes, and *uṃ* and *ūṃ* on the two ears;
*ṛṃ* and *ṝṃ* on the two cheeks, and *ḷṃ* and *ḹṃ* on the two nostrils.

One should apply the letter *e* to the two lips and the letter *auṃ* to the two rows of teeth respectively; then the letter *aṃ* to the tongue and the letter *aḥ* to the palate in due order. One should place the *ka*-group (the gutturals) upon the five joints of the right hand.
Likewise, one should place the *ca*-group on the joints of the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group on both feet;
then *pa* and *pha* on the two sides, *ba* on the back, and *bha* on the navel.
One should place the syllable *ma* in the heart, and [the letters] from *ya* to *sa* in order upon the skin and the other [elements].
One should place the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *sa* upon the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*).
One should place the syllable *haṃ* within the heart and the syllable *kṣa* between the two eyebrows.
Having thus assigned the phonemes by way of the fifty paths of Rudra,
one should assign the five Brahmans according to the divisions of limbs, faces, and kalās;
and having performed the assignment on the hands and so forth with those [phonemes], either in sequence or not at all.
One should assign these [mantras] to the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet.
Then, one should assign the faces starting from the upward one and ending with the western one.
And the five kalās of Īśāna should be assigned to these five [limbs] in sequence.
Then, four portions of the Puruṣa should also be assigned to his four faces,
according to the sequence starting from the east;
[and further] at the heart, throat, shoulders, navel, belly, back, and chest.

One should contemplate the eight digits (kalās) of Aghora in the two feet and the two hands; thereafter, one should contemplate the ten digits of Vāmadeva in the anus, the genitals, the thighs, and the knees, as well as in the calves, the hips,
the waist, and the sides.
The knower of ritual procedures should perform the assignment [of mantras] upon the nose, the head, and the two arms.
Having thus performed the assignment of the thirty-eight *kalās* in due order,
the wise one, skilled in the *praṇava*, should thereafter perform the assignment of the *praṇava*.
Likewise on the two arms, the two elbows, and the two wrists;
on the sides, the belly, the thighs, the shanks, and the feet, as well as on the back—
having thus performed the placement of the *praṇava*, one who is skilled in ritual placement (*nyāsa*) [should proceed].
One should perform the Haṃsanyāsa as it is taught in the Śiva-śāstra:
having divided the seed-syllable of the Haṃsa, one should place it on the two eyes and the two nostrils;
and having divided it again, one should place it on the two arms, the two eyes, the mouth, the forehead, and the two nostrils.

Having performed this *haṃsanyāsa* on the two armpits, the two shoulders, the two sides, the two breasts, as well as the two hips, the two hands, and the two ankles— or alternatively, by way of the five limbs— one should then install the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*).
By the path previously described, through which the state of Śiva is produced:
one who is not Śiva should not practice Śiva, nor should one who is not Śiva worship Śiva;
one who is not Śiva should not meditate on Śiva, nor should one who is not Śiva attain Śiva.
Therefore, having assumed the body of Śiva and abandoned the state of being a bound soul (paśu),
one should contemplate "I am Śiva" and perform Śaiva rites.
The sacrifice of action, the sacrifice of austerity, and the sacrifice of recitation (japa)— each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.

The sacrifice of meditation and the sacrifice of knowledge—these are proclaimed as the five sacrifices. Some are devoted to the sacrifice of ritual action, others are devoted to the sacrifice of austerity; still others are devoted to the sacrifice of recitation, and likewise, some are devoted to the sacrifice of meditation.
Others are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*), and they are distinguished in an ascending order.

The sequential sacrifice (*kramayajña*) is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by desire (*kāma*) and lack of desire (*akāma*). Having enjoyed desires through the sacrifice of desire, one who is attached to desires will be born again.
Having enjoyed pleasures in the abode of Rudra against his will, he falls from there;
having become devoted to austerity and sacrifice, he is born again—of this there is no doubt.
And as an ascetic, having again enjoyed pleasures therein, he falls from that state.
Having become devoted to recitation and meditation, a mortal is born as a human being on this earth. By virtue of that excellence, a mortal devoted to recitation and meditation shall,
after attaining knowledge, very soon reach union with Śiva.

Therefore, for embodied beings, even the sacrifice of action (karmayajña), when performed without desire and authorized by Śiva, leads to liberation; whereas when joined with desire, it leads only to bondage. Therefore, among the five sacrifices, one should be devoted to meditation and knowledge.

He who possesses both meditation (dhyāna) and knowledge (jñāna) has crossed the ocean of existence. Free from defects such as violence, pure, and having perfected the means of the mind, his sacrifice of meditation is supreme; it bestows the fruit of liberation beyond all others.
Just as laborers outside [the palace] do not partake significantly in the fruits [of the king's wealth],
so too here, those who perform ritual actions (karmiṇaḥ) are seen in the royal palace [of the Lord].
For the subtle body of those who meditate (dhyāninām) becomes directly perceptible as divine (aiśvaram).
Just as here [in this world], the gross [forms] of deities are fashioned from materials such as clay and wood through ritual action,
those devoted to the sacrifice of meditation do not regard stone or clay images as the ultimate reality,
because they possess knowledge of the true nature of Śiva.
The man who, having abandoned Śiva who resides within himself, worships him externally,
is like one who discards the fruit held in his own hand and licks his elbow.
From knowledge comes meditation, and from meditation, knowledge arises once again.

Liberation arises from both of these; therefore, one should be devoted to meditation. [One should meditate] at the end of the twelve-finger space, as well as on the crown of the head, the forehead, between the two eyebrows, on the tip of the nose, or on the mouth, the throat, and likewise the heart.
Or, at the navel— the seat of the eternal— with a mind pierced by faith,
one should worship the God and the Goddess through the ritual offerings of the external sacrifice;
or else, one should worship them constantly in a linga, whether it be fashioned or natural.
Either in the fire or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should worship the Supreme Lord with devotion according to one's means;
or else, one may worship the Supreme Lord both internally and externally. One who is devoted to internal sacrifice may perform external worship or not at all.

Om. Thus, in the venerable Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh section, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Daily and Occasional Rites as Taught in the Śiva-śāstra.
Upamanyu said:
I shall explain, in brief,
the ritual procedure for worship as it was taught by Śiva himself to Śivā within the Śiva-śāstra;
this includes the external and internal limbs of the sacrifice, concluding with the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
Whether he has performed the external sacrifice or not, he should subsequently perform it there;
having mentally conceived the ritual substances and purified them,
and having meditated upon the god Vināyaka and worshipped him according to the prescribed rule.
Having properly worshipped Nandīśa to the south and Suyaśas to the north in his mind, the wise one should prepare the seat,
such as the lion-seat (siṃhayogāsana) and others, being fully engaged in the rites of worship and so forth.
Or one may meditate upon the pure lotus posture, endowed with the three principles;
above that, one should meditate on Śiva together with Ambā, who is enchanting to all,
perfected in all auspicious marks, and beautiful in every limb.
Endowed with every excellence and adorned with all ornaments,
with red face, hands, and feet, his countenance possessed a smile like the kunda flower or the moon;
resembling pure crystal, he had three eyes like full-blown lotuses.
Hara has four arms and noble limbs, bearing the beautiful crescent moon;
his hands grant boons and protection, and he carries a deer and an axe;
he wears serpents as necklaces and bracelets, and his throat is beautifully blue.
Devoid of all comparison, together with his attendants and retinue;
then one should meditate upon Maheśvarī at his left side,
whose complexion is like the petals of a full-blown blue lotus, and whose eyes are wide and long.

Her face possessed the luster of the full moon, and her hair was dark and curled; she resembled the petals of a blue lotus and wore the crescent moon as her crest-ornament. Her breasts were exceedingly round, firm, lofty, smooth, and full.
She had a slender waist and broad hips, was dressed in excellent, fine yellow garments,
was adorned with every ornament, and was radiant with a tilaka mark upon her forehead;
she was further graced by a mass of hair interwoven with various flowers.
With a form entirely graceful and her face slightly bowed with modesty,
she sat upon a great throne, holding a radiant golden lotus in her right hand and placing another like a staff in her other hand.
Having thus meditated upon the God and the Goddess— who are the direct embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who sever the bonds [of worldly existence]—
one should worship them with devotion using flowers of pure emotion, along with all the ritual offerings, upon an auspicious and excellent seat.
Alternatively, one may thus mentally conceive of any one of the forms of the All-pervading Lord—
whether that known as Sadāśiva belonging to Śiva, or the supreme form of Maheśvara,
or the one designated as the twenty-sixth principle, or even the one called Śrīkaṇṭha.
Having performed the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and other rites upon one's own body, one should likewise meditate upon Śiva—
the embodied one who transcends both being and non-being— within this image;
then, by means of the intellect, one should perform the worship according to the external ritual sequence.
Thereafter, one should perform the oblation in the navel with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and other offerings;
and one should meditate on Śiva in the space between the eyebrows, having the form of the flame of a pure lamp.
Thus, in this auspicious yoga consisting of meditation—whether performed as part of the body or independently—ŚivP_7.2.23.20cd–23.21ab.
And the ritual procedure, ending with the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), is the same everywhere.
Then, having completed the entire sequence of worship consisting of mental contemplation,
one should worship the Lord in a *liṅga*, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or even in the fire.

Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh section, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Explanation of the Ritual of Worship," ends here.
Chapter 24.
Upamanyu said:
One should sprinkle the place of worship with the root mantra for the sake of purification;
one should cast flowers there with water scented by sandalwood.
Having driven away the obstacles with the Astra-mantra and having veiled [the space] with the Varma-mantra, [one should proceed].
Having assigned the weapon-mantra (*astra*) to the directions, one should prepare the ground for worship.
There, having strewn *darbha* grass, one should wash [the area] with sprinkling and other rites.
Having purified all the vessels, one should perform the purification of the ritual substances.
The sprinkling vessel, the arghya vessel, and after that the pādya vessel,
as well as the vessel for the ācamanīya— this is the quartet.
Having washed, sprinkled, and inspected them, one should then pour auspicious water into them.
One should deposit all meritorious substances as they are available:
gems, silver, gold, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth;
fruits, sprouts, and *darbha* grasses—these are the various kinds of meritorious substances.
In the bathing water, and especially in the fragrant water for drinking,
one should place cool and pleasing flowers and the like;
and for the water for washing the feet, one should provide uśīra and sandalwood.
One should especially throw nutmeg, kakkola, camphor, bahumūla,
and tamālaka into the water for sipping (ācamanīya) after having powdered them;
likewise, one should place cardamom, camphor, and sandalwood in all the vessels.
Kuśa grass tips, unbroken grains, barley, rice, and sesame seeds;
clarified butter, white mustard seeds, flowers, and sacred ash—these should be placed in the arghya vessel.
Also, kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, bahumūla, and tamālaka.
One should sequentially cast the sacred ash into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel;
having applied the mantra everywhere and encircled it on the outside with the *varman* (armor) mantra,
one should thereafter protect it with the *astra* (weapon) mantra and display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having sprinkled all the articles of worship with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using the root mantra, one should then purify them according to the prescribed rule.
In the absence of a *prokṣaṇī* vessel for any ritual acts, a single vessel may be used for all the vessels.
The best of practitioners should prepare the *arghya* offering with water; this is the general rule.
Then, having worshipped the god Vināyaka according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, he should proceed to the right side of the door.
One should properly worship Nandin himself as the lord of the inner apartments—
resembling a mountain of gold, adorned with all ornaments,
with the crescent moon upon his head, gentle, three-eyed, and four-armed.
The Lord held a blazing trident, a deer, a goad, and a sharp cane;
his face had the luster of the moon’s orb, or else it was like that of a monkey.
To the north, by the side of the gateway, stood the wife of the Maruts, the daughter of the Wind.
Having honored his mother Suyaśas, who was devoted to virtuous vows and intent upon adorning his feet,
he entered the inner chamber of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Having worshipped the Liṅga with those ritual materials, he should remove the remains of the previous offering (nirmālya).

Having washed it, he should place the flower upon his head for the sake of its purification. With flowers in hand, he should recite the mantra according to his ability for the purification of the mantra. Having worshipped Caṇḍa in the northeast, he should offer him the *nirmālya* (the remains of the offering).
Thereafter, one should fashion the seat, beginning with the *ādhāra* and so forth, in due order.

One should meditate upon the auspicious *ādhāra-śakti*, dark-complexioned, down below on the earth. In front of her, one should visualize Ananta, coiled in the shape of a serpent, with his neck uplifted.
[He saw] a white [serpent] with five hoods, as if licking the sky.
Above that was an auspicious seat supported by four lions.
Indeed, Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya were its feet.
One should contemplate the [limbs] starting from the southeast (Āgneya) as white, red, yellow, and dark blue in color;
and the [qualities] beginning with unrighteousness (adharma) and ending with ignorance (ajñāna), located in the directions from the east to the north in sequence,
resembling the rājāvarta gem, one should meditate upon them as the limbs.
Its upper covering is a pure, white lotus-seat.
They say its eight petals are the eight qualities beginning with *aṇimā*. And the filaments are the Rudras, Vāma and the others, together with the powers, Vāmā and the rest.
The seeds are those very powers, Manonmanī and the rest;
the pericarp is supreme detachment, and the stalk is knowledge whose essence is Śiva.
And the bulb (kanda), whose nature is the dharma of Śiva, is located within the triple circle at the end of the pericarp.
Upon the three circles, the triple reality consisting of the Self and so forth is the seat. Upon all seats, comfortably spread with a variegated covering,
one should fashion a divine seat, radiant with pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
One should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation (*sthāpana*), the confinement (*sannirodha*), and the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*),
as well as the prostration (*namaskāra*), forming each of the respective mudrās in turn.
Following that, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), fragrance (*gandha*), and flowers (*puṣpa*).
Having offered incense, a lamp, and betel-leaf, one should then cause the two Śivas to rest;
or else, having thus prepared a seat and a form,
one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the root mantra, the Brahma-mantras, and other mantras as well.
Then one should invoke Śiva, the supreme cause of the Goddess—
the god who resembles pure crystal, who is immovable and imperishable,
the cause of all worlds, and the highest being who comprises all worlds.
Pervading both the internal and the external, subtler than the subtle and yet greater than the great,
the immutable Lord is perceived by devotees without effort;
he is beyond the reach even of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
It is heard that the essence of the gods is beyond the reach of the learned;
it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, the medicine for those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence.
Known as the *śivatattva*, it remains steadfast in the world for the sake of Śiva.
One should worship the supreme Liṅga with devotion, accompanied by the five offerings (pañcopacāra).
This is the Liṅga-form of Maheśvara, of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
At the time of bathing, one should perform auspicious rites such as the utterance of the word "Victory" (jaya).
With the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), ghee, milk, curd, honey, and so forth;
with roots, fruits, and essences; with sesame, mustard, and parched grain flour;
and with auspicious seeds such as barley, and with powders derived from black gram and other legumes.
Having bathed him and anointed him with flour and other substances, one should bathe him with warm water.
One should rub him with bilva leaves and other items to remove the scent of the ointment.
Then, having bathed him again with waters according to the royal protocol (*cakravarty-upacāra*), [one should proceed].
1. The neuter form *klībatva* is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
2. Regarding the word *mahataḥ*, [the reading] *kṣeṣa-* [is intended]. 573a.
One should give fragrant myrobalan (*sugandhāmalaka*) and turmeric (*haridrā*) in due order. ŚivP 7.2.24.43ab.
Then, having cleansed the liṅga or the image with water,
one should bathe it with scented water and water infused with kuśa grass and flowers,
and subsequently with water containing gold and gems empowered by mantras, in the proper sequence.
But in the absence of these materials,
one should bathe Śiva with faith using whatever substances are available, or even with mere mantra-water,
using either a water-pot (*kalaśa*), a conch (*śaṅkha*), a *vardhanī* vessel, or the hand.
One should bathe [the deity] with water containing grains and flowers, preceded by mantras:
with the *pavamāna*, the *rudra*, the *nīla*, and the *tvarita* hymns;
with the *liṅgasūkta* and other *sūkta*s; and with the *śiraḥ* hymn of the *Atharvaveda*.

One should bathe the Lord of the gods with Ṛg verses, Sāman chants, Śaiva hymns, and the five Brahma-mantras, as well as with the Śiva-mantra and the Praṇava. Just as one performs the bathing and other rites for the God, so too should one perform them for the Goddess.
However, there is no distinction whatsoever between them, since they are similar;
having first performed the rites such as bathing directed toward the God,
one should subsequently perform them for the Goddess, according to the command of the God of gods.
When Ardhanārīśvara is worshipped, no distinction of priority or posteriority exists;
whether at the Liṅga or elsewhere,
one should perform the ritual services there, having first performed the consecration of the Liṅga with pure and fragrant substances.

Having wiped [the image] with a cloth, one should offer a garment and a sacred thread (*upavītaka*). Then one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), fragrance, flowers, and ornaments;
as well as incense, a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), drinking water, and a means for cleansing the mouth.
Furthermore, there was water for sipping and mouth-perfume thereafter;
then a beautiful and auspicious crown adorned with all kinds of gems,
as well as pure ornaments and various garlands.
Having offered a fan, a chowrie, an umbrella, a palm-leaf fan, and a mirror,
one should perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) accompanied by the sounds of all auspicious instruments,
as well as songs, dances, and the like, together with shouts of "Victory! (*jaya*).
In a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or a beautiful earthen one,
[one should worship] with lotuses, beautiful flowers, seeds, curd, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth,
as well as with tridents, pairs of conchs, lotuses, and nandyāvarta designs made from cow-dung.
Having arranged eight lamps around [the central area], marked with the signs of fire and so forth— namely the *śrīvatsa*, *svastika*, mirror, and thunderbolt— and placing one lamp in the center,
one should contemplate and worship the nine powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vāmā within them.
Having covered [the vessel] with the *kavaca* mantra and protected it on all sides with the *astra* mantra,
one should display the *dhenumudrā* and lift up the vessel with both hands;
or else, one should place five lamps in the vessel in their proper order.
Then, either in the intermediate directions, in the center, or even with a single lamp,
one should lift that vessel and, by means of the root-mantra, rotate it three times clockwise above the *liṅga* and other objects in due order.
Then one should offer the *arghya* upon the head and fragrant sacred ash (*bhasita*).
After making an offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should present the sacrificial offerings (*upahāra*).
Then one should give water for drinking, and having again offered water for sipping (*ācamana*), [one should proceed].

One should offer betel-leaf accompanied by the five fragrant substances (pañcasaugandhika). One should sprinkle the items to be sprinkled and perform songs and dances. Having meditated upon the two Śivas within the Liṅga and other icons, one should chant the name of Śiva according to one's capacity.

One should perform circumambulation, prostration, praise, and the surrender of oneself; one should also make a formal request regarding one's tasks with humility. Having offered the *arghya* and a handful of flowers, and having formed the ritual gestures (*mudrā*) according to the prescribed rule.
Afterwards, one should ask the deity for forgiveness and, having dismissed it, contemplate it within oneself.
In times of extreme distress, one may perform the rites from the water for the feet up to the mouth-freshener, beginning with the *arghya*,
or even merely scatter flowers while being filled with devotion.
By that alone, the supreme dharma becomes well-cultivated through meditation.
One should not eat without having first worshipped Śiva as long as one’s life-breaths remain.
If a sinner should eat according to his own will, there is no atonement for him.
But if one eats [the offering] through negligence, having diligently vomited it up,
one should bathe, worship the God and the Goddess twice as much, observe a fast,
and practice the recitation of the name of Śiva ten thousand times while observing celibacy.
On the following day, having given gold and other gifts to Śiva according to one's capacity,

or having performed a great worship for a devotee of Śiva, one shall become pure. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Śiva as Prescribed by the Scriptures," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 25.
Upamanyu said:
"And here, out of fear of [exhausting] the lotuses, that which remains unsaid regarding worship—" Śiva Purāṇa 7.2.25.1ab.
That which I shall declare further, in brief and not in detail:
before the offering of the oblation and after the presentation of the lamp,
one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇābhyarcā*), or else when the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) has arrived.
There, from Īśāna to Sadyojāta, and likewise from Rudra to Astra,
one should recite [the mantras] for Śiva or Śivā in the first enclosure;
in the northeast, the eastern part, the south, and likewise the north.
In the west, as well as in the southeast, the northeast, and the southwest;
then again in the northwest and the northeast— in these four directions,
the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) is declared, which consists of the collection of mantras.
Alternatively, one should worship [the deities] beginning with the Heart and ending with the Weapon-mantra.
Outside of that, the wise one should worship Śakra in the east, Yama in the south,
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Dhanada in the north.
One should worship Īśa in the northeast (aiśa), Anala in his own [southeastern] quarter, and Nirṛti in the southwest (nairṛta).
One should worship Māruta in the northwest (māruta), Viṣṇu in the southwest (nairṛta), and Brahmā in the northeast (aiśvara).
Outside the lotus, one should also worship the weapons, beginning with the thunderbolt (vajra) and ending with the lotus (abja).
One should worship the world-protectors in their well-known forms in their respective directions in due order.
Having clearly visualized the God and the Goddess, all the deities of the surrounding enclosures should be meditated upon as seated at ease with their palms joined in reverence.
One should perform the worship of all the deities of the enclosure with their own names preceded by "namaḥ," having bowed down to them all in due order.
One may also worship the innermost enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) with its own specific enclosure.
In yoga, meditation, recitation, or fire-offering— whether external or internal—
the sixfold oblation should be offered: pure rice mixed with mung beans,
milk-rice, and curd-mixed rice, as well as rice prepared with jaggery and soaked in honey.
Among these, one or several kinds [of food], combined with various condiments,
along with molasses and sugar-candy, and excellent churned curd,
as well as edible foods such as cakes and other delicious fruits, should be offered.
Water rich with red sandalwood and flowers, exceedingly cool;
soft betel-nut smeared with the juice of cardamom;
and leaves of the betel vine combined with catechu and other ingredients.
White substances, those of golden hue, and auspicious items are prescribed;
likewise, white powder from stone that is neither too dry nor defiled,
as well as camphor, kaṅkola, and fresh, pure jasmine and other flowers.
The ointment should be sandalwood, or made from the powder of radish wood;
the paste should consist of musk and saffron.
The flowers should indeed be fragrant, pure, and auspicious.
Flowers that are scentless, foul-smelling, spoiled, stale,
or naturally withered should not be offered in the worship of Śiva.
Likewise, garments should be soft and made of gold.
The ornaments, especially those resembling circles of lightning—
all of these were fumigated with camphor, resin, agallochum, and sandalwood,
and scented on all sides with heaps of flowers.
Incense prepared with the powders of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and guggulu wood,
along with clarified butter and honey, is highly praised;
likewise, incense made from the exceedingly fragrant clarified butter produced by a tawny cow (kapilā) is commended.
Lamps that are perpetually lit and blended with camphor are recommended.
Furthermore, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)— namely, sweet milk, curd, and ghee—
as well as [milk] derived from a tawny cow, are desired by Śambhu for bathing and drinking.
And there were auspicious seats made of ivory,
adorned with gold and jewels, along with variegated coverlets provided with soft pillows and made of fine cotton.
There were various beautiful and comfortable beds, high and low;
and there was water brought from rivers flowing to the ocean,
or water drawn from a well— cool, purified by cloth, and superior for bathing and drinking.
A beautiful parasol, moon-like and radiant with strings of pearls;
divine, set with the nine gems, and enchanting with its golden handle; and two white fly-whisks, delicate and adorned with gold.
It was shaped like a pair of royal swans and adorned with jeweled handles;
there was also a mirror, very glossy, anointed with divine fragrances,
covered all over with jewels, and decorated with various garlands.
The conch shell, deep-sounding and resembling a swan, a jasmine flower, or the moon,
was adorned with jewels and gold upon its back and other parts;
and there were delightful trumpets (*kāhalas*) that produced various sounds.
They should be fashioned from gold and adorned with pearls; likewise,
kettledrums (bherī), clay drums (mṛdaṅga), cymbals (muraja), timiccha, paṭaha, and other such instruments,
which possess a resonance like that of the ocean, should be prepared with great care.
One should likewise fashion beautiful vessels and all the leaves entirely of gold,
as well as the entire abode of Maheśvara, Śiva, the Supreme Self.
It should be constructed like a royal residence, possessing the characteristics described in the treatises on architecture;
it should be enclosed by high walls, with gate-towers (gopuras) shaped like mountains,
covered with many jewels, and featuring golden doors and panels.
It was made of refined gold, surrounded by hundreds of jeweled pillars,
enriched with canopies of pearl necklaces, and featured door-arches of coral;
it was adorned with divine golden crowns marked by the sign of the water-pot.
Its summit was adorned and marked with the insignia of the king of weapons;
it was graced by royal thoroughfares and dwellings worthy of kṣatriyas,
and surrounded on all sides by palaces with lofty, towering peaks.
It was surrounded by excellent men of high station stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
as if by inner enclosures with their borders exquisitely adorned,
and by thousands of noble women skilled in dance and song.
It was filled with many men skilled in the playing of flutes and lutes,
and protected by heroic guards accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots;
it was adorned with numerous flower gardens and many lakes.
It was resplendent in all directions and intermediate quarters with many oblong ponds,
and it was graced by devotees who were experts in the truth of the Vedas and Vedāntas, devoted to the Śiva-śāstras,
intent on the way of life prescribed for Śiva’s followers, and possessing the characteristics described in the Śiva-śāstras.
[It was filled] with peaceful, broad-faced [devotees], ever devoted to virtuous conduct—
Śaivas and Māheśvaras, illustrious twice-born ones who were served [there].
Thus, both internally and externally, it was constructed according to their capacity.
In a suitable location—whether made of stone, wood, or brick;
or even one made solely of clay; or in a sacred forest, on a mountain, by a river, in a temple, or in another place or an auspicious house.
For him there is no transgression, since he is the Lord who is subject to his own will.
Even if one should worship with wealth acquired by righteous means, yet without devotion, one does not obtain the fruit thereof; devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Whatever is performed with devotion for the sake of Śiva according to one's means—
whether it be small or great— the fruit is equal for both the wealthy and the poor.
Impelled by devotion, even a man of little wealth should perform [such acts].

Even one who possesses the essence of great wealth would not achieve anything if he were devoid of devotion. Even if one should give away all his possessions to Śiva while being devoid of devotion, he would not partake of the fruit thereof; in this matter, devotion alone is the cause.
Neither by extremely fierce austerities nor by all the great sacrifices can one go to the divine city of Śiva, except through devotion whose essence is Śiva. (ŚivP 7.2.25.53ab–cd) [Note:

The commentary states that the suffix -ghañ may sometimes result in a neuter form when it follows the sense of "continuing a relationship" (*sambandham anuvartate*). For this very reason, expressions such as *śeṣaṃ rāmavat* ("the remainder is like Rāma") are logically consistent.]
The meaning is "by means of the trident" (575a).
O Kṛṣṇa, devotion to Śiva—the Supreme Lord—is more secret than the secret in all respects;
there is no doubt about this, and by that devotion, the devotee is liberated. (ŚivP 7.2.25.54ab–54cd)

The recitation of Śiva-mantras, meditation, burnt offerings, sacrifice, austerity, sacred learning, charity, and study—all these are for the sake of inner disposition (bhāva); of this there is no doubt. A man devoid of such disposition is not liberated even after performing everything.
Furthermore, one endowed with devotion is liberated even without performing anything at all.
What need is there to mention the case of a devotee of Śiva, who has performed thousands of Cāndrāyaṇa penances, hundreds of Prājāpatya rites,
month-long fasts, and other such austerities?

In this world, non-devotees perform austerities in mountain caves for the sake of meager enjoyments; yet the devotee is liberated through his devotion. Indeed, yogis abide in the quality of *sattva*, wherein *sāttvika* action bestows liberation.
Performers of ritual action, enveloped by passion (rajas), perform [the sacrifice] for the sake of attaining supernatural powers (siddhi).
Asuras and Rākṣasas, endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas),
as well as other men of that same nature, worship the Lord for the sake of worldly ends.
Whether one resorts to a *tāmasa*, *rājasa*, or even a *sāttvika* disposition,
by performing worship and other rites with devotion, one attains well-being;
for devotion has been fashioned like a boat to rescue one from the ocean of sin.

Therefore, for one endowed with devotion, what is the use of passion or darkness? O Kṛṣṇa, whether he be an outcaste, or even the lowest, or a fool, or even a fallen man— if he has taken refuge in Śiva, he is worthy of worship by all gods and asuras.

Therefore, with every effort and through devotion alone, one should worship Śiva; for there is no fruit anywhere for those who have not worshipped him. Hence, O Kṛṣṇa, listen to my words as I shall tell you a supreme secret.
Having been deliberated upon by the Vedas, the scriptures, and those who know the Vedas, this has been well-determined.

Om. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship Prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 26.
Upamanyu said:
"Whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed;
whether a killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a slayer of a hero, or even a killer of an embryo."
Having worshipped with devotion the Supreme Cause, Śiva, even without mantras,
one shall be gradually liberated from those various sins over the course of twelve years.
Therefore, with every effort, even one who has fallen [from grace] should sacrifice to Śiva.
If there is no other devotee who subsists on alms, has conquered his senses, and—
having committed even a very great sin— worships the Lord of Gods with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra, he is liberated from that sin.
Those who subsist on water, those who subsist on air, and others who are emaciated by various vows—
none of them attain union with the world of Śiva through those observances alone.
However, he who worships Śiva even once with devotion using the five-syllabled mantra [attains it].

He too shall go to the abode of Śiva by virtue of the majesty of the Śiva-mantra. Therefore, all austerities and sacrifices in which one’s entire possessions are given as dakṣiṇā are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of the worship of the form of Śiva.

Whether bound or even liberated, if one subsequently worships [Śiva] with the five-syllabled mantra, that devotee is released; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. Whether one is without Rudra or with Rudra, one should worship Śiva with the Sūkta.
A man who has fallen even once, or one who is deluded, is liberated;

or he should worship the Lord with the six-syllable mantra or with the hymn-mantra (sūkta-mantra). Indeed, a devotee of Śiva who has conquered anger is truly "obtained" even if he was previously unobtained.
In this matter, that which is obtained from one who has not yet attained [the goal] is indeed superior; of this there is no doubt.
By means of that [attainment], or through the limb of Brahman, he is liberated along with the *haṃsa*.
Therefore, one should always worship Śiva with devotion using the hymn-mantra (*sūktamantra*).

Those who worship Mahādeva once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or indeed constantly, should be known as Maheśvaras. Without the aid of self-knowledge, the Blessed Lord Śiva is not truly worshipped.
He wanders for a long time in this cycle of existence, an ocean of suffering. Having obtained the rare human birth, the fool does not worship Śiva;
therefore, that birth of his is fruitless, as it does not lead to liberation.
Having attained this human birth which is so difficult to find, those who worship the wielder of the Pināka bow—
their birth is indeed fruitful; they are the best of men, having accomplished their purpose,
being devoted to Bhava and with their minds bowed in reverence to Bhava.
Those who are intent on remembering Bhava do not partake in suffering. Charming palaces, women adorned with playful ornaments,
and wealth that knows no satiety— these are the fruits of the ritual of worshiping Śiva.
Those who desire great enjoyments and sovereignty even in the abode of the thirty gods,
they always long for the lotus feet of Hara.
Good fortune, radiant beauty, virtuous character, and a disposition tender with generosity— these they seek.
Indeed, for one who worships Śiva, valor and fame shall arise in the world.
Therefore, having renounced everything, with a mind solely intent on Śiva,
one should perform the ritual of Śiva’s worship if one desires welfare for oneself.
Life passes swiftly; youth passes swiftly.
Disease approaches swiftly; therefore, the wielder of the Pināka bow should be worshipped, while death has not yet arrived and old age has not yet overtaken one.
"As long as there is no impairment of the senses, so long should you worship Śaṅkara.
There is no other dharma equal to the worship of Śiva in the three worlds;
realizing this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort."
If one should perform worship in the temple, one should conduct the door-sacrifice, the curtain-rite, the offering of oblations to the retinue,
and the daily festival;
this should be done either by oneself or by an attendant after the presentation of the sacrificial food.

One should offer the oblation (bali) to the attendants of Prasāda in due order. Having gone forth with musical instruments, one should stand facing that direction and offer flowers, incense, a lamp, and food together with water.
Then, standing upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) and facing north, one should offer the bali-oblation.
Then, whatever food and other offerings were previously presented to the God,
all of that— whether with remnants remaining or not— one should present to Caṇḍa.
Having offered the oblation according to the rules, he should afterwards complete the remainder of the worship.
Having performed the ritual application according to the rules and recited the mantra as many times as prescribed,
he should then conduct the daily festival as described in the teaching of Śiva.
In a vast vessel of radiant gold, adorned with red lotuses,
one should invoke and worship the divine Pāśupata weapon.
Having placed that vessel upon Śiva, it should then be offered to a decorated twice-born brāhmaṇa.
With his body having laid down his weapons, he [was honored] by him who held a blazing staff;
and from the surroundings of the palace, with auspicious sounds,
along with dancing, singing, and the like, together with lamps, banners, and so forth.
Having performed three circumambulations— neither too fast nor too slow—
and having completed the triple circumambulation around the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha),
the patron (yajamāna) re-enters and stands at the doorway with palms joined in reverence.
Having taken [the weapon] and led it inside, one should then discharge the weapon;
having performed the circumambulation and other rites in the sequence previously described,
and having taken eight flowers, one should then conclude the worship.

Om. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Worship with its Principal and Subsidiary Limbs," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh part of the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Upamanyu said:
Now I shall describe the fire-rite (agnikārya), whether performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila),
or indeed upon a raised platform (vedī), or in a new and auspicious vessel made of iron or clay;
having established the fire according to the rule and subsequently consecrated it.
There, having propitiated Mahādeva, one should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
One should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring either two cubits or even just one cubit;
it may be circular or square, and one should likewise construct an altar (vedi) and a mandala.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be as deep as it is wide; in its center is an eight-petaled lotus.
Its height should be four finger-breadths or even two finger-breadths;
they declare that the navel within it should have a height of two spans (vitasti).
The middle [measurement] is taken from the middle joint of the middle finger;
by the wise, a hand is said to consist of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
There should be three, two, or even one girdle (*mekhalā*).
One should fashion it as is aesthetically pleasing, smooth, desirable, firm, and made of clay.
One should make the *yoni* like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, or indeed like the frontal globe of an elephant,
in the middle of the girdle, either toward the west or the south.

One should slowly fashion a beautiful *unmīlikā* (elevated mound) slightly lower than the fire-altar (*agni*), facing the front of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) and leaving a small space from the girdle (*mekhalā*). There is no fixed rule for the height of the altar (*vedi*); it may be made of clay or of sand.
The mandala should be prepared with cow-dung and water; the measurement for the vessel has not been specified. One should plaster the earthen pit and the altar with cow-dung and water.
Having washed the vessel, one should heat it, while other items should be sprinkled with water.
Then, having drawn [the mandala] in the pit and so forth according to the method taught in one's own scripture,
he should sprinkle it with water and prepare a seat for the fire using *darbha* grass or flowers.
For the purpose of worship and for the fire-oblation (*homa*), he should prepare all the necessary materials.
Having washed those things that require washing and having sprinkled them with the *prokṣaṇī* water, one should purify them.
[The vessel] may be made of gemstone or wood, or produced from the house of a *śrotriya*. (Note: The absence of the dental *t* [in *adantatva*] is an archaic Vedic usage.)
Or else, one should bring another worthy fire from its usual receptacle; then,
having circumambulated the sacrificial pit and other sites three times in a clockwise direction,
one should recite the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) and place the fire upon its seat in due order.
Whether by way of the *yonimārga* or likewise facing oneself,
the wise one should prepare the entire sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the prescribed measurement.
[He should visualize] the fire situated within his own navel as sparks [emerging] from that aperture.

Having emerged from the external fire, one should meditate on [the deity] in the form of a *bimba* (image) as merged within it. Following the sequence prescribed in one's own *sūtra*, the knower of mantras should perform the rites up to the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*), preceded by the *anvādhāna* ceremony, using the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Having worshipped the form of Śiva, one should then place the mantra on the right side; having offered it into the clarified butter, one should display the mudrā known as the "cow. The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of precious metal; those made of brass, iron, or lead are not to be used.

They may be made of sacrificial wood, or according to the Smṛtis, or approved by artisans; or they may be made from the leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* or similar trees, provided they are unblemished and grown from the center. Having joined those two with *darbha* grass and heated them in the fire, one should sprinkle them again.

For the sake of accomplishing the consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*), one should offer oblations with the eight seed-syllables beginning with *Śiva*, according to the sequence prescribed by the venerable Pārāśarya in his own Sūtra:
namely, *bhruṃ*, *stuṃ*, *bruśruṃ* in due order, followed by *puṃ* and *draṃ*.
There are seven seed-syllables for the seven tongues in successive order.
The middle tongue is three-pointed and is called Bahurūpā;
the southeastern tongue is red, the southwestern is black, and another is considered to be Suprabhā.
The tongue named Atiriktā has a radiance corresponding to its own name;
after its own seed-syllable, the word "vācyā" should be uttered, ending with "svāhā," according to the sequence.
Having offered clarified butter with those tongue-mantras, one should worship each of the tongues individually in order.

Having offered three oblations into the center with the mantra "Raṃ Vahnyai Svāhā," one should perform the sprinkling (pariṣecana) with clarified butter or sacrificial fuel-sticks. When this has been done, it becomes the fire of Śiva; there, one should meditate upon the seat of Śiva.
There, having invoked the Lord Śiva as Ardhanārīśvara, one should worship him;

then, having sprinkled [the area] up to the lamps, one should perform the oblation of fuel-sticks (samidh-homa). Those sticks should be made of Palāśa wood or other sacrificial woods, twelve finger-breadths in length.
They should not be crooked, nor naturally dry, but should have their bark intact, be free from wounds, and even.
They are prescribed to be ten finger-breadths long, or measured by the little finger;
or, in the absence of such, even all those measuring only a span (prādeśa) may be offered.
Having offered an oblation of clarified butter shaped like a blade of *dūrvā* grass and four fingers in length, one should afterwards offer food in the measure of an *akṣa* fruit,
as well as parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
If available, one should offer ten, five, or three oblations of foods to be chewed, licked, or sucked, anointed with clarified butter; or,
according to one's capacity, one may offer even a single oblation.
One should offer clarified butter with the *śruva* ladle, and other materials such as fuel-sticks with the *sruk* ladle or with the hand;
in that rite, one should likewise offer with the divine or the *ārṣa* sacred portion (*tīrtha*).
If only a single substance is available, or if nothing is obtained, one should nevertheless offer with faith.
For the sake of expiation, one should offer three oblations after consecrating them with mantras. Then,
having filled the *sruk* ladle with clarified butter distinguished by the *homa*,
and having placed a flower before it, one should [cover] it with the *śruva* ladle turned face-down.
Having covered [the vessel] with Darbha grass, standing with his hands joined in añjali at the base [of the fire],
he should offer a continuous stream of oblation equal in measure to a barley grain, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
Having thus performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), he should sprinkle water around [the fire] as before.
Then, having dismissed the Lord of Devas, one should conceal the sacrificial fire;
or, having dismissed even that, one should constantly perform worship after merging it into the navel. Alternatively, one may bring forth the fire according to the path prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra.
Having consecrated [the deity] born from the womb of Vāgīśī, one should worship according to the rules;
having performed the *anvādhāna* again and having laid the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*),
one should place the vessels in pairs and then worship Śiva.
Having purified the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, he should sprinkle those [implements] with its water.
Having placed the *praṇītā* vessel, filled with water, in the northeast,
and having performed everything up to the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), he should purify the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles.
Having performed the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*,
and *sīmantonnayana* rites separately and having offered oblations for each, one should contemplate the fire that has arisen as having three feet,
seven hands, four horns, and two heads.
Honey-tawny, with three eyes, wearing matted hair and the moon as his crest-jewel;
red-hued, clad in red garments and smeared with [sandalwood paste], adorned with garlands and ornaments;
endowed with all auspicious marks, wearing a sacred thread and three girdles.
Having meditated on him thus born, bearing a spear and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in his right hands,
and likewise a *tomara* lance, a palm-leaf fan, and a vessel of clarified butter with the others,
one should perform the birth rites (*jātakarman*).
Having performed the removal of the [birth] tube and then purified the impurity (sūtaka),
and having offered oblations preceded by the rite for one named after the fire of Śiva,
he performed the dismissal of the parents and the rites of tonsure, initiation, and so forth.
Having performed the rites up to the conclusion of the *aptoryāma*, he should then perform the consecration for him;
having offered the stream of clarified butter (*ājyadhārā*) and other oblations, he should then perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
After that, he should sprinkle [the vessel] with the seed-syllable "Raṃ."
Having performed worship in due order around Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Īśāna, and likewise the world-protectors (lokeśas), as well as their weapons,
the knower of ritual procedures should kindle the fire for the sake of accomplishing the incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Having again prepared the ritual substances beginning with clarified butter (ājya),
and having fashioned a seat for the fire, he should invoke [the deities] there as before;
then, having worshipped both the God and the Goddess, he should perform the rites ending with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Alternatively, having understood that the fire-ritual prescribed for one's own stage of life (āśrama) is to be offered to Śiva, the follower of the Śiva-āśrama should perform it; there is no other rule in this matter. One should collect the ashes from the Śiva-fire, or else those produced from the Agnihotra fire.
Food cooked on the domestic marriage fire is pure and fragrant; likewise,
the dung of a tawny cow is commended when it is caught falling from the sky,
being neither wet, nor too hard, neither foul-smelling nor dried up.

Having discarded what is above and below, if [the ash] has fallen, one should collect it; having formed it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire or elsewhere with the root mantra. Having discarded what is uncooked and overcooked, [one should take] the white ash.
Having taken [the ashes] or having stirred them together, one should deposit them in an ash-receptacle. One should prepare an ash-receptacle that is either made of metal, wood, clay, or stone,
or any other beautiful and pure vessel.
In a level, auspicious, and pure place, one should deposit the ashes along with wealth.
One should not give them to an unworthy person, nor should one cast them upon an impure surface. One should not touch them with the lower parts of the body, nor neglect them, nor step over them.
Therefore, having taken the ashes, one should employ them according to the mantra;
one should not give them at times other than those prescribed, nor should one bestow them upon the unworthy. One should collect the ashes while the deity has not yet been dismissed.
O Prajāpati,

once the dismissal [of the deity] has been performed and the fire-rite (agnikārya) completed according to the path taught in the Śiva scriptures or according to the method prescribed in one's own Sūtra, one should then perform the bali-offering.
Then, having assigned the seat of knowledge (*vidyāsana*) upon the well-anointed mandala,
and having established the treasury of knowledge (*vidyākośa*), one should worship it in due order with flowers and other offerings.
Having prepared a mandala for the Guru as well, situated in front of the [mandala] of Knowledge...
Having prepared an excellent seat there, one should worship the Guru with flowers and other offerings.
Then, one should honor those worthy of worship and feed those who are hungry.
After that, one should eat pure food oneself at ease.

Or, O Lord, having offered it to the deity, one who possesses faith should consume the remainder for the sake of self-purification— not out of greed, nor that which has been offered to a Caṇḍāla. This same rule applies to perfumes, garlands, and whatever else [is offered there].
But a wise person should not form the notion "I am Śiva" in that state.
Having eaten and sipped water, and having meditated on Śiva in the heart, one should recite the root mantra.
One should spend the remainder of the time with those who are worthy, through discourses on the scriptures of Śiva and other such activities.
When the first watch of the night has passed, having performed a captivating worship,
one should prepare a single, most beautiful bed for the two Śivas,
as well as food, edibles, garments, ointments, flower garlands, and so forth.
Having performed everything that is pleasing to the mind through thought or deed,
one who is pure should sleep at the feet of the God and the Goddess;
a householder together with his wife, while others may do so alone.
Having recognized the time of dawn, one should recite the primary *mātrā*;
having mentally prostrated before the immutable Lord Śiva, together with Ambā and his attendants,
and having performed purification and other rites as appropriate to the place and time according to one's capacity.

One should awaken the God and the Goddess with divine sounds of conchs and drums. Then, having performed the worship of the two Śivas with flowers that are exceedingly fragrant and blooming at that very time, one should commence the rite previously described.
Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh section, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the twenty-seventh chapter titled "Description of the Fire Ritual" (Agnikārya-varṇana).
Chapter 28.
Upamanyu said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the sequence of occasional rites (*naimittika-vidhi*) as taught in the *Śiva-śāstra* for those who dwell in the hermitages of Śiva,
to be performed in all months and during both fortnights.
On the eighth and fourteenth days, as well as on the lunar festivals (parvan) in their proper order,
