during the solstices, the equinoxes, and especially during eclipses,
a great worship— or even one exceeding that— should be performed according to one's capacity.
Having prepared the *brahmakūrca* according to the rule every month,
one should bathe Śiva with it and, while fasting, drink the remainder;
[this purifies] even the most grievous of faults, such as the killing of a Brahmin.
No other expiation for the *brahmakūrca* rite is considered superior to its consumption.
In the month of Pauṣa, under the Puṣya asterism, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for the Lord.
In the month of Māgha, under the asterism called Maghā, one should offer a blanket of ghee.
In the month of Phālguna, at the end of the Uttarā constellation, one should indeed commence the great festival.
In Caitra, on the full moon day of Citrā, one should perform the ritual of the swing according to the rules.
And in Vaiśākha, under the Viśākhā constellation, one should establish a great pavilion of flowers.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the asterism called Mūla, one should cause a cold-water jar to be offered;
likewise, in Āṣāḍha, under Uttarāṣāḍhā, the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should be performed.
In Śrāvaṇa, one should also arrange the ordinary mandalas.

Then, under the lunar mansion called Śraviṣṭhā on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, one should perform the sprinkling rite; thereafter, on a day when the moon is in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, one should engage in water sports. Then, on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, one should offer milk-rice and fresh grain.
And on the day of Śatabhiṣaj, he should perform the fire-ritual with that very [substance].
On the full moon of Kārttika, when the moon is in conjunction with Kṛttikā, he should offer a thousand lamps.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is in Ārdrā, he should bathe Śiva with ghee.

If one is unable [to perform these] at those times, one should instead hold a festival; or else, an assembly, a great worship, or an especially extensive adoration. Even when an auspicious occasion has passed, or even during other praiseworthy rites, [one should perform worship].
In times of mental distress, misconduct, bad dreams, or the sight of evil omens; during portents, or when other inauspicious events occur, or when a disease is severe—
then acts such as bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and charity [should be performed].
The rites preceded by *puraścaraṇa* should be performed in accordance with the consecrated [liṅga].
And when the fire of Śiva has been extinguished, one should perform the re-establishment (*punassandhāna*).
He who thus conducts himself, ever diligent and most devoted to the dharma of Śarva—

Maheśvara grants liberation to him after a single birth. He who performs these [rites] in successive order during the obligatory and occasional ceremonies goes to the divine, primordial abode of the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for hundreds of millions of kalpas, that man,
when his time there has passed, falls from that state and attains the worlds of Aum, Kaumāra,
Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and especially the world of Rudra.
Having dwelt there for a long time and having enjoyed the pleasures as described,
he ascends again from there, passing beyond five stations.
Having attained knowledge from Śrīkaṇṭha, he shall go from there to the city of Śiva.
And he who is devoted to half-practice likewise, having performed it twice over in this very manner,
shall thereafter attain knowledge and reach union with Śiva. But that embodied being who has practiced half of half [the path], after the destruction of the body, [attains the same].
Having transcended the two worlds above, up to the unmanifest (avyakta) at the end of the cosmic egg,
he reaches the domain of Rudra belonging to the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain King.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures there for many thousands of yugas, he [proceeds further].

When his merit is exhausted, having reached the earth, he is born into a great family. There too, by the power of his previous impressions, that man of great luster abandons the ways of the fettered (paśu-dharma) and becomes devoted to the dharma of Śiva.
By meditating solely out of reverence for that Dharma, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
Having enjoyed various pleasures, one shall attain the station of a Vidyeśvara.
There, together with the Vidyeśvaras, one shall enjoy many pleasures in due succession.
Whether within or outside the cosmic egg, he then returns once more;
having thereafter obtained the knowledge of Śiva and attained supreme devotion,
and having reached a state of similarity with Śiva, he does not return again.
Even one who is intensely devoted to Śiva, though his mind remains attached to sense objects,
is liberated whether he performs the duties of Śiva or not.
One who has turned back [from worldly life] may have done so once, twice, or thrice.
Furthermore, one who holds authority over the Śiva-dharma shall not become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Therefore, having taken refuge in Śiva for whatever reason,
one who has exerted effort for the sake of the highest good should direct the mind toward the Śiva-dharma.
We shall not insist upon anything here for anyone;
by its very nature, this [teaching] is not pleasing to those who engage in persistence or excessive debate.
However, it is pleasing to others due to the weight of their meritorious latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
For those for whom the cause of saṃsāra is no longer able to sprout,
one should therefore reflect upon this entirely according to one's innate nature;
if one desires one's own welfare, one should apply oneself to the Dharma of Śiva.

Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the twenty-eighth chapter titled "Description of the Rules for Daily and Occasional Rites" concludes.
Chapter 29.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

O Blessed One, I have heard from your own lips that which is equal to the Vedas: the eternal and occasional rites proclaimed by Śiva for those who take refuge in him. Now, I desire to hear [the rules] concerning those who are entitled to the Śiva-dharma.
"If there is also karma that is performed for the sake of desired rewards, you should speak of it now.
Upamanyu said:
"There is indeed some [karma] that has results pertaining to this world, and likewise some that has results pertaining to the next world."
Furthermore, that [action] pertaining to this world and the next is again fivefold:
some action consists of ritual performance (*kriyā*), some action consists of austerity (*tapas*),
some consists of recitation and meditation (*japa-dhyāna*), and likewise some consists of all [these combined].
Likewise, ritual action is divided according to the sequence of fire-offerings, gifts, and worship;
it bears fruit only for those who possess all powers (sarva-śaktimat), and not for others.
And that power is the command of my Lord, Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Therefore, a twice-born man who observes the command should perform rites for the fulfillment of desires;
now I shall describe those rites which indeed bestow fruits both in this world and the next,
to be performed by the Śaivas and Māheśvaras, internally and externally, in due order.
Śiva and Maheśvara do not differ here at all;
just so, the Śaivas and the Māheśvaras are not divided.
For those men who take refuge in Śiva and are devoted to the sacrifice of knowledge are indeed Śaivas.
Those on earth who are devoted to ritual sacrifices are designated as Māheśvaras.
Therefore, the Śaivas should perform [the rites] internally, while the Māheśvaras should perform them externally;
however, there should be no difference in the application of the rite that is about to be described.
Having examined the ground according to the rules by its scent, color, taste, and other qualities,
one should prepare a surface on the earth that is well-smeared, resembling the surface of a mirror, and where the canopy is spread out in the sky as desired by the mind.
First, one should determine the east according to the path prescribed in the scriptures;
one should prepare a mandala measuring either one cubit or two cubits,
and draw a pure eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
With powders of jewels, gold, and other materials gathered as available,
[one should construct] that which is endowed with five enclosures and possessed of great splendor.
On the petals, the Siddhis are to be imagined, and on the filaments, those accompanied by their Śaktis.
The eight Rudras, beginning with Vāma, are located in order upon the petals starting from the east;
on the pericarp is dispassion (vairāgya), and in the seed-syllables are the nine powers (śaktis).
On the [pedestal] of Skanda is Dharma whose essence is Śiva, and on the stalk is knowledge (jñāna) which has Śiva as its refuge.
Upon the pericarp are the mandalas of Fire, the Sun, and the Moon;
beyond these is the triad of principles known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman.
Above all the seats, it is pleasant and adorned with various flowers.
One should worship [the Lord], who is joined with the five veils, together with the Mother;
he who resembles pure crystal, is serene, and possesses a cool radiance,
adorned with a crown of matted locks resembling a circle of lightning.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a lotus-like face slightly smiling,
his feet, palms, and lips resembled the petals of a red lotus;
he was endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
He was endowed with excellent divine weapons and anointed with divine perfumes;
he had five faces and ten arms, with a crescent moon as his crest-jewel.
His eastern face was serene, possessing a luster like that of the newly risen sun.
It was enriched with three lotus-eyes, adorned with the crescent moon as its crest,
and its right side possessed a beautiful luster like that of a dark blue cloud;
it was formidable, with a frowning brow and three red, circular eyes.
With fangs formidable and difficult to withstand, his sprout-like lower lip quivering;
his upper lip resembling coral, adorned with dark locks of hair;
playful in expression, three-eyed, and crowned with the moon as an ornament.
The western face has the luster of the full moon and is radiant with three eyes;
it bears the crescent moon, is gentle, and is enchanting with a mild smile.
The fifth [face] resembles crystal and is brilliantly illuminated by the crescent moon.
Extremely serene, blazing with three wide-open eyes;
on the right side, radiant with a trident, axe, thunderbolt, sword, and fire;
and on the left, radiant with a serpent, iron arrow, bell, noose, and goad.
Up to the knees it is bound by Nivṛtti; up to the navel by Pratiṣṭhā; up to the throat by Vidyā; likewise, up to the forehead by Śānti;
and above that, by the supreme Kalā known as Śāntyatītā.
He is the one who directly pervades the five paths, whose form consists of the five kalās;
the God whose crown is Īśāna, the ancient one known as Puruṣa;
likewise, Maheśvara, whose heart is Aghora and whose secret organ is Vāma.

And that form of his has feet that appear instantly; it consists of thirty-eight kalās, is composed of the Mātṛkās, and likewise consists of the five Brahmans. It is composed of what is called the syllable Om, and is endowed with the power of the Haṃsa.
Thus,

Sadāśiva— the very embodiment of Vidyā, consisting of the three principles— is directly perceived with his lap occupied by the Power whose nature is Will; on his right side is the one called Knowledge (Jñāna), and on his left is the one called Action (Kriyā).
Having conceptualized [the deity] through the root-mantra of the form and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in due order,
one should worship according to the rule up to the arghya offering with the root-vidyā—
[worshipping] Śiva himself in embodied form, together with the supreme Śakti.
There, having invoked Mahādeva— who is devoid of the manifestation of existence and non-existence—
and having prepared the five ancillary offerings, one should worship the Supreme Lord with the Brahma-mantras,
the six limbs, and then with the Mātṛkā.
One should worship the Supreme God sequentially with the *praṇava*, with Śiva joined by Śakti,
or likewise with peaceful mantras and all other Vedic mantras,
or even with Śiva alone.

Having performed the rites from the water for the feet (*pādya*) up to the mouth-freshener (*mukhavāsa*), and excluding the ritual dismissal (*prasthāpana*), one should indeed commence the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā*) in due order.
Om. Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of Rituals for Specific Desires," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious *Śiva-mahāpurāṇa*.
Chapter 30.
First of all, one should worship the two deities Heraṃba and Ṣaṇmukha with perfumes and other offerings on the right and left sides of the two Śivas, respectively. ŚivP_7.2.30.1ab / ŚivP_7.2.30.1cd.
Then, one should worship the Brahmans, beginning with Īśāna and proceeding in order,

together with their Śaktis, ending with Sadyojāta, in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa). One should also worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), beginning with the Heart, in that very same place, in their proper sequence.

One should worship [the deities] starting from the southeast for both Śiva and Śivā. Therein, one may or may not worship the eight Rudras, Vāmā and the others, together with the powers (śaktis), Vāmā and the others, subsequently in order around the east and the other directions.
The first enclosure has been described by me to you, O delighter of the Yadus.
Out of affection, the second enclosure is now being told; listen with faith.
On the eastern petal and the others, [one should worship] Ananta, and his Śakti to his left.
One should worship Sūkṣma together with Śakti on the petal in the southern direction;
then, on the petal in the western direction, one should worship Śivottama together with Śakti;
likewise, one should worship Ekanetra on the petal in the northern direction.
One should worship Ekarudra and his Śakti thereafter on the petal in the northeast (Īśāna).
One should worship Trimūrti and his Śakti on the petal in the southeast (Agni).
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha on the petal in the southwest (Nairṛta), and his Śakti to his left.
In that very manner, one should worship Śikhaṇḍīśa on the northwest petal;
in the second enclosure, the offerings are to the sovereign rulers of all seasons;
and in the third enclosure, the eight forms (Aṣṭamūrtis) are to be worshipped along with their Śaktis.
In the eight directions, starting from the east and proceeding around them in order: Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Rudra, Paśupati,
Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva— these are the eight forms (mūrtis) respectively.
Immediately thereafter, Mahādeva and the others,
the eleven forms (mūrtis), are to be worshipped there in sequence along with their Śaktis:
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, Śaṅkara, and Nīlalohita.
Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, Bhavodbhava, and Kapardīśa are proclaimed; likewise, there are eleven Śaktis.
Among them, eight are to be worshipped first, beginning with the southeast (āgneya) in due order.
The God of gods is on the eastern petal, and Īśāna is in the southeast;
Bhavodbhava is between those two, and Kapālīśa follows after that.
In that enclosure, one should further worship the Lord of Bulls (Vṛṣendra) in front.
One should place Nandin to his right and Mahākāla likewise to the north;
Śāstṛ on the petal in the southeast direction, and the Mothers on the petal in the southern direction;
Gajānana on the southwestern petal, and furthermore, Ṣaṇmukha on the western petal.
One should worship Jyeṣṭhā on the petal of Vāyu (the northwest), Gaurī in the north, and Caṇḍa in the northeast (Īśvara). Between Śāstṛ and Nandīśa, one should worship Munīndra and Vṛṣabha;
furthermore, one should worship Piṅgala to the north of Mahākāla.
Then, one should worship Bhṛṅgīśvara in the midst of the assembly of the Teacher and the Mothers; Vīrabhadra in the midst of the Mothers and Vighneśa;
and one should worship the goddess Sarasvatī in the space between Skanda and Vighneśa.
Between Jyeṣṭhā and Kumārī, one should worship Śrī, who is honored at the feet of Śiva;
between Jyeṣṭhā and Gaṇāmbā, one should worship Mahāmoṭī;
and between Gaṇāmbā and Caṇḍa, one should propitiate the goddess Durgā.
In this very section, moreover, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite while meditating upon the assembly of Śiva’s attendants—
known as the Rudras and the Bhūtas— along with their various Śaktis,
and the circle of Śivā’s female companions.
When the third enclosure has been thus expanded and worshipped,
one should meditate upon the fourth enclosure and worship it outside of that.
The Sun is to be worshipped on the eastern petal, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) on the southern.
Rudra is on the petal in the direction of Varuṇa (the west), and Viṣṇu is on the petal in the northern direction.
Then follow the separate enclosures for each of the four deities.
First, there are the six limbs of that [deity], along with the powers beginning with Dīptā.
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā,
Amoghā, and Vidyutā are situated in order around the east and the other directions;
these four forms are to be worshipped in sequence in the second enclosure.
Beyond that are the powers (śaktis) beginning with the East and ending with the North;
then, in successive order, Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi;
and Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu—these are the forms of Vivasvat.
Vistārā is situated in the eastern quarter, while Sutarā is located in the south;
Bodhanī is in the western part, and Āpyāyinī is in the north. Furthermore, beyond that are Uṣā, Prabhā, Prājñā, and Sandhyā.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in the directions beginning with the northeast (aiśāna), one should worship [the deities] in the second enclosure:
Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha—the best among the intelligent;
Bṛhaspati of vast intellect, and Bhārgava, the treasury of splendors.
One should worship Śanaiścara, Rāhu, Ketu, and the smoke-colored,
terrifying [Ketu] on all sides in the third enclosure in due order;
or alternatively, one should worship the twelve Ādityas in the second enclosure.
And in the third enclosure, one should worship the twelve zodiac signs;
and outside of that, all around, the seven groups of seven,
as well as the sages, gods, gandharvas, serpents, and hosts of apsarases.
One should likewise worship the village chiefs, the Yakṣas, the Yātudhānas, and the horses;
one should also worship the Vālakhilyas, who consist of the seven Vedic meters.
Having thus worshipped the Sun-god in the third enclosure, [one proceeds].
Thereafter, one should worship Brahmā along with his three enclosures.
One should worship Hiraṇyagarbha in the east, Virāj to the south,
Kāla in the western quarter, and Puruṣa in the north.
Hiraṇyagarbha is the first Brahmā, resembling a lotus;
Kāla is like collyrium of a dark complexion; and Puruṣa is like crystal.
He consists of the three qualities: indeed, the rājasa, the tāmasa, and likewise the sāttvika.
These four are situated respectively in the first enclosure;
they are to be worshipped in the second enclosure, proceeding in order from the east and around.
They are Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana.
In the third enclosure, one should subsequently worship the Prajāpatis:
eight in the east and other directions starting from the east, and three in the east and west in due order—
Dakṣa, Ruci, Bhṛgu, Marīci, and likewise Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, Kaśyapa,
and Vasiṣṭha— these are renowned as the Lords of Progeny (Prajāpatis).
Their wives, together with them, are to be worshipped in due order.
Prasūti, Ākūti, Khyāti, and Sambhūti;
Dhṛti, Smṛti, Kṣamā, Sannati, and Anasūyā;
Devamātā and Arundhatī—all of them were indeed devoted wives.
One who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva [should worship] the four Vedas— glorious and of pleasing appearance—
in the first enclosure;
furthermore, one should worship the Itihāsas and Purāṇas in the second enclosure.
In the third enclosure, all Vedic sciences, preceded by the Dharmaśāstras,
are to be worshipped on all sides.
The Vedas are to be placed in the east and other directions, while the others are to be arranged according to preference.
Having performed worship on all sides, either eightfold or fourfold,
and having thus honored Brahmā together with his three enclosures,
one should thereafter worship Rudra along with his enclosures in the south and the west.
The six ancillaries of Brahman (brahma-ṣaḍaṅga) are remembered as the first enclosure;
likewise, the second enclosure consists of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras).
There is a distinction regarding the third enclosure, which shall now be described.
His four forms are to be worshipped in order, starting from the east:
the deity endowed with the three qualities (triguṇa), known as Śiva, is in the east;
the rājasa form, Brahmā, the creator, is worshipped as Bhava in the south.
In the west, the fire is tamasic; it is Hara, the destroyer, who is to be worshipped.
In the north, Viṣṇu—the lord of the universe, the benevolent one—is sattvic and the bestower of happiness.
Thus, in the western quarter of Śambhu, there is the twenty-sixth Śiva.
Having worshipped [the central deity] thoroughly, one should then worship Vaikuṇṭha on the northern side.
Placing Vāsudeva at the forefront, one should sacrifice in the first enclosure;
then Aniruddha to the south, and Pradyumna to the west.
In the north, one should worship Saṃkarṣaṇa, and in the west, these two [Rāma and Kṛṣṇa] either in their natural order or reversed.
This is declared to be the first enclosure; now follows the auspicious second enclosure:
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana.

Rāma, another Kṛṣṇa, and you, Aśvamukha—these they placed in the third enclosure; one should worship them in the eastern quarter. One should worship the weapon called Nārāyaṇa in the south, which is in some places unimpeded.

In the west, [he should worship] Pāñcajanya, and in the north, the bow Śārṅga. Thus, having manifested the supreme Hari known as Viśva— Mahāviṣṇu and Sadāviṣṇu— in embodied form, he should worship him with these three enclosures.
Having thus worshipped the fourfold manifestation of Viṣṇu according to the sequence of the four forms,
one should then worship his four powers (śaktis) in order:
Prabhā in the south-eastern quarter, and Sarasvatī in the south-west.
One should worship Gaṇāmbikā in the northwest and Lakṣmī in the northeast.
Having thus performed the worship of the forms beginning with Bhānu and their respective powers,
one should then worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) in that very enclosure.
One should worship Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa,
as well as Vāyu, Soma, Kubera, and Īśāna;
thus, having worshipped the fourth enclosure according to the prescribed rule.
One should worship the weapons of Maheśa in the outer area behind [the deity]:
the glorious trident (triśūla) in the northeast (aiśāna), the thunderbolt (vajra) in the direction of Indra (māhendra),
the axe (paraśu) in the region of the fire-quarter (vahni-dig-bhāga), and one should worship the arrow (sāyaka) in the south (yāmya).
One should worship Khaḍga in the southwest and Pāśa in the domain of Varuṇa (the west).
One should worship Aṅkuśa in the northwest quarter and Pināka in the north.
One should worship Raudra Kṣetrapāla facing toward the west.
Having worshipped the fifth enclosure immediately thereafter on the outside,
one should worship the deities of all the enclosures either outside or in the fifth enclosure.
In the fifth enclosure, one should sacrifice to the Great Bull (Mahokṣa) together with the Mothers in front.
Then, all those born of divine origins are to be worshipped on every side:
the sky-dwellers, the sages, the Siddhas, the Daityas, the Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas;
as well as the lords of the Nāgas, beginning with Ananta, together with the Nāgas born of their respective lineages.
The ḍākinīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, and the leaders of the bhairavas; others dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla) born from various wombs;
as well as rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, and lakes.
Animals, birds, trees, insects, and other such low-born creatures;
humans of various forms, and wild beasts of low birth;
the worlds within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), and from those, millions of cosmic eggs.
There are countless external cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*), together with their presiding lords;
and the Rudras who support these cosmic eggs are stationed in the ten directions.
Beyond that [egg] lies that which belongs to Gauḍa, that which belongs to Māmeya, and that which belongs to Śākta.
Whatever exists that is denotable by words, consisting of both conscious and unconscious principles—
all that, having understood it generally, one should worship at the side of the two Śivas;
all [the deities] with palms joined in reverence, inconceivable, and likewise with smiling faces.
And always gazing with affection upon the God and the Goddess;
having thus performed the worship of the enclosures for the sake of pacifying distraction,
one should again worship the Lord of Gods, prepare the food, and utter the imperishable syllable (akṣara).

Thereafter, he should offer to Śiva and Śivā an excellent, pure, and beautiful great oblation (*mahācaru*) that is like nectar, well-prepared with various side dishes; the best portion consists of thirty-two *āḍhaka* measures, while the lowest is less than one *āḍhaka*.
Having prepared [the offerings] according to one's means, one should present them with faith.
Then, having offered water, betel-leaf, and various side dishes,
and having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and so forth, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
One should procure specifically those excellent materials suitable for enjoyment;
one who possesses devotion should not practice stinginess with wealth when it is available.
[This applies even] to one who is deceitful, negligent, or who acts with hypocrisy.
"The rites performed for specific desires do not bear fruit at all"— this is the teaching of the wise.
Therefore, having completely abandoned indifference,
one who desires the attainment of results should perform the rites for specific desires with the application of all their constituent parts.
Having thus completed the worship and having bowed to the God and the Goddess, one should then recite the hymn of praise with devotion and a concentrated mind. Then,
at the conclusion of the worship, one should recite the hymn at least one hundred and eight times.
Eagerly, one should recite the five-syllabled mantra more than a thousand times;
having performed the worship of the Vidyā and the worship of the Guru,
one should thereafter worship the members of the assembly in due order, according to one's means and according to one's faith.
Then, having dismissed the Lord of Devas along with all his retinues,
one should present the mandala to the guru together with the implements of sacrifice;
or else, one may give everything in due order to those who have taken refuge in Śiva.
Alternatively, one should offer it for the sake of that very Śiva in a sacred field (śivakṣetra) of Śiva;
or one should worship the Lord in the Śiva-fire with the seven oblation-substances,
having duly honored all the deities of the surrounding enclosures according to the prescribed rule.

He is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Yogeśvara. There is no sacrifice anywhere in the world superior to him. Indeed, there is nothing in this universe that cannot be accomplished by him.
Whether its fruit be some worldly result or a result pertaining to the hereafter,
it cannot be restricted by saying, "This is its fruit, and not that.
This is the supreme means for attaining the entirety of that which constitutes ultimate well-being.
It cannot be said that whatever is worshipped by a person from this [Lord]—
just as from a *cintāmaṇi* jewel— that fruit is obtained by him.
Nevertheless, one should not employ this for the sake of a trivial result.
For one who seeks small gain becomes himself smaller than the great [object of desire].
Whether the fruit be great or small, if an action is performed, it succeeds;
let that action be undertaken dedicated to Mahādeva.
Therefore, a wise person should perform this [rite] for fruits— whether visible or invisible— that cannot be obtained by other means, such as victory over enemies or death;
and even during great calamities, such as intense passion or fear.
"In times of famine and other such calamities, one should perform a rite of pacification for the sake of peace by means of this [mantra].
What is the use of much talk? This weapon of his own, which wards off great misfortune, Maheśvara has declared to be for the Śaivas."
"Therefore, there is no protection for the self here beyond this.
Thinking thus, one who performs this auspicious rite attains its fruit.
Whoever, having become pure and being well-composed, should recite even just this hymn—*Śiva Purāṇa* 7.2.30.100–101ab.
He shall obtain one-eighth of the fruit of even his most cherished object. Having kept that purpose in mind, he should recite [the text] while fasting on a festival day;
or by doing so on the eighth or the fourteenth day, he shall obtain half the fruit.
But he who, intent upon the goal, likewise observes the vow on the festival days and other occasions, and recites this hymn for one month, shall obtain the full fruit. Om.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Optional Rites of the Śaivas," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 31.
Upamanyu said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I shall recite to you a hymn of praise according to the path of the five enclosures."
This meritorious act is completed by the Lord of Yoga.

Victory, victory to you, O Śambhu, sole Lord of the world, naturally enchanting, whose nature is eternal consciousness! You are the reality that transcends the path of both speech—which is inherently impure and manifold—and of the mind.
Victory to you, whose effortless activity is beautiful and naturally stainless!
Victory to you, O ocean of pure qualities, whose great power is equal to your own self! Victory to you, endowed with infinite splendor, whose form is beyond compare!
Victory to you, O support of inconceivable majesty, whose auspiciousness is undisturbed!
Victory to you, the stainless one, the supportless one, who arises without cause! Victory to you, the uninterrupted supreme bliss, the cause of liberation!

Victory to you, O supreme sovereign! Victory to you, the abode of exceeding compassion! Victory to you, the independent essence of all things! Victory to you, whose majesty is peerless! Victory to you, who pervade the great universe! Victory to you, who are not encompassed by anything!

Victory to you, O Supreme One of all; victory to you, O Utterly Unsurpassed! Victory to you, O Wondrous One; victory to you, O Non-minuscule; victory to you, O Undecaying; victory to you, O Imperishable! Victory to you, O Immeasurable; victory to you, O Free from Māyā; victory to you, O Non-existence; victory to you, O Stainless!

O you of mighty arms, of great essence, of great virtues, and of great renown; O you of great strength, of great illusion, of great flavor, and of the great chariot! Salutations to the supreme deity; salutations to the supreme cause!
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one; salutations to you, who are even more auspicious than auspiciousness.
Indeed, this entire world, including the gods and the asuras, is dependent upon you.
Therefore, who would dare to transgress the command ordained by you?
Furthermore, these people always rely solely upon you;
therefore, may you show them favor and grant what they have requested.
Victory to you, O Ambikā! Victory, O Mother of the World! Victory, O you who consist of the entire universe!
Victory to you whose sovereignty is infinite! Victory to you whose form is incomparable!
Victory to you who transcend speech and mind! Victory to you who shatter the darkness of ignorance!
Victory to you who are free from birth and old age! Victory to you who are ever superior to time!
Victory to you who abide in manifold forms; victory to you, beloved of Viśveśvara!
Victory to you, worshipped by all the gods; victory to you, who cause the universe to expand!
Victory to you whose divine limbs are auspicious; victory to you, the lamp of auspiciousness!
Victory to you whose conduct is auspicious! Victory to the bestower of auspiciousness!
Salutations to the embodiment of the accumulation of supreme and most auspicious qualities!
Indeed, the entire world has arisen from you alone, and into you alone it dissolves.
Without you, even the Lord himself would not be able to grant the fruit from this [act].
O Queen of the Gods, since birth this person has relied upon you;
therefore, fulfill the heart’s desire of this devotee of yours.

Five-faced and ten-armed, resembling pure crystal, his body is composed of the phonemes, the Brahman-mantras, and the kalās; he is the Lord who is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). Established in devotion to Śiva, he is Sadāśiva, who has transcended even the state of peace (śāntyatīta).
May she, worshipped by me with devotion, grant me the welfare I have prayed for.
May the Power named Śivā, who is called Icchā (Will) and who has ascended the lap of Sadāśiva,
the mother of all worlds, grant my heart’s desire.
The two gods, Heramba and Ṣaṇmukha, are the beloved sons of the two Śivas;
they possess the power of Śiva, are omniscient, and subsist on the nectar of Śiva-knowledge.
Satisfied with one another and affectionate toward each other, they are eternally honored by the two Śivas.
The two gods are always honored even by the thirty deities led by Brahmā;
they are ever intent on protecting all the worlds,
manifesting incarnations at their own will through numerous divisions of their own portions.

These two, who have been thus constantly worshipped by me at the side of Śiva and Śivā, shall grant my request, honoring their command. [Grant it] to Sadāśiva, known as Īśāna, who resembles pure crystal.

The form of Śiva, the Supreme Self, is characterized by the conceit of being the head (mūrdhābhimāninī). It is devoted to the worship of Śiva, peaceful, beyond the state of peace (śāntyatīta), and established in sacrifice. It is the final seed-syllable of the five syllables, endowed with the five kalās.
May that supreme Brahman, the sacred thread (pavitra) which was first worshipped together with Śakti in the first enclosure, grant my prayer;
it is ancient, known as Puruṣa, and resembles the rising sun.
And the conceit of being the eastern face of Parameṣṭhin Śiva—
consisting of peace, abiding in the wind, and devoted to the worship of Śambhu’s feet—
is the first among the seeds of Śiva and among the kalās, possessing four kalās.
In the eastern quarter, I have worshipped with devotion and according to my ability;
may that supreme Brahman, the Purifier, grant my prayer.
[May He grant it who is] like collyrium and other substances, who is non-terrible (Aghora) yet possesses a terrible form.
The right face of the God, which worships the feet of the God of gods,
is mounted upon the Vidyāpāda and situated in the middle of the fire-mandala;
it is the second among the seeds of Śiva, endowed with the eight kalās among the kalās.
May the Middle Brahma, worshipped together with Śakti on the southern side of Śambhu,
grant me that which has been requested.
May he who is called Vāma, resembling powdered saffron and wearing excellent attire, [bestow it].
The face of the Lord is established in the *pratiṣṭhā* [tattva];
it resides in the midst of the circle of water and is intent upon the worship of Mahādeva.
It is the fourth among the seeds of Śiva (*śivabīja*), endowed with thirteen kalās.
May the Supreme Brahman, worshipped together with Śakti in the northern quarter of the Lord, grant my prayer; it is pure,
white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, known as Saṃdhyā, and possessing gentle characteristics.
The western face of Śiva is devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet;
it is established upon the earth, fixed in the state of *nivṛtti*,
and is the third among the seeds of Śiva, endowed with eight *kalās*.
Worshipped together with Śakti on the western side of the Lord,
may the supreme Brahman, the sacred thread (*pavitra*), grant my prayer.
O you who are the heart-form of both Śiva and Śivā, and who are permeated by the nature of Śiva!
Placing their command before you both, grant my desire to me—
[the desire] directed toward Śiva and Śivā, who are the embodiments of the crest [of the Lord] and who take refuge in Śiva. Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, grant my desire to me.
O you who are purified by the armor of Śiva and Śivā,
having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they both grant my desire. O you who are devoted to the form of the Eye of Śiva and Śivā!

Honoring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may you two grant my desire; and you two, who are the embodiments of the weapons of Śiva and Śivā and are eternally intent upon their worship— honoring the command of Śiva and Śivā, may you two grant my desire.
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Rudra, Kāla, Vikaraṇa,
Bala, Vikaraṇa, and the supreme Balapramathana,
as well as Sarvabhūtadamana— such are the eight powers (aṣṭaśaktayaḥ).
"By the very command of Śiva and Śivā, let them grant what I have requested.
Then Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śiva, Ekanetra,
the one named Ekarudra, Amṛti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍaka [spoke].
Likewise, their eight Śaktis are worshipped in the second enclosure;
by the very command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant me my desire.
Furthermore, there are the eight forms beginning with Bhava, and also their Śaktis.
Mahādeva and the others, as well as the other eleven forms [of Śiva],
all together with their Śaktis, are stationed in the third enclosure.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant the desired fruit.
The king of trees was of great splendor, with a voice like that of a massive cloud;
he resembled the peaks of Mount Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and the Himālayas;
he had the form of a white mountain peak and was graced by a hump.
He was adorned with a tail like that of the lord of great serpents;
his face, horns, and feet were red, as were his eyes for the most part;
all his limbs were stout and elevated, and he was radiant with a beautiful gait.
Possessing auspicious marks, glorious, and adorned with blazing jewels;
beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and having the bull as his vehicle for both Śiva and Śivā;
likewise, his own body was purified by the placement of their feet.
The illustrious bull-king’s attendant, whose excellent weapon is the glorious trident—
placing their command before him, may he grant my desire.
May Nandīśvara, of great splendor, the son of the daughter of the mountain king, [grant it].
Constantly worshipped and saluted by the gods together with Nārāyaṇa,
he stood at the gate of Śarva’s inner apartments along with his attendants;
he was equal in splendor to the Lord of All and the crusher of all Asuras.
He was consecrated as the presiding authority over all the duties of Śiva;
he was beloved by Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and bore the glorious trident as his excellent weapon. He was deeply attached to those who had taken refuge in Śiva, and they, in turn, were devoted to him.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant my desire.
May the mighty-armed Mahākāla, like another Mahādeva,
eternally protect those who have taken refuge in Mahādeva.

He who is dear to Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and always a worshiper of the two; having honored the command of the two, may he grant my desire. He knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, he is the teacher, and the supreme body of Viṣṇu.
The son of Mahāmoha, who is fond of honey, meat, and fermented liquors—
placing their command before him, may he grant my desire.
And likewise Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā of fierce prowess—
these indeed are the seven Mothers, the mothers of all the worlds.
By the command of the Supreme Lord, may they grant me my request.
He has the face of an intoxicated elephant; he is the son of Gaṅgā and Śaṅkara;
his body is the ether, his arms are the quarters of the sky, and his eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire;
he is eternally worshipped by the divine elephants of the quarters, beginning with Airāvata.
Having burst forth through the intoxication of the knowledge of Śiva, he causes no obstacle for the gods;
yet, being meditated upon by Śiva, he is the Lord of Obstacles who creates hindrances for the Asuras and others.
Having honored the command of the two Śivas, may he grant my desire.
The six-faced one, born of Śiva, the lord who wields the spear and the thunderbolt;
he is indeed the son of Agni, and furthermore the son of Aparṇā,
as well as of Gaṅgā, Gaṇāmbā, and the Kṛttikās.
He was surrounded by Viśākha, Śākha, and Naigameya;
likewise by Indrajit, the commander of Candra’s army and conqueror of the Asura Tāraka,
and by the piercer of mountains, chief among whom is Meru, by means of his own splendor.
Resembling molten gold, with eyes like the petals of a hundred-petaled lotus,
Kumāra is the supreme exemplar of beauty among those who are delicate.
He is dear to Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and always a worshiper of the feet of Śiva.

Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may she grant my desire; Jyeṣṭhā, the most excellent, the giver of boons, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva and Śivā— placing their command foremost, may she grant my desire.
Worshipped by the three worlds, the Mother of the Gaṇas appeared in person with the form of a meteor;
at the request of Brahmā for the sake of the creation and expansion of the world from Śiva,
she emerged from between the eyebrows of Śivā as she was being divided.
She was Dakṣāyaṇī, Satī, Menā, Haimavatī, and Umā;
she was the mother of Kauśikī and likewise of Bhadrakālī,
as well as the mother of Aparṇā and Pāṭalā.
May Rudrāṇī, who is ever devoted to the worship of Śiva and is the beloved of Rudra,
grant my desire after honoring the command of Śiva and his consort.
May Caṇḍa, the lord of all the Gaṇas, who was born from the mouth of Śambhu, [grant it].

Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant my desire. May the illustrious Piṅgala, the leader of the Gaṇas, who is devoted to Śivā and beloved by Śiva, grant my wish by the very command of Śiva and Śivā.
The leader of the Gaṇas named Bhṛṅgīśa is devoted to the worship of Śiva;
by virtue of our general relationship,
may he grant my desire, preceded by his husband’s command.
Vīrabhadra, of great splendor, resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon,
is eternally dear to Bhadrakālī and the protector of the Mothers;
he is also the one who severed the head of the sacrifice and of the evil-minded Dakṣa.
Taksaka, who dwells among the gods such as Upendra, Indra, and Yama,
is the illustrious attendant of Śiva and the protector of Śiva’s command.
By the very command of the two Śivas, may he grant my desire.

Sarasvatī, born from the lotus-like mouth of Maheśa, is intent upon the worship of the two Śivas; may she grant my desire. Lakṣmī, residing on the chest of Viṣṇu, is devoted to the worship of the two Śivas.
By the very command of the two Śivas, may she grant my desire;
Mahāmoṭī, who is devoted to the worship of the feet of the Great Goddess—
by her very appointment, may she grant my desire.
Kauśikī is mounted upon a lion; she is the supreme daughter of Pārvatī.
She is the sleep of Viṣṇu, the Great Māyā, and the slayer of the great buffalo-demon. She is the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and she is fond of honey, meat, and wine.
Having honored the teaching of my mother, may she grant my desire.
There are the Rudras, equal in splendor to Rudra, foremost and renowned for their power;
and those called Bhūtas, of great heroism, possessing a radiance equal to Mahādeva.

They are eternally liberated, incomparable, free from dualities, and undisturbed; they possess their powers (śaktis) and are accompanied by their attendants, being honored by all the worlds. They are capable of the creation and destruction of all the worlds.
Mutually affectionate and devoted to one another,
exceedingly tender toward each other, and saluting one another,
they were eternally beloved by Śiva and marked by the characteristics of Śiva.
Those with gentle streams, those that are mixed, and those consisting of two intermediate types;
those that are deformed, those that are beautiful, and likewise those assuming various forms—
having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they indeed grant my desire.
The group of the Goddess’s dear friends, endowed with the characteristics of a queen,
together with many Rudra-maidens and Śaktis,
is constantly worshipped with devotion in the third enclosure of Śambhu.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant me auspiciousness.
Divākara is a form of Maheśa, a radiant orb of light;
he is both devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), permeated by qualities (*guṇasaṃkīrṇa*), and likewise consisting solely of qualities (*guṇakevala*).
The primordial one is of an unchanging nature, yet he possesses the common modification;
he is also the possessor of unique actions through the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Thus, he is divided threefold, fourfold, and again fivefold.
In the fourth enclosure, may he who is worshipped along with the attendants of Śambhu—
He who is dear to Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent on the worship of Śiva’s feet—
having honored the command of the two, Śiva and Śivā, grant me auspiciousness.
The six limbs of Divākara and the eight powers beginning with Dīptā;
Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Ravi in their proper order;
Arka, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu—these are the forms of Āditya.
Furthermore, there are other powers (śaktis), namely Vistarā, Sutarā, Bodhinī, Āpyāyinī, Uṣā, Prabhā, Prājñā,
and Sandhyā; and the planets, beginning with the Moon and ending with Ketu, are all permeated by Śiva.
Impelled by the command of the two Śivas, may they grant me auspiciousness.
Or else, may the twelve Ādityas, as well as the twelve Śaktis,
the sages, the gods, the Gandharvas, and the hosts of Pannagas and Apsarases [grant it].
The village chiefs, as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and asuras—
these seven groups of seven are the horses composed of the seven Vedic meters.
And all those beginning with the Vālakhilyas are worshippers of the feet of Śiva.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant me auspiciousness.
Now, Brahmā is the form of the God of gods, the sovereign of the terrestrial sphere,
possessing the sovereignty of sixty-four qualities, and established in the principle of intellect (buddhitattva).

The Lord is without qualities (*nirguṇa*), yet he is mingled with qualities (*guṇasaṃkīrṇa*) and likewise consists solely of qualities (*guṇakevala*). He is the immutable Self (*avikārātmaka*), and thereafter he becomes the common one before [creation].
And he possesses uncommon actions through the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Divided the earth into three parts, four parts, and again into five;
O Śambhu, he was worshipped in the fourth enclosure along with his followers—
he who is dear to Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent on the worship of Śiva’s feet.
Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant me auspiciousness.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of the World, Virāṭ, Kāla, and Puruṣa;
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana—[may they grant me auspiciousness].
The lords of progeny, Dakṣa and the others, who are the sons of Brahmā—
these eleven, together with their wives, as well as Dharma and Saṃkalpa,
are devoted to the worship of Śiva and are entirely dedicated to devotion toward Śiva.
May all those who are subject to the command of Śiva grant me auspiciousness.
Likewise, may the four Vedas, together with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
and the Dharmaśāstras endowed with Vedic sciences, [grant me auspiciousness].
May those [deities] whose purposes are mutually opposed, yet who establish the nature of Śiva,
bestow auspiciousness upon me after honoring the command of Śiva and Śivā.
Now, Rudra, the Great God, is the most venerable form of Śambhu.
The lord of the Āgneya-maṇḍala is the sovereign endowed with the power of *puruṣa*;

he is filled with the self-concept of Śiva, being both devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and yet consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*). He is purely *sāttvika*, as well as *rājasa* and *tāmasa*.
Formerly he delighted in changelessness, and thereafter he was entirely free from modification.
Possessing extraordinary deeds, he is distinct from the performance of creation and other cosmic functions.
He is the one who severed even the head of Brahmā, and Janaka was his son.
Janaka’s son is the controller even of Viṣṇu;
the Lord is the eternal awakener of those two and the bestower of grace.
Rudra, the sovereign of the two worlds, exists both within and outside the cosmic egg.
Beloved of Śiva, devoted to Śivā, and intent upon the worship of Śiva’s feet—
placing the command of Śiva before him, may he grant me auspiciousness.
His [mantra] consists of the six limbs of Brahman, as well as the group of eight ending with Vidyeśa.
And the four manifestations beginning with Śiva, who worship Śiva—
Śiva, Bhava, Hara, and likewise the other, Mṛḍa—
placing Śiva’s command before them, may they grant me auspiciousness.
Now, Viṣṇu is the supreme body of Maheśa Śiva himself;
he is the direct lord of the water-element, established in the state of the unmanifest (avyakta).
He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), yet abounds in the quality of sattva, and likewise consists solely of the [unmanifest] guṇa.
He prided himself on being changeless, yet he was subject to the three common transformations;
he possessed extraordinary power through his distinct performance of creation and other cosmic functions,
even while vying with the Self-born One (Brahmā) who had arisen from his own right limb.
Directly created by the primordial Brahmā, he is indeed his creator;
Viṣṇu dwells both within and outside the cosmic egg as the sovereign of two worlds,
the wielder of the discus who brings an end to the asuras, and likewise the younger brother of Śakra.

And he manifested here in ten forms under the pretext of Bhṛgu’s curse; for the sake of suppressing the burden of the earth, he descended by his own will into Kṣiti. Possessing immeasurable power and a master of illusion, he deluded the world through his *māyā*.
Having fashioned an image of Mahāviṣṇu or even of Sadāśiva,
he is constantly worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas upon a seat consisting of the three forms. Devoted to Śiva, attached to Śivā, he is intent on the worship of Śiva’s feet.
Placing the command of Śiva before him, may he grant me auspiciousness.
Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and thereafter Saṃkarṣaṇa—
these are declared to be the four forms of Hari.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and then the Dwarf;
likewise the three Rāmas, Kṛṣṇa, and Viṣṇu with the horse’s face (Hayagrīva). The discus is the weapon of Nārāyaṇa, as are the Pāñcajanya conch and the Śārṅga bow.

Having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may they grant me auspiciousness. May Prabhā, Sarasvatī, Gaurī, and Lakṣmī, who are devoted to Śiva, grant me auspiciousness by the decree of Śiva and Śivā.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa;
Vāyu, Soma, Kubera, and likewise Īśāna, the wielder of the trident—
all these are devoted to the worship of Śiva and are permeated by the true being of Śiva.
Having honored the command of the two Śivas, may they bestow auspiciousness upon me. Furthermore,
[may] the trident, the thunderbolt, as well as the axe and the arrow,
the sword, the noose, the goad, and the Pināka, the supreme weapon, [grant me blessings].
These divine weapons of the God and the Goddess shall always,
having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, provide me with protection forever.
May the bull-formed God, the son of Surabhi, who possesses great strength, [do the same].
Surrounded by the five Mother-cows, he entered into a competitive emulation with the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala);
through his ascetic penance, he attained the status of a vehicle for the Supreme Lords. Placing their command before him, may he grant my desire.
Nandā, Sunandā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanā—
these five mothers of the cows reside in the world of Śiva;
they are eternally devoted to devotion for Śiva and dedicated to the worship of Śiva.
By the very command of the two Śivas, may they grant my desire.
The protector of the field (Kṣetrapāla) possesses great splendor and resembles a dark blue cloud;
his face is formidable with fangs, and it shines with quivering, red lips.
The glorious one has blood-red hair standing upright, with eyes curved in a frown;
he has three round, red eyes and is adorned with the moon and serpents.
Naked, his hands hold aloft a trident, a noose, a sword, and a skull-cup.
Bhairava is surrounded by Bhairavas, Siddhas, and Yoginīs;
he is seated in every sacred field (kṣetra), standing as the protector of the virtuous,
devoted to bowing to Śiva, and permeated by the true nature of Śiva.
Protecting those who have taken refuge in Śiva especially, like his own biological sons,
and having honored the command of Śiva and Śivā, may he grant me auspiciousness.
Tālajaṅgha and others are worshipped in his first enclosure.
Having honored the command of the two Śivas, may the four [Gaṇas] protect me;
and may Bhairava and the others who surround him on all sides likewise show me favor out of respect for the ordinance of Śiva.
The sages beginning with Nārada, who are divine and honored by the gods;
the Sādhyas and those gods who dwell in Janaloka;
and those who have ceased their offices and dwell in Maharloka.
Likewise, the seven ṛṣis and others, together with the qualities of those who dwell in celestial chariots—
all of them devoted to the worship of Śiva and subject to the command of Śiva— may they,
by the command of the two Śivas, grant my desire to me.
The four divine classes of beings, beginning with the Gandharvas and ending with the Piśācas; the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others who move through the sky;
and the Asuras and Rākṣasas who dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
The serpent lords beginning with Ananta, the birds beginning with Vainateya,
the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pretas, the Vetālas, the Grahas, and other hosts of Bhūtas; as well as the Ḍākinīs, Yoginīs, and Śākinīs of similar kind.
Fields, groves, houses, and the like; sacred fords and shrines;
islands, oceans, rivers, streams, and other lakes;
mountains such as Sumeru and others; and forests on all sides.
Domestic animals, birds, trees, worms, insects, and the like, as well as wild beasts;
all the worlds, the Lord of the worlds;
the cosmic eggs along with their coverings, the months, and the ten elephants of the quarters.
The phonemes, words, and mantras, as well as the principles (tattvas) together with their presiding deities;
the Rudras who sustain the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and other Rudras along with their Śaktis;
and whatever else is seen, inferred, or heard in this world—[all these are pervaded by Him].
"May they all grant every desire by the very command of Śiva and Śivā.
Now, there is the supreme Śaiva Vidyā, which liberates from the bonds of Paśus;
it is known as the Pañcārtha, divine, and excluded from the [lower] Vidyās of the Paśus."
The scripture known as the *Śivadharma*, and that which follows it called the *Dharma*;
the *Śaiva* and the *Śivadharmākhya* Purāṇa, which is equal to the Vedas;
and those other Śaiva Āgamas, fourfold in kind, beginning with the *Kāmika*.
Having been honored and worshipped here without distinction by the two Śivas,
they were commanded by them alone for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal— meaning, for the fulfillment of all my wishes.
"May these teachers—
beginning with Śveta and ending with Nakulīśa, together with their disciples— and the gurus belonging to their lineages,
especially my own gurus, acknowledge that this rite has been properly performed and is fruitful."
"May the Śaivas and Māheśvaras, who are devoted to knowledge and action,
approve of this rite as fruitful and well-performed;
likewise may all the worldly Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas [approve] in due order."
Those who know the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, those proficient in all the scriptures; men who are followers of Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Yoga, and Nyāya;
as well as other men who are devotees of the Sun, Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu.
May all the learned and the distinguished, restrained by the teaching of Śiva,
approve of this action which accomplishes my intended purpose—
those Śaivas who abide in the path of the Siddhānta, as well as the Śaivas who follow the Pāśupata tradition.
The Śaivas who observe the great vow (mahāvrata), and the other Śaivas, the Kāpālikas—
those who uphold the command of Śiva are worthy of worship even by me, according to the teaching of Śiva.
May they all favor me and declare my ritual action to be fruitful.
May those established in the knowledge of the South and those who follow the southern and northern paths abide without conflict for the sake of my spiritual welfare through these mantras;
as do the atheists, the deceitful, the ungrateful, and those of a tamasic nature.

May heretics and those of extreme wickedness remain far away from me! What is the use of many praises here? Whatever virtuous people there may be who possess faith, may they all favor me and proclaim auspiciousness.
"Salutations to Śiva, who is with Ambā, together with his sons, and the primordial cause;
to you who are enveloped by the phenomenal world in the form of the five enclosures. Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff before Śiva and Śivā.
One should recite the five-syllabled mantra at least one hundred and eight times;
likewise, having recited the Śakti-mantra, one should perform its dedication.
Having asked the Lord for forgiveness, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
This most meritorious hymn is dear to the hearts of Śiva and Śivā;
it directly bestows all desired objects and is the sole means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Whoever constantly recites this or listens to it with a concentrated mind—
Having quickly shaken off all sins, he shall attain union with Śiva.
Even a killer of cows, an ungrateful person, a slayer of heroes, or even a destroyer of an embryo;
one who kills those who have come for refuge, or one who betrays the trust of a friend—[all such persons shall likewise attain it].
Even one who has practiced wicked and sinful deeds, such as a matricide or a patricide,
is liberated from those very sins by reciting this hymn.
And [it delivers one] from fears indicated by evil dreams and other great calamities.
If one should recite this, one shall not fail to obtain its fruit.
Through the chanting of this hymn, a person attains longevity, health, sovereignty, and whatever else is desired. May you remain steadfast in the recitation of this praise.
The fruit that is proclaimed for reciting the hymn to Śiva without first performing worship is one thing;
but when one recites it after having performed worship, the fruit thereof cannot be described.
Let alone the attainment of such fruits when this [hymn] is chanted!
Having heard this, the Lord remains in heaven together with Ambikā.
Therefore, having worshipped the God along with Umā in the sky,
one should stand with palms joined in reverence and recite this hymn of praise.
Om. Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Hymn to Śiva," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva-mahāpurāṇa.
Upamanyu said:
O Kṛṣṇa, this supreme rite, consisting of the combination of ritual action, austerity, recitation, and meditation, has been told to you; it grants success both in this world and the next.
Now, I shall describe that which bestows fruit upon men even in this very life for the devotees of Śiva.
Therein, one who is most proficient in the meaning of mantras should first accomplish the great mantra consisting of worship, fire-oblation, recitation, meditation, austerity,
and charity; for ritual action that produces visible results does not yield fruit otherwise.
Even one who has mastered a mantra may find that his fruit is obstructed by some powerful unseen force; therefore, a wise man should not act precipitously.
However, a remedy can be found here for that obstruction.
Having first examined [the suitability] by means of omens and other such signs, one should then perform the rite of expiation (*niṣkṛti*).
That man who, out of delusion, performs the rite for the sake of worldly results in any other way shall not partake of its fruit and will incur ridicule.
One should never perform an action with visible results without full confidence;
for such a person would indeed be lacking in faith, and one who lacks faith does not attain the fruit.
There is no fault on the part of the Lord, even when an action results in failure.
Because the fruit is seen even in this very life for those men who act according to what has been taught, the practitioner—
whose mantra is perfected and whose obstacles have been dispelled,
being confident and full of faith— attains that fruit by performing [the rites].
Alternatively, for the sake of attaining that fruit, one should be devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
At night, one should eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), or milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or fruits.
One should not perform, even in thought, any prohibited act such as violence (*hiṃsā*) and the like.
One should always go about smeared with ashes and be pure in one's attire. Having thus become observant of these practices, on an auspicious day favorable to oneself,
in a location possessing the previously mentioned characteristics and adorned with garlands of flowers and other ornaments—
Having smeared the ground with cow dung to a size of at least one cubit,
he should draw an auspicious lotus, blazing with its own luster,
made of refined gold, possessing eight petals and filaments.
In the center, it was provided with a pericarp and adorned with all kinds of jewels;
it was also endowed with a stalk corresponding to its own form.
In such a bulb made of gold, [the lotus was placed] according to the proper ritual injunctions.
There, having again mentally conceived all the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, one should duly install a *liṅga*—
made of gems, gold, or crystal, and possessing the proper characteristics—
along with its pedestal (*vedikā*).
There, having invoked the Lord, one should worship the imperishable God together with Ambā and his attendants.
Therein, the form of the embodied Lord Maheśvara is to be conceived;
[the word] "cow" is the understood remainder.
She has four arms and four faces, adorned with all ornaments;
she wears a tiger skin, her face is slightly smiling,
and her hands likewise hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a deer and a *ṭaṅka* axe.
Alternatively, she may be visualized with eight arms according to the meditator’s preference:
then, she holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and a thunderbolt in her right hands;
and likewise, she bears a noose, a goad, a shield, and a serpent in her left hands.
Resembling the rising sun, she has three eyes in each face.
Her eastern face is gentle, with a radiance corresponding to its pleasant form;
her southern face resembles a dark blue cloud and is terrible to behold.
The northern face resembles coral and is adorned with dark locks of hair;
the western face has the luster of the full moon and is gentle, bearing a digit of the moon. Seated upon the orb of that [western] face is the supreme Māheśvarī Śakti.
Known as Mahālakṣmī, she is dark-hued and captivating to all.
Having thus fashioned an image of this form and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa in due order,
one should then invoke the Embodied One and worship the Supreme Cause.
For the purpose of bathing, one should prepare there the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) from a Kapila cow,
as well as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), full vessels, and especially seeds.
Having first fashioned a mandala adorned with powdered gems and other ornaments, [one should perform the rite].
One should then place the pitcher of Īśāna upon the pericarp;
subsequently, one should arrange the pitchers of Sadyojāta and the others around it.
Then, one should place the eight pitchers of the Vidyeśvaras in order, starting from the east.
Having filled them with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and wrapped them with thread as before,
one should place within them auspicious substances accompanied by mantras and ritual procedures,
and cover them completely on all sides with a garment such as fine silk (dukūla).
Having assigned the mantra everywhere, preceded by each respective mantra,
when the time for bathing has arrived, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with the sounds of all auspicious instruments and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances.

Then, having repeatedly drawn out water with *kuśa* grass, and even water with gold and jewels— water consecrated with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and perfected by various mantras— he bathed Maheśvara in due order with those respective mantras.
One should perform the act of worship with perfumes, flowers, lamps, and the like.
The unguent for anointing should consist of one *palāvara* (a specific measure) plus eleven *palas*.
One should also offer auspicious and fragrant flowers made of gold and precious gems.
Blue lotuses and other varieties of water-lilies, numerous bilva leaves,
red lotuses, and white ones [were offered] to Śambhu;
as was incense produced from black aloe-wood, along with camphor, clarified butter, and guggulu resin.
Lamps prepared with the ghee of a tawny cow and made with camphor wicks [should be lit].
The five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇas) are to be worshipped.
The food offering consists of the great sacrificial porridge (mahācaru), prepared with milk, jaggery, and clarified butter.
Water made fragrant with *pāṭala*, *utpala*, *padma*, and other such flowers;
betel-leaf well-prepared and endowed with the five aromatics (*pañcasaugaṃdhika*);
and especially ornaments fashioned from gold and jewels.
And various garments— fine, new,
and beautiful— should be given along with songs, instrumental music, and other such offerings;
furthermore, the root mantra should be recited one hundred thousand times according to the highest count.
In this world, according to the power of the fruit [sought], the worship consists of at least one and at most three [offerings].
The fire-oblation (homa) for each substance shall consist of at least ten and at most one hundred [oblations].
For rites such as killing and expulsion, Śiva should be meditated upon in his terrible form.
Upon the *liṅga* of Śiva, in the fire of Śiva, and indeed upon other images,
Śambhu should be meditated upon with a gentle form for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
For rites such as killing (*māraṇa*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of iron.
But in all other cases, such as in rites for peace (*śāntika*) and so forth, [the ladles] should be made entirely of gold.
[One should offer oblations] with *dūrvā* grass mixed with ghee and cow’s milk, as well as with honey,
or with sacrificial porridge (*caru*) mixed with ghee, or even with milk alone.
One should offer oblations with sesame seeds for victory over death and for the pacification of disease; likewise,
one who desires prosperity and the pacification of great poverty should offer oblations with ghee, milk, or even lotuses alone.
One who desires subjugation (*vaśya*) should offer oblations with *jātī* flowers together with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
O twice-born one, with clarified butter and *karavīra* flowers, one should perform attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).
One should perform eradication (*uccāṭana*) with oil, and furthermore, immobilization (*stambhana*) with honey.
Stambhana (paralysis) is achieved even with mustard seeds, while pātana (bringing down) is done with garlic.
Tāḍana (striking) is performed with the blood of both a donkey and a camel.
One should perform māraṇa (killing) and uccāṭana (expulsion) with rohi seeds mixed with sesame seeds.
One should perform the rite of inciting enmity with *lāṅgalaka* oil;
likewise, one may effect binding with *rohi* seeds, as well as the paralyzing of an army.
This is accomplished entirely by means of oblation materials mixed with red mustard seeds.
In rites of malevolent magic (ābhicārika), one should perform oblations with oils produced from hand-presses;
likewise, one should offer oblations in rites of malevolent magic with cotton seeds combined with *kaṭukī* and husks,
and with mustard seeds mixed with oil.
Milk likewise bestows the pacification of fever as well as the fruit of good fortune;
a fire-oblation (homa) performed with honey, clarified butter, and curd brings about all spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
[One may also perform it] with milk and rice, or with sacrificial porridge (caru) alone.
Whether for pacification (śāntika) or nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should perform the fire sacrifice with seven types of materials, such as sacrificial fuel (samidh) and others;
specifically, through these substances in the homa, one achieves subjugation (vaśya) and likewise attraction (ākarṣaṇa).
Indeed, through this, one especially attains subjugation, attraction, and the state of prosperity (śrīpada).
An oblation with *bilva* leaves likewise bestows victory over an enemy.
For rites of pacification (*śānti*), sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) such as those from the *pālāśa* and *khadira* trees are used;
for acts of cruelty, those from the *karavīra* and *arka* plants; and for conflict, thorny wood.
One who is tranquil should perform rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and especially those for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*);
but one who is pitiless and of a wrathful mind should perform rites of sorcery (*ābhicārika*).
This applies when one is in an extremely dire situation and there is no other remedy available.
One may perform a malevolent rite (*ābhicārika*) directed against an assassin (*ātatāyin*);
however, one should not perform a malevolent rite directed against the ruler of one's own kingdom,
whether he be a believer, very righteous, honorable, or whoever he may be.
One should not act [against him] even with intent to kill, even if he is an assassin;
for whoever— whether by thought, deed, or word— is a devotee of Śiva,
whether it be the ruler of one’s own kingdom or even another who has taken refuge in Śiva.

Having performed a malevolent rite (*abhicārika-karma*), a man would fall into ruin immediately. Therefore, if one desires one's own happiness, one should not harm anyone who protects one's own kingdom or is a devotee of Śiva by means of malevolent rites or other such acts.
Having performed acts such as killing directed against anyone else,
one who is possessed of remorse should perform an expiation;
whether he be poor or wealthy, he should do so even at a *bāṇaliṅga*.
Whether it be at a self-manifested (*svayambhūta*) linga, one established by the seers (*ārṣaka*), or even a Vedic (*vaidika*) one;
in the absence of gold and gems, or when there is an inability to acquire them,
one should perform this [worship] with the mind alone, or with materials that are mere representations.
But he who is capable in some part [of the rite] yet incapable in another part,
even he attains the fruit if he performs according to his capacity.
Even when this ritual action has been performed, if no fruit is seen therein—
One should repeat [the mantra] there two or three times; in every way, the fruit is seen.
Whatever materials were used for the worship—gold, gems, and the like, most excellent—all that one should give to the Guru, and then separately offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
If he does not desire it, one should offer all of that to Śiva;
or else, it should be given to the devotees of Śiva and not to others.
This applies to one who, by his own power and without dependence on a guru or others, would accomplish [the rite] himself.

He too should act in this manner here and should not take [the materials] himself. That fool who, out of greed, takes for himself the excellent materials that are the components of the worship, shall not obtain what he desires; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Whether one should personally take that consecrated liṅga or not,
if one does take it, one should always worship it oneself or have another do so;
he who performs this rite exactly as prescribed shall do so without any lapse.
The fruit [of this] shall never fail; therefore, what need is there for further inducement?
Nevertheless, I shall describe the supreme accomplishment of this rite by way of summary:
even one who is assailed by enemies or afflicted by manifold diseases [shall succeed].
Even one who has entered the jaws of death is released from harm;
the most wretched is honored, and the destitute becomes like Vaiśravaṇa.
Even the deformed becomes like the god of love, and the aged becomes like a youth.
An enemy immediately becomes a friend, and an adversary becomes a servant;
nectar acts like poison, and even poison acts like nectar.
Even the ocean becomes dry land, and even dry land becomes an ocean.

The chasm acts like a mountain, and that mountain acts like a chasm; the fire acts like a lotus-pond, and the pond acts like the sacrificial fire. The garden acts like a forest, and that forest acts like a garden.
The lowly deer acts like a lion, while the lion acts like a pet animal;
women act like women going to meet their lovers, while Fortune acts like one of virtuous conduct;
Speech acts like a servant sent at will, while Fame acts like a courtesan.
Wisdom acts like one who behaves according to her own will; the mind acts like a diamond needle;
power acts like a great wind; strength acts like an intoxicated elephant;
and action, directed toward the enemy's side, acts like a pillar through its exertions.
To his enemies, every single person belonging to the enemy's side acts as an adversary;
even while still alive, those enemies, along with their kinsmen, act like corpses. Even one who has fallen into calamity, being himself freed from misfortune, truly acts like nectar.
Even that which is unwholesome, when consumed, constantly acts as an elixir;
even when practiced incessantly, pleasure remains ever new;
and everything, including the future and so forth, becomes like a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of one's hand.

Even the supernatural powers (*siddhis*), such as *aṇimā* and the rest, yield their fruits by chance. What more need be said here? When this rite is completed, there is nothing that cannot be attained among the accomplishments of all desires and goals.

Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh section, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, in the Uttarakhanda, the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Rites for Attaining Siddhis in this World," ends.
Chapter 33.
Upamanyu said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the rite that bears fruit solely in the hereafter;
there is no ritual in the three worlds equal to this.
It is endowed with a preeminent merit and is practiced by all the gods.
By Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and especially by Rudra;
by the world-protectors beginning with Indra; by the nine planets beginning with the Sun;
and by the great ṛṣis who know Brahman, such as Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and others.
By Śveta, Agastya, Dadhīci, and others like them, as well as by us who have taken refuge in Śiva;
by the lords of the Gaṇas such as Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, and Bhṛṅgīśa;
and by the Daityas dwelling in Pātāla and the great serpents beginning with Śeṣa.

By the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas, each has attained their respective station; this [path] has been practiced by all. By this very method, all the gods attained the state of divinity.
Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā; Viṣṇu reached the state of Viṣṇu;
Rudra attained the state of Rudra; Indra reached the state of Indra;
and Gaṇeśa attained the status of Gaṇeśa through this very method.
Having bathed the Liṅga of Śiva and Śivā with water scented with white sandalwood,
and having worshipped them with blooming white lotuses and prostrated before them,
he should there prepare a beautiful lotus-seat endowed with all the proper characteristics.
When there is wealth, one should, according to one's own capacity,
place a small *liṅga* made of gold or other precious gems in the center of the mass of filaments;
it should be beautiful, resembling a thumb in size, composed of all fragrances, and auspicious.
Having placed [the vessel] on the right, one should worship it with bilva leaves.
One should place agallochum on the right side, realgar on the west,
sandalwood on the north, and yellow orpiment on the east.
One should worship with fragrant, beautiful, and diverse flowers.
One should offer black aloe-wood incense along with guggulu on all sides,
and present extremely fine and radiant garments.
One should cause milk-rice mixed with ghee and ghee-lamps to be offered;
having presented everything with the mantra, one should then perform the circumambulation.
Having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods and praised Him, one should at the end ask for His forgiveness.

Then, relying upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should offer the Liṅga, mixed with all types of offerings, to Śiva while reciting the Śiva-mantra. He who thus constantly worships the auspicious [Liṅga] composed of the five fragrances— 589a.

Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. This supreme, secret vow, the great vow of the Śiva-liṅga, has been fully declared to you because of your devotion; it must not be given to just anyone.
And it was declared by Śiva in the past that [this] should be given to the devotees of Śiva.

Om. Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Rituals Pertaining to the Next World," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 34.
Upamanyu said:
Whatever accomplishment is proclaimed here as resulting from obligatory, occasional,
or optional rites— all that may be obtained immediately by the consecration of the *liṅga* and the *bera*.

The entire world consists of the *liṅga*; everything is established within the *liṅga*. Therefore, when the *liṅga* is installed, everything becomes firmly established—whether by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, or anyone else.
Setting aside the installation of the *liṅga*, one establishes oneself in one’s own state.
What else need be said here regarding the cause for installation?
For even the *vaiśveśvara-liṅga* was indeed installed by Śiva himself.
Therefore, with every effort, for the sake of happiness both in this world and the next,
one should install a *liṅga* or even an image (*bera*) of the Supreme Lord.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"What is this called the *liṅga*, and how is Maheśvara the possessor of the *liṅga* (*liṅgin*)?
How does he possess the state of being a *liṅga*, and for what reason is Śiva worshipped in this [liṅga]?
Upamanyu said:
The unmanifest is declared to be the *liṅga*, the source and place of dissolution for the three *guṇas*.
It is without beginning or end, the material cause of the universe;
