that very thing is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), as well as *māyā* and the essence of space.
From that very source this entire world of moving and non-moving beings has arisen.
It is threefold: the impure, the pure, and the pure-impure.
From that [proceed] Śiva, Maheśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.
And the elements, having arisen through the senses, dissolve here by the command of Śiva;
for this very reason, Śiva is the *liṅgin*, because he commands the *liṅga*.
Since that [universe] would not be capable of acting on its own without being commanded.
Since the entire universe, once born, dissolves back into that very same place,
its nature as a *liṅga* (the sign/source) arises through this alone and not by any other means;
for the *liṅga* is the body of Śiva and Śivā, since it is presided over by them both.
Therefore, one should always worship Śiva together with Ambā there;
the pedestal of the liṅga is the Great Goddess, and the liṅga is Maheśvara himself.
By worshipping those two alone, both he and she are worshipped.

In ultimate reality, those two do not possess the nature of a subtle body (*liṅgadeha*); however, because they are pure, that [body] is designated as such figuratively. That very thing is the supreme power (*paramā śakti*) of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
When Śakti receives the command, she brings forth this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
Her majesty cannot be fully described even in hundreds of years—
she by whom even Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa were first deluded.
Long ago, when the dissolution of these three worlds had arrived,
Viṣṇu, having gone to his bed upon the waters, slept peacefully and undisturbed.
By chance, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, went there.
He beheld the lotus-eyed one sleeping there, undisturbed;
deluded by the *māyā* of Śambhu, the Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke to Viṣṇu:
"Who are you? Speak! Having struck Mādhava with indignation, he roused him.
Struck by that violent blow of the hand, he woke up instantly and rose from his bed; there he beheld the Supreme Lord.
Then Hari, though inwardly enraged, spoke to him as if he were not angry at all.
"From where have you come, my child? Tell me, why are you so distressed?
Hearing these words of Viṣṇu, which indicated his quality of sovereignty, Brahmā—who harbored enmity toward him due to the quality of passion (rajas)—replied once more.
"Why do you address me as 'child,' as a teacher addresses his own disciple?
Do you not know me, O Lord, whose handiwork this phenomenal world is?
Having divided myself threefold, I have created this [world] and now sustain it."
"I shall withdraw [the world]; there is no creator whatsoever to be found in this universe.
When this was said, the imperishable Viṣṇu spoke to Brahmā:
"I alone am the primordial creator of this [world], its destroyer, and its protector."
In ancient times, you too descended from my very own imperishable body.
By my command, having divided yourself into three, you create the three worlds,
preserve them, and at the end, you dissolve them and then create them once again.
"You have forgotten Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who is free from all ailment;
you thus disregard me, his very father.
There is no fault of yours in this; you have been deluded by my *māyā*."
"By my grace, this delusion of yours shall depart before long.
Listen to the truth, O Four-faced One: I am indeed the Lord of all the gods;
as creator, sustainer, and destroyer, there is no sovereign equal to me."
In this very way, a dispute arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu; and a great battle occurred, terrifying and hair-raising, as the two,
bound by enmity through passion, struck each other violently with their fists.
To remove the pride of those two gods and to awaken them,
a wondrous, divine *liṅga* appeared between them—
rich with thousands of garlands of flames, immeasurable, and incomparable.
Free from decay and growth, devoid of beginning, middle, and end—
by its thousand flames, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were utterly bewildered;
abandoning their battle, they then wondered, "What indeed is this?"
When the true nature of those two did not become manifest to him,
then they both prepared to examine his beginning and end.
There, Brahmā appeared in the form of a swan, possessed of wings on all sides.
Having become as swift as thought, he ascended upwards with great effort.
Nārāyaṇa,
the soul of the universe, also assumed an immeasurable boar-form resembling a mass of black collyrium and went downwards.
Thus, for a thousand years, Viṣṇu in his boar form hurried downward;
yet he did not see even the slightest root of this Liṅga.
Desiring to know its end, he likewise traveled upward for that same length of time.
Not seeing the end, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became utterly exhausted and fell downward.
Likewise, the Lord Viṣṇu, weary and with agitated eyes,
quickly rose upward from below with great effort.
Then, having come together, they gazed at one another with eyes smiling with wonder;
deluded by the Māyā of Śambhu, they did not perceive what ought to be done or what ought not to be done. Both stood behind him, at his side, and in front of him.
Having prostrated, they then wondered, "What is this?
Oṃ. Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Delusion of Hari and Brahmā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 35.
Upamanyu said:
Then there appeared there a resonant sound characterized by its own nature—
the single-syllabled Brahman "Om," which is the means of realizing Brahman.
Even that remained unknown to Brahmā as well as Viṣṇu,
because their minds were obscured by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Then that single, imperishable [Principle] became divided into four parts.
The syllable *a* is situated with three morae (*trimātrā*) and beyond that, with half a mora (*ardhamātrā*).
There, the letter *ā* rests on the right side of the blazing liṅga;
likewise, the letter *u* is on the left, and the letter *m* is in its center.
The sound consisting of half a mora was heard at the top of the *liṅga*;
even though that supreme syllable (*praṇava*) was then divided,
those two gods did not perceive anything for the sake of discernment.

Then the unmanifest *praṇava*, having undergone transformation, became the soul of the Vedas. Therein, the letter *a* became the *Ṛgveda*, the imperishable *u* became the *Yajurveda*, the *m* became the *Sāmaveda*, and the resonance (*nāda*) became the *Atharva* scripture.
He established Ṛgaya as the embodiment of his own purpose in brief;
he established Brahmā among the qualities of *rajas*, as the first among the forms, and also among the activities;
he established the Earth among the worlds for the sake of creation, and the imperishable Self among the principles (*tattvas*).
On the path of the *kalās*, one attains *nivṛtti* (cessation) and the five Brahmans;
in the lower portion of the parts of the *liṅga*, there is that which is called the seed (*bīja*) within the three causes.
Therein lies the intellectual sovereignty consisting of the sixty-four qualities, such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Thus, the entire world was pervaded by these ten meanings through the Ṛgveda.
Then, the Yajurveda presented its own tenfold meaning:
Sattva among the qualities (guṇas), Viṣṇu among the forms (mūrtis), and the Primordial One (Ādya) among the actions (kriyās).

He established Sthiti among the worlds, Antarikṣa among the three principles (tattvas), and Vidyā among the paths of Kalā; he established Pratiṣṭhā among the five Brahmans and Vāma among the five Liṅgas;
he established Madhya among the three causes and Yoni among the three.

And just as primordial sovereignty [is established], from that [source] the universe consists of the Yajus; thereafter, he manifested the Sāman aspect of the tenfold Self. Then, among the qualities of Tamas, he established Rudra as the first in the forms and in the ritual actions.
He performs the withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) into the three worlds and the [three] principles (*tattvas*), [worshipping] the supreme Śiva;
likewise, he worships Aghora in the *vidyā* and *kalā* [principles], and in the five Brahmās.
Above the pedestal (*pīṭha*), in the portions of the Liṅga, he worships the Bījin in the three causal [principles].
In this manner, the world was pervaded by the power of manhood and likewise by sovereignty through peaceful means.
Then Atharvan declared the primary meaning of his own self to be freedom from qualities (*nirguṇya*);
thereafter, he [perceived] Maheśvara directly as Sadāśiva even within the various forms.
Even though Śiva, the Supreme Self, is devoid of action,
he performs actions for the sake of favoring living beings, by which creatures are liberated;
for even speech, together with the mind, has turned away from him in the worlds.
Above that world of Unmanā is the extraordinary world of Soma,
where the Lord Soma dwells eternally together with Umā.
Above that world of Unmanā is [the realm] which, once reached, one does not return from.
[He perceives] Śānti and Śāntyatītā, as well as Vyāpikā among the Kalās;
likewise Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna among the five Brahmans;
and also the unsurpassed Mūrdhan at the portion of the Nāda within the Liṅga.
In that [state], where the partless (niṣkala) Śiva alone is to be invoked and worshipped—
then even within those [levels], it is beyond the bindu, beyond the nāda, and beyond the śakti;
it is a reality higher than reality, for in the ultimate sense, it is beyond all categories (atattva).
Beyond the causes, from the cause that agitates Māyā which transcends the triad;
beyond Ananta and Śuddhavidyā;
and beyond Maheśvara, the sovereign lord of all the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras), from Sadāśiva who is supreme.
From that God who is the body of all mantras, endowed with the three powers,
possessing five faces and ten arms, manifest as both the differentiated (sakala) and the undifferentiated (niṣkala);
from that supreme Bindu, and from the half-moon beyond that.
Then from the Lord of Night (Soma), then from the one called Ānāda, then from the one beyond that,
then from Suṣumneśa, and also from the Lord of the Brahma-aperture;
then from the one beyond that, from Śakti, and further beyond from the Śiva-tattva.
The supreme cause, directly manifest as the self, the auspicious one who is himself without cause;
the creator of all causes, the meditator, the object of meditation, the imperishable;
situated in the midst of the supreme ether, abiding above the Supreme Self.
He is endowed with all sovereignty, yet he is the Lord of all while himself being without a lord. Due to the impurity of illusory sovereignty, such as that of humans and others,
and because of the lower [state] which must be abandoned, he is distinct from the higher state that is the domain of the path of supreme purity.
Beyond that, from the supreme beyond the supreme— beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Unmanā—
there is the supreme sovereignty, which is beginningless even for Unmanā and the rest;
it is boundless, independent, free from all excelsior, and eternal.
Thus, because this Atharvaṇa Śruti is most weighty by virtue of these ten kinds of meanings, the entire universe is pervaded by the Atharvaṇa.
Furthermore, the Ṛgveda declares: "The waking state is described by me."
Because I am the eternal declarer of the reality of the Self,
the Yajurveda has declared that state which is called by me the dream state;
for therein, Vidyā, transformed into the nature of objects of enjoyment, is to be known within me.
Sāman spoke of that which is called deep sleep; thus everything is spoken by me.
This is designated by my name, Śiva, as being of the nature of *tamas*. Then Atharvan spoke of that which is called the Fourth (*turīya*) and that which transcends the Fourth (*turīyātīta*).
Therefore, I declare that I am beyond the path (*adhva*). However,
the triad consisting of the path— known as Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman— is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*),
is to be accomplished through the triple Veda (*trayī*), and must be thoroughly purified by one seeking the supreme state.

That which transcends the paths is called the Fourth (turya), the supreme state of Nirvāṇa. Because it is beyond the qualities (nirguṇya), it is the purifier of this path. Nāda is the means of valid cognition for both [the Fourth and the Beyond], and Nadānta is of the nature of intoxication (mada).

Therefore, because he possesses independence regarding all objects, the Supreme Lord is the primary reality. Whatever object exists, all of it— whether in its entirety or individually— is declared to be the meaning of the syllable *praṇava*, according to the application of secondary and primary qualities.
Therefore, this single imperishable Brahman expresses its own meaning;
by means of it, as "Om," Śiva first brings forth the entire universe.
For Śiva is indeed this Praṇava, and the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva.

Since there is no absolute difference between the signified and the signifier, Rudra is devoid of thought; for speech, along with the mind, turns back without reaching him. Yet, he is signified by the single syllable.
From the single syllable called *a*, the Self (*ātman*) is designated as Brahmā;
from the single syllable called *u*, Viṣṇu is declared to be twofold;
and from the single syllable called *m*, Śiva is proclaimed as Rudra.
From the right side of Maheśa was born the one known as Brahmātman;
from his left side arose Viṣṇu, who is designated as Vidya.
From the heart of Śiva came Nīlarudra, who is designated as Śiva.

Brahmā is the initiator of creation, Viṣṇu is the sustainer and the deluder, and Rudra is likewise the agent of dissolution; he is the eternal controller of those two. Therefore, these three are declared to be the causes of the world.

And Śiva, the supreme cause, is the cause of the three causes. Without understanding this truth, a Liṅga appeared between you two, who were bound by enmity through the quality of passion (rajas), in order to awaken your understanding.
"In this way, they said 'Om' to me when it was spoken here by Atharvan.
Even though the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as thousands of other branches,
themselves declared through their own mouths that [the truth] was thus manifest within the Vedas," so he spoke.
Like something experienced in a dream, that [reality] is not determined by those two;
for their awakening and for the removal of darkness therein,
everything has been sealed within the *liṅga*, just as it is proclaimed by the Vedas.
Seeing that [the Linga] had been sealed upon the Lingin by his grace,
the two gods then became awakened with tranquil minds;
they understood the origin, the dissolution, and the true nature of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Beyond that is the supreme abode and the Puruṣa who possesses all abodes;
the unsurpassed Brahman, the partless, auspicious Lord,
the eternal master of this phenomenal world consisting of both the individual soul (paśu) and its bonds (pāśa).
It is entirely free from fear from any quarter, devoid of increase or decrease, and immutable;
it pervades both the external and the internal, yet is itself devoid of exterior or interior;
it is eternally beyond all comparison and distinct from the entire world.
It is without characteristics, indefinable, and beyond the reach of speech and mind;
its sole essence is luminosity, it is peaceful, serene, and eternally manifest;
it is the abode of all auspiciousness, endowed with such a power.
Then, having recognized the god Virūpākṣa, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa,
filled with fear, placed their joined palms to their heads and spoke these words.
Brahmā said:
"O Lord, whether I am ignorant or wise, I was created by you from the very beginning;
who, then, is at fault here for having fallen into such delusion?
O Lord, let this ignorance of mine rest upon you, for you are ever present."
Who, being fearless, would speak of his own or another's duty? Indeed,
even a dispute between us two is auspicious,
since it yields the fruit of prostrating at the feet of our Lord, the God of gods.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord, there is no speech capable of praising you in a manner worthy of your greatness. For those who are to be commanded in the presence of their Master, silence itself would be a transgression."
"What task should be undertaken here?"— thinking thus, appropriate for the occasion,
though not knowing anything at all, I have prattled on and now bow to you.
The state of being the cause was granted by you, yet it has been forgotten through your *māyā*.
I was deluded and possessed by egoism, yet I have been instructed once again.
O Lord, what is the use of many words? I am utterly terrified, for I endeavored to define you who are indefinable.
"They long for you, O Mahādeva, the destroyer of the suffering of the terrified.
Therefore, O Śaṅkara, you ought to forgive my transgression today.
Thus was Maheśvara entreated by those two lords.
Pleased, the Lord favored those two gods and spoke with a smile. The Lord said:
"O child, child Vidhi, O Viṣṇu! You have both been deluded by my Māyā."

Having become arrogant in their power, you two, O Buddha and Vairocana, engaged in a dispute that culminated in battle and did not cease. Consequently, the creation of progeny by you two, who were the causes of the world, was brought to an end.
"Because of the discord arising from ignorance and pride, even in you two,
I have now,
through the play of manifesting this Liṅga, thus restrained your arrogance and delusion."
Therefore, completely casting aside further dispute and shame,
may you two perform your respective duties free from envy.
Previously, by my command, together with me, you held all the compendia of knowledge.

Indeed, I bestowed upon you both the supreme five-syllabled mantra known as the Sūtra— a jewel among mantras— for the sake of establishing my status as the cause. All that was taught by me has today been forgotten by you both.
"And furthermore, by my command, I shall restore everything as it was before;
for without you two, they are not capable of creation and protection.
Having spoken thus to Nārāyaṇa and Pitāmaha, Mahādeva—

He bestowed the king of mantras upon them along with the Jñānasaṃhitā. Having received that great, divine, and supreme command of Maheśvara, as well as the jewel of mantras of great significance and all the kalās, they [were established].
Having prostrated like a staff at the feet of the God of gods,
they then stood there, free from fear, motionless with the stillness of bliss.
In that interval, the wondrous power of the Lord appeared like a magical illusion.
The *liṅga* had vanished somewhere and was not perceived by them;
then, lamenting "Alas! Alas! due to the sudden shattering of their affection, they said to one another, "How can this event be untrue?"
Having reflected upon the inconceivable majesty of Śambhu, they became free from all distress;
having entered into a state of supreme friendship and embraced one another,
those two foremost of gods departed for the sake of the world's affairs.
From that time forward, all the gods and asuras, beginning with Śakra,
as well as sages, men, nāgas, and women, perform the installation of the liṅga according to the prescribed rules and worship Him within the liṅga.
Om. Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Warding Off of Hari’s Delusion by Brahmā," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 36.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the supreme procedure for installation,
just as it was ordained by Śiva for both the *liṅga* and the *bera*.
Upamanyu said:
On a day that is auspicious and favorable, during the bright fortnight,
one should fashion a Liṅga of the prescribed dimensions according to the path taught in the Śiva-śāstra;
having then selected an auspicious site and performed the examination of the ground (bhūparīkṣā).

One should perform the ten services (upacāras), preceded by the removal of [any] defects. Prior to those ten services, having first worshipped Vināyaka and performed the purification of the site and other rites, one should lead the Liṅga to the bathing pavilion.
Then, one should mark the characteristic features as prescribed by the treatises on iconography (śilpaśāstra) using a golden stylus smeared with the juices of saffron and other pigments;
alternatively, this may be done with water mixed with eight kinds of clay or likewise with water mixed with five kinds of clay.
One should purify the *liṅga* together with its pedestal using the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having worshipped the water reservoir along with its altar,
one should bring the *liṅga* together with its pedestal there and perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).

In a pure dwelling place for the consecration, endowed with every splendor, provided with archways and enclosures, draped with garlands of *darbha* grass, furnished with the eight elephants of the quarters, and accompanied by the eight jars of the world-protectors; ŚivaP 7.2.36.8ab–9ab.
In a place adorned with the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalaka) and where the guardians of the directions have been worshipped,
one should fashion a seat made either of metal or wood, marked with a lotus design;
there, in the center, one should install a spacious and magnificent throne.
Having worshipped the four gatekeepers in due order, beginning with Bhadra—
namely Samudra, Vibhadra, Sunanda, and Vinandaka—
and having bathed and worshipped the Linga together with its pedestal (vedikā), [he should proceed].
Having wrapped it all around with two cloths together with their fringes,
one should slowly bring it to the water and place it upon the pedestal (pīṭhikā),
with its head toward the east and its thread-mark facing downward, while the pedestal itself is placed to its west.
One should consecrate the Liṅga there, endowed with all auspicious rites,
for five nights, three nights, or even for one night.
Having performed worship there and having purified it as previously described, one should then dismiss it.
Having worshipped him according to the festive rite, one should lead him to the bedchamber.
There, one should prepare a place for the bed in the center of the maṇḍala;
having bathed the Liṅga with pure waters, one should worship it in the prescribed sequence.

Having drawn a lotus in the northeast on a ground surface that has been smeared clean— [the form] *aiśānyām* is an archaic usage [of the locative], and the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* in *ḍiḍhḍhaṇañ* is an archaic usage. 592b.
Having purified the Śiva-pitcher and having invoked Śiva therein, one should worship him.
Having fashioned a white lotus in the center of the altar according to the prescribed rite,
one should also draw a lotus for Caṇḍikā to its west.
Having prepared a bed there with unwashed linen garments or flowers, or even with *darbha* grass, one should place a golden flower upon it; then,
having brought the *liṅga* there amidst the sounds of all auspicious instruments.
Having wrapped it all around with a pair of red garments and a *kūrca* grass-bundle,
together with the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), one should lay it down as before.
Having drawn a lotus in front, one should [place the deities] upon its petals in due order.
One should place the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa) in the center, and the Vardhanī jar of Śiva as well.
Having circumambulated the triad of lotuses, the best of the twice-born should perform the oblation.
These should be conceived as the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) of Śiva, situated all around starting from the east.
Furthermore, there should be four well-reciters who are practitioners of *japa* located in the cardinal directions;
they are known as the four forms beginning with Virañci (Brahmā), and they should perform the oblations.
The preceptor should be positioned first to their northeast or to the west.
One should perform the principal oblation (pradhānahoma) with seven substances in their proper order.
Other twice-born ones may offer either a quarter or a half of what the preceptor offers.
Alternatively, the preceptor alone may perform the principal oblation here.

Having first offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should place the "Hand of Śiva" upon the head of the *liṅga* with the root mantra using clarified butter one hundred and eight times. Then, one should perform [the offerings] in sequence with the seven substances, either one hundred times, fifty times, or twenty-five times.
Having offered oblation after oblation, he should repeatedly touch the liṅga and the pedestal. Then,
having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should duly give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor,
the hotṛ priests, and the architect, in the proportions of one-quarter, one-half, or even a third.
Half of that should be given to the other members of the assembly according to one's capacity.
Then, having placed a golden bull or even a tuft of grass within a pit,
[he should purify it] with earth and water, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and again with pure water.
One should cast the purified Brahma-stone, smeared with sandalwood paste, into the pit;
then, having performed the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the nine names of the Śaktis,
one should [apply] minerals such as yellow orpiment, along with seeds, perfumes, and medicinal herbs.

One should cast [the linga] upon the Brahma-stone according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra. Having established a linga for each [image], and perceiving that the milk produced from the tree has settled, one should place that linga upon the Brahma-stone.
One should place the pedestal slightly inclined toward the northeast while reciting the root mantra; then,
having joined it with the pedestal and meditating upon the Śakti-mantra,
one should perform the binding with binding materials and purify the site.
Having offered the *arghya* and flowers, they should again set up a curtain.
Then, in front of the *liṅga*, they should perform the *niṣeka* (consecration) and other rites as appropriate.
Having brought the water-pots from the place of rest, they should arrange them in due order.
Then, having commenced the great worship and fully worshipped the ten jars,
and having recollected the Śiva-mantra, one should take [the water] from within the water of the Śiva-jar by joining the thumb and ring finger and utter it.
The knower of mantras should place [the deities] in the center of the northeastern portion of the *liṅga*.
Likewise, he should place the *Śakti*, the *Vidyā*, and the *Vidyeśas* in their proper order.
Then, at the base of the *liṅga*, he should consecrate the *liṅga* with the waters of Śiva.
Having consecrated the *piṇḍikā-liṅga* in the *vardhanī* vessel with the jars of the *vidyeśas*,
one should thereafter prepare the seat, beginning with the *ādhāra*.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the five *kalās*, one should meditate upon the radiant *liṅga*.
Facing east or north with palms joined in reverence, one should invoke Śiva and Śivā directly;
one should meditate upon the Lord as He arrives from the sky, mounted upon the king of bulls or a celestial chariot,
adorned and accompanied by the Goddess.
Richly adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by the sounds of every auspicious instrument,
[the assembly] consisted of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Arka, Śakra, and other gods and dānavas,
whose entire bodies were drenched with tears of joy and who stood with their heads bowed in joined palms.
Surrounded on all sides by those praising, dancing, and singing,
one should then complete the worship by performing the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra).
There is no ritual procedure superior to this fivefold offering.
One should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) for images in every respect just as one does for the *liṅga*.
At the time of the extraction of the marks (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*), the opening of the eyes (*nayanamocana*) must be performed.
During the preliminary consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*), one should lay them down face-down upon their bed.
One should cause that [deity], which has been made to lie within a water-pot, to enter into the heart by means of mantras.
They say that consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) performed when the deity has already taken up residence is superior to that performed when it has not yet taken up residence.
One who is capable may subsequently perform the rite of consecration after the deity has taken up residence.
If one is incapable [of building a temple], one should first install a *liṅga* or even an image (*bera*),
and afterwards construct a temple for Śiva according to one's means.
Furthermore, I shall describe the supreme ritual procedure for installation regarding domestic worship.
Having fashioned a small *bera* (image) or a *liṅga* endowed with the proper characteristics,
when the northern solstice has arrived on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight,
one should place the Goddess in a pure location and draw a lotus there as previously described.
Having scattered leaves, flowers, and other offerings, and having placed the central jar in the middle,
one should arrange four jars around it in the cardinal directions. With their respective seed-syllables, one should install the five Brahmans within those five jars using the five [mantras].
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worshipped [the deity], displayed the mudrās and so forth, and provided protection,
one should purify the *liṅga* or the image (*bera*) with earth, water, and other substances as before;
then, covered with flowers, one should install it upon an excellent seat situated toward the north.
Having placed a flower upon [the image's] head, one should sprinkle it with the waters from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Having worshipped again with flowers preceded by shouts of "Victory!
(*jaya*), one should bathe [the deity] with the jars using the *Mūlavidyā*, ending with the *Īśānavidyā*.
Then, having performed the placement of the five kalās (pañcakalānyāsa) and the worship as before,
one should constantly propitiate the three-eyed God there with the Goddess. Or else, one may use a single water-pot (kumbha) endowed with the form-mantra (mūrtimantra).
Having deposited everything within the lotus, one should perform the remaining rites as before.
A linga that is utterly ruined should be purified and installed again;
one that is slightly impaired should be consecrated with sprinkling, while one that is not impaired at all should be worshipped.
The liṅgas known as Bāṇa may or may not be installed,
because they were previously consecrated by Śiva himself; however,
the remaining ones that appear like those of Bāṇa should be installed.
In the case of a self-manifested (*svayambhū*) linga, as well as in those that are divine (*divya*) or of the sages (*ārṣa*),
one should perform the rite of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) and, having established a pedestal (*pīṭha*) even where there was none,
worship Śiva there; for these, no formal installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) is prescribed.

One should cast into a body of water a liṅga that is burnt, loose, or has its parts damaged. Having joined together those parts that are fit for rejoining, one should perform the rite of installation.
Alternatively, from a defective image (bera) or liṅga, preceded by the worship of the deity, [the rite should be performed].

Having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsya*), one should practice either the internal concentration (*saṃdhāna*) within the heart or the formal renunciation (*tyāga*). If the worship for one day is interrupted, one should perform double the amount of worship.
For an interruption of two nights, one should perform a great worship (*mahāpūjā*); beyond that, a consecration (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) is required.
If worship is interrupted for many days beyond one month,
some say a re-consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is required, while others prescribe the procedure of ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
In the case of ritual sprinkling, however, one should first dismiss the deity from the *liṅga* and other objects as before.
Having bathed [the deity] with clay and water according to the sequence of the eight pentads,
and having bathed [him] with the products of the cow and purified [him] with water from *darbha* grass,
one should sprinkle [the deity] one hundred and eight times with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the root mantra.
Placing his hand, adorned with flowers and *kuśa* grass, upon the top of the *liṅga*,

he should then mutter the root mantra five times and subsequently one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, he should also touch [the *liṅga*] from the crown down to the pedestal while reciting the root mantra.
And one should perform a great worship after invoking the God as before.
Whether a *liṅga* has not been obtained or has been installed, or in a sacred place (*śivasthāna*), or in water,
or likewise in fire, in the sun, or in the sky, one should sacrifice to the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh section, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Installation," ends.
Chapter 37.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Having extracted the essence from knowledge, action, and conduct, and having summarized it, everything has been spoken by the Blessed One; I have heard it all, which is equal to the Vedas. Now I desire to hear about yoga, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
If death should occur prematurely, before the destruction of yoga and the like, [then this method]— which is complete with its authority, its constituent parts, its procedure, and its purpose—
is capable of being accomplished immediately, so that the man shall not be a self-destroyer.
"You ought to explain, according to the truth, that [liberation], its cause, the means for its attainment at that time, and the gradations of its various types.
Upamanyu said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you who know the meaning of all questions have asked what is appropriate.
Therefore, I shall explain all of that in due order; listen with a concentrated mind.
For one whose other mental fluctuations are restrained, the steadiness of the mind upon Śiva [is attained]."
That which is the mode of practice is, in brief, Yoga; it is indeed fivefold:
Mantra-yoga, Sparśa-yoga, and likewise another, Bhāva-yoga;
Abhāva-yoga is considered the supreme Mahā-yoga, greater than all others.
By the power of the practice of mantra alone, the mental activity that has the meaning expressed by the mantra as its object,

being free from distraction, is declared to be *mantrayoga*. That same [mental activity], when preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and directed toward the tactile [perception], is designated as *sparśayoga*.
That which is free from the touch of mantras is proclaimed as the yoga of existence (bhāvayoga),
because the form of the universe is perceived therein with its constituent parts dissolved.
That which arises from the non-appearance of the existing reality is declared to be the yoga of non-existence (abhāvayoga).
Only the single nature of Śiva, devoid of all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), is contemplated;
this mental state of the mind directed toward Śiva is here called Mahāyoga.
When the mind is detached from objects perceived through the senses as well as those heard of in scripture, [this state arises].

Whoever possesses this qualification has the right to yoga, and no one else. Merely by the constant perception of the defects of the two objects of experience, as well as the qualities of the Lord, the mind becomes dispassionate.
In brief, every yoga consists of either eight limbs or six limbs:
restraint (yama) and observance (niyama), as well as postures such as the svastika;
breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and meditation (dhyāna).

"Samādhi": thus the eight limbs of yoga have been declared by the wise. Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these, in brief, are the six limbs of yoga.
The distinct characteristics of these have been proclaimed in the Śiva-śāstra,
as well as in other Śiva-āgamas— especially in the Kāmika and others—
and likewise in the Yoga-śāstras and certain Purāṇas.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness— these,
through their fivefold application, are called *yama* by the virtuous.
Purity, contentment, austerity, recitation, and meditative concentration likewise [constitute *niyama*].
Thus, there are five varieties of *niyama* according to the division of its own parts:
the *svastika*, the *padma*, the *ardhacandra*, the *vīra*, the *yoga*, the *prasādhita*, the *paryaṅka*, and the *yatheṣṭa*; these are declared to be the eight types of postures (*āsana*).
Prāṇa is the wind born from one's own body; its *āyāma* is its restraint.
That is said to be threefold: *rocaka*, *pūraka*, and *kuṃbhaka*.
By pressing one nostril with a finger, while [blocking] the other with the [other hand],...
One should expel the air from the abdomen; this is known as *recaka* (exhalation).
One should fill the body with external air like a leather bag;
because of filling through the other nostril, it is considered *pūraka* (inhalation).

One neither releases nor inhales the air situated within or without; remaining motionless like a full pitcher, that indeed is *kumbhaka*. This triad, beginning with *recaka*, should be performed neither too quickly nor too slowly.
Therefore, the practitioner of yoga should practice in a gradual sequence;
that practice consisting of exhalation (*recaka*) and the rest, preceded by the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śodhana*),
is declared in the *Yogānuśāsana* to extend up to voluntary departure from the body (*svecchotkramaṇa*).
The restraint of breath (*prāṇāyāma*) occurs through the sequence beginning with the *kanyaka* [breath];
it is taught as being fourfold according to the division of the qualities of the measures (*mātrā*).
The *kanyaka* itself is fourfold, and it consists of twelve measures.
The middling [prāṇāyāma], however, consists of twenty-four mātrās and involves two suppressions;
the superior, moreover, consists of twenty-six mātrās and involves three suppressions. Beyond that is the prāṇāyāma which produces perspiration, trembling, and so forth.
The arising of bliss, horripilation, and the shedding of tears from the eyes;
the uttering of incoherent speech, wandering, fainting, and so forth—these arise in the supreme yogin.
Having circumambulated the knee neither too quickly nor too slowly...
One should perform the snapping of the fingers; this is proclaimed as the "mātrā.
These are to be understood according to the sequence of mātrās and through the application of the sequence of exhalation (udvāta).
One should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) preceded by the purification of the channels (nāḍīviśuddhi).
Prāṇāyāma is traditionally said to be of two kinds: *agarbha* (without seed) and *sagarbha* (with seed).

That which is devoid of recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) is *agarbha*; it is *sagarbha* when accompanied by those. Prāṇāyāma conjoined with the "seed" is more than a hundred times superior to the *agarbha*.
Therefore, yogins perform breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) along with the internal retention (sagarbha). Only through the conquest of the vital breath (prāṇa) are the bodily winds (dehavāyu) subdued:
namely, prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkala*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya*—
because it initiates the act of departure (*prayāṇa*), it is therefore called *prāṇa*.
That which is known as *apāna* leads downward that which is consumed, such as food and the like.
Vyāna causes all the limbs to expand;
Udāna is so called because it agitates the vital points (marmas).
Because it leads everything equally throughout all the limbs, it is celebrated as Samāna.
Nāga is said to be in the belching; Kūrma resides in the opening of the eyes.
Kṛkala is to be known in the sneeze, and Devadatta in the yawning.
Dhanañjaya, the all-pervading one, does not leave even the dead.

Practiced gradually in this manner, this breath control (prāṇāyāma) which possesses the proper measure burns away every defect and protects the body of the practitioner. When the vital breath (prāṇa) has been properly conquered, one should observe its signs.
First, there arises a diminution of feces, urine, and phlegm;
likewise, the capacity for eating much, slow respiration,
lightness, swift movement, enthusiasm, and excellence of voice.
The destruction of all diseases, as well as strength, splendor, and beauty;
fortitude, intelligence, youthfulness, stability, and clarity;
penances, the destruction of sin, and sacrifices, gifts, vows, and so forth—[all these arise from him].

These [other practices] do not equal even a sixteenth part of that *prāṇāyāma*. When one forcibly restrains the senses here, which are attached to their respective objects, that is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
The senses, preceded by the faculty of speech, lead either to heaven or indeed to hell;
when restrained or unleashed, they result in heaven or hell respectively.
Therefore, a wise person seeking happiness should abide in knowledge and detachment.
Having quickly restrained the horses of the senses, one should uplift the self by means of the self. Briefly stated, *dhāraṇā* (concentration) is the binding of the mind to a specific location.
And that location is none other than Śiva alone, because he is free from the three defects.

Having fixed the mind upon a specific place for a certain duration of time, it does not deviate from the object of focus; this is *dhāraṇā*, and not otherwise. Through *dhāraṇā*, the first stability of the mind is produced.

Therefore, one should make the mind steady through the practice of concentration (*dhāraṇā*). The verbal root *dhyai* is traditionally understood to mean "reflection"; thus, it is called *dhyāna* when there is repeated reflection upon Śiva with an undistracted mind.

And that similar cognition which arises for one whose mind is established upon the object of meditation—this continuous flow, free from other intervening cognitions, is called *dhyāna* (meditation). (ŚivP 7.2.52cd–53ab) (Note: There is a variant reading, "daśa vāyavaḥ," at the beginning of verse 53a.)

Abandoning everything else, Śiva alone is the bringer of auspiciousness; he is the supreme object of meditation, the Lord of the presiding deities. Thus concludes the Atharvaṇa scripture. Likewise, the supreme Śivā is to be meditated upon; both Śiva and Śivā reside within all beings.
They are heard of in the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures as all-pervading and ever-manifest;
they are omniscient and should be constantly meditated upon through their various distinct forms.
Liberation is the primary realization, while the secondary realization consists of the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
These two are to be known as the purpose of this meditation:
the meditator, the act of meditation, the object of meditation, and that which is the purpose of meditation.
Having understood these four, the knower of yoga should practice yoga.
Endowed with knowledge and dispassion, full of faith and possessed of forbearance, free from the sense of "mine" and always energetic—a person who meditates in this manner is so described.
When weary from recitation, one should meditate again; when weary from meditation, one should recite again.

For one who is devoted to recitation and meditation, yoga is swiftly accomplished. Twelve *prāṇāyāmas* constitute one *dhāraṇā*, and twelve *dhāraṇās* constitute one *dhyāna*. That which lasts for twelve *dhyānas* is designated as *samādhi*.
Samādhi is proclaimed as the final limb of yoga.
Through samādhi, the light of wisdom (prajñā) arises everywhere;
it shines forth as the object alone, remaining motionless like curdled milk.
The appearance of [the object] as if devoid of its own nature is called *samādhi*.
Having fully absorbed the mind in the object of meditation, the yogi should behold it with great steadiness.
Established in *samādhi*, the yogi is proclaimed to be like the fire of extinction (*nirvāṇa*).

He does not hear, nor does he smell; he does not speak, nor does he see. He does not perceive touch, nor does his mind form any volitions. He does not conceive anything at all, and like a piece of wood, he is not bound.
Thus, one whose self is dissolved in Śiva is said here to be established in *samādhi*.
Just as a lamp placed in a windless spot never flickers,
so too the wise man established in *samādhi* should not waver from it.
As the yogin thus practices this supreme yoga,
all obstacles and impediments that stand in his way gradually perish.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Course of Yoga," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the seventh part of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Vāyu and the sages of Naimiṣa.
Chapter 38.
Upamanyu said:
"Laziness, intense diseases, negligence, and doubt regarding one's station," *Śiva Purāṇa* 7.2.38.1ab.
Unsteadiness of mind, lack of faith, distorted vision,
suffering, dejection, and longing for sense objects—
these ten are proclaimed as the obstacles for men engaged in yoga.
Laziness and impurity of being belong to the body and consciousness of yogins;
diseases arise from the imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātus), while afflictions arise from the defects of karma.
Negligence is the name for yoga, and cultivation is the name for its means.
The consciousness that is occupied by both "this" and "that" is doubt regarding the locus.
Indeed, the instability of the mind is called lack of foundation (*apratiṣṭhā*).
Lack of faith is the state of being devoid of conviction on the path of yoga.
That intellect which is perverted is designated as "delusion" (bhrānti).
They know that the suffering of men born of ignorance is internal, pertaining to the mind;
and that which is physical suffering arising from [external] beings, as well as that which arises from deeds performed in the past.
That which arises from celestial causes is said to be lightning, weapons, poison, and the like;
that which arises from the frustration of one's desires is declared to be despondency. Delusion regarding diverse objects of the senses is what is called longing.
When these obstacles have been stilled, for the yogin intent on yoga,
there arise divine portents that indicate spiritual perfection (*siddhi*):
intuition, hearing, discourse, vision, tasting, and tactile sensation.

These six are the obstacles; these are the perfections of yoga. Intuition (*pratibhā*) is said to be the appearance of an object exactly as it is, even when it is subtle, hidden, past, remote, or yet to come.
The hearing of all sounds without effort in the act of hearing; the knowledge of all livelihoods among those who follow various vocations for all embodied beings;
and what is called the vision of divine things, which occurs effortlessly—these are [the fruits].
Likewise, the tasting of divine flavors is called *āsvāda*.
Similarly, the perception through touch is renowned by the name *vedanā*.
And [the lords] up to the sovereigns of the world of Brahmā [experience] divine fragrances and so forth.
Precious gems appear and bestow many gifts;
a voice, sweet and spontaneous, issues forth from his various mouths;
and likewise, all elixirs and divine medicinal herbs manifest.
Having prostrated before him, the celestial women grant their success;
even when only a single portion of the perfection of yoga is seen, the mind turns toward liberation.
Just as this has been witnessed by me, so too shall liberation come to pass.
Leanness, stoutness, childhood, old age, and youth;
the diverse and wondrous forms, and the maintenance of the four bodies;
and the constant collection of fragrant scents without any portion of earth—[these belong to the body].
Thus they say that the Paiśāca state possesses eight qualities, O King:
dwelling in water, as well as on the earth, and likewise emerging from them;
being able, when one so desires, to drink even the ocean oneself without distress.
Wherever he desires it in this world, there alone is the sight of water;
even without jars or other vessels, he holds a collection of water in his hand.
Whatever substance is even tasteless, he desires to consume it at that very moment.
There shall be taste and the other [sensory qualities], as well as the sustenance of the body for the [other] three;
and the bodilessness of the body, endowed with the qualities of earth.
This is the wonderful sovereignty of water, possessing sixteen attributes.
The creation of fire from his body and the avoidance of the fear of its heat;
the power to burn this entire world effortlessly if he so desires;
the establishment of fire within water and the holding of fire in his hand.
When the creation has been consumed by fire, the cooking of food and so forth occurs in the mouth as before;
through two [powers], the construction of bodies endowed with sovereign power [is accomplished].
This twenty-fourfold [power] is declared to be *taijasa* (fiery).
The swiftness of thought for living beings, entering within [them] in an instant,
the effortless bearing of great weights such as mountains,
heaviness and lightness, and the holding of the wind in the hand.
By the mere touch of the tip of a finger and so forth, he causes even the earth to tremble;
by a single [breath], he effects the formation of bodies, endowed with radiant enjoyments. The wise know the power of the wind to consist of thirty-two qualities.
The complete disappearance of one's shadow, the non-perception of the sense organs,
the power of moving through the sky at will, the simultaneous engagement with all objects of the senses,
the leaping across space, and the absorption of those [powers] within one's own body.
The ability to solidify space and the state of being bodiless,
endowed with the sovereignty of the wind— this great fortyfold power is declared to be the sovereignty of Indra; they call it "Āmbara."
The attainment of objects according to one's desire, the departure according to one's desire,
the overcoming of everything, the vision of the meaning of all secrets,
the creation of forms in accordance with one's karma, mastery, and a pleasing appearance.
The vision of cyclic existence, endowed with the enjoyments of Indra—
this is the sovereignty of the moon, which is superior to that of the mind in its qualities. Furthermore,
there is cutting, striking, binding, and likewise liberation.
The grasping of all beings who are subject to the power of saṃsāra,
as well as the grace toward them all, and likewise the conquest of death and time—
this they declare to be the sovereign power of Prajāpati, which consists of self-conceit.
This great [state] is fifty-six times greater than the enjoyments of the lunar [gods].
It consists of creation by mere volition, as well as protection and withdrawal;
it includes the authority over all and the impelling of the minds of all beings.
And the creation of the entire world is distinct and dissimilar;
it is the instrument for both the auspicious and the inauspicious, joined with the powers of Prajāpati.
They declare that the sovereignty of Brahmā possesses sixty-four qualities.
Beyond this Buddhist [state], they know the sovereignty of Prakṛti to be secondary;
that which is called Vaiṣṇava is declared to be the very abiding place of that [sovereignty].
That entire state cannot be described by others except by Brahmā.

That state of Viṣṇu— which is both personal and subordinate, as well as the supreme state of Gaṇeśa— cannot be fully known by others. All accomplishments of higher knowledge and all supernatural powers are merely incidental to it.
However, those whose minds are attached to impure manifestations and to the *guṇas* must strive with supreme dispassion to bring them to cessation;
otherwise, they shall not attain the supreme sovereignty that is fearless and fulfills all desires.

Therefore, for one who would cast aside like a blade of grass the virtues and enjoyments of gods, asuras, and kings, there shall be the supreme perfection of yoga. Alternatively, if he desires to show grace to the world, the sage may wander about.
Having enjoyed qualities and pleasures according to his desire, he shall attain liberation.
Now, I shall describe the practice of yoga; listen with a concentrated mind.
Furthermore, [it should be practiced] at an auspicious time and in an auspicious place, such as a sacred field of Śiva.
In a secluded place, free from living beings, silent, and devoid of disturbances; on a pleasant ground well-smeared and perfumed with incense, fragrances, and the like;
strewn with loose flowers and adorned with canopies and other decorations.
Provided with *kuśa* grass, flowers, fuel, water, fruits, and roots;
not near fire or near water, nor even on a heap of dry leaves;
nor crowded with gadflies and mosquitoes, nor infested with snakes and wild beasts.

Nor [should one recite] in a place infested with wicked wild animals, nor in fear, nor where surrounded by the wicked; nor in a cremation ground, at a sacred tree, on an anthill, in a ruined house, or at a crossroads;
nor on the banks of rivers, streams, or the ocean, nor even in the middle of a street.
One should not [perform it] in a dilapidated garden or a cow-pen, nor in an undesirable or censured place;
nor when suffering from indigestion, nor when there is an upward gurgling of sour fluids, nor in a place defiled by feces or urine;
nor during vomiting or diarrhea, nor after eating too much, nor when overcome by fatigue.
Neither distracted by excessive anxiety, nor afflicted by excessive hunger or thirst,
nor preoccupied with one's own teachers or ritual duties, should one practice yoga; rather,
one should be moderate in diet and recreation, and disciplined in one's activities.
One should practice proper sleep and awakening, free from all exertion. One should use a seat that is soft, pleasant, spacious, level, and pure;
and one should practice upon postures such as the lotus (padmaka) and the cross-legged (svastika).

Having paid homage to his own gurus and having saluted those worthy of respect in due order, he should stand with neck, head, and chest erect, with his gaze fixed on the ground; with his head slightly inclined, he should not let his teeth touch one another.
Having placed the tongue motionless against the edge of the teeth,
protecting the testicles with the two heels and likewise the generative organ,
he should rest his arms effortlessly across his thighs.
Placing the back of the right hand upon the palm of the left,
slowly raising the back [of the body], and bracing the chest forward;
gazing at the tip of one's own nose and not looking toward the directions.
Having mastered the movement of the vital breaths and remaining as motionless as a stone,
one should meditate upon Śiva together with Ambā within the abode of one’s own body;
in the center of the pedestal of the heart-lotus, one should worship Him through the sacrifice of meditation.

One should meditate [on the Lord] at the root, at the tip of the nose, at the navel, at the throat, or at the two cavities of the palate; or between the eyebrows, at the region of the gateway, on the forehead, or on the crown of the head. Having prepared the supreme seat for the two Śivas according to the rule, one should meditate there.
There, one should meditate upon Śiva— whether with attributes (*sāvaraṇa*) or indeed without attributes (*nirāvaraṇa*)—
in a lotus of two petals, sixteen spokes, or twelve spokes according to the rule;
or in a ten-spoked, six-cornered, or four-cornered [mandala].

Between the two eyebrows is a two-petaled lotus, brilliant as lightning. On the right and left petals of this lotus situated between the brows, which are colored like lightning and mark the end of the phonemes, [the letters] appear in succession.

The sixteen petals of this sixteen-spoked [lotus] are indeed the sixteen vowels; starting from the east and proceeding in order, this lotus extends from the root of the bulb. The letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭa* are the petals in their respective sequence.
That [lotus] with the color of the sun is to be meditated upon within the heart;
it is said that the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, white as cow’s milk, are situated in due order upon the petals of this lotus below. And its petals are six.
The letters beginning with *va* and ending with *sa* reside,
like leaves, upon the golden-hued lotus of the *mūlādhāra*,
which has the color of smokeless embers, according to their sequence.
Then, upon whichever of these lotuses the mind finds delight,
one should meditate with a steady intellect upon the God and the Goddess right there—
pure, the size of a thumb, and blazing forth on all sides.
Having the form of a pure lamp-flame, adorned with its own power;
having the appearance of a crescent moon, or even the form of a star;
resembling the awn of a grain of wild rice, or like a lotus fiber.
Even if the meditator desires the conquest of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth— which is shaped like a kadamba bud and resembles a drop of frost—
he should contemplate the gross form of the presiding deity of each respective principle.
The eight forms (mūrtis) beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva, as well as those beginning with Abhava,
are determined in the Śiva-śāstra to be the gross forms of Śiva;
these forms are classified by the lords of sages as terrible (ghora), mixed (miśra), and tranquil (praśānta).

Those skilled in contemplation should meditate on these [mantras] while remaining free from desire for fruits. If even terrible ones are thus contemplated, they will bring about the destruction of sins and diseases.
In the case of mixed mantras, the result occurs after a long time; but in the case of gentle ones, it occurs neither immediately nor after a long duration.
In the north (Saumya), liberation is attained especially; peace, wisdom, and success are accomplished here.
The supernatural powers (siddhis) are also achieved here in due order; of this there is no doubt.
Om. Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Arising of Obstacles in the Practice of Yoga," in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā within the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 39.
Upamanyu said:
For those who remember the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, all goals are immediately accomplished.
Thinking that [the mind] becomes tranquil, some yogins indeed meditate upon Him.
Some perform gross meditation for the sake of stabilizing the mind;
for when the mind becomes steady through the gross, it becomes firm in the subtle.
When Śiva is meditated upon directly, all supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished.
Even when other forms [of deities] are meditated upon, one should contemplate them as having the form of Śiva.
One should observe the steadiness of the mind and meditate on that [form] again and again.
They say that at first meditation has an object, and thereafter it is without an object.
Regarding this, the view of the wise is that there is no such thing as objectless meditation.
For meditation is defined as a certain continuous flow of the intellect.
Therefore, the intellect devoid of an object proceeds here in its pure state.
Consequently, meditation with an object takes recourse in the rays of the rising sun;
that which has a subtle object is [also] without an object, for there is nothing else in the ultimate sense.
Alternatively, meditation that possesses an object is based upon a formal aspect (sākāra);
whereas the self-awareness of the formless (nirākāra) Self is considered meditation without an object (nirviṣaya).
That very same meditation is said to be both "with seed" (sabīja) and "seedless" (nirbīja).
Likewise, by means of having a form as its support, and then by means of having no form as its support;
therefore, having first performed meditation with an object— that is, with seed—
one should at the end make it without an object, that is, seedless, for the sake of attaining all perfections.
Through *prāṇāyāma*, the states of the Goddess beginning with *śānti* are accomplished in succession:
*śānti*, *praśānti*, *dīpti*, and *prasāda* beyond that;
as well as *śama*, which is the pacification of all calamities—this is designated as *śānti*.
The destruction of darkness, both internal and external, is celebrated as tranquility (*praśānti*).

That which is the illumination within and without is designated as radiance (*dīpti*). That state of being established in one's own nature (*svasthatā*) is proclaimed as the clarity of the awakened mind (*prasāda*).
And all causes, both external and internal,
indeed become quickly serene through the clarity of the intellect.
Likewise, the meditator, the meditation, the object of meditation, and whatever the purpose of the meditation may be— [all these become clear].
Having understood this fourfold [set], the meditator should practice meditation.
Endowed with knowledge and dispassion, always with an undistracted mind,
full of faith and a serene soul— such a person is described by the virtuous as a true meditator.
The root *dhyai* is traditionally understood to mean "thought," specifically the repeated contemplation of Śiva.
Likewise,
even a brief practice of yoga, such as meditating upon the Supreme Lord with faith for even a single moment, can destroy sin.

Meditation is defined as that which is performed with an undistracted mind. The support for this meditation, which consists of a continuous flow of the intellect, is called the "object of meditation" (dhyeya) by the wise; and that is Śiva himself, together with Ambā.
The complete sovereignty consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā* and the conditions for liberation are declared to be the direct purpose of perfect meditation upon Śiva;
for through meditation, one attains happiness, liberation, and fearlessness.
Therefore, having renounced everything, a person should be devoted to meditation.
Without meditation there is no knowledge; for one who lacks yoga, there is no meditation.
He who possesses both meditation and knowledge has crossed the ocean of worldly existence.

Knowledge that is serene, one-pointed, and free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is indeed attained by the yogi who is disciplined through the practice of yoga. For those whose every sin has been utterly destroyed, the mind becomes intent upon knowledge and meditation.
For those whose intellects are struck down by evil, even news of that [state] is very difficult to obtain.
Just as a great, blazing fire would consume both the dry and the moist,
so too does the fire of meditation burn away both auspicious and inauspicious karma in an instant.
Just as even a very small lamp can destroy a vast darkness,
so too even a slight practice of yoga can destroy great sin;
this occurs by meditating upon the Supreme Lord with faith for even a single moment.
Whatever great spiritual welfare there may be, its end is never found.
There is no sacred site equal to meditation; there is no austerity equal to meditation;
there is no sacrifice equal to meditation; therefore, one should practice meditation.
Yogins do not resort to sacred fords filled with water, nor to deities made of stone or clay, because they possess the conviction of their own Self. Furthermore,
the subtle body of yogins becomes directly perceptible as divine.
Just as [a palace] is constructed for those who are unrefined using materials such as clay and wood;
and just as in this world, those who move within the inner circle are dear to a king, while those who move outside are not—
so too, those devoted to internal meditation are dear to Śambhu, but not those engaged in ritual action.
Just as in the world those who are excluded do not enjoy much fruit,
so too here, even those who perform ritual actions are seen in the palace of the Lord of Men;
yet, if those striving for the sake of knowledge and yoga meet with misfortune in the interim, [they suffer likewise].
By the mere exertion of yoga, he shall go to the world of Rudra.
Having experienced happiness there, he will be born into a family of yogins;
and having again attained the yoga of knowledge, he transcends the cycle of worldly existence.
The destination that even a man who merely desires to know yoga attains—
that destination cannot be reached even by all the great sacrifices. Nor can that fruit be obtained by honoring ten million twice-born ones who are learned in the Vedas.
By the mere gift of alms to a Śiva-yogin,
one obtains that same fruit which is gained through sacrifices, the agnihotra, gifts, pilgrimages, and burnt offerings;
by giving food to a yogin, one attains all that fruit in its entirety.
And those fools who utter slander against the practitioners of Śiva-yoga,
they shall fall into hells by the ears of those who hear it, until the destruction of the earth.
For there must be a listener for there to be a speaker of such slander against the yogins.
Therefore, it is the opinion of the great ones that the listener who is wicked should be punished.
Furthermore, those who constantly worship the yogis of Śiva with devotion enjoy great pleasures and, in the end, attain the yoga of Śaṅkara.
Therefore, those who seek worldly enjoyments should fully honor the Śiva-yogins with shelter,
food, drink, and the like, as well as beds and clothing.
Because it possesses such essential strength, the dharma of yoga cannot be shattered by the hammers of sin.

The yogin is to be known as being like a diamond grain (*vajrataṇḍula*); likewise, he is not smeared by sins, nor is he affected by floods of suffering, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. In whatever place a sage who is constantly devoted to the yoga of Śiva may dwell, [that place becomes pure].

That place itself would become purified; how much more so, then, one who is already pure! Therefore, having abandoned all other duties, a wise person should practice the yoga of Śiva for the sake of abandoning all suffering.
The yogin who has attained the fruit of perfected yoga, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
may enjoy pleasures according to his wish and either wander about or remain here;
or else, considering sensual pleasure to be truly trivial, he may renounce it.
Having abandoned action through the yoga of dispassion and by one's own will, let him be liberated.
But that mortal who perceives death to be near and observes many portents of death should,
intent on the commencement of yoga, take refuge in a sacred field of Śiva.

If that man, while dwelling there with a steady mind, should voluntarily renounce his life even without illness or other causes; or if, having practiced fasting, he offers his own body as an oblation into the fire of Śiva; ||| ŚivP_7.2,39.48ab–49ab |||
Or, by casting one's own body into the sacred waters of Śiva (śivatīrtha) and plunging therein,
or by abandoning one's life according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra,
one shall be liberated immediately; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Or if one, rendered helpless by disease and other afflictions, takes refuge in a sacred field of Śiva (śivakṣetra) and dies there, he too is likewise liberated; of this there is no doubt.
[The meaning is that this applies even to one who is making an effort.]
And there is another reading: "na cāsāv ātmaghātakaḥ" (nor is he a suicide).
For just as they desire death as the highest good through means such as fasting, since it is performed with a mind made firm by confidence in the scriptures.
Having killed one who delights in reviling Śiva, or having been tormented by him himself,
he who gives up his life— which is so difficult to abandon— is not born again. He who is unable to kill one delighting in reviling Śiva, yet dies of his own accord, [attains the same state].

He shall be liberated immediately, together with twenty-one generations of his kin. No man standing on the path to liberation is equal to him who gives up his life for the sake of Śiva or for the sake of a devotee of Śiva.
One should not perform funeral rites for him here on earth, as one would for animals;
nor should one observe impurity, especially his sons and others.
This is whether it be for the sake of the conduct of Śiva or for the sake of the knowledge of Śiva.
One should either bury that body in the earth or cremate it with pure fire;
or one should cast it into auspicious waters, or abandon it like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
Furthermore, if one desires to perform a ritual act dedicated to him as well—
One should perform only what is auspicious according to one's ability and satisfy those who are devoted. A devotee of Śiva should share his wealth with him if his progeny is also devoted to Śiva;
if not, he should give it to Śiva, for he should not give it to one whose progeny belongs to the lower beings (paśu).
Om. Thus, in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of Śaiva Yoga," ends.
Śrī Sūta said:

Having thus declared to the sages who had approached him with prostrations the yoga of knowledge obtained from Upamanyu by the Yadava who has conquered all enemies, that self-exalted one suddenly vanished into the sky at evening like the wind. Then, at the time of dawn, the ascetics of Naimiṣa—
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, everyone set out together to perform the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
Then, by the command of Brahmā, the goddess Sarasvatī herself appeared;
gracious and with sweet waters, that auspicious river began to flow.
Having beheld the river Sarasvatī, the sages, their minds filled with joy, concluded the sacrificial session they had commenced and performed their ablutions there. Then,
having gratified the gods and others with her auspicious waters, they continued their rites.

Remembering their former history, they set out toward Vārāṇasī. Then, seeing the Bhāgīrathī falling from the foot of the Himavat mountain and flowing toward the south, they bathed there and proceeded along its bank.
Then, having reached Vārāṇasī, they were all filled with joy;
and having bathed in the northward-flowing Gaṅgā,
they beheld the Liṅga of Avimukteśvara and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites.
As they were preparing to set out there, they beheld in the sky a divine and most wonderful light,
resembling ten million suns;
by the radiance of that self-effulgent light, the entire expanse of the quarters was pervaded.
Then the perfected Pāśupatas, their bodies covered in ashes—
sages by the hundreds— approached and merged into that splendor.
While those high-souled ascetics were thus dissolving away, [the Lord spoke].
That splendor vanished instantly, and it was like a marvel.
Having seen that great wonder, the great ṛṣis of Naimiṣa,
not knowing what this could be, went toward the forest of Brahmā.
Even before their departure, the Wind-god, the purifier of the world,
[bestowed] upon the inhabitants of Naimiṣa the vision of the Great-souled One and his discourse with them;
thereafter, he [instilled] faith and understanding in them regarding Śiva, together with Ambā and his attendants.
Having informed Brahmā— the creator of the worlds and source of the Vedas— of the completion of that long-standing sacrificial session of the performers of the *sattra*,
he, having received his permission regarding his own task, departed toward his own city.
Then Brahmā, having arrived at that place, while Tumburu and Nārada were disputing with one another over their singing out of mutual rivalry,
maintained his neutrality through the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) arising from the songs they had produced.

He dwells in happiness, attended by Gandharvas and Apsarases. Then, because there was no opportunity, the sages were turned away at the gate by the doorkeepers and sat down on the side outside the Brahma-abode.
Then, having attained equality with Tumburu in singing, Nārada was authorized by the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin to perform as his companion;
abandoning their mutual rivalry, they entered into the highest friendship.
Accompanied by him and surrounded by Apsarases and Gandharvas,
he went forth from the abode of the Creator to play the lute for the Lord, the sovereign Nakulīśvara,
like the sun emerging from a cloud.

Seeing him, those members of the six clans bowed down to Nārada, the bull among sages, and with great reverence asked for an audience with Śambhu. He replied, "This is indeed the right moment; enter within."
Then,
intent on hospitality and filled with the utmost haste, those who were stationed at the gate announced him to Brahmā.
By his command, they entered the abode of the Egg-born one, having gathered together as a single mass.
Having entered from afar and prostrated before the God on the ground like a staff,
they were permitted by him to approach and stood around him. Then,
having inquired after the welfare of those who were stationed there, the lotus-seated Brahmā—
"I have learned the account from you because Vāyu himself told it to us. What did you do afterwards once Māruta had vanished?
When the Lord of the Gods had spoken thus, the sages [replied] after their ritual ablution (*avabhṛtha*).
Going to the sacred ford of the Gaṅgā and making a pilgrimage toward Vārāṇasī;
beholding there the Liṅgas installed by the lords of the gods;
and even once worshipping the Liṅga of Avimukteśvara.
The vision in the sky of that great mass of splendor;
the dissolution of the sages therein, and the subsequent cessation of that radiance;
and the realization of its true nature, even as it was being meditated upon by their own selves.
Having bowed down repeatedly, they told him everything in full detail. Having heard what was related by the sages, the four-faced Viśvakarman shook his head slightly and spoke in a deep voice.
"Your supreme success in the world beyond is drawing near;
for the Lord has been propitiated by you for a long time through this long sacrificial session,
and he has become inclined toward showing grace"— thus was the true state of affairs indicated.
That radiant light which you beheld in the sky over Vārāṇasī is the supreme,
manifest splendor of Maheśvara known as the Liṅga;
there the sages, observers of the Śrauta Pāśupata vows, have merged into it.
They became liberated, established in their own true state, steadfast, and with their sins burnt away.
Just as liberation was attained by this [teaching], may it soon come about for you as well;
and this very matter shall be indicated by the splendor seen by you.
In this matter, this very time has come to you of its own accord through destiny.
Depart for the southern peak of Meru, which is frequented by the gods,
where my son Sanatkumāra, the supreme sage, resides.

In the past, even Sanatkumāra, having seen the Supreme Lord in person, was corrupted by a lack of humility because he considered himself the master of all yogis due to ignorance. He waited for the arrival of Nandin, who had appeared before him as his lord.
Because he was utterly fearless and failed to perform his duties, such as rising to greet me,
he was turned into a great camel by Nandin, who was provoked to anger by that offense.
Then, after a long time, I grieved for him.
Having worshipped the God and the Goddess, and having indeed entreated Nandin,
his state of being a camel was somehow averted through effort;
for he was restored to his former childhood, as he had been before.

Then Mahādeva, as if smiling, said to the Lord of the Gaṇas: "Indeed, having shown me contempt, that sage has spoken thus with such arrogance. Therefore, O sinless one, you yourself must explain my true nature to him."
The first-born son of Brahmā,
who is the propagator of my knowledge, will instruct me as if I were deluded;
he alone shall perform your consecration as the presiding authority over Dharma.
Thus addressed, he— the leader of all hosts of beings—
received that command of his superior upon his head at dawn;
likewise did Sanatkumāra, by my instruction, on Mount Meru.
"For the sake of winning the favor of this Gaṇa, he performs difficult penance;
therefore, you must see him before meeting the Lord of the Gaṇas.
For the sake of his grace, Nandin will arrive there before long."
Having thus commanded them with haste, they were sent forth by the Universal Yogin;
the sages then went to Kumāraśikhara, the southern peak of Mount Meru.
Om! Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pilgrimage of the Naimiṣa Sages," in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the seventh book, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, of the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter 41. Sūta said:
There is a lake named Skandasaras, which resembles the ocean.
Its water was as sweet as nectar, cool, clear, deep, and light;
it was surrounded on all sides by heaps of crystal stones,
and its entire expanse was covered by blossoming flowers of every season.
With *śaivala* moss, blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white water-lilies resembling stars;
with waves like clouds, it was like the sky descended to the earth;
and with landing places made of blue stone that were easy to ascend and descend.
The two stairways shone with beautiful [stones], illuminating the eight directions;
they were filled with those who had mostly descended there and those who had ascended again,
wearing white sacred threads and white loincloths or bark garments.
[He was surrounded] by young ascetics with matted locks, crests, or shaven heads, adorned with the triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra),
their faces smiling helplessly out of dispassion;
and [he saw] jars, lotus-leaf cups, and auspicious water-pots.
With water-pots, other similar vessels such as *karakas*,
and especially for their own sake, for the sake of others, and particularly for the sake of the deities,
they constantly brought water and gathered flowers.
By sages who were observant of proper conduct, whose limbs were grey with smeared ashes, who had climbed onto rocks within the water for fear of touching those of low birth,
and who remained on the stones while plunging here and there into the waters— those who were both beloved and disciplined.
Having performed the libation for the ancestors with sesame seeds, unbroken grains, flowers, and discarded *darbha* purifiers,
he should announce to those who are knowledgeable the twice-born who have come for their daily bath.
In various places, [the scene was filled] with the breezes from numerous offerings of flowers made at each spot,
while others performed worship and other rites upon the sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*), preceded by the offering of *arghya* water to the Sun;
in some places, herds of elephants were seen sinking and emerging from the water, their leaders utterly exhausted.
In some places, deer, antelopes, and horses had come there out of thirst;
in other places, excellent peacocks and elephants had emerged after drinking;
and in others, it was illuminated by bulls and rival bulls striking against the banks.
In some places with the excellent cries of *kāraṇḍava* ducks, in some with the warbling of cranes,
in some with the calls of ruddy geese, and in some with the songs of bees;
[the place was filled] by those who lived upon the trees of their own prosperity, performing bathing, drinking, and other such acts.
As if repeatedly speaking out of affection to those various living beings with the warbling of flocks of cuckoos perched on the tops of trees along the banks,
he seemed to call out day and night to all those afflicted by the heat.
On the northern bank of that lake, beneath a *kalpa* tree,
upon an altar made of diamond-stone and on a soft deer-skin,
