he saw Sanatkumāra seated, eternally maintaining the form of a youth.

Those inhabitants of Naimiṣa beheld him, who had momentarily ceased from his meditation while remaining unwavering in soul, who was being attended by sages and honored even by the lords of yogis; they bowed down and stood before him in reverence.
Just as they explained the reason for their welcome to him who had questioned them,
a tumultuous sound of celestial drums was heard in the sky;
at that very moment, a celestial chariot (vimāna) radiant like the sun appeared.
It was surrounded on all sides by innumerable lords of the Gaṇas,
crowded with hosts of Apsarases, and filled with Rudra-maidens;
it resounded with the beating of mṛdaṅgas and murajas, and was accompanied by the sounds of flutes and lutes.
It was enriched with canopies of variegated jewels and adorned with strings of pearls;
it was surrounded by sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras,
who were dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments.
With a banner bearing the emblem of a heroic bull and a staff made of coral wood— a banner that was a cause for honor and served as a worthy decoration for the gateway—
in the center of that celestial chariot, between two chowries, [he stood].
Beneath the umbrella and the jewel-encrusted staff, which were as pure as the moon,
he was seated upon a divine throne together with the goddess Suyashā and Śrī;
he was endowed with a magnificent body and possessed three eyes.
The walls of the abodes served as a means of recognition for the Lord;
they appeared like the inviolable command of the Creator of the universe arrived in person,
and like the very grace of Śambhu standing manifest before one.
He saw the son of Śilāda in person, who bore the glorious and excellent trident as his weapon;
he was the presiding lord of the Gaṇas of Viśveśvara, like another Viśveśvara himself,
capable of both punishing and favoring even the creators of the universe.
With four arms and noble limbs, adorned with the crescent moon,
he was further decorated by a serpent around his neck and the moon upon his crown.
He was like sovereignty incarnate, and like power endowed with action.
Seeing him who was like the perfection of Nirvana and like the embodiment of omniscience,
the son of Brahmā, his face beaming with joy, stood up together with the sages;
with palms joined in reverence, he remained there as if offering himself to Him.
Then, in the meantime, when that celestial chariot had descended to the earth,
they prostrated themselves like a staff before the god, and having offered praise, they addressed the sage:
"These members of the six families have been engaged in a long sacrificial session at Naimiṣa."
Commanded by Brahmā, they had already arrived out of longing [to see him].
Having heard the words of the son of Brahmā, Nandin immediately severed their bonds with a mere glance;
then, having bestowed upon them the Śaiva dharma and the yoga of divine knowledge, he returned once more to the presence of the God.
Sanatkumāra told all of that to Vyāsa, my direct preceptor;
and the honored Vyāsa told it to me, and I have now related it to you in brief.
This jewel of a Purāṇa concerning the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) must not be told to those who do not know the Vedas.
Indeed, given out of delusion to a disciple who is not devoted or to atheists, it bestows hell.
But for those by whom it has been given, received, recited, or heard according to the path and accompanied by service,
it invariably grants them happiness, the gateway to Dharma, the threefold aims of life, and ultimately liberation.
"Mutual assistance has been rendered by you and by me through the application of the ancient path.

Therefore, I shall depart with my desires fulfilled; may there always be auspiciousness for us all. When the Sūta had thus offered his benedictions and departed, and the great sacrificial performance was concluded, the sages of virtuous conduct [proceeded].
In this Kali age, when the world was being defiled by sense objects, they took up residence in the vicinity of Vārāṇasī.

Furthermore, desiring liberation from all the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), they performed the Pāśupata vow in its entirety. Having mastered all knowledge and meditative absorption, those blameless ones attained supreme bliss.
Vyāsa said:
This Śiva Purāṇa is indeed concluded;
it is beneficial and should be recited with devotion and likewise listened to with great effort.
This should not be spoken to an atheist, nor to one who lacks faith, nor to a rogue;
neither to one who is not a devotee of Maheśa, nor to one who merely displays the banner of righteousness.
For by hearing this even once, sin shall indeed be reduced to ashes.
One who is not a devotee attains devotion, and a devotee partakes in the abundance of devotion.
Furthermore, through hearing [this] again, there is true devotion, and from that hearing, liberation arises.
Therefore, those who desire liberation must indeed hear it again and again.
This ancient Purāṇa should be recited five times with a virtuous mind, aiming for the supreme fruit;
one shall attain that, without a doubt.
So too did the kings of old, as well as the most excellent Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas.
By repeating this seven times, they obtained the vision of Śiva. Furthermore,
any human being who, devoted to faith, hears this,
shall enjoy all pleasures in this world and attain liberation at the end.

Indeed, this Śiva Purāṇa is supremely dear to Śiva; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is equal to the Veda, and increases devotion. For the speaker and the listener of this Śiva Purāṇa, [it always grants]— ŚivaP 7.2.41.50–51ab.
May that Śaṅkara grant welfare to you, O son of Ambā, together with your attendants.

Om. Thus ends this work, the forty-first chapter titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Śrī Śiva Mahāpurāṇa," within the Vyāsopadeśa section of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā in the glorious Śiva Mahāpurāṇa. Om.
The book is complete.
